This is in my Top Ten Games Ever, at least until they release a game that just pumps dopamine directly into my brain, or they redefine the number 'ten'.
I am told the demo is hard.  I'm led to believe its harder than the actual (full paid) game; you just don't have that many parts to work with, and there isn't much for a new player to go on.  The tutorials have improved, but I have a few friends who have tried this game, found it too difficult, and given up.  This is a shame.
I found Kerbal Space Program hits the sweet spot between too easy and too hard.  After watching a couple of tutorials on YouTube (hint: watch the tutorials on YouTube and read the wiki) I found I could reliably put spacecraft in orbit with an  iteratively developed rocket.  KSP is forgiving enough to permit you to design a TLAR ("that looks about right") spacecraft, but if you're willing to develop and tweak it, or even do some math, KSP will reward that, too.
My greatest accomplishment was as a result of what the Brits delightfully refer to as an own goal.
I wasted fuel pottering around on the Mun, and found I didn't have enough to get home.  I had a kerbal stranded in a highly eccentric Munar orbit, and the only way to get him back was to build a rescue vehicle, send it out to him, match orbits and then perform a  dangerous spacewalk, which I had never done before.
I briefly considered abandoning him to circle the Mun forever, without ever getting home to do whatever it is these gormless creatures do when they're not strapping themselves on top of hundred-meter columns of high explosives and duct tape, but it was my mistake, not his, that got him into this mess.  His slack-jawed wonder at the sterile beauty of space was a reflection of my own. No way was I not bringing my man - I mean Kerbal - back.
This is as good a time as any to mention that Kerbonauts are differentiated from each other by five lines of code in the save file, and that their models and animations are all alike.
So I did it.  I was leaning with my eyes three inches from the screen, wiping my palms every minute on my lap, for an hour, trying to get that rescue rocket as close as possible.  (Now I've learned how, it's routine, but at the time, this was all seat-of-the-pants flying for me.)  There was no in-game reward, other than the fact I'd done it: the crisis proceeded naturally as a result of the game's engine (and my own incompetence.)  Similarly, the planets you land on are all pretty boring; the game leaves it up to you to find the meaning and reward in what you're doing.  (Getting to those planets is not easy.)
Herdman Kerbal - or Hernman Kerbal, I forget which - I got you home.
Awesome game with a huge modding community.  Really need to work out the bugs for the x64 bit version because the x32 bit can't handle large amounts of mods loaded.

Steep Learning curve, but stick with it and the game will blow your mind.
This game takes a while to get into.  If you download the game, boot up, and try to go to space, you will not go to space today.  It takes hours of trial and error, building and revising, and reading tutorials online to even get yourself into orbit.  hours more each to learn transfers to moons, other planets, landings, plane changes, rendezvous, docking, aerobraking, and all the other things this game will teach you about orbital mechanics and space travel.
Once you learn how the game works, though, the sky is (literally) the limit!  Your first landing on the Mun will feel like the greatest accomplishment of your gaming life.  Hundreds of dockings later, the feeling of watching two ships latch together still brings a smile to my face.  300+ hours in, and there's tons I still have left to do.  I just launched my first interplanetary mission.  I still haven't gotten an SSTO into orbit.
All of this isn't even looking at the community that surrounds this game.  It's been around for years, and when you post pictures of your first successful orbit to the KSP subreddit, people will jump in and congratulate you, because we all remember how hard it was and how great it felt.
And then you get into the mods, and the game explodes from there.  You can build colonies with Umbra Space Industries, massive star cruisers with B9 Aerospace, extensive comms networks with RemoteTech, star fighters with BDArmory, and the list goes on. Your space stations are given purpose with Station Science, your satellites with SCANsat.  There is literally no end to what you can do with this game.
Buy it.  you will not be disappointed.

This game is wonderfull and wonderfully hard.
You start small, learning how to fly by trial and error, learning how to orbit by even more trial and error, doing interplantary missions by even more trial and error. Once you find out parachutes and the moon aren't a functional combination you scrape your Kerbal off of the ground and try again, this time with an engine. And so it goes for everything.
If you manage to do all there is to do in this game (which I'm not even a tenth of the way from after 300 hours), there are mods. Thousands of mods. New parts, new engines, new resources, new planets, new physics, new machinery. There is a mod for everything. This way the game never stops being fun.
If you are worried that you might get stuck, no matter. Either you try a campaign, being carefull and micromanaging, or you try sandbox, building multimilion dollar rockets and crashing them into buildings. You can go all the way from serious to playing around, whenever you want.
This is by far the best money I've ever spent on a game, and even though I hesitated at first, I'm incredebly glad I did buy it.
Even more so, it gets constantly updated and the mods are in very close contact with the community, asking their opinions on certain things. NASA has even joined up and made the Asteroid Update with the mods. Exciting stuff!
Very much recommended!

This game is so amazing and one of, if not the best, story driven games I've ever played. I did not expect it would end up having such a strong emotional impact on me. It was a pretty decent drama story at first, then it shifted into heavy topics that were deeply disturbing, heinous, bizarre, sad and bittersweet. Honestly, going back into games without stories and characters as well fleshed out as this feels pretty empty. The game plays like an interactive novel (WITH TIME TRAVEL) as the world comes to life around you, very immersive and shocking. The game builds up character storylines and mystery through 1-3 and pays off incredibly well by episode 4 as you go into full Sherlock mode. This is without even mentioning the game mechanics, which adds depth to the story, the puzzles, and Max's character. Max's empathy and kindness is without equal. Her personality makes you want to be a better person, to always make the right choices when helping those in need (depending on how you play her). Her friend Chloe livens up the adventure and pushes the story forward as you bond with her.

In my opinion, the best games are those that make you forget your just playing a game and the characters in it seem like real people.

I cannot help but make a biased review for this game. It's truly a masterpiece. If game is art, this is a great example. Not only can you do pretty much whatever you want, there's mods that let you do even more of that be it look at even more beautiful sights, blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, fly with different pieces and engines, start a turn based war with someone by sending saves back and forth, make movies, etc., but you can get an inkling of what accomplishing something as incredible as touching down on another celestial body than the one you've been stuck on your entire life thus far save a very very small few number of the population. This game will make you feel like you've actually accomplished something, because in essence you have. Everyone has their own style, their own speed they play at. For some it is easier than others. There is a huge learning curve, anyone will tell you. But when you begin to figure things out, that's when the true fun begins. I won't ruin the rest for you. You must discover what KSP means for you. And if at first you don't succeed, add more boosters!

The game reminded me strongly of the time when I drove through Eureka CA, and Coos Bay OR during a storm this past Spring.

[EARLY ACCESS REVIEW] KSP is a challenging space-sandbox simulation game.
Pros:
+Vast open area (space) to play in
+Highly detailed planets
+Amazing customization for the space planes/rockets
+Detailed base for launches.
+Complex physics
+Nothing is easy (might be a con for others)
+Cool easter eggs here and there. (Space kraken, monoliths, pyramids, etc.)
+Science and career mods are amusing (I prefer science)
+Highly detailed UI, but fairly easy to learn.
+Mod support
+Cheat tab (ctrl+alt+f12)
+Kerbals, they add some comedy to the game, and are just great in general.
+Out of spaceship walking is fluid and smooth
+Graphics are great.
+Regular updates, keep the game new and fresh
+Able to speed up time (this prevents the game from getting boring most of the time)
+First person cockpits are a nice addition to the game
+Controls for the spaceships/planes are nice
+Animations are excellent
+Graphics options are detailed
+Well optimized
I could name more, but I think I'll stop here.
Cons:
-Occasionaly glitchy and sometimes crashes (but this doesn't matter that much since it's in Early Access)
-No steam workshop (there is so many mods already, and it is so easy to install them, adding Steam Workshop support to the game would be amazing)
-Price is a little high
-sometimes you cannot speed up time in certain areas, which causes the player to wait 10 minutes just to get to the interesting parts of the game.
Overall, KSP is a excellent game, and I see a bright future ahead for the developers and the game.

What's great about Kerbal Space Program?
A short list:
1) Great music! Once you get into space, the music kicks in, and it creates an atmosphere of wonder and accomplishment. There's a good variety of tracks, too!
2) EXPLOSIONS! And by that I mean MORE than just how fun it is to watch a crazy rocket design crash and explode (although such crashes are spectacular and amusing), but also that the sounds of the different rocket types all have distinct  and different sounds... and some of the bigger ones have a satisfying rumble to them!
3) Challenge! It doesn't matter if you're the n00bliest of n00bs or an actual rocket scientist, there's challenges to be had here. It's not unfair in its challenges, and with a bit of experimenting (or watching some Let's Plays) it's pretty easy to get a grasp of the basics, and then you can move on to bigger and tougher challenges! And with the new tweakable Difficulty settings, you can custom-tune difficulty to your personal preference. Supreme Easy Mode, or Iron Man's Worst Nightmare, or anything in between!
4) SCIENCE! NASA literally has helped this game get into its current form! While the in-game solar system is entirely fictional and scaled down a bit, the orbital mechanics are quite realistic, and if you're at all familiar with space-based technology, you'll recognise the various homages to real-life rockets and fuel tanks.
The only "cons" this game has imo is that it's still a bit jittery in the physics sometimes, and that since SHIFT cranks up the throttle it's not very SHIFT+TAB-friendly.
Overall, a great rocket-building creative game that can actually teach you a few things. I highly recommend it! And if my word alone isn't enough for you, I highly recommend that you check out some videos on youtube by Zisteau or Danny2462.

Kerbal Space Program is a space-simulator which is able to inspire, because the possibilities are so endless like the universe. There are two modes
, the career-mode where you have to complete some goals, research for better rocket parts and so on and you have the sandbox-mode where you have  all parts from the beginning and where you can set your own goals. An orbit around "Kerbin" (corresponds earth)? Fly to the "mun" (corresponds moon) or one of the other planets? Build a Lander and land somewhere? Or build a rover and make a trip on the "mun"? It lies by you! A successful launch is even an special goal for the first time. It's harder as it sounds. While playing, your physics-knowledge will increase, you will see what i mean. You can explore many planets, moons, comets and asteroids which each have their own challenges.
You will find lots of mods which make the game unbelievable. More parts for rockets or space-stations, better atmospheres for your planets and moons and more. As well as other games, the mods aren't free of risk but for me there were only a few game-crashes after hours of playing (>100h).
It's nearly perfect, so you have the feeling to get an full game. Some Special-features like an multiplayer will follow. So don't be disappointed if updates are slow in coming.

Magnificent.
Here's a recent experience:
After painstakingly designing an interplanetary vehicle with limited funds, I lifted off and headed towards Ike (a small moon orbiting Duna, KSP's Mars analogue). I was playing in career mode, where rocket parts cost money that must be earned by completing contracts. This ship had very nearly bankrupted me, but with pending contracts for planting a flag on ike and recovering scientific data from it's orbit, I stood to make a tidy profit... if my ship could manage the round trip.
The trip to Ike went largely as planned. I was able to bring my interplanetary vehicle into a low orbit around the irregular moon and make various scientific observations. My Kerbal pilot made a successful spacewalk from the main cockpit into an attached lander module, which I then decoupled and landed gently on Ike's surface. I planted a flag, took soil samples, and made some more observations before returning to orbit and docking with my interplanetary vehicle (successfully docking, by the way, feels like being declared King of Space). My mission at Ike completed, I headed for home.
However! All was not well. Due to poor maneuvering, bad design, or perhaps a voodoo space curse, I ran out of fuel just as I entered Kerbin's (Earth's) orbit. I was adrift, millions of kilometers from home, unable to land and recover my precious scientific data.
Desperate, I quickly designed a recovery module, build for the sole purpose of grabbing my wayward ship and pulling it out of orbit. After a precarious orbital rendezvous, I managed to clamp onto the ship and gently, gently pushed back against its orbital velocity so it would fall back to Kerbin. But alas! The recovery module was insufficient, and my ship remained stranded in an insane elliptical orbit, brushing the top of kerbin's atmosphere on one end and peaking at several million kilometers away on the other.
I was broke, my ship to Ike was lost at my very doorstep, and it seemed my Kerbal Space Program would have to shutter its doors.
Suddenly I had a flash of realization: My lander, the tiny ship I'd used to touch down on Ike, had a few small tanks of monopropellant for docking with the main vehicle. Docking had gone smoothly, and so I had plenty of propellant leftover. Trying to stop an interplanetary vehicle with a tank of monopropellant is like trying to stop a 747 in flight by sitting on top and blowing into the wind, but it was my last hope. I waited until I was at the point of lowest orbital velocity, millions of miles from Kerbin, and... I blew into the wind.
It was just enough to dip the low point of my orbit into the atmosphere, allowing my ship to gradually brake on each orbit. About 15 orbits later, the atmosphere had finally slowed the ship enough for me to land. And land I did, at considerable speed. The word "crash" might be more apropos. Tragically, all hands were lost. But some parts survived, including scientific apparatuses with precious data from across the solar system. With these parts recovered, I fulfilled my contracts, and the Kerbal Space Program had the funds to fly another day.
I can't express to you the thrill of seeing a mission succeed this precariously. You have to play KSP to experience it for yourself.

I heard a lot of great things about Kerbal Space Program, so I finally decided to take the plunge and get it.  This is not an arcade-type game.  It really does aim to be a simulator and in that regard it is on the mark.  So far, all I have done is the sandbox mode, but even in that realm there's plenty to do and plenty to learn.  Some things are very intuitive - for example, using symmetry mode to set the hold-down arms on your rocket - while others not so much - another example, from what I've seen, you have to use a side-mounted parachute if you want to plop a launch escape tower on top of your Kerbal's space capsule.
I love what I've seen in this game so far, and I'm looking forward to seeing more.  Space buffs who want to slip the bonds of Kerbal will be in love with this game.

This game will really mind♥♥♥♥ you. There's so many things happening, that you won't expect while playing it. And since you make the choices, there's different ways the game can end, which is great, since you can play the game multiple times, without getting tired of it.

What's great about Kerbal Space Program?
A short list:
1) Great music! Once you get into space, the music kicks in, and it creates an atmosphere of wonder and accomplishment. There's a good variety of tracks, too!
2) EXPLOSIONS! And by that I mean MORE than just how fun it is to watch a crazy rocket design crash and explode (although such crashes are spectacular and amusing), but also that the sounds of the different rocket types all have distinct  and different sounds... and some of the bigger ones have a satisfying rumble to them!
3) Challenge! It doesn't matter if you're the n00bliest of n00bs or an actual rocket scientist, there's challenges to be had here. It's not unfair in its challenges, and with a bit of experimenting (or watching some Let's Plays) it's pretty easy to get a grasp of the basics, and then you can move on to bigger and tougher challenges! And with the new tweakable Difficulty settings, you can custom-tune difficulty to your personal preference. Supreme Easy Mode, or Iron Man's Worst Nightmare, or anything in between!
4) SCIENCE! NASA literally has helped this game get into its current form! While the in-game solar system is entirely fictional and scaled down a bit, the orbital mechanics are quite realistic, and if you're at all familiar with space-based technology, you'll recognise the various homages to real-life rockets and fuel tanks.
The only "cons" this game has imo is that it's still a bit jittery in the physics sometimes, and that since SHIFT cranks up the throttle it's not very SHIFT+TAB-friendly.
Overall, a great rocket-building creative game that can actually teach you a few things. I highly recommend it! And if my word alone isn't enough for you, I highly recommend that you check out some videos on youtube by Zisteau or Danny2462.

Kerbal Space Program is a space-simulator which is able to inspire, because the possibilities are so endless like the universe. There are two modes
, the career-mode where you have to complete some goals, research for better rocket parts and so on and you have the sandbox-mode where you have  all parts from the beginning and where you can set your own goals. An orbit around "Kerbin" (corresponds earth)? Fly to the "mun" (corresponds moon) or one of the other planets? Build a Lander and land somewhere? Or build a rover and make a trip on the "mun"? It lies by you! A successful launch is even an special goal for the first time. It's harder as it sounds. While playing, your physics-knowledge will increase, you will see what i mean. You can explore many planets, moons, comets and asteroids which each have their own challenges.
You will find lots of mods which make the game unbelievable. More parts for rockets or space-stations, better atmospheres for your planets and moons and more. As well as other games, the mods aren't free of risk but for me there were only a few game-crashes after hours of playing (>100h).
It's nearly perfect, so you have the feeling to get an full game. Some Special-features like an multiplayer will follow. So don't be disappointed if updates are slow in coming.

I've just reached my first 50 hours playing this game, and I must say this game is absolutely amazing in all aspects! Good and bad points, in my opinion.
Gameplay: Three totally configurable game modes, depending on your way of playing: Career mode, if you want to be a space tycoon; Science mode, if you want to plan real expeditions inside the vast universe and go back home with something to continue; and Sandbox, BECAUSE SPACECRAFTS!
Creativity: God's sake,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥shaped rockets! Better if I add thrusted balls! Now, seriously, you will be building your first Mun-landing machine and thinking about how to add wheels to it to ride across.
Well documented: Do you need hints to build your first unmanned rover? You have a full how-to-use wiki. You don't know how to reach planet X riding a metal cucumber? Forums, official page, videos...
Mods: MODS, MODS, MODS!!!!! Modders are great, their ideas are great, everything is right in the world this way. You feel there's something empty in your space life? Mod it!
Science: Well... It's not exactly con for me. But take this advice: If you are not some astronomy curious or you expect to fly over aliens in a emotive FPS, dont buy this.
Details: Physics are right, game is funny, kerbals jump too high and can put asteroids in a planet's orbit but... It's lack of some details. It's in pre-alpha, I know, but I found some useful tools that, simply, aren't -connection between satellites, lack of planet terrain details, 90% can be solved by modding-. If you want to play this seriously, expect to mod it at some point.

Review, spoiler, and analysis of reactions:
I am a gamer, I play lots of different genre, though lately I mostly focus on Blizzard games.
I picked this up for three reasons, a friend had played it, got good reviews, and they offered chapter one for free.
I am a disabled veteran so I am trying to pick out which emotions have a trigger, which are based on how I feel at the moment, it is not always easy to separate the two. For example this morning I am in pain, angry, slightly despondent, and a bit mentally drained. In part from finishing this game late last night. So let me start with what I know. Some games can get you anxious, sometimes they can get you annoyed or angry for Brief periods of time, I don't think I have been this affected by a Movie, or a book, let alone a Video game in a loooong time. This game PROVES that you can use video games to tell stories EVERY bit as effectively as any book or movie, period.
Life is Strange is a story based game, it does not have a lot of action, it's not face paced, and does not require a lot of manual dexterity to play. It took me 12 hours to complete, though I rushed chapter 5, which I will get into later. I compare my Steam purchases to movie prices. It cost me about 20$ for all 5 episodes via the bundle. Great price for for the content!
Towards the start of the story you get the power to rewind time to mitigate choices to some extent. This is a choice based game. What you do at one point can and probably will affect the game later. There is A LOT of dialog and character development. You get attached to some of the characters. The game is far better at getting you attached to some, rather than disliking others. Though it did illicit concern I never felt the threat that some might from one of the main bad guys. Moving on, they had great attention to detail, the setting drew you in. It is so well done that you Identify with the characters no mater what sex, creed, persuasion to an extent if you were raised in a western culture. I would say most middle class will identify with at least some of the issues that are addressed in this game. PTSD, Assault, suicide, loss, hopelessness, depression, it also has some hope that pulls you along thinking that YOU can affect change. Here is the key point, you are so attached and drawn in that it is YOU making the moral decisions and dealing with the outcomes. YOU feel the weight and responsibility of those actions.
I do not want to use any spoilers because I feel this game is worth the time and money to play. That being said there was a point about mid way though that something happened that got so under my skin, that I couldn't change, that left me a bit hollow. Did I mention that I spent two decades protecting people? Not helping some of these people affected its own guilt. Sometimes I got i'm moral discussions with myself about if it was supposed to happen should I change it. At what point do you draw the line to help someone. This thought process will repeat and becomes perhaps THE main moral dilemma at the end.
Acts 1 though most of 4 absolutely brilliant. End of Act 4 and Act 5 was a solid B for me, The game as a whole is overwhelmingly a A+ in my book. I think for me why the end of Act 4 though end of Act 5 was a B/B+ is it made me rush thought it and miss some stuff and get frustrated all because of one thing. The conversations and the feel took too long. Let me be very specific as to why this is a factor. There were situation that had a certain amount of Gravitas that should also have had a certain amount of urgency that I thought the timing lacked by a few seconds. I started to get really angry waiting for SLOW dialog to finish so that I could affect some change. That being said I am former military and my mind in emergencies kicks into high gear. So I already mentioned it drew me in, so here I am concerned about someone or something, my mind is telling me that this is dangerous or important, and the feel and dialog does not affect this. For others it would be a bit like watching the horror movie where the person is about to get killed and you know its coming, your trying to get them to realize its coming to no avail. But it in this game this is a issue, you have got rid of a certain amount of disbelief and your connected a certain amount to the characters, so that feeling of common lets go, let me do something is Freaking frustrating. I think I actually yelled at the computer a few times in Act 5. So if anyone from there actually ever reads this, the tone of her voice, the cadence of what she was reading, and how long before you could do something was OFF, at least a few seconds to convey Urgency correctly. I am purposefully being a bit picky here, because it was such a brilliant game.
The ending, I have only seen one side of the ending and currently cant bring myself to go though the another. I probably should do it while its fresh. But I am literally a bit wary of how it may affect me for a bit, and I have family stuff tomorrow. I already am a bit estranged, angry and depressed so will have to pass for now.
One last note, I do not want this to stop people from playing BUT again this is so well done that it can affect you. If you are a loner, someone that's gone through any kind of trauma, have PTSD, or any of a multitude of issues keep in mind you may not come though the other side of the rabbit hole untouched.
AFTERMATH: SPOILER
I Saved her the first time, and let Arcadia Bay burn, maybe I was and am tired of saving people, maybe I didn't want the loss, maybe it was the pang of love, and that I hoped something still would change. What ever the reason, today I went back and chose to Sacrifice Chloe, I went back to capture the mood to the point of the dinner, this was enough to suspend disbelief for a bit. Poignant and touching, it still got to me. Though I still want to see SuperMax and Chloe ride off into the sunset in that broken down truck, I will have to settle for a very touching piece of storytelling.
Kudos to the team for giving us a Life is Strange ending after all.

I've just reached my first 50 hours playing this game, and I must say this game is absolutely amazing in all aspects! Good and bad points, in my opinion.
Gameplay: Three totally configurable game modes, depending on your way of playing: Career mode, if you want to be a space tycoon; Science mode, if you want to plan real expeditions inside the vast universe and go back home with something to continue; and Sandbox, BECAUSE SPACECRAFTS!
Creativity: God's sake,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥shaped rockets! Better if I add thrusted balls! Now, seriously, you will be building your first Mun-landing machine and thinking about how to add wheels to it to ride across.
Well documented: Do you need hints to build your first unmanned rover? You have a full how-to-use wiki. You don't know how to reach planet X riding a metal cucumber? Forums, official page, videos...
Mods: MODS, MODS, MODS!!!!! Modders are great, their ideas are great, everything is right in the world this way. You feel there's something empty in your space life? Mod it!
Science: Well... It's not exactly con for me. But take this advice: If you are not some astronomy curious or you expect to fly over aliens in a emotive FPS, dont buy this.
Details: Physics are right, game is funny, kerbals jump too high and can put asteroids in a planet's orbit but... It's lack of some details. It's in pre-alpha, I know, but I found some useful tools that, simply, aren't -connection between satellites, lack of planet terrain details, 90% can be solved by modding-. If you want to play this seriously, expect to mod it at some point.
9/10, is a cult game, no doubt.

As an aerospace engineer, I've got to say that I love this game. It does a great job of letting the player experience some of the aspects of my work without being overwhelmed or having to worry about killing anyone by accident. :)
I recommend new players start out with the Sandbox mode while they learn to build and fly their spacecraft. Keep the early spacecraft simple, and learn the controls step by step. I also recommend watching the KSP Tutorial on Youtube by Scott Manley if you're not familiar with the sort of flight profile an actual rocket uses to get to orbit.
You'll learn more than you thought you could from a game, and have a great time doing it, especially if you're the sort of person who loves construction and strategic style games. If you've ever stayed up too late on a game of Civilization, this one is probably a good pick for you, too.

Here's the TL;DR:
_____________________________________________
If you've seen even one trailer for this game, that should be enough for you to know if the aesthetic is a good match for you. It's got a sort of indie-movie coming-of-age vibe to it with an outdoorsy northern-California feel to the environments and setting, with great big oak trees and a town that feels somewhat rural but charming at the same time. As far as settings go, think something similar to the show "Twin Peaks" or the game "Alan Wake"
The game's visual art style is simple, but it works very well for the setup. It's not quite as gritty in its stylization as something similar to it, like Telltale's "The Walking Dead" game is. Life is Strange has a much softer look to it, and makes the game seem much lighter than what it might actually be under this aesthetic. The facial animation can be somewhat lacking at times, but it's almost completely mitigated by all the voice actor's fantastic performances. Yes,
. There wasn't a single person in this game who's dialogue I didn't believe, and that alone is pretty amazing. While some of the dialogue can be cringey or seem like it's trying to hard to appeal to a demographic of young hipsters who understand digital-age lingo, most of the script is very well written, definitely on-par with that of a good television series.
On the subject of music, the soundtrack to Life is Strange is just fantastic. Most of the game's environmental soundtrack is done by Jonathan Morali, but some of the most memorable parts are done by various alternative indie bands. Lots of acoustic guitar, minor electronic effects and soft vocals. Think "The Shins" or "Radiohead" in terms of tone. It is a perfect fit for the game and it just simply makes you want to lose yourself to this world that's been put before you.
The biggest draw of a game like this is that you, as a player, can affect the story and change the outcome of it based on the unique choices you make. Well, that's
of true. Ultimately, there are multiple endings, but by the very end of the game, you are only given a canned ending of some sort. It would be great if there were hundreds of final outcomes to the story, but from a production standpoint, it's just impossible for a single game studio to make that many different final endings. And honestly, the final ending doesn't even matter. This really is the kind of game were you as a player are meant to enjoy the journey and not the destination.
Many choices you make actually do have a pretty significant amount of gravity on how things turn out. It's actually pretty amazing to me how much effort the makers of this game put into allowing the player to explore different ways to do things. There are three kinds of choices you can make. One beings small choices, choices that don't really change anything at all or are only done for fun. The second being choices that are small, but they actually change the game in some way later, usually a character talking about something differently than they might have otherwise. The third kind of choice you can make is what I'm calling a "big choice" The game  freezes for a moment and lets you make a decision that will dramatically alter the way things unfold later on.
One of the great things about Life is Strange is that the game's protagonist, Max, discovers very early on that she has the power to rewind time, and because of this, you can just about always rewind time after making a decision, just to see what kind of alternative outcome you could have gotten. It's fun to see the different ways things can unfold, and it makes the decisionmaking process that much more engaging since you can't simply undo every single decision you make.
That's not to say that the only gameplay here is clicking one of two buttons to make a choice. Even though the game is mostly linear, there are lots of distractions to keep you occupied. I looked at just about everything I thought would be important at some point, and I don't think I can overstate how much effort the developers of Life is Strange have put into the extras you can find. Everything you can find in this game is interesting to some degree and just loaded with small touches that make it come to life. There are so many optional things to look at and read through it is absolutely insane. That and the occasional time-travel based puzzle sections make the game interesting and engaging moment to moment.
Once you finish one of the five chapters, the game will stop for a moment so you can look at the decisions you've made, and compare the choices you made to the choices that other people made. There are several you will look at and think "huh, I didn't know you could do that" It might not sound like a big deal, but it actually makes for a pretty great motivator to keep moving through the game. Once the next chapter begins, it does a TV series-esque recap of important things that have happened in case you need to be caught up to speed.
The game's length feels just about right. It doesn't linger on for too much longer than it needs to, although I certainly wouldn't have minded if there was more to get into here. I beat the game in about 12 hours, although it probably could have done it in 6-8 hours or so if you just chose to rush through everything. There's a pretty hefty amount of replay value here as you can go through things individually by chapter if you want to explore all the possibilities available to you.
_____________________________________________
Life is Strange is now the gold standard for what story-driven games of this genre should be. It's by no means perfect, but for the price and the things it will make you feel, there really isn't anything else like it.

This game is beautiful, in many ways.
The essentially standalone game mechanic is simple enough that it's almost completely story-led.
It's well written despite some wonkey dialogue (if you get irrationally annoyed by teenage girl slang, you may want to avoid).
The art style is gorgeous and beautifully executed. The lighting in particular is fantastic. Animations are fluid, the way characters move is surprisingly realistic. It feels extremely polished.
The story is interesting and well paced, and the use of episodes means you can play for small stints of an hour or two and have a very satisfying gameplay experience each time. The choices you make do have impact, and with the rewinding mechanic you have the opportunity to see how different decisions would have played out in the short term, without ruining the long term affects. This gives you the feeling of granting extra weight to the decision you make.
I especially liked the collectible nature of the journal, taking photos, etc. It clues you in to what would be described in other games as 'secondary objectives', but isn't explicit about it.
I've only finished a couple of episodes so far, but already looking forward to jumping back in.
I came with pretty high expectations and left satisfied. If you liked the Telltale 'Walking Dead', 'Game of Thrones' etc. series of games, you will love Life Is Strange. It feels very much like those Telltale games, but done with much more polish.

A high quality episodic game which allows you to turn back time to undo certain actions or avoid mistakes.
Unfortunately it would quite often break my immersion by not allowing me to do what seemed most sensible.
Some examples (SPOILERS!):
- When you open Chloe's stepdad's files they fall in oil. To avoid this you can reverse time. But when you try it again it falls in the oil again and Max states that is going to keep happening. Well, not if you climbed on a chair so you can reach it properly it wouldn't, but apparently the player character isn't intelligent enough to approach a problem from more than one angle.
- When you find Chloe's stepdad's pictures of Kate, it's not possible to confront Chloe about this. Apparently finding tools to fix your camera is more important than warning your best friend about her stepdad's potential serial killer behaviour.
- Chloe asks you to put on some music. But the player is unplugged and has no CD in it. You are apparently mute since asking Chloe where you can find a CD is impossible. So you have to go through all of Chloe's personal belongings with her RIGHT THERE only to eventually find a CD in a lockbox under her bed. A very cheap trick by the game to just have you explore her room, despite it making no sense to do so, realistically.
I could go on, but my point is clear. The game offers a very interesting, well delivered story, and I'll definitely pick the other chapters up in a sale. I'm intrigued by the story  and the characters and I'm interested in seeing the long term consequences of my actions.
But the game is just not very immersive when half the time the actions I as a player think are most sensible are just not available. Too often I was just going through the motions of what the game wanted me to do instead of it giving me a little bit of freedom to do what would thematically make the most sense.

This won't be the most helpful review ever, but this game already has plenty of reviews that say more eloquently what I already think. Read some of the Top Recommended Reviews, and you'll see what I mean. But in a nutshell, if you like modern episodic adventure games where your choices matter, but feel like in most of them your choices don't *really* matter? This might be the game for you.
Its main hurdle for some may be the setting and protagonist (e.g., 18-year-old girl at a prestigious school in Oregon), but if you allow yourself to get past that, it becomes one of the series' strengths. I am neither 18 nor a girl, but it was interesting to be put in the position to make choices in that role, and as part of an interesting time travel story, one of the better ones I've seen in recent years. It's also a dramatic game that deals with the human condition as well as some controversial subject matter, so if you don't feel like playing a game along those lines, I would advise against this for now.
Despite what may initially seem like just a gimmick, the main gameplay element becomes key to the storyline, and adds a paradoxically agonizing weight to decisions that one doesn't always feel in similar fare. And while the 'core' story may remain more or less the same, some elements can change drastically depending on what you choose. (I've only gone back and made a few different choices, but saw that it drastically changed parts of the game, as well as the end.)
The last episodic choice-related games I played before this included "Tales From The Borderlands" and "Game of Thrones", and while I enjoyed them, neither of them felt as meaningful or made me think like this one did. I can't imagine having to wait months between episodes, and by the time I'd finished the third episode, I was compelled to move on to the fourth and fifth ones just to see where it was ultimately going.
Without spoiling any details, I will say that I wasn't entirely happy with the last hour of the last episode, from both a gameplay perspective as well as a plotpoint perspective, but it was still dramatic enough that it didn't detract significantly from the overall experience, and I am glad I played it.

This is, according to the developers, an unfinished game as of October 2014, with the next major update being the first that they consider to even be 'in-beta'.  Despite that, it's one of the most time consuming, nerve-wracking, awe-inspiring pieces of software I've owned from the time I was playing Sierra adventure games on a Tandy 1000 TL in the early 90's.
The best part about it is that it can appeal on dozens of levels.  I'm a spaceplane addict; I can't build enough Single-Stage To Orbit spaceplanes and build in-atmosphere jets just to see how well I can thrash a particular design around.  But other people spend hours upon hours building or flying/driving heavy-lift rockets, unmanned probes, space stations, rovers, bizarre steampunk looking creations, etc.
The learning curve can be high.  I strongly recommend Youtube tutorials, registering on the game forums and learning as much as you can about the basics of flying and designing rockets.  But the payoffs, when your much-tinkered-with jet finally performs just like you want it to or when you see the sunrise on the Moon for the first time...it's a tangible thing.
The only words of warning I'd offer are that it is unfinished (though I've seen 'complete' popular releases that were far more bug-ridden) so there are the occasional glitches and if you can't handle something COMPLETELY free form you might have trouble coming up with things to do.
I...totally don't have that problem.  Not with an entire solar system as my sandbox.

This won't be the most helpful review ever, but this game already has plenty of reviews that say more eloquently what I already think. Read some of the Top Recommended Reviews, and you'll see what I mean. But in a nutshell, if you like modern episodic adventure games where your choices matter, but feel like in most of them your choices don't *really* matter? This might be the game for you.
Its main hurdle for some may be the setting and protagonist (e.g., 18-year-old girl at a prestigious school in Oregon), but if you allow yourself to get past that, it becomes one of the series' strengths. I am neither 18 nor a girl, but it was interesting to be put in the position to make choices in that role, and as part of an interesting time travel story, one of the better ones I've seen in recent years. It's also a dramatic game that deals with the human condition as well as some controversial subject matter, so if you don't feel like playing a game along those lines, I would advise against this for now.
Despite what may initially seem like just a gimmick, the main gameplay element becomes key to the storyline, and adds a paradoxically agonizing weight to decisions that one doesn't always feel in similar fare. And while the 'core' story may remain more or less the same, some elements can change drastically depending on what you choose. (I've only gone back and made a few different choices, but saw that it drastically changed parts of the game, as well as the end.)
The last episodic choice-related games I played before this included "Tales From The Borderlands" and "Game of Thrones", and while I enjoyed them, neither of them felt as meaningful or made me think like this one did. I can't imagine having to wait months between episodes, and by the time I'd finished the third episode, I was compelled to move on to the fourth and fifth ones just to see where it was ultimately going.
Without spoiling any details, I will say that I wasn't entirely happy with the last hour of the last episode, from both a gameplay perspective as well as a plotpoint perspective, but it was still dramatic enough that it didn't detract significantly from the overall experience, and I am glad I played it.

Have you ever wondered how being an astronaut is?
If you have an interest in space, engineering, physics and exploration, then this is the game for you! There's definitely a steep learning curve, but this only enchanses your feelings of achievement. The game packs a powerful physics-generator, and although it's not a simulator, you will learn a whole lot about what it takes to perform advanced missions in space.
The two basic forms of gameplay is construction of rockets, spaceships and planes, and flying them to a wide range of planets and moons in a fictional solar system not unlike ours.
If you choose to play the Sandbox-mode, all your missions are entirely designed by you - be it achieving orbit around the home planet, going to one of their moons or even going to other planets. There's a whole solar system to explore! Among the list of places to go, you have planets both with and without an atmosphere, their moons or even asteroids.
If you choose to play the Career-mode, you can choose to complete various contracts. These range from testing new parts to landing on planets far, far away. Completing contracts gives you money and science-points, which you can use to develop new parts. When in space, you can also gather science-points by doing different experiments.
All in all, this is the most fulfilling game I have ever played. Be warned, though - playing this game will most certainly teach you a whole lot about orbital mechanics, and watching films about space will have you going "Hey! That's not how you land on a planet! You have to burn retrograde!"

A high quality episodic game which allows you to turn back time to undo certain actions or avoid mistakes.
Unfortunately it would quite often break my immersion by not allowing me to do what seemed most sensible.
Some examples (SPOILERS!):
- When you open Chloe's stepdad's files they fall in oil. To avoid this you can reverse time. But when you try it again it falls in the oil again and Max states that is going to keep happening. Well, not if you climbed on a chair so you can reach it properly it wouldn't, but apparently the player character isn't intelligent enough to approach a problem from more than one angle.
- When you find Chloe's stepdad's pictures of Kate, it's not possible to confront Chloe about this. Apparently finding tools to fix your camera is more important than warning your best friend about her stepdad's potential serial killer behaviour.
- Chloe asks you to put on some music. But the player is unplugged and has no CD in it. You are apparently mute since asking Chloe where you can find a CD is impossible. So you have to go through all of Chloe's personal belongings with her RIGHT THERE only to eventually find a CD in a lockbox under her bed. A very cheap trick by the game to just have you explore her room, despite it making no sense to do so, realistically.
I could go on, but my point is clear. The game offers a very interesting, well delivered story, and I'll definitely pick the other chapters up in a sale. I'm intrigued by the story  and the characters and I'm interested in seeing the long term consequences of my actions.
But the game is just not very immersive when half the time the actions I as a player think are most sensible are just not available. Too often I was just going through the motions of what the game wanted me to do instead of it giving me a little bit of freedom to do what would thematically make the most sense.

Its main hurdle for some may be the setting and protagonist (e.g., 18-year-old girl at a prestigious school in Oregon), but if you allow yourself to get past that, it becomes one of the series' strengths. I am neither 18 nor a girl, but it was interesting to be put in the position to make choices in that role, and as part of an interesting time travel story, one of the better ones I've seen in recent years. It's also a dramatic game that deals with the human condition as well as some controversial subject matter, so if you don't feel like playing a game along those lines, I would advise against this for now.
Despite what may initially seem like just a gimmick, the main gameplay element becomes key to the storyline, and adds a paradoxically agonizing weight to decisions that one doesn't always feel in similar fare. And while the 'core' story may remain more or less the same, some elements can change drastically depending on what you choose. (I've only gone back and made a few different choices, but saw that it drastically changed parts of the game, as well as the end.)
The last episodic choice-related games I played before this included "Tales From The Borderlands" and "Game of Thrones", and while I enjoyed them, neither of them felt as meaningful or made me think like this one did. I can't imagine having to wait months between episodes, and by the time I'd finished the third episode, I was compelled to move on to the fourth and fifth ones just to see where it was ultimately going.
Without spoiling any details, I will say that I wasn't entirely happy with the last hour of the last episode, from both a gameplay perspective as well as a plotpoint perspective, but it was still dramatic enough that it didn't detract significantly from the overall experience, and I am glad I played it.

*Review applies to the whole game, i.e. episodes 1-5*
Life Is Strange is an amazing experience on one condition - accept right off the bat that it's more of an interactive movie than an actual game. That said, just sit back, relax, have a glass of good wine or a cup of tea and be told a story that balances between intriguing, heartwarming and absolutely gutwrenching. The choices you make in the game, even the tiniest and insignificant-seeming ones, can come back to reward you ot bite you in the most unexpected ways, making you feel guilty as hell for what you thought was the best choice and/or make you cry like a little ♥♥♥♥♥. It's a thoroughly enjoyable (sometimes in a horrible, depressing, but-i-want-to-know-what-happens kind of way) emotional rollercoaster that I definitely plan to ride again to see how different choices would turn out. On a sidenote, I recommend immersing yourself into the story and making the choices you would make, not what obviously seem the most moral ones. Might end up getting to know yourself a little better. For example, turns out that I would let a town be destroyed in exchange for the life of one friend of mine. I think it's fair to say this game ♥♥♥♥ed me up.  Onto the pros, cons, and meeh.
Pros:
+ a brilliant, thrilling story that draws you in like no other
+ great voice acting
+ very atmospheric and relaxing gameplay
+ the graphics style I think is very fitting for the game
+ good soundtrack, again very fitting for the game's overall feel and the developers have definitely thought about supplying a good flow of music for players who might take longer in one or another part of the game.
+ awesome detail to the game in terms of NPC-s and interactions.
+ has decent replay value
+ the game does an excellent job of illustrating the butterfly effect - even the smallest choices (or choices you didn't make and things you didn't change) have consequences.
Cons:
- Some of the playable parts just seem unnecessary and almost like the makers thought "hmm, we haven't let the player do anything for a while, let's interrupt the cutscene just to have them fetch some stuff for no discernible reason".
But still. 10/10.

This is where it's at. For its relatively high price tag, you'll get the smartest, and probably most fun game of the decade.
While far from perfect (at this point, Unity seems to have been a wrong decision at project kickoff), it's probably the best thing that has happened to computer games since Tetris. Think Minecraft, and space simulation. :)
Like Minecraft, it's open ended, vast and teems with possibilities. Also like Minecraft, it exposes an impressive API for modders and plugin writers to utilize, and there are mods out there to change the entire solar system, to replace stock physics with a more realistic one, to build giant robots, whatever you want.
As you start, the game puts you in a lead role of a space program on Kerbin - an incredibly dense planet roughly 1/10 in size of Earth, with the same G value at sea level, inhabited by little green people who, by the looks of it, aren't very bright. It never ceases to be endearingly humorous, while commanding quite some investment of your time in learning about actual space exploration, and stuff like orbital physics.
You don't have to hit up the Feynman Lectures to enjoy the game, but you might actually be tempted to. Whether carefreely launching badly designed craft and - sometimes - failing hilariously, or making Excel sheets for TWR and Delta-V calculations, and painstakingly plotting your launch and transfer windows, and exploring the solar system, if you think space is cool, you'll definitely have fun.
(I do wish the 1.1 release will fix the terrible instability on OS X though...)

I have been playing this game for a signficant amount of time and through many, many updates. I have to say, this is one of the best games i have ever played. KSP offers a unique experience that simulates managing you own space program through trial and error and the support of a great community. The game lets players explore the in's and out's of aerospace engineering in a fun way - it has certainly created a love for all things space for me. In the game itself, players create rockets and space-planes to reach other planets in a fictional solar system. The game has realistic orbital physics and orbital mechanics, which is easily taught by the games simple to follow tutorials. Even if you cannot complete a task, such as orbital rendezvous, the game's community will happily help you out or direct you toward a good youtube video.
There is a huge modding community following this game because of the simplicity of adding mods to this game. Mods are recomended after awhile, as they can create an entirely  new experience. Since KSP is in Early Access, there is much to be done. At the time I am writing this. the development of the game has reached a "Scope Complete" level, where the breadth of the game features have been implemented, but not to the depth of detail and functionality that Squad (the developers) is looking for in those features. Mods help in this area, creating a rich game experience even though the game even isn't complete. Regardless, the game itself is amazing and under pretty much regular update, so new things are always around the corner.
If you are skeptical, try out the demo!

This game is on the outside a cute little unrealistic space game. Do not judge a book by it's cover. It has a surprisingly realistic sort of engine that gives kids and even adults a fun way to learn REAL rocket science! As a game, it is unfinished but it is constantly updated with new features and items to build your spaceship to fly from the launch pad at the Kerbal Space Center to the Mun (Moon) or even Jool (Jupiter!) The solar system in Kerbal Space Program is at a very small scale compared to real life where the planet farthest out is about 0.76 AU away from the sun in game but Earth in real life is about 0.98 AU away from the sun, which makes for a simple space program and less waiting for your ship to orbit (granted the game has time acceleration up to 100,000 times normal time.) Overall, a solid and educational game that will be fun for tens or even hundereds of hours in my case. Get this game.

The first thing you will notice are the vastly outdated graphics, which just hurt your eyes and are nothing like the trailers and the screenshots. Everything is downgraded as usual. However, this is not the biggest of surprises in the game industry these days, so in my generosity, it can be forgiven.
What I and many others fail to understand is the concept of the game, for it simply isnt very well thought out before put into use. This is very obvious when you really start to understand the gameplay and try to execute the things you observe the game showing you, which eventually feels clunky, outdated and sometimes, unfortunately, even flat-out depressing.
Gameplay-wise, the game holds your hand almost all the time and it becomes really annoying, when you start to notice you have no real difference in the course of action. There are moments where you just feel completely lost and get annoyed at how everything doesnt quite fit together.
The controls dont feel fluid at all, and occasionally you feel like you're either stuck in the mud or glue, or the game intentionally was made hard and frustrating to control. Why would anyone want to offer the players of their game an experience like this?
And what's really frustrating are the sounds. It's like someone literally wanted to hire one of the worst composers, voice actors and the sound designers for this kind of a game! Could it be simply a bad decision from the lead of this project or very, very dark humor from the entire team of the game developers? You decide!
And dont even get me started on the AI. It's rather non-existent. Some games are famous for their silly bot-AI that keeps doing mistakes and failing at the only thing it was designed to do. The only difference between those games and this is that the AI here isn't even funny. It just wants to make you shout at it's actions in utter rage.
The performance of the game tends to be lackluster. Ive seen it perform badly on many different specs and machines, which cannot garner much respect, but at this point it doesn't really surprise, either.
All this could be fixed with at least a long, interesting story that would give content for your money and/or time, but it doesn't really offer either.
When you thought it couldn't get any worse, the game has more bugs here and there, hindering your already non-existent progressing and sucking the last drops of joy out of the experience
On top of all of this, the game is insanely difficult to progress in. Everything has been made non-intuitive for the average gamer, to the point even hardcore difficulty masochists will find it unpleasant to experience.
It all makes you think: Where is the gaming industry heading these days?
One can only hope for improvement on this one, although it seems unlikely, as this game was most likely just another cash-grab. Pity..

I'm very surprised I haven'r reviewed this yet.
Kerbal Space Program is, well... you guessed it, a game about launching stuff into space. For profit, and science, and fun. Mainly for fun.
While there is a career mode, where you have to take care of budgets and reputation, take up contracts etc, there is a sandbox mode for those rocketeers who just can't seem to get up off the launchpad without a little practice, or explosions.
Another highlight of the game is this: there is no real story. Sure, there are contracts that tell you to reach space and get into orbit, but once you have mastered that, you can do whatever your heart desires. Build a massive space station in orbit! Start a program to the Mun (Moon) or even create a base there! Try and emulate what Voyagers 1 and 2 did and do a Grand Tour of the Planets! Your unique aspirations are exactly that: yours. You decide everything.
Even if you're not the best at flying rockets into orbit, there are plenty of mods for the game to help you get there. If you have experience in modelling, designing or even coding, you could potentially create the next best mod for KSP. Who knows, your ideas might even be incorporated into the final game.
All in all, this game can suit anyone, from a casual space tourist to an absolute space nerd. I personally fall into the latter category.

This honestly plays almost like a finished game. There are simply so many places to go and study, that you will never really "finish" the game. There is also a very active mod community; you can get mods to improve realism (such as TAC Life Support or Ferram Aerospace Research), as well as many mods that add more things for you to do (such as KSP Interstellar or KW Rocketry). The base game does have some issues with realism, but the recent addition of lifting bodies and destructible buildings is a massive step forward. If you like physics, this game is for you. My current gameplay:
After the first probes, it was about time to send someone to the Moon. There goes Jebediah Kerman! He made it, but... the rocket landed in the wrong position, and could not be used anymore.
So it was time to design a rescue mission. Which became rescue missions. After 5 tries, I've managed to design a rocket able to land at the exact location where Jebediah was on the Moon, and bring him back safe and sound. Now the other planets and moons wait for the bold explorer!
This game is just awesome. No violence or war; it's all about designing missions and sophisticated multi-stage rockets and thinking about every possibity. If you leave anything to luck, it'll go wrong. You are completely free to choose how to design your ships and thus solve the challenges they present. Same about exploration: you choose what to do first, no linear sequence of gameplay.
The story of its development history is amazing and the game is wonderfully unique.  Can't wait to see its systems fleshed out more.

Ok, first of all - its not a game. Its not even a "point and click" adventure. You just sit in your chair, watch lots of animations and occasionally move the character to another place. The game is rated amazingly high for its story, but should the game consist ONLY of it? Start reading books, there are plenty of way better and more intriguing stories, or at least watch some movies. The only thing I liked was music, but for this we got youtube, spotify, etc. My expectations were lower than I expected, so thumbs down for this one.

Due to the lack of serious/in-depth reviews on this game here, I will attempt not to be diluted with the behemoth of other Steam users writing reviews for this game.
When I first bought this game I would always mess around in sandbox. Does that sound like you? Build rocket, go straight up, find myself empty of fuel.
Build rocket, only reach 10km before my fuel was out, exit game.
This game is so much more than that. The default aerodynamics aren't simplistic, they're just wrong. Mods like FAR or NEAR (simple version of FAR) greatly improve the aerodynamics to make the game a lot more fun. If you're new to the whole rocket thing, MechJeb is also recommended. It'll show you your TWR and Delta V so you can hopefully get to the Mun, or just get into orbit without your Thrust-to-weight ratio holding you down.
The game is built off Unity, but despite other projects I have seen on this engine, KSP utilises it much better. The graphics are somewhat cartoony and the whole idea of "Kerbodyne" parts and such have lots of puns.
If you've been to the Mun (or Minimus is you're smart enough to know that Minimus has less Delta V requirements than the Mun...), then you'll often find yourself kind of bored of the game.
Well, there's mods to keep you interested. Ever seen Scott Manley's videos? Interstellar quest? A big part of KSP is imagination - making your own [italics]space program[/italics]. There's mods to help you colonise other planets (or moons), build solar system sattelite relays to help your interplanetary voyages relay back science data to the Kerbal Space Centre.
KSP really has no end. It's well worth the $30 and I'm sure if you hold out for a month or so there's a high chance it will go on sale in that period. The amount of updates are consistent every month or so, and bring lots of new content.

There was a time where Kerbal Space Program was a total sandbox: there was no map, no action keys, only one flight flown at a time, with bugs were commonplace...but never have I had so much fun on such a raw product, battling the space kracken and attaining orbit with the aid of community altitude/velocity tables.
Kerbal Space Program has been a working alpha for at least three and a half years now, and has picked up an amazing community of contributors and modders, who add so much unofficial content and dedicatedly update/revise it on every new version. For myself, what I love about what KSP is how it has stayed true to its core premise of being a /Kerbal Space Program./ Squad has realized all this so well: through traditional staged rockets, SSTOs, the much newer R+D unlockable parts from science, and now the economic aspects of it: you truly control the fate and direction of the KSP. And Squad is not done yet.
The game itself is a mostly a simulator: most of your gameplay is flying your creations and accomplishing tasks using them. There is a very steep learning curve, not unlike that of 1950s-60s NASA. ;) You build and fly your rockets by trial and error - and as you invest more and more time and effort into the game, you turn to mods to extend the experiance for you: utilizing tools to help make the most efficent spacecraft. After probably thousands of hours, I still find it fun because of there /sheer amount of things you can do./ Bigger rockets = more power = more fun.
TL;DR pick up a demo and give it a go. You're going to have a blast crashing for first few rockets.

A beautifully crafted experience enhanced by being able to live through the eyes of the protagonist.
This, to me, is a game you can put at the tip of a spear and argue that it is a true work of art. Granted, art is a subjective term, and everyone has opinions. However, as reflcted in many other reviews this games breaks a barrier and puts you in an all too familiar world that we all live in.
The design of the west coast Arcadia Bay makes for a solid, believeable world. Blackwell, the Diner, the Beach, and Chole's home are all reminiscent of our current world. School parking lots fillled with junkers and hot rods, Science class with all the works, and some beautiful moments in nature. Part of the enjoyment of the game is taking in the world that you walk and seeing all the tiny easter eggs the designers have put (hats off to the Dontnod, the French team that created this west coastal world).
The same goes for sound design, well thought out and always appropriate (or not, when you can hear your peers banging in the dorm down the halll). And an awesome soundtrack, noting Syd Matters- Obstacles as more or less the theme of the game, which can play more than once depending on your choices.
More than anything, the driving force of the game is the plot: A girl (Max) learns she can turn back time, and joins forces with her friend Chloe to find a missing girl in Arcadia Bay. All while a huge impending natural disaster seems right at their doorstep. Some people have found that somewhere in Episodes 4 and 5 the writers became "lost". I can't see why, I actually found episode 4 incredibly dense (and episodically was my favorite), and the choices and twists that occur in these two episodes made me want more. The mechanic of reversing time is perfect for a game like this, you can always see every option you have and craft each situation the way you want it to be.
The first episode is free, I tried it, and immediatly bought the season pass after, you can easily get 10 hours out of this, or if you really want to experience this world it can take 15-20 hours. Well worth the money.
My only warning: I am not a parent, but I do teach, and I would not recommend this game to anyone below the 17 M rating. Not for graphic violence, but because of the thematic material of the game (Semi SPOILER- Suicide attempts, sexual hazing, torture).
Go be Max and save the world.

Ingredients:
1 cup of butter
1 cup of sugar
1 cup of brown sugar
2 eggs
2 teaspoons of vanilla extract
3 cups of flour
1 teaspoon of baking soda
2 teaspoons of hot water
1/2 teaspoon of salt
2 cups of chocolate chips
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C).
2. Cream together the butter, white sugar, and brown sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the vanilla. Dissolve baking soda in hot water. Add to batter along with salt. Stir in flour, chocolate chips, and nuts. Drop by large spoonfuls onto ungreased pans.
3. Bake for about 10 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are nicely browned.
Additional Notes:
*Prep Time - 20 minutes
*Cook Time - 10 minutes
*Ready in 1 hour!

Ingredients:
1 cup of butter
1 cup of sugar
1 cup of brown sugar
2 eggs

3. Bake for about 10 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are nicely browned.
Additional Notes:

*Cook Time - 10 minutes

If you like well-written dialogues, great story and decisions which actually do have impact on it, this game was made for you. You'll likely immediately feel immersed by the atmosphere of the enviroment, scenery, music and characters. Square Enix definitely did a well done job by balancing slow-paced serene pauses the main character finds herself in and the action-adventure moments, when you actually have to think fast. The characters, which mostly consist of high school senior students or their friends/family and the prestigious photography art school setting might sound a bit 'meh' at first, but you'll quickly get to sympathize with the protagonist, explore the areas and people around and eventually you'll realize you just spent several hours without even noticing.
Just to point out some of the cons too, sometimes you might get stuck at a spot with an unnecessarily hard-to-notice clickable object which you'd never have expected to be of use. Also, the dialogues tend to feel a bit too long at times, but it's possible to avoid the long talk by selecting right choices. Later on the game might feel a little confusing, at least it did to me, as there's a lot happening - literally - at the same time. There's also no save/load option, but you certainly won't need it, as you'll figure out quickly throughout the game.
Be perceptive, click everything that can be clicked, make wise choices and you'll enjoy 12 hours of a great, movie-like game.
This is easily one of the best games I've ever played and quickly made it onto my top 5 games of all time list.  I would recommend this game to anyone who likes space, exploration, and explosions.

This game is definitely worth it. You'll have lots of fun designing rockets and learning how orbital mechanics works.
But there's a lot of lost potential here. Once you've done everything, it starts to get tedious to build rockets. I'm not a huge fan of the "management" of a space program -- obviously that's what most people wanted, but I find it tough to care about career mode. There isn't enough science in the end game. There's no use for space stations. There's no use for space stations orbiting other bodies in the solar system. There's hardly any use for rovers. Once you've gone to a planet/moon, there's not really any reason to explore it further.
However, launching things, learning how to orbit, how to do hohmann transfers, and how to adjust your orbital plane and catch up to other spacecraft will take you dozens of hours and is very very fun. I wasn't as enthused with space planes and the aeronautics, but I think that's just me -- many people seem to find that fun as well.
Also, the game has a number of annoying bugs, still: broken/unselectable Maneuver nodes, crashes, slow physics when there's a lot in the frame, weird accelerations, spontaneous spacecraft crashes, and windows that won't close / buttons that won't work. The bugs aren't that bad, but if you play for a little while you're guaranteed to encounter them.
Mods make this game a lot better, but don't go overboard on installing them; most aren't that great.
To summarize: a fun game for the first couple/few dozen hours, then very disappointing.

The intense conflicts in the story feel surreal, with choices feeling so mundane but yet foreshadowed as so consequential. Minor spoiler: There's also a time reversal mechanic that allows you to reverse time and essentially try out things differently in the game. Life is Strange... is absolutely incredible
It isn't a question of whether you should buy this game or not; but rather a question of when you should buy this game.
In basics I would describe it like this:
Pros
+Episode 1 is totally free for you to play and demo the game with, if you enjoy episode 1 then you will enjoy the following episodes and if you don't like it then you haven't lost anything...
+Amazing soundtrack that creates a real ambience and sets the mood in each scene
+Engaging and in-depth storyline that will want you craving more at the end of each episode
+Realism. Though of course not overboard the themes and elements of the story can be touching to many who have experienced things that occur in the story in the past.As many others have said that the game shows what it FELT like to be a teenager rather than what it WAS like.
+Gorgeous graphics, even though I had to run the game at the bare minimum graphics they were amazing to look at and I loved just watching
+Choices Matter. Though of course it is always an illusion your choices do impact parts of the story and will shape your character/ your view of the character as the story progresses, it does this well and I enjoyed the ability to choose how certain things play out.
+Emotional attachment. Even if you think you're a tough person who can handle anything and doesn't show emotion Life is Strange will slap you right in the cheek and prove you otherwise. If you get emotional easily I can almost guarantee you will cry at some point throughout the story and regret the very moment you bought a game that could do this to you. The ending will put you in emotional turmoil and the journey itself will grow you in a way that you never thought a humble video game could.
+So many more things for you to discover, this is only a short list of positive things about the game, just read the other reviews to cement the idea that this game is incredible.
Neutrally Positive
+=Even if you are only getting 5-10fps it does not derail the story at all and I still managed to have a very enjoyable experience.
+=Costs about the same price as a standard novel ($24) and will entertain
+= At least 20 hours playability depending on your playstyle, if you just play the game through and avoid any extra dialogue and don't take a seat then of course this will be a lower number.
Neutrally Negative
-= Reskip. Though only a minor issue which can be easily fixed, if you choose to rewind and restart a conversation and choose to skip it you will be stuck in a constant state of attempting to rewind and skip the dialogue and will have to restart from the previous checkpoint.
-= Very little replayability value. As in many novels and movies and various things with a storyline ultimately you will know what happens and though it is fun to try and play things from a different perspective you know what will happen in the end and you can't remove that from your memory.
Cons
-Perhaps weak ending (under some interpretation) that makes everything you've done feel pointless; though this may have been the point of the ending itself.
-Many plot holes. There are a lot of questions that are left unanswered throughout the story which does weaken it a lot when you reach the end.
-Lip Syncing. It is bad at the best of times, though improved on from initial release, quite easily can still be frustrating for some, though I had no major issue with this myself.
-Interactivity Issues. Sometimes (depending on the screen size) you will find yourself unable to select objects while staring right at them and will need to decrease the screen size to be able to get it without carefully adjusting your mouse until you can select it
.
