Kerbal Space Program is at its heart, simpily a physics sandbox. However, the scope and detail of physics it encompasses surpasses the hasty calculations of "good enough" for physics models that start to creep on computer algebra systems territory. The main point of this advanced sandbox is hinted at by the title, you build a rocket, pray, and orbit celestrial bodies in the name of science, honor, or money.
What is fantastic about this sandbox, is that the player can invest how involved he or she wants to be in the game. If the player wanted to be percise, using the correct amount of delta V, and efficent use of fuel as guided by the player's mathmatics, so they can spend as little money as necessary, they can do that. Or, they can be heavy handed, state a massive rocket is good enough, and launch with as many boosters as they like without bouncing off the atmosphere to send a minimal probe into orbit.
Kerbal Space Program is a "early alpha/beta release" game. It is a sucessful one, with the community healthy, and the development active. Kerbal Space Program supports all big 3 OSes. KSP supports mods (which are also platformless), which can add new depth to the gameplay. There is over 150 mods (my estimate) that are at or above developer quailty based on asthetics, resource use, and gameplay value.
It is ultimately fun, educational, and challenging.
Highly recommended.

Time travel will run into a paradox or two and that's inevitable. The writers were not aware of this, or perhaps they were, and decided to actively create the most painfully obvious of paradoxes where they could be avoided, or at least dampened. There's also the countless times where you could have used the power to your advantage but simply weren't able, even though you have done the same thing for every other mundane activity, because it would hurt the plot.
The player has a camera. Early on a major secondary character stresses the importance of documenting everything you do, to always take the picture. You, in all your glory, then take it upon yourself to never take a single picture of the dozens of incriminating things you find. It's not even an option. But you can take pictures of squirrels and your blue-haired hipster friend.
Every character is written to be so utterly incompetent and brain dead that the only thing keeping them from complete disaster is your ability to rewind time and tell them not to do the very stupid thing they're about to do.
Bonus round: I've heard the player say "...so apropos." three times now. I get it, she's a quirky hipster who just heard the word for the first time in english-lit. ♥♥♥♥ off already.

Kerbal Space Program is at its heart, simpily a physics sandbox. However, the scope and detail of physics it encompasses surpasses the hasty calculations of "good enough" for physics models that start to creep on computer algebra systems territory. The main point of this advanced sandbox is hinted at by the title, you build a rocket, pray, and orbit celestrial bodies in the name of science, honor, or money.
What is fantastic about this sandbox, is that the player can invest how involved he or she wants to be in the game. If the player wanted to be percise, using the correct amount of delta V, and efficent use of fuel as guided by the player's mathmatics, so they can spend as little money as necessary, they can do that. Or, they can be heavy handed, state a massive rocket is good enough, and launch with as many boosters as they like without bouncing off the atmosphere to send a minimal probe into orbit.
Kerbal Space Program is a "early alpha/beta release" game. It is a sucessful one, with the community healthy, and the development active. Kerbal Space Program supports all big 3 OSes. KSP supports mods (which are also platformless), which can add new depth to the gameplay. There is over 150 mods (my estimate) that are at or above developer quailty based on asthetics, resource use, and gameplay value.
It is ultimately fun, educational, and challenging.
Highly recommended.

"Orbital mechanics meets Lego" would be my single-phrase summary of Kerbal Space Program. It's also absurdly addictive.
The premise is simple: you are in control of the space program for the people of the planet Kerbin, cute green schmucks called Kerbals. You design and build rockets by gluing various components together, and see if it makes it off the launchpad.
It probably won't. Then after a bit more fiddling, it'll make it into the sky before it all goes horribly wrong. But you'll make progress. A step at a time your design skills will get better, and your rockets will get further, and a few hours later you'll have your first rocket in orbit and you'll feel like a god among men (or kerbals). You'll realise you forgot to figure out how to land the blasted thing, but hey, that's what the next rocket is for right?
At some point you'll finally figure out how to do an orbital rendezvous, and suddenly you're building space stations via multiple launches, docking and undocking, making reusable space planes, conducting science missions with robotic probes and landers on other planets, or trying to figure out how to "safely" get a manned (er, Kerballed) science lab down to an island on one of the moons around the Jupiter analogue. (And bring them back, right? Right???)
This game is an insane joy to play, a wonderful hands-on "try it and see" education in orbital mechanics and other aspects of physics and so far has eaten almost as much of my life as Skyrim: not bad going for a game that's still in early access and still has entire sections of gameplay yet to be implemented.

A simple aerospace simulator where you can build and fly spacecraft and/or aircraft of many types. This game can be modded quite a bit, and a few mods include WW2 era plane parts, extra rocket parts, and weapons such as machine guns and missiles that can be put on your fighter (yes, you can make fighters in this game, whether they be prop fighters or jet fighters). If you aren't into all this military stuff, then there are other things you can do, including making a space program (obvious, indicated in the name of this game), or building something really crazy and out of this world (such as a heliplane, a jet-powered helicopter that I built). At first, the basic concepts of building spacecraft or aircraft (aircraft especially) can be quite confusing, but thankfully, there is a helpful KSP community that is always there to help. Once you get a grip on the basic concepts, just let your imagination fly. Eventually, you'll end up like me, making copies of the F-16 out of stock parts. If you're interested, I would suggest playing the KSP Demo first in order to see if you like the game, and if you do enjoy playing it, then by all means, purchase it.

Have you ever wished for a rewind power that could  bring you back to almost any previous point in your life, so you could re-embrace a lost moment, do something silly (kick your bully in the face and rewind back), or fix a mistake in the past? If you do, play this game and THINK AGAIN.
Despite a weak final episode and an unpopular ending  -ONLY BECAUSE OF HOW AMAZING THE FIRST 4 EPISODES WERE- Life Is Strange is an AMAZING game, one that will impact you (perhaps very deeply by causing you to develop depression, you've been warned!) if you invest your emotions into the story of Max Caulfield, whose sudden mysterious superpower to rewind time is bringing her -and you- to desperately try to fix everything that is wrong with life: saving her childhood friend, solving a missing person case, helping high school bully victims ...
The story doesn't shine because it has a grandiose plot with gripping twists at every turn, or overly complex mind♥♥♥♥s that you would expect in a sci-fi involving time travel story. Instead, as you are playing through the game, you realize that the themes of the game are those that we struggle with in our daily lives: lost friendship, everything everyone has gone through in highschool, broken families, and the inevitability - that some of us may have unfortunately experienced in real life- of losing someone we love to the finality of death.
The game's gorgeous handpainted artystlye graphics, beautiful soundtracks and the phenomenal voice acting for the main characters both make the protagonists come to life and bring your heart into their world. The secondary characters feel less developed despite the game's attempts to illustrate everyone's humanity, the good characters with their shades of grey and the bad ones with their redeeming qualities, but are nonetheless humane enough for you to feel anger and empathy towards them throughtout most of your journey (until the last episode where the disparity between the quality of the protagonists and the secondary characters finally takes a toll on the game which is a major reason why the last episode is a bit of a let-down).
So you may ask, why the heck should I play this thing, if all it is going to do is make me depressed, or even make me go through all the **** I have already dealt with in real life? True, I'm not the one to judge what's the best for you. But sometimes, experiencing things similar to your own through someone else's eyes can be surprisingly refreshing, and lend insights that you could not have obtained going through it yourself. Perhaps you would realize that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s treating you badly are victims themselves, and what you need to do is not to antagonize them further, but reach out a helpful hand; Perhaps it would make you come to terms with something, to realize that it is better to just bravely face the consequences and walk down the road, no matter how difficult it appears, than holding onto the written past and living in pain, regret, and denial; perhaps, it would make you realize, that it is better to just...let it go.
I wish I could constantly rewind back to time and  experience this game in a fresh way over and over again. But at least, this game will forever remain in my catalogue as a mesmerizing memory. I hope it will be the same for you :)
Treasure what you have, for sometimes you will never know the true value of a moment until it becomes a memory.

Have you ever wished for a rewind power that could  bring you back to almost any previous point in your life, so you could re-embrace a lost moment, do something silly (kick your bully in the face and rewind back), or fix a mistake in the past? If you do, play this game and THINK AGAIN.
Despite a weak final episode and an unpopular ending  -ONLY BECAUSE OF HOW AMAZING THE FIRST 4 EPISODES WERE- Life Is Strange is an AMAZING game, one that will impact you (perhaps very deeply by causing you to develop depression, you've been warned!) if you invest your emotions into the story of Max Caulfield, whose sudden mysterious superpower to rewind time is bringing her -and you- to desperately try to fix everything that is wrong with life: saving her childhood friend, solving a missing person case, helping high school bully victims ...
The story doesn't shine because it has a grandiose plot with gripping twists at every turn, or overly complex mind♥♥♥♥s that you would expect in a sci-fi involving time travel story. Instead, as you are playing through the game, you realize that the themes of the game are those that we struggle with in our daily lives: lost friendship, everything everyone has gone through in highschool, broken families, and the inevitability - that some of us may have unfortunately experienced in real life- of losing someone we love to the finality of death.
The game's gorgeous handpainted artystlye graphics, beautiful soundtracks and the phenomenal voice acting for the main characters both make the protagonists come to life and bring your heart into their world. The secondary characters feel less developed despite the game's attempts to illustrate everyone's humanity, the good characters with their shades of grey and the bad ones with their redeeming qualities, but are nonetheless humane enough for you to feel anger and empathy towards them throughtout most of your journey (until the last episode where the disparity between the quality of the protagonists and the secondary characters finally takes a toll on the game which is a major reason why the last episode is a bit of a let-down).
So you may ask, why the heck should I play this thing, if all it is going to do is make me depressed, or even make me go through all the **** I have already dealt with in real life? True, I'm not the one to judge what's the best for you. But sometimes, experiencing things similar to your own through someone else's eyes can be surprisingly refreshing, and lend insights that you could not have obtained going through it yourself. Perhaps you would realize that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s treating you badly are victims themselves, and what you need to do is not to antagonize them further, but reach out a helpful hand; Perhaps it would make you come to terms with something, to realize that it is better to just bravely face the consequences and walk down the road, no matter how difficult it appears, than holding onto the written past and living in pain, regret, and denial; perhaps, it would make you realize, that it is better to just...let it go.
I wish I could constantly rewind back to time and  experience this game in a fresh way over and over again. But at least, this game will forever remain in my catalogue as a mesmerizing memory. I hope it will be the same for you :)
Treasure what you have, for sometimes you will never know the true value of a moment until it becomes a memory.

Love this game.  Even in early release, its one of the best simulation sandboxes I've ever played.   It is a physics joyride through the star system of the green Kerbals that inhabit a planet called Kerbin, which is a loose analogue of our own Earth.   The mechanics are easy enough for anyone to understand, but challenging enough to be rewarding for those who already understand rocket science.   The game offers two open ended modes--career mode and sandbox mode.   In sandbox mode, the constraints on design are limited only by the player's imagination while career mode attempts to add a strategy element to the player's "space program", primarily by adding additional engineering constraints to the design process.   In career mode, players start out with a limited amount of cash and "scientific" understanding of the kerbal universe.  Starting with simple flights, the player acquires points that can be used to unlock scientific discoveries which in turn unlocks more advanced parts that can be used to perform more difficult missions including missions to the moons of the kerbal home planet and to other planets in their solar system.   Selecting career mode is an option, but for those players who are looking for a quick fix or interested in trying out a "what if" scenario, sandbox mode unlocks every part from the very beginning.
Another strength of KSP is its modding community and the openness of the KSP game as a modding platform.  Some of the best parts and game mechanics have been created by community modders.   Squad actively encourages the creation of mods and has set up a dedicated website for sharing them.   Mods are free additions from members of the KSP community and include everything from new parts for establishing orbital and terrestrial bases, adding robotic kits or adding a feature that requires unmanned rockets to be in radio contact with mission control in order to receive commands and send back data.   These are just example of the kinds of mods that are available that take this game to the next level.
The game is great for kids, too.  My preschool-aged son loves just pushing the staging buttons, throttling his space ships up and down, and we plan our little moon adventures together.  My daughter in elementary school is learning the important parts of a rocket from the engine, and how the engine burns fuel to produce thrust, and where the kerbals sit during the flight.   Both are learning about solar systems, planets, moons and stars in a much more fun and hands on way while playing this game.
I highly recommend this game to casual or more dedicated players who are interested in a space simulation sandbox challenge or to parents with children learning about the science of the universe, basic engineering, physics and math.

Garrys Mod is an open sandbox game, where you are allowed to do anything, depending on what you play. There are many games within Garrys mod, The most populaur being DarkRP, A gamemode where you roleplay as a normal citizen, crime stopper, or even cause crime. Garrys mod also holds lots more games, such as hide and seek, prop hunt, sandbox,  TTT (Trouble in terrorist town), jailbreak, and many more. I believe garrys mod has lots of good aspects to it, and also bad.
Pros:
-The variety of different gamemodes you are able to play.
-If you find a good server you may also be able to make some friends. ;)
-Did I mention gamemodes?
-Great game to play if you have extra time.
-Really low price (Especially on sales).
-Many players, lots of interaction, good or bad, I enjoy a bit of both because sometimes they can be funny.
-Really fun to play, lots of different servers with lots of different things, one is almost very likely to fit what you like.
-Not really much of my favorite Pro, but there are lots of fandoms, so you won't feel left out, I guess.
-Also supports lots of different other games that you can play, but roleplay, play the game having a role, an example, SCP RP, one of my most former favorite gamemodes, has a story of basically monsters that try to escape a facility where they're kept in, the guards prevent this from happening, or atleast try to. These roles can be played by players but most servers set a limit on how many people can be on one specific role.
-You are allowed to create your own servers to play with your friends, without having to buy one, but it runs off of you, so if you have lag, everyone else will lag.
-You are able to download addons which will let you have more things to play with and have fun with, but if you are hosting a server everyone joining will have to download those addons. (It auto-downloads while in the loading screen).
Cons:
-Since this game is mostly based on servers, which different people own, there can be lots of limits, which can make this less fun. Would be good if you were the type of person to like playing really slowly, however i'm not.
-Keeping that in mind there are also lots of administrators that help the server run properly by stopping rule breakers of the server, those administrators can cause lots of problems too. Such as abuse of their power, this is very common in "DarkRP".
-Not only can the people in charge or with power can cause problems to gameplay, it can also be the people. Most of the time Garrys mod isnt too friendly too people, but sometimes it can be. (I've met a bit of my friends on Garry's mod.)
-As mentioned before, players can be a problem, as trolling is very populaur. Trolling could happen with people using their microphones to play very loud music, going against the server rules and probably end up killing randomly.
-Following server rules is a MUST. If you wan't to play almost any game on Garry's mod, you MUST follow the rules. Most servers have an "MOTD" Which stands for message of the day, appear when finished loading the server, server owners and administrators expect you to follow these rules.
-Most servers have not been good to my likings so i've resorted to playing on my own server with friends.
-Lots of servers have an abundance of addons, most of those aren't even accesible unless you buy a server rank. This means your computer is going to have to have a bit of space, maybe 10 GB if you're the type of person to go on LOTS of servers. I reccomend about 2 GB for downloading servers, It's probably more than enough.
-Not many, but some servers have ingame purchases, for ingame money, ranks, or even levels, these things are good for the server but sometimes servers turn it to pay to win.
The game is great if you have space, but you need to avoid other players if you want to have a peacful experience with the game. I recommend because I've had lots of great experiences and memories with this game.

Ralph Waldo Emerson one said "life is a journey not a destination", so im going to keep this in mind while recommending this game. Im sure many of the negative reviews harp on the episode 5 ending so i wont really get into it. However, while i was upset about the binary choice i was forced upon regardless of my decisions throughout the game, I really enjoyed the storyline and the progression i made with my decisions up until that point.
Positives:
-Graphics are done well and i really enjoyed the animations and voice acting
-The open ended nature of the game and the dialogue was really well thought out and i did multilple playthroughs of chapters so i would see what different choices led to.
-The story is fantastic and very bioshock infinite-like, showcasing how time travel and fixing our mistakes could lead to bigger problems.
------
The negatives:
-some of the highschool archetypes are groan inducing, the mean girls-esque Victoria really made me groan in all of her scenes. "go ♥♥♥♥ your selfie"... really? people say that in highschool?
-some of the puzzles and gameplay seem to be used solely to pad gameplay time and make it longer, for example in episode 2: collecting the 5 bottles seems arbitrary, but that seems to be the case for most click-and-point games.
-the "ending" (though the more i think about it, the more it seems brilliant in the theme of time travel within this game)
-the whole "missing girl plot" and resolution also seems arbitrary to the games story, almost like it was a side story forced to be the main storyline
- *this may be just me and my inferior IQ ... but this is one of those games where you NEED a strategy guide. For example the dialogue trees in certain set pieces seem to be so arbitrary and random, yet required to progress to the next area. Really dampens the pace of the game when youre scratching your head to 20 minutes figuring out which minor dialogue will help in a critical piece.
Overall: Despite my gripes and complaints, I enjoyed myself and would recommend to anyone looking for a story focused game to kill time.

Below, I'd like to reflect on my time spent in this game. The following applies to current major version 0.24, vanilla game with no mods.
First up my thoughts on the game as a whole. This game is unique and interesting. You build space planes and ships and launch them into space. You control comical characters (your crew) and some pretty hilarious things can happen along the way. You learn various aspects of ship building pretty quickly on the launch pad. You understand how much fuel is required to get through Kerbin's atmosphere, how to build uniform designs, how to stage properly and efficiently, how many engines are required to lift certain loads, etc. The tutorial taught me enough to understand how to get into space and orbit. Pre-built ships exist in the hangar to use and learn from if you desire. The theme of the game is cute and the mood is certainly lighthearted.
The graphical fidelity of the game is alright and fitting for the price and scope involved. Ships are beautiful, burning in and out of the atmosphere looks pretty neat. World design, from what I have seen of it, is pretty empty. Kerbin itself (the planet you start on) is void of detail, there are mountains, snowcaps, deserts, green landscape, water, but nothing there. There is no reason to explore it, no thriving world, no plants, no trees, no species of any sort. Audio is a mixed bag. On my setup the audio skips, crackles, pops in and out, and for the most part makes me want to mute it. This is especially true when you have a stage with a lot of rockets, just a disaster on the ears when they fire up and burn in concert. Something should be done to this aspect of the game. Browsed the game forum and found complaints about the audio that are over a year old. I find myself either muting the game audio, or turning the volume WAY down so I can still try to fly my ship somewhat observantly.
One of the biggest issues with KSP building is the camera. You can never position the camera where you need it to install parts and carefully make connections. The camera appears to be stuck rotating around a fixed location in the center of the hangar. This makes building difficult. Another major issue is with message box popups that occur during the building process. When you answer the popup you end up clicking through the box and onto your ship. When you click parts of your ship they become disconnected. I cannot tell you how many times I clicked a critical part of the foundation of a ship and destroyed the entire build. This is massively frustrating, SAVE your ship designs early and OFTEN.
The building process is also oddly limited, I am always looking for a part which doesn't exist. You just cannot build space ships out horizontally, the parts available are largely to build vertically. Why can't I build a small main rocket with layers of modular horizontal rockets/boosters that branch off from this core? Then I can stage off the structure bits and rockets as I burn fuel, revealing the only important center exploration rocket? Instead, it is required to use massively flimsy joint structures and ruin the build by spamming struts. Ironically, the selected name of my crew is the Strut Co, but I avoid using struts 99% of the time. This ends up with most of my ship's designs relying on similar layouts either using those staging plates (which don't offer enough space between parts, nor big enough for big designs) or slamming rockets to other rockets with no ability to stage off.
More issues with building are involved with uniform building. The uniform building process can allow you to mirror parts to other sections of your ship. This is very handy, but it mirrors in odd ways. You are out of luck to decide which source parts to mirror to which destination parts. And where are counterweights? I always have to build a ship uniformly so it flies straight. Of course this makes sense and I understand, but sometimes I'd like to build an asymmetrical design and have counterweights to balance the ship, which could then be staged off as required. If I counter balance a pod piggy backed to a big rocket by another rocket, I cannot burn that rockets fuel as the weight would change during burn and then I'd lose balance. There is just an all around limitation of parts and ways to build different ship designs. Maybe it is my problem and I just have a big imagination, but I always think, WOW I have a great idea, and then find out it cannot be done or requires a hundred struts and joints, which destorys the physics engine and framerate. (not to mention painfully difficult to build with those camera issues)
To load up the game, build a rocket for fun, launch it into space, and have a good time, it can certainly be done with this game. This IS the game. (and basically the reason why most of this review covers building) The game is with building ships, crashing ships, and coming to compromises with your imagination. With everything considered, my typical time spent with KSP involves picking it up on the weekends, getting frustrated with the ship building, and then shelving it once again. When a new update comes out I find myself jumping back in to see if any of the issues have been addressed. At this time I cannot recommend the game. Maybe the scope is too big. I worry that it will go final version and be stuck with these starter issues. I appreciate the stuff that has been added to the game over time, at some point though it would be wise to finish foundational areas before time and money runs out.

A sandbox game, before the world knew how much they loved sandbox games.
Truly limitless possibilities, not only via spawning barrels and sending them into orbit with thrusters and trails - but through modding, multiplayer, etc.
Garry's Mod has spawned several very successful gamemodes that could easily stand on their own and be critically acclaimed. Trouble in Terrorist Town, Murder, Prophunt (Though it did not originate in GMod), Cloud16/Clockwork RP frameworks. Despite being way ahead of it's time, it's easy to make a case for Garry's Mod being the best sandbox game ever created, to date.
A wonderfully refreshing game, its not often you find ones like this. Recommend it if you enjoy either A: Physics, or B: Space Travel.

Kerbal Space Program can be an incredibly frustrating experience, but when a player succeeds at a mission, there are few better feelings of accomplishment in noncompetitive gaming.  The challenges are oftentimes not very well spelled out, and players can invest hours into this game only to discover that their efforts were in vain (for example sending a lander to another planet only to discover that its gravity is five times that of your home planet, so you need to completely revamp your approach).  While frustration abounds, it challenges the player to improve and fine tune his approach to the game.  KSP is still a work in progress, but it is a pleasure to play.
Be aware that this game can be very taxing on your system, and you will need to shut down any background programs if you're running it on an average or outdated system, like mine.

Now before you scroll down to read the next review, let me just say now I've clocked in over 200 hours of my time into this game alone. Now, Kerbal Space Program is a game like no other. It's a space sim, compiled with a comedy game. It's like Take on Mars extended their game to the entire Solar System and slammed into some comedy game I've never heard of. It's truly amazing.  It's only in Alpha and it still has as much to do as a mall, something for everyone. Now before you scroll down to read the next review, let me just say now I've clocked in over 200 hours of my time into this game alone. Now, Kerbal Space Program is a game like no other. It's a space sim, compiled with a comedy game. It's like Take on Mars extended their game to the entire Solar System and slammed into some comedy game I've never heard of. It's truly amazing.  It's only in Alpha and it still has as much to do as a mall, something for everyone. This game has single handedly taught me the basics of NASA's work like orbital mechanics and aerodynamics, and only at the cost of most of my PC's harddrive! Pretty good deal, right? Now, even though the game has enogh to do on it's own, people have still seen too less stuff in it, so they made mods. It goes from little mods that add in like 2-3 parts, to autopilot mods like MechJeb, to resource mods like Kethane or Karbonite. Point is, if you like space, want to learn more about space through gaming (yeah, take that stereotypical teachers, games can be educational!), or kill your employed Kerbals in numerous firey explosions, then this be the game for you!

Garry's Mod is a game developed by Garry Newman. The game uses textures and other stuff from a few other Source games, you can either install these games or download these textures from another website but you might get a few errors that way. The game consist of alot of custom made gamemodes, Zombies, Murder, alot of RolePlaying gamemodes and much much more!
Pros:
- The Gameplay is okay. It's basically just standard gameplay from the other Source games with a few twists here and there depending on the gamemode.
- Graphics are okay (but that doesn't really matter in these kinds of games)
- Alot of custom gamemodes that will keep you busy for a while (Murder, Zombies, Slenderman, RolePlaying etc.)
- Alot of fun to play with friends.
Cons:
- You have to own the other source games or get the textures from a third party website in order to run the game properly.
- Alot of servers use different addons, meaning you've to download alot.
Overal it's a great game and my second most played game on steam so far. It's fun to play with alone or with some friends. There are alot of different gamemodes to choose from, I'm sure that there's something for everyone! At the time of writing this review I've 250+ hours invested into this game, and I still play it from time to time. I recommend this game!

* A spoiler-free review, followed by spoilerful analysis. *
A masterful execution of a slightly overshot plot.
Although advertised as a mystery adventure revolving around a missing girl, with photography and time travel added in - this game is quite a heavy drama, enough for it to deserve a mention in the first words of this review. Themes range from poverty, drug abuse, bullying and domestic violence only to ramp up to suicide and murder, with terminal illnesses and psychiatric issues sprinkled in for flavor. With the game's excellent voice acting, decent motion capture and mostly well written dialogue, these subjects may resonate all too well with some players. The authors even went as far as to include a bunch of helpline numbers, "just in case", and that's saying a lot.
Heavy subjects aren't the only thing one might want to be warned about. The game's plot revolves heavily around photography, and - just as cooking shows will invariably make you hungry - if you have at least a tiny bit of a photographer in you, this game will make you crave a new lens, go a photo field trip, take a few walks at the "golden hour", or start obsessively looking at everyday objects in hopes of framing them in some interesting context.
Warnings aside, this game is an atmospheric marvel. A small seaside American town and boarding school is captured in an absolutely gorgeous manner. No location is bland, there are contextual odds and ends sprinkled everywhere - from mildew on ceilings and post-it notes on random household objects, through garbage lying about and random everyday items scattered every which where, to scratches, cracks, dirt, scuff marks and traces of DIY repairs. Apparently, not to make the mistake of creating a game about a subject without consulting an expert, some photography professionals were brought on board - as every screenshot begs to be captured on grainy, analog film and displayed in a gallery. Really, visually, this game is a work of art - it's not entirely photorealistic, mind you, there's a distinct hand-painted quality to it, but it does the job perfectly, together with contrasting lighting and clever camera angles. To top it all off, anyone who's ever done a bit of photography will quickly notice the game's graphics engine adds a chromatic aberration to the third-person camera, which has an unusually wide angle for a TPP game, but it perfectly enhances the visual experience. Some recent games have abused this effect, most notably Bloodborne or Alien: Isolation, for reasons unknown - Life is Strange, in turn, uses it well to enhance the photography focus (sorry, pun necessary) of the game. My only gripe is that characters' models themselves are slightly dated by today's standards, and - for example - could use animated strands of hair instead of modeled blobs, but I'm not sure it would even work with the hand-crafted style.
What makes the plastic-haired characters come to life, however, are their voiceovers, and these are simply perfect, both in casting and delivery. Nerds speak in either excited or calmly analytic speech patterns, jocks have a slightly simple vocabulary but make up for it with bravado, teachers have their "teachy" voices on, parents are caring, shady characters you immediately don't want to have anything to do with by the way they sound... It all seems obvious, but many games either overdo it and voices end up apt but cartoonish, or botch it and scrawny shopkeepers sound like fat thugs and vice versa (The Witcher 3, looking at you). Oh, and the voice acting itself! All the lines are delivered without a hitch, without a single breath taken in the wrong moment, without any "reading from the prompter"; instead, they're all acted correctly for the situation, they're whispered, shouted, growled, sobbed, cried, trembled and gasped. Even the heroine's voice when narrating "examined objects" changes from scene to scene, depending on her mood at the moment. Together with how most of the dialogue seems specifically motion-captured, with facial expressions, gestures, walking about and interacting, the conversations are simply real, almost unlike any other title I've played, well, maybe with Telltale games coming close.
Speaking of characters - they're characters. They're not default stick figures with stock heads on top. Some may seem a bit cardboard, but hey, not everyone is a secret genius with a mind-blowing agenda - some of us are just laid-back skateboarding stoners. But even the least interesting individuals have their mannerisms, quirks, a cohesive dress style, a dorm room matching their personas (or not!), enough to feel alive and not just brought out of a characters library and placed at certain coordinates. And you'll never really know who is or isn't a flat stereotype, as the game does a great job at screwing with your assumptions.
This brings us to the plot. The heroine's newly discovered superpower, enabling her to rewind a few minutes of time, results in either being able (or forced) to replay certain scenes over and over again, trying not to make any mistake - and the game's quite creative about how much you can screw up. What could have been the worst bag of plot holes is cleverly turned into a plot device.
What seems lacking, though, is a more tangible explanation for how strong Max's attachment to her old childhood friend is - despite being best friends when they were 13, they fell out of touch for a whole five years and are now young adults with not a lot in common, having grown up in completely different directions, and yet suddenly there's absolutely nothing Maxine wouldn't do for her friend. One would think they'd need at least a bit more time to reacquaint themselves with each other, more than the mere one day they get, before going into "together forever" mode.
One obvious catch when playing with rewinding time is how much it could possibly affect the world as we know it - the well known "butterfly effect". (Watch out, this is just slightly spoilerish.) The plot makes a big point of the fact that small actions may have disastrous consequences - but instead of being clever about it, and showing a nice, logical, action-and-reaction explanation of why playing with time might not be a great idea, the game invents an artificial problem that stems from a vague "unexplained scientific mystery", which the protagonist only assumes to be a side effect of her powers.
However, what puts a serious dent in the game's plot (and here come HUGE SPOILERS!) is the final decision and its meaning. The game's two endings are so disproportionate, and the "sacrifice" option is so heavily hinted at, that it's obviously the "right" choice: Chloe has to be sacrificed and there's no other way, unless we're fine with a bodycount going into hundreds. However, this is where I say "wait a minute". If the tornado is indeed a side-effect of Max's messing with the timeline, then she "sacrifices" Chloe to save everyone from… herself! From her meddling, from her sticking her nose into everyone's business like she's a superhero or something. The shadowy figures from Max's nightmares were right, then - in the end she did more harm than good. The moment she decides to stay passive, everything just ends up working itself out without any more deaths or drama. Thus, if you ever find yourself having superpowers, or any real-world equivalent thereof, the right choice is not to use them. The world will be better off without your heroism. You'll only make things worse. You'll only cause more hurt. Go sit in the dark corner of a decrepit toilet and cry, that's where you belonged all along. Well, that's a nice message, DONTͶOD, thanks a bunch, good thing you included those depression helpline numbers, they'll surely come in handy now.

This game is fun and challenging, even if you are like me and hate math or advanced trig/rocket science there is still a place for you here. For example, I'm a 24 year old college senior who is a Psychology and Poly-Sci major, and yet in my short time with KSP I've highly enjoyed learning way more about Gravity, G-forces, Properties of Mass and Volume, Propulsion types, Chemical types, Barometric Pressure, 'etc.', than I have in 20 years of academic study. Seriously, I've even learned the exact definitions and characteristics of words like 'Periapsis', 'Sub-Orbital Trajectory', 'Rocket Fuel/Oxidizer' , 'Pitch/Yaw/Roll', 'Monopropellant', and everything in between, things I've always thought wouldn't be my cup of tea, actually make the game special.  It's heavy on rewarding content that is expanding at a rapid pace. Although, to me the single drawback could be that the scope can be a little unnerving the first time you open up Sand-Box Mode and see all the different parts available so I recommend all the tutorials first, at least to the Lunar Landing section. Once you finish those the physics start to click. I've only owned it way less than a month, and you can see by my 'time played' that it's left me completely enthralled.... and left my girlfriend....very very angry! Haha. Also if you are only interested in aviation within an atmosphere: Awesome jets can be crafted piece by piece. So far in career I've been able to learn how to make custom maneuvers, reach orbit above Kerbin, land and return from Kerbin's first moon called 'Mun' and land but not return from the second moon known as 'Minmus. Each one of these things seems inconsequential, but to me and others who play they have been some of the most rewarding experiences ever in a video game. They should make a freshman level elective course for this game! Oh.. and did I mention its chucked completely full of witty humor! You have to buy this. Especially since the game is worth at least $100.00. At below $30.00 do not hesitate. If you are still hesitating watch Scott Manley's videos. Metacritic will score this game 90+ when its fully released, I've seen nothing that comes close to KSP in this genre, in fact it basically is a genre of its own. Enough of my love letter tho, just go press the 'Purchase' button above and thank me later! Mun or Bust!

- You have to own the other source games or get the textures from a third party website in order to run the game properly.

Overal it's a great game and my second most played game on steam so far. It's fun to play with alone or with some friends. There are alot of different gamemodes to choose from, I'm sure that there's something for everyone! At the time of writing this review I've 250+ hours invested into this game, and I still play it from time to time. I recommend this game!

What more do you need to know, that 520+ hours dosen't tell you.
Build, launch, then gather science.  Control your own space program.  When you get sick of the stock game parts, a ton of mods are waiting for you.  KSP is a sandbox like game, that has a career mode.  The career mode challenges you to build, launch, and fly your creations to gather science.  That science allows you to unlock more parts.  More parts, means more creations.  It is a vicious cycle of building a new vessel, gather science, land (or crash), repeat.
Squad has been updating about every month or so.  Other developers should look at KSP and Squad as a how to properly do “early access”.  Squad is up front about what state the game is in.  Almost every week a dev blog report is published on their site, giving insight as to what each developer has been working on that week.
By Squad's own admission, this game is built to be modder friendly. Mods exist to do many different things, mine-able resources, mapping, future engines, props for planes, autopilot modules, just about anything you can think of.
If you like space, and you like sandbox style open end games, this is for you.
(Written during 0.24.2 KSP Build)

I could describe this game in a lot of ways. A spacecraft simulator, a space agency tycoon, a sandbox ship builder, an educational physics game, among other things. But none of them can grasp just how vast this game truly is from the in-game universe that's already quite large, to all the things added in by mods that make the game even more worthwhile.
But one thing is for sure, it is a wonderful game that does more than it advertises and is probably worth more than how much it currently costs. It has grasped my attention and pulled on my heart strings in ways that I have never thought a game could. From the tedious engineering of building ships with as much complexity as making Sims and their houses to exploring the solar system following real world physics which affects not only how you fly but also how you eventually build when you realize that you've run out of fuel half-way through or have just happened to land(edit: crash) your first ship on the Mun.
And all that from a game that on the surface is about sending little green space frogs that tend to scream in their helmets a lot to their deaths all for the sake of science and snacks.
To put it simply, this game is the closest incarnation of love in a video game I've ever found.
There are no other games that I'm aware of that can be so fun while also teaching you about orbital mechanics.
Worth.

This game is fun and challenging, even if you are like me and hate math or advanced trig/rocket science there is still a place for you here. For example, I'm a 24 year old college senior who is a Psychology and Poly-Sci major, and yet in my short time with KSP I've highly enjoyed learning way more about Gravity, G-forces, Properties of Mass and Volume, Propulsion types, Chemical types, Barometric Pressure, 'etc.', than I have in 20 years of academic study. Seriously, I've even learned the exact definitions and characteristics of words like 'Periapsis', 'Sub-Orbital Trajectory', 'Rocket Fuel/Oxidizer' , 'Pitch/Yaw/Roll', 'Monopropellant', and everything in between, things I've always thought wouldn't be my cup of tea, actually make the game special.  It's heavy on rewarding content that is expanding at a rapid pace. Although, to me the single drawback could be that the scope can be a little unnerving the first time you open up Sand-Box Mode and see all the different parts available so I recommend all the tutorials first, at least to the Lunar Landing section. Once you finish those the physics start to click. I've only owned it way less than a month, and you can see by my 'time played' that it's left me completely enthralled.... and left my girlfriend....very very angry! Haha. Also if you are only interested in aviation within an atmosphere: Awesome jets can be crafted piece by piece. So far in career I've been able to learn how to make custom maneuvers, reach orbit above Kerbin, land and return from Kerbin's first moon called 'Mun' and land but not return from the second moon known as 'Minmus. Each one of these things seems inconsequential, but to me and others who play they have been some of the most rewarding experiences ever in a video game. They should make a freshman level elective course for this game! Oh.. and did I mention its chucked completely full of witty humor! You have to buy this. Especially since the game is worth at least $100.00. At below $30.00 do not hesitate. If you are still hesitating watch Scott Manley's videos. Metacritic will score this game 90+ when its fully released, I've seen nothing that comes close to KSP in this genre, in fact it basically is a genre of its own. Enough of my love letter tho, just go press the 'Purchase' button above and thank me later! Mun or Bust!

If your dream involves working at or running Nasa, this games for you. If you'd love to deisign aeronautical space planes and rockets, then be able to immediately test those craft around Kerbin or better yet around the solar system, this game is for you. If you like to see just how creative,   innovative, and clever you can be, this game is for you.
To me this game does not feel like an early access game and naturally feels the most complete out of any I have played (check my library, I do own a few) and at only a quarter done has almost endless gameplay. There are bugs and glitches to work out and in the entire time i've spent playing i've encountered only minor ones that have not ruined or broke gameplay, things like audio and grapic hiccups.
This is one of, if not my most, loved game. I've put 51 hours into this game over about 2 weeks (would be alot more but I work 70+ hours a week so comparatively it's a big chunk of my time) and see no signs of slowing down or the tiniest inkling becoming burnt out. I've even developed the Tetris effect(Kerbal Effect?) and while working I'll catch my self day dreaming all about it. During lunch breaks I'll propose and draft challenges while sketching designs for craft to take them head on. All while i count the seconds down to quitting time so that then I can rocket(I'm terrible, I know) home to attempt what has been on my mind all day. I haven't had a game consume my attention like this since I was a great deal younger.
The stock game has a steep learning curve and in my opinion makes successful missions all the more rewarding.

They do have mods, and mods are a big factor and fully supported in this game. Some adjust the difficulty in both directions(Better and easier ,lol, i kid. i kid). From MechJeb(An autopilot system, "just set it and forget it"), Infinite fuel(No Fun), all the way to implementing life support systems(extremely challenging RIP nameless Kerbals 6-17). There are amazing texture packs that are outta this word (Couldn't help myself), and cosmetic/aerodynamic parts(Procedural Fairings which look and work beautifully).
So if this sounds like a game you may be interested in then I highly recommend checking out the demo. It will give you a small glimpse into what this game is about and it's free, come on who can argue with that, or for that matter not just try it out.
I hope this review(though littered with bad puns and my excited rantings) helped or persuaded you to check out the demo, I mean at the very least peaked your interest enough to maybe look into the game alittle more?(Please?)

Garry's Mod is a game developed by Garry Newman. The game uses textures and other stuff from a few other Source games, you can either install these games or download these textures from another website but you might get a few errors that way. The game consist of alot of custom made gamemodes, Zombies, Murder, alot of RolePlaying gamemodes and much much more!
Pros:
- The Gameplay is okay. It's basically just standard gameplay from the other Source games with a few twists here and there depending on the gamemode.
- Graphics are okay (but that doesn't really matter in these kinds of games)
- Alot of custom gamemodes that will keep you busy for a while (Murder, Zombies, Slenderman, RolePlaying etc.)
- Alot of fun to play with friends.
Cons:
- You have to own the other source games or get the textures from a third party website in order to run the game properly.
- Alot of servers use different addons, meaning you've to download alot.
Overal it's a great game and my second most played game on steam so far. It's fun to play with alone or with some friends. There are alot of different gamemodes to choose from, I'm sure that there's something for everyone! At the time of writing this review I've 250+ hours invested into this game, and I still play it from time to time. I recommend this game!

So far I have 44 hours playing this game, and here's what I can say:
Pros:
-Includes a Sandbox and Career mode
-Sandbox mode allows you to build any spaceplane or rocket you imagine, and you can travel to any planet you'd like, which are all unique.
-Career mode is significantly harder, in the way that you have to manage science points, money and reputation to make a successful space program.
-lots of places to go, complete with many planets you can travel to, various areas in Kerbin (KSP version of Earth) to visit
-A lot of mod support!
-64-bit version included
-And much much more!
Cons: (Yes, It's early access and there's still problems but still listing them)
-Performance issues, many of them solved by the 64-bit version
-bugs, less than a handful major
-Can't think of any others!
While the game is still early access, all current problems are being worked on and will be fixed in the future.
I do enjoy the game very much and can't wait to see the upcoming major releases, including multiplayer in the future!
I highly recommend this game.

Arma 3 is a must-have game for those looking to have a realistic and immersive experience. However, this is not provided by the game itself, but by the communities that make this game bring out it's full potential.

If you are a space geek like me (former NASA contractor), or you are really interested in building spacecraft and orbital mechanics, this is the game for you.  I really enjoy the game, and even though it is still in an alpha state the game continues to improve much more.
Warnning though, this game does have something of an initial high learning curve and does require some effort to learn how to play.  This isn't a mindless FPS, where you are full action from the word go.  The claims that this is a simulation based game are very accurate.  You'll find often times a lot of time being spent performing manuvers, designing space craft, and, by all indications from the development team, much more.    Patience is very much needed with this game, and if you don't have it then it is not for you.
There are some pretty good built-in tutorials with the game that shows the basics of how do to many of the activities.  There are also other supporting sites that can give you help where needed.  I am impressed by breadth of available information for playing the game given it is still in it's infancy.
I really do it an injustice to call it still in its infancy.  This game is very playable, but there are still some pretty serious quirks.  In my experience I have not seen many problems, and I am impressed with the game support to resolve those issues. (I have no experience with the support staff having not   contacted anyone over issues I encountered).  I look forward to seeing how this game develops and becomes a production release.
This game is an excellent opportunity to turn on your inner rocket scientist.  It can be frustrating sometimes, but very rewarding when you finally figure it out.

I don't think I've ever had a video game bring me to tears. Oh Squaresoft... er... Square-Enix... always fuding the tear-jerkers. After finishing all five episodes, I have been put on the craziest emotional roller coaster a game has ever put me through. Life is Strange's characters primarily center around young college women at an art school, but don't let that put you off.
As a 29 year old father, I had some very small reservations. The game initially reminded me of how Final Fantasy X-2's target demographic was young female gamers. I was worried the game would be a little too feel-good and girly. Kudos for Square-Enix for allowing DONTNOD studios to keep the story with a strong female protaganist. If you search around, you'll see many developers did NOT want a female lead. Having a female protaganist only helped to strengthen the story.
Some might find there's too much "mumbling exposition" but the game as a complete package is just emotionally stunning.
As a musician, when I hear something musically that strikes me, I get this tingle in the back left of my head. This game constantly tapped into that feeling.
Give the game a chance, especially for the price.

This game plays like an outdated pollaroid would photograh, and reads like a cheap teenage oriented novel would read. That is to say, on both accounts, horribly.
The graphics being outdated wouldn't bother me that much if the adventure-style gameplay mechanic and artstyle were actually engaging - but they aren't. Both are lazy and streamlined and offer absolutely no captivating elements.
The narrative is weak, clichéd and the characters are as interesting as watching freshly painted walls dry. Also, the amount of "awesomesauce", "rawk on", "how lame...", *sigh* and the like elements are enough to construct a watermill that can be powered by the flow of vomit alone. The protagonist - bland pseudo-shy cliché neo-hipster #19293 Max - is the antithesis of engaging, interesting or in any way captivating of any human empathy. Adult teen girl drama is simply never interesting - and you only make it worse if you create a typical teenage unraveling into adulthood with "special power" metaphor arc. And this game does exactly that - 10/10 effort in plummeting its own weak story further down the proverbial drain.
The soundtrack, or "music", is simply terrible and droll, offering no actual contextual compass to the situation unfolding and constitutes the musical equivalent of a fart orchestra playing during a high-level corporate meeting: unintentionally funny at best, tiresome and unnecessary at worse.
All in all: an objective bust, with bland artstyle to go with bland character development, a protagonist that offers the player no compelling reason to give two sh*ts about anything going on, largely and unnecessarily overwhelmed by teenage pop linguistic and cultural references, a dry and uninteresting soundtrack, and a story arc that is equivalent to Twilight but with less vampires and more (kind of) time-travel.

Kerbal Space Program is probably the best Early Access game out there. Yes, it's even better than DayZ. It's an amazing game, and I don't even purchase simulators. If I buy a game from a genre I don't like/care less about, then you know that I knew something was up with the game. I'm not much of a Early Access guy, but this game was quite an exception.
The visuals, unfortunately, are pretty weak so far. The textures look like those from games where the textures are glitched and it's all blurry. The Kerbonauts are also not much better. However, the graphics look nice on occasion, so it's not bad everywhere. Not much to say about visuals in this game.
The gameplay is much like a simulator (which it is) where you build a ship and launch it, and with the proper ship, you can either get to the Mun and beyond, or crash and burn and possibly kill Jebediah Kerman. And if you DO kill Jeb, then I will find you and make sure that neck of yours makes a mighty fine snapping noise as you collapse to the ground. Anyway, the construction is solid and is easy to learn. Just be warned though, you will need to know the basics to physics if you want to make a decent ship. To add on to that, the pilot controls are also solid and makes the game more difficult in a good way. Why else do you think I enjoyed FTL, Super Meat Boy, Dark Souls, and all of the other throw-your-controller/keyboard-at-the-wall simulators? The only con to the gameplay is that the learning curve can be quite steep and requires lots of blood, sweat, and tears (Okay, that's a bit of an exaggeration) into the game. But, we'll get into replayability later.
The story? Well, there is absolutely no story in this game whatsoever. No trace. There's a small amount of lore, but that's it. The story to this game will NOT be counted towards KSP's final score.
The audio is decent, but the noises keep looping and it sounds repetitive and it needs lots of work. However, I love the songs a lot, so that'll boost the score quite a bit for this game.
The replayability is very, very, very, high. This is one of the few games on Steam that could easily take 1000 hours of your life, sitting on the throne alongside Team Fortress 2, Dota 2, Skyrim, and a few others. There is so much trial and error in the game that for you to actually get to the Mun, it would take you hours after hours after hours. Look at the other reviews' hours. I only have a small amount, but let's use common sense: Most of the reviews have over 1k hours logged into the game, so what does that mean? Does it have high or low replayability? That's what I thought. The reasons the game is highly replayable was explained in the Gameplay part of the review already.
In the end, Kerbal Space Program is an impressive and difficult space simulator. Despite a few flaws, this game is well worth the price and is worth buying, Early Access or not. I highly recommend the game. Why waste your time dealing with connecting into servers and getting captured by bandits all the time in DayZ when you could build a bunch of ships and then watch them all burn to the ground after failing miserably and then decide that if Jeb dies, you need to restart the launch or else I WILL FIND YOU- I mean, you will get sad. Oops.

It's an excellent simulator. Despite it's early development hiccups(lacking flight control support for one. My G940 throttle does not go to absolute zero and there are lacking some control options for sensitivity, dead zone and other things that are essential if you truly wish to pilot the craft you design). But, having said that it is both a very good flight and space simulator where the design of the craft themselves are completely dependant on your ability to design and understand center of gravity, center of thrust and center of lift dynamics. If the rocket spins out of control it's your own fault!
Lots of great mods for both beginners and those that have been educated in the field, allowing for both very complex or simple designs depending on what you desire and what you want to do. There are also historical mods to let you re-make or re-enact historical launches and missions. I myself put a moon base on the moon complete with the kerbalnaut's own moon transport, moon space craft and moon structures. And I've lost as many kerbals to pilot error as much as design flaws. It also gives you a tremendous appreciation for what NASA and the world's space programs have been able to achieve! I found myself attempting to mimick their techniques in getting craft both airborne and spaceborne with minimal weight, drag and fuel requirements.
I enjoy the game and bought it while I was flight modeling for a world war 2 flight simulator game and it helped as a relief from stress as well as enhancing more acute understanding of the fundementals and dynamics of rocket and flight designs.
Highly recommended for those that enjoy design, strategic and simulator games. Or those that wish to send hydrogen-powered spacecraft across the solar system to only have them crash land on one of the planets - usually because of a design flaw or pilot error!

My goodness. Where to begin on this game? Kerbal Space Program has a bit of a steep learning curve. I highly recommend checking out the tutorials section. That said, this is one of the most incredible games I have ever played. This game has taught me more about rocket science and orbital mechanics than any of my college-level aerospace classes. There are moments of excitement as you achieve new heights, like orbiting Kerbin (the home of the Kerbals), landing on the moon (aptly named the Mun) and landing on other planets. Then there's the moments of dread and unadulterated frustration as your rocket runs out of fuel, you discover you forgot the parachutes (again), and the all-too-familiar "Space Kraken," a glitch which not only rips apart your ship and sends it to the farthest reaches of the universe at impossible speeds, it breaks the game and requires a restart. That said, if you enjoy space, building and testing your own vehicles (not all of them spacecraft), or just straight-up exploding things, then you'll love Kerbal Space Program. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

Where do I even start with this game? What can I say to describe this game? Well I can for one say that this game is just like pandoras box. It's full of crazy stuff that you could never think of. I bought this game around 2010 or 2011. When I first played this game I was amazed at what I could do, but I didn't know how to do anything. At this time I had just made $10 when I was around 8, and I decided to buy CS source and Gmod since you could buy them both for $10. My dad kept discouraging me to buy the game, but as the rebelious soul I was I decided to buy the game anyways. When I first bought the game I was met with a menu. I had no idea what to do with this menu, and I just played around with it until I finally joined a TTT server. I had no idea what gamemode I was playing, and I just walked around uknowingly I was the Traitor. So eventually while I was walking around with people who were like 17 or 18 talking (Which I had no idea what they were saying). I eventually got killed. After that I thought the game was absolute garbage so I stopped playing it for about a month. So eventually I got back on, and I started playing around in the single player, and I created so many cool stuff.(Which I thought at my age, but now I look back and think all my old creations were lame.) After a week or two I realized that I've racked up 50 hours on the game by just playing singleplayer. I eventually got onto another server that was sandbox, and just built my own creations while getting yelled at by older players about how my creations were absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ After that I stumbled into the DarkRP community which was Ehh... barely alright in the 2010 years. Eventually I racked up around 345 hours after 2 months of playing the game. Gmod eventually decided to update, and with that update I got an error. I couldn't play any gmod with that update because of that error. I searched and searched to find a solution to that error, but I couldn't find any on youtube. So about 6 years later of not being able to play gmod on my main computer, but only being able to play on a reative's crappy laptop. I finally found a steam forum of a guy saying he knew how to fix it. I almost jumped out of my skin excited to add this guy. After about an hour of so he added me and we started talking. He helped me to fix it in about 5 minutes. I was so excited to jump back on the DarkRP servers, only to find out that the community has turned into a complete hell hole of little kids who love to see you get introuble, and other people making unfunny jokes about racism, and staff who are terrible at their job. (I've yet to find an actual server that turned out good in the end.) I still play gmod and I'm about to gain 1,000 hours on the game, but the community on the main deal is absolute aids. It's fun to mess around with friends, but don't expect to get any far without a dumbass admin banning all of you because you shot one another once. This game is really good, but the community isn't.
Basicly I give this game a 7.5/10. A very fun game, and a very CREATIVE game that leaves you to play for HOURS, but I'm racking off a few points just because of how toxic the community is, but this game is really fun and I recomend you should buy it!

I'm going to give an introduction to people who have no idea what Garry's mod is and why it's one o the most popular games available on steam. Garry's Mod isn't necessarily a game, it's a tool, it's a tool that the steam community have been able to turnaround and make into a game with servers, game modes, weapons and armour. I personally don't think Face punch are the developers of this game, they gave the community a basis to form their own game. If you get Garry's mod and nothing else, you are probably going to be confused why people like it this much. However, if u get around 10 mods off of the steam workshop, you will see why.
One of the main reasons people love Garry's Mod this much is due to the community mods, it's not the game necessarily but the mods made by the community. Garry's Mod was originally released in 2004 as a mod for Half-Life 2 and escalated in popularity when it was brought onto Steam. A game that was released in 2004 still has 1000s of players going on each day, I have tons of friends that just play Garry's Mod an nothing else on their steam profile, because of the variety this game has.
There's a sandbox mode which is what it is. You can do whatever the hell you want. You can make a zombie apocalypse happen, you can make NPCs into a happy family or you can shoot an NPC in the face. There are online servers dedicated to each of the Garry's Mod game modes so you can play multiplayer in sandbox which furthers the possibilities of what you can do. You can role-play, you can have a death match with your friends there are endless possibilities.
There's Trouble in Terrorist Town which is best to be played with at least 4 players and is not possible to be played with 1 player. There are a group of players in a server, all of them are innocent except for one (depending on how many people are in the server there can be two terrorists and there can also be one detective who can examine a corpse and determine information about him) the terrorists' goal is to kill all the innocent without being suspected and not to be killed by the innocent. The innocents' goal is to stay alive for 5 minutes and find the terrorist and kill them. I personally don't play much of TTT mainly due to neither me or my friends having a mic but if you have a group of friends with a mic, this game is perfect.
My personal favourite game mode is Prop Hunt. There are two teams, Hunters and Props. The Props are given 30 seconds to disguise themselves as props and hide in the map. After 30 seconds, the Hunters are released and they are given 4 minutes and 30 seconds to find all of the props. There's something about Prop Hunt which I find addicting. I always find achieved and feel like I outsmarted someone when I'm on either of the team. If you feel like you aren't accomplishing anything in life, give Prop Hunt a try.
Another game mode that I've spent a lot of time on is death run. There are two teams (again), the Deaths and the Runners.The runners are unleashed upon a map and their goal is to get to the end. However there are traps hidden around the map which the Deaths need to activate to prevent the Runners from reaching the end. I found this game to probably be the most frustrating out of all of the game modes as I kept on dying half the time because of my own stupidity and not because of the traps. I only recommend that you play death run if you're experienced at Garry's m=Mod as there are a few things in death run that inexperienced players won't understand how to do.
There's also Hide and Seek which is self explanatory. There are two teams, the hiders and the seekers, the hiders need to hide in the environment and the seekers have a certain amount of time to find all of the hiders. This is a bit like prop hunt but it's harder, when in prop hunt the "Hiders" could disguise themselves as props and blend in with the environment and the "seekers" had a full arsenal of weapons, in Hide and Seek, the Hiders won't be able to blend in with the environment and the Seekers don't have any weapons to kill the hiders with, they need to chase them and catch up with them. I only recommend this if you're finding Prop Hunt either boring, tedious or you're sick of winning each time as if you are still enjoying Prop Hunt there isn't much else here, it's only for the players that want a bit more of a challenge.
The next game mode is Murder. Murder is basically like TTT but harder. In Murder there are two teams, Bystanders and the Murderer. The Murderer is given a knife and they need to kill everyone with it and the bystanders are defenceless except for one of them that has a Magnum revolver. Their goal is to figure out who is the murderer and the person who has the gun needs to shoot and kill the murderer. Similar to Hide and Seek, I only recommend this to people who are getting sick of TTT or are finding it too easy as if you're enjoying TTT there won't be anything here for you.
The last game mode that I'm going to talk about is Jailbreak. This is basically like the Minecraft mod Cops and Robbers, There are two teams, the Prisoners and the Officers and one of the officers is the Warden. The prisoners' goal is to escape the prison, which will take about 10 minutes or to kill all of the officers. The officers goal is to keep the prisoners in check and stop them from leaving the prison and they win if all of the prisoners are all either dead or if they're still in the prison after the time limit has expired. This one is a breath of fresh air as this one has cooperation involve with it, it isn't necessarily every man for himself, the prisoners have to work together in order to escape the prison and the officers have to work together to keep the prisoners in check. I recommend this game mode to anyone getting GMod or anyone who has gotten it.
I've just scraped the tip of the iceberg as there are tons of other game modes in GMod I haven't talked about like, Base Wars (a game where you defend your own base) and Zombie Survival (a game where you need to survive a zombie apocalypse.) If I have not convinced you to pick up GMod then I fail at being a reviewer. Just get GMod and enjoy it for what it is along with 1000s of other players.

With Scott Manley's video tutorials, (see youtube) this game is utterly astounding. No loading screens between planets or the like, like in the olden days; just make your rocket/ship, take off, and visit other worlds!
Even though it's still in development, Kerbal is now so far progressed (as of 2.4) that it's really feeling like a fully fledged game. Indeed it wont be till the end of the research tree that you start to feel things need to be more fleshed out.
I thought i was a begginer at the intricacies of spaceflight knowledge. What little i picked up from star trek down the years and watching Nasa and the like. This game teaches you about orbital mechanics in a way i thought i would never comprehend. So much so, that once you've learned all that's necessary to land on the Mun (Kerbal's version of the Moon), and land on it for the first time, you feel an amazing satisfaction level that ive not experienced in maybe a decade or more of playing games.
Building up your spacestations, satellites, probes and colonies to make exploring the Kerbol system easier leads to a huge, never-ending scope of creativity and adventure in a way few games currently on the market can even come close to.
- If you're worried you arent brainy enough for this game. Dont be.
- If you think its a space agency accountancy and/or mangement game, you're wrong, it's about exploration and adventure.
- If you don't know what a Kerbal is, it's the little green men that are far more adventurous than the human race.
Seriously, this game is one that you will really feel you missed out on if you didn't at least try it.

This is the first time I've felt a deep rooted need to write a review for a game on Steam. I can't stress enough how
one­-dimensional and ridiculous both the plot and the characters are. Maybe for those who are not
accustomed to games that actually offer choices, they would be deceived by the butterfly icon at
the top left of the screen which reminds you that "This action will have consequences..." And yet,
the first chapter is riddled with Max's (the playable character) incessant internal dialogue
indicating the 'right' choice to make, or at other times, the only choice available to progress in the
game. What's even worse, for a game that offers little interaction with its environment and instead
focuses on the "story based" aspect, the texture and movement of the charcter models and
objects are underwhelming. From the user feedback, I was expecting a much better game than
what I received. The mountain of positive reviews must only come from adolescent acoustic guitar
players, who are more excited about inserting themselves into a teenage angst film, than playing
an entertaining video game driven by dynamic characters and interesting conflict. Considering the
first chapter is entitled "Chrysalis," I think it's entirely fitting that this game never seems to
transform into anything more than hype.

It's obvious from the popping-up of my friends' list that lots of people are playing Kerbal Space Program.  Never-the-less, I avoided it until recently because the little green Kerbals made the game appear to be a whimsical and smirking jaunt more appropriate for a fan of 'The Sims' (oh look my guy is peeing on the floor! Haha!) than for the hardened gamer whose enjoyment of games is based mostly on his level of personal annihilation while playng, like myself.
Two days later, when the tail of my robe gets caught in the castor of my computer chair, I curse and tug on it a couple of times, but decide to leave it because my launch window is about to close.  Burn!  Full prograde burn!  I'm frantically watching my liquid fuel deplete and trying to stay on target as I burn for home, my onboard computer full of data I collected from my first successful landing on Duna.  I can already imagine what technologies I might unlock with the trove of scientific knowledge I've picked up on this flight.  I collected temperature and barometric pressure readings at several altitudes in Duna's thin atmosphere, I collected surface samples from two different substrates, I have a pod full of goo reacting strangely to the radiation in space, damnit I have to get home!  My robe is still caught in the wheel and the cat is eating his food out of the can.  Anhillation level: high.
Is Kerbal Space Program a whimsical jaunt?  Yes, but is also a deep and involving sim where you are creating the story of your space program as you play.  I recently landed on the Mun (the moon) and recued a marooned Kerbal who'd crash landed there on one of my earliest missions.  I planted a flag saying "Bob Kerman was here 636 days escaped to space.  Tell Kelly Frears, Memphis TN I love her."  I've fretted over what technologies to unlock and had a blast piecing together launch vehicles and watched in horror as they broke apart during staging before breaking atmo, pounded my desk in triumph as my lander touched down after dropping my first rover on the Mun.  Career mode is the only mode I have played, collecting science and earning money completing contracts, e.g. testing a new parachute high in the atmosphere for the manufacturer, but if you are more of a creative tinkerer who needs to be unhinged, other game modes exist where you don't need to manage cash or unlock tech.
I highly recommend this game in its current state of pre-release 0.25 (i think).  It is already more of a game than most finished products.  Evey feature implemented works and adds to the experience, nothing is broken and there is loads more on the way.  I'll try to get my robe untangled by the time they release multiplayer.
