For ANYONE out there that has ever been fascinated by space, I truly recommend  Kerbal Space Program.
INTRO: KSP stars the Kerbals; plucky green space men looking to explore the solar system they live in. In KSP, you control the kerbnauts in a user progressed solar system, where you decide what they do, and where they go.
GAMEPLAY: 3 game modes allow you to pick whichever type of journey you would like to experience; full carrer mode, (which involves balancing all aspects of your space program), science mode( gather data to access new parts), and sandbox mode (all parts unlocked, unlimited pilots, full experience right away).
Personally, I play a lot of Sandbox mode, as the full experience is great for keen space-lovers. Carrer mode is usually recommended for begineer players, to ease them into the games many aspects.
All flights start out in the SPH or VAB (space plane hangar, and vehicle assembly building) where the user gets to design the perfect craft for their mission. Want a rover? No probem. Want to build a space station? You can do that. The full range of parts allows for nearly endless possibilities. After building, ships are launched on the respective launch pads, and gives full control of the craft to the user.
REALISM: While not 100% realistic, KSP still contains lots of things that are realatable to real space travel. Jet engines dont work in space (duh), and orbiting a planet takes A LOT of fuel and time. Even orbiting the earh-like planet, Kerbin, can be a hard task for beginners.
Throughout your spacey-adventures, the HUD adds to the realism; altimeters provide accurate altitude readings, while the NAVball provides incredible spherical presicion for direction. Fuel, electricity, and compressed oxygen levels are also dispayed in a drop down resource bar.
Planets and Moons in KSP provide awe-inspiring destinations for Kerbanauts. Some of the celestial bodies have real world analogies, such as the green gas giant Jool, an obvious hint to the monstrous Jupitar. These destinations allow you to set up bases, habitats, and stations around the game's solar system, the Kerbol system. Each celestial body has detailed information on its mass, diameter, orbit time, rotation time, atmosphere, and more. Included is a quirky description of each planet, and how it was discovered :p
The game has full physics on every thing, from the weight of your ship to the thickness of an atmosphere.
FLEXIBILITY: KSP's massive part count allows for extreme flexibility when designing craft. Not only can you build rockets, but design space planes, rovers, landers,boats, space stations, bases, probes, and my favourite..ASTEROID INTERCEPTORS.
With all the parts and places in the game, it's up to you where you send your kerbals. Some people prefer Moons, some people prefer the Mars analogy Duna , while others may never leave Kerbin, staying within it's atmosphere, creating polar bases and research stations.
For myself, I prefer the Jool system, a system of 5 moons orbiting the gas giant of Jool. the Innermost moon, Laythe, is almost as large as kerbin, and boasts the only atmosphere out of all the moons, making it an incredible 5-year "vacation" for your kerbals, especially with a view of Jool within the atmosphere.
Ive played over 150 hours of KSP (including  my steam logged hours, ive had an old version before I got the complete version on steam) and STILL HAVENT RUN OUT OF IDEAS. Throughout my hours, I've made  bases on the Moon, Mars, Venus( all of the respective in-game analogies), Laythe, and many others. Ive made refuelling stations, and have even intercepted a 2000+ ton asteroid at a 50 degree incination (south) before it slammed into Kerbin.
Believe me, this game is incedible for anyone out there who has ever considered rocket science as a possible career, and anyone looking for a taste at space exploration.
If someone sees you playing KSP and asks, "WTF is this, rocket science?" say, "yes, yes it is"

Basically, this game is awesome.
Cool orbital mechanics, space that actually works like space, lots of things to do. Hard to explain WHY the game is so much fun. It just feels very good to plan a complex mission, have everything go wrong, and then solve the problems that occured in some creative way.
For example, today i launched a rocket that should transport a Kerbal in a rover to the Mun, then dock again in Orbit and bring him back to Kerbin as a test for my interplanatary program. So when i got to the Mun, i noticed that i a) built the decoupler incorrectly on the main vessel so its docking port couldn't be reached, and b) Forgot to attach engines to the Lunar rover. So i decided to just let him in Munar orbit indefinitively, and send a second similar vessel with these problems fixed. Only i didn't have enough fuel on board the rover to get into Munar orbit again. Then i had a genius revelation. I could use the main vessel with the working docking port to save Jeremiah from his Munar orbit, crash the bad rocket into the Mun, and build a third unmanned rocket to save Bill who was stuck in his rover on the Mun. Luckily i didn't have to land exactly on top of him since my rover had wheels. For ANYONE out there that has ever been fascinated by space, I truly recommend  Kerbal Space Program.
INTRO: KSP stars the Kerbals; plucky green space men looking to explore the solar system they live in. In KSP, you control the kerbnauts in a user progressed solar system, where you decide what they do, and where they go.
GAMEPLAY: 3 game modes allow you to pick whichever type of journey you would like to experience; full carrer mode, (which involves balancing all aspects of your space program), science mode( gather data to access new parts), and sandbox mode (all parts unlocked, unlimited pilots, full experience right away).
Personally, I play a lot of Sandbox mode, as the full experience is great for keen space-lovers. Carrer mode is usually recommended for begineer players, to ease them into the games many aspects.
All flights start out in the SPH or VAB (space plane hangar, and vehicle assembly building) where the user gets to design the perfect craft for their mission. Want a rover? No probem. Want to build a space station? You can do that. The full range of parts allows for nearly endless possibilities. After building, ships are launched on the respective launch pads, and gives full control of the craft to the user.
REALISM: While not 100% realistic, KSP still contains lots of things that are realatable to real space travel. Jet engines dont work in space (duh), and orbiting a planet takes A LOT of fuel and time. Even orbiting the earh-like planet, Kerbin, can be a hard task for beginners.
Throughout your spacey-adventures, the HUD adds to the realism; altimeters provide accurate altitude readings, while the NAVball provides incredible spherical presicion for direction. Fuel, electricity, and compressed oxygen levels are also dispayed in a drop down resource bar.
Planets and Moons in KSP provide awe-inspiring destinations for Kerbanauts. Some of the celestial bodies have real world analogies, such as the green gas giant Jool, an obvious hint to the monstrous Jupitar. These destinations allow you to set up bases, habitats, and stations around the game's solar system, the Kerbol system. Each celestial body has detailed information on its mass, diameter, orbit time, rotation time, atmosphere, and more. Included is a quirky description of each planet, and how it was discovered :p
The game has full physics on every thing, from the weight of your ship to the thickness of an atmosphere.
FLEXIBILITY: KSP's massive part count allows for extreme flexibility when designing craft. Not only can you build rockets, but design space planes, rovers, landers,boats, space stations, bases, probes, and my favourite..ASTEROID INTERCEPTORS.
With all the parts and places in the game, it's up to you where you send your kerbals. Some people prefer Moons, some people prefer the Mars analogy Duna , while others may never leave Kerbin, staying within it's atmosphere, creating polar bases and research stations.
For myself, I prefer the Jool system, a system of 5 moons orbiting the gas giant of Jool. the Innermost moon, Laythe, is almost as large as kerbin, and boasts the only atmosphere out of all the moons, making it an incredible 5-year "vacation" for your kerbals, especially with a view of Jool within the atmosphere.
Ive played over 150 hours of KSP (including  my steam logged hours, ive had an old version before I got the complete version on steam) and STILL HAVENT RUN OUT OF IDEAS. Throughout my hours, I've made  bases on the Moon, Mars, Venus( all of the respective in-game analogies), Laythe, and many others. Ive made refuelling stations, and have even intercepted a 2000+ ton asteroid at a 50 degree incination (south) before it slammed into Kerbin.
Believe me, this game is incedible for anyone out there who has ever considered rocket science as a possible career, and anyone looking for a taste at space exploration.
If someone sees you playing KSP and asks, "WTF is this, rocket science?" say, "yes, yes it is"

To begin with, I must warn that this game is a time-stealer. I have only had it for a couple of months, and look at my playtime!
I have spent countless hours just trying to get my fancy newly designed interplanetary rocket assembled in orbit, only to realise that I had forgotten to account for the fuel needed for the return-trip, leaving my poor kerbonaut stuck in orbit around the sun. Well... Time to build another rescue-rocket...
PROS: The game in its current state could easily be classified as more or less finished, yet the newest patch out is only called 0.24. Can't wait to see what's in store in the future!
With this new version a new career mode has been added, having you manage your funds (that is litterally their name for it), reputation and science points used for further development of rocketry. You are still able to choose to play the previous career mode, where science points are the only thing to worry about, or the sandbox mode, where there is basically no limit to what you can build.
In all the hours I have played this game, I have only once, (as in: ONE TIME!), experienced a crash to desktop, despite ALT-TAB'ing out of the game quite often for instructional videos or design tips.
Adding to all this there is also a very active modding community with a lot of extra gear to play around with, although with this new version, it might take some time for some of them to fix compatibility issues.
All in all a truly well-designed experience, and despite my many hours of gameplay, I still find myself learning new things every time I play.
CONS: Since this is an early access game, there are of course some bugs (though not as many, as you would expect) the most infuriating one being the fact that time-acceleration also accelerates the physics, causing your otherwise incredibly sturdy and stable rocket to compress, spin out of control and break apart. The rule of thumb seems to be to never use time-compression when powered up in any way or entering atmospheres.
Another problem is the fact that there is no in-game tutorial explaining space planes or aerodynamics. There are however plenty of videos on youtube, particularly by Scott Manley, that explain very well all the different workings of the game elements.
Final thoughts:
I can highly recommend this game for anyone interested in trying out all kinds of ludicrous rocket designs or is intersted in learning a bit of simple rocket science. This game could easily be applied for educational purposes (and I know that some are actually doing this), since the principles of space flight used in-game are developed to mimic real life as closely as possible. So if you are interested in crafting and space, BUY THIS GAME!

I've played Kerbal since mid-alpha, and it's continued to pique my attention. I've always been a big flight simulator buff, and I always bemoaned the lack of any real space simulators on the market. The majority of them were clunky and didn't offer any real sense of space flight beyond shuttle orbit. The others out there were overly simplistic and didn't really cater to those with a real interest in space.
When I first bought KSP, I was really intimidated by its sheer complexity. So many options, so many ways to do things, and no real explaination of how to do them. That's where Kerbal Space Program's genius really lay, though. Even without playing in career mode, the game rewards experimentation and creativity. It allows the player to set their own goals by presenting a fully functional solar system and a box of toys, and tells you, "Go outside and play."
Rocket creation is immensely rewarding and the progression of being able to continue to challenge yourself never gets old. I remember the immense sense of satisfaction I felt when I was able to manage a munshot free return trajectory without the aid of mechjeb on a limited fuel supply. I've learned more about physics than I ever would have sitting in a classroom, and I really think there's value here with this game not only for entertainment, but as a learning tool for physics, aerodynamics, orbital mechanics, etc.
The game also has an incredible community and a respectable mod support. Also, there are plenty of videos to teach you specifically how to do certain things, or dicuss theory in general. I would highly recommend watching Scott Manley's videos on Youtube, as he's constantly posting KSP content that's informative and entertaining.
Spaceplane creation still eludes and frustrates me, but I find myself continuing to tinker with it.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys space and wanted to be an astronaut as a kid.

First, I love this game soo much I've even renamed my steam name after the game's chief astronaut. If that's not saying something I don't know what is! Space sims in the past have been mainly in the vain of wing comander and xwing vs tie fighter with the occasional actual space flight sim like the famed Orbiter for real hard core astronauts who enjoy the spectacle of orbital mechanics and real world physics. Orbiter has the same newtonian style physics modeling as kerbal, and in many ways more as it has re-entry effects by default and the planets are too scale unlike the Kerbol system where everything is tiny.
However with that said, I think I've put only ten hours into Orbiter and several hundred into KSP. Why is that? Well how many other space sim, or for that matter flight sim games, let you build your own craft exactly the way you want to with pre defined parts? I mean that's insane! In Flight Simulator and games like Orbiter if you want to make your own custom ship you need to break out a three dimensional modeling program like 3d Studio Max etrc, export the files, and do the animations. What about in Kerbal? Oh they give you all the parts you need, fuel tanks, command pods, engines, utilities, decouplers, etc, and just snap them togther to your liking! No need to break out 3d studio max, unless you want to make new sub components :), just use the predefined parts to build the craft of your dreams! And thankfully, if you find the stock parts too limiting, there's dozens of great parts mods like KW Rocketry, B9, Firespitter, and the list just goes on and on!
There's even an RPG aspect! As you lift off into orbit, you get to watch your Kerbonauts squrim and and scream inside their glass visored helm for mercy as they race their way into orbit, unless they happen to have the "badass" tag like a certain Jebediah Kerman! Nothing scares Jebediah, not even death.. okay maybe plummiting straight into the ground at one and half kilometers per second does but aside from that he's similing :D! I so wish Squad would actually give the stupidity and courage characteristics real meaning with some sort of character promotion system dependent on time spent on missions etc but hey the game is in constant development so who knows?
Now with that said, the game is missing things which are added by mods. Mainly re-entry effects, no clouds,  the stock areo dynamics are kind of wierd. Kerbin's atmosphere for example is all the same thickness, there's only one type of gear bay for aircraft, no female Kerbalnauts, and so and so on. All of which have unofficial fixes to them with mods to make re-entry as deadly as it is in Orbiter with Deadly Re-entry and of course Ferram Aero space to redo the areo dynamics, and lastly the Visual Ehnachment mod to add clouds into the game. And if you even want female kerbonauts, well there are texture packs for that too. I love that the modding community is so huge and vast for the game, though I think it does also at the same time make me feel that Squad, the developer, is ignoring certain improvements because mods include many of them already rather than including better areo dynamics, clouds, female kerbals, more space plane parts, re-entry heating effects, etc into the core game which is good and bad. Thankfully there are mods to add these features in. And if you want to go to war, Kerbal against Kerbal, well there' s weapons mods too :D! If you like flight sims and space sims, plus having the ability to custom design all your crafts, whether it's a plane or a rocket, this is the game for you!

Kerbal Space Program is such an amazing game for those who have done physics in the past and want a challange or for those who want to learn physics - or even just those who want to succeed by trial and error. As someone who's done plenty of maths and physics in the past I none the less ended up being too lazy to do the calculations and ended up doing things by trial and error.
After my tenth attempt and many explosions I finally managed to land on the Mun and return to Kerbin, and I can now confidently say I can manage to fly by eye to the Mun and land there every time. The sense of achievement you get from having mastered the game sufficiently to do something like that easily when once it was impossible is fantastic.
For those of you that enjoy engineering, have some patience and/or are commited enough to actually do the math (Unlike me, I'm way too lazy) This game is a must buy, even if it was double the price - And that's just at the current beta state.
And then there are the mods - want to make the game even harder/even more realistic? There's a mod for that, Want the game to do all the maths for you? There's a mod for that, Want new and fantastic space ship parts? Mod for that.
TLDR: Why haven't you bought this already?

This game holds my personal record for most hours played. It keeps drawing you back in. Even in sandbox mode you feel what it was like in the real space program, learning to build a stable ship, learning how to orbit, learning to dock, and finally standing on another world. The new career path has made this even more noticable. The physics are outstanding and are what you would expect from a advanced flight sim. The freedom to build in sandbox mode, and spending hours trying to land on the Mun, then actually pulling it off is a great feeling, even for a video game.
The only real feature missing is mission planning. There are addons and mods that help you plan your missions, but I feel that should be part of the game. You shoudl not have to speed up time and wait for Mars to be in the right position for landing. Nor should you have to create your manuevers on the fly. I think a real mission control woul be worth while. An ability to know when to launch, know when to manuever ahead of time, that would really make the sim come alive.
Other than that 10/10 for me personally. One of my favorite games to have come out in the last few years, and one that keeps finding ways to bring me back.

Due to recent update to .24 I decided to give it another go, and was excited to see that the game was much more difficult than before in the career mode. The new update has present the opportunity to worry about funding, projects and reputation. The game still gives you the chance to play in sandbox mode, or scientific mode if you don't want to worry about funds.
The developers are supportive of the community, and the community is supportive of beginners as they launch their first rockets into space. The community has made some great mods to help or slow your progress as you launch your spacecraft into orbit. The type of mods that can help is having your craft launch automatically to the planets or moons, while another that can slow you down is constantly requiring radio contact to your base of operation.
The game can run on all operating systems and now support 64bit. But don't be surprise if the game does crash on you, especially if you have a lot of parts nearby or mods installed. But don't let this discouraged you either from buying it, because the game itself is great as an educational tool or to just have fun.

Kerbal Space Program is both hilarious and horrifying, all at the same time and all without meaning to be so. The Kerbals are funny. The physics is not; it's dead serious. This is not a game for the impatient or the unprepared. I hope you've taken at least one college level physics course, if not you are going to be at a disadvantage. Additionally, you need to be willing to learn how to work the controls for your ships; I highly recommend using a joystick if you can.
The game is still very much in a pre-release state. There is a fair bit of wonky physics and weird programming choices/oversights, but it is very much a fully playable game. Overall, I'd give Kerbal Space Program a solid B. It definitely needs improvements in certain aspects, but it is also obvious that the developers have put a lot of time and energy into making the game what it is currently. Plus, at time of writing (18-07-14), a large update was just released adding in a plethora of new features (like a real career mode).

"Life is Strange" is an interactive, episodic, and adventure game developed by Dontnod Entertainment and published by Square Enix. The release date of this game was January 29, 2015, and was distributed through platforms including the PS4, Xbox, Ps3, and the PC.
I first came in contact with this game when there was a deal on Steam advertising this game by offering the first episode as free for download. Without much thought, I downloaded the game and immediately played the first episode, titled "Episode 1: Chrysalis". In this review, I will cover my general impressions of playing the first episode and my overall experience of playing through all of the other episodes and the subsequent stories, too. THERE WILL BE SPOILERS, SO IF YOU HAVE NOT PLAYED THE GAME I ADVISE YOU TO STOP READING FROM THIS POINT ONWARDS.
First of all, the entire premise of the game is so captivating for me. As someone who is drawn to the conept of time travel and the interaction between the past, present, and future when a time twisting mechanism is involved, I felt this game really hit home. In this game, you step into the life of Max Caulfield, who transfers to Blackwell Academy to pursue her dreams of photography. After a strange encounter in the bathroom that results in the shooting of her best friend Chloe (whom she has not been in contact with for five years), she realizes she has the ability to rewind time (let's be real, that's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing cool). With this power, she rewinds time and saves her best friend.
This leads to the one of many authentic strenghts of this game: the immerisve and engrossing nature presented by the protagonist and the environment. To me, I believe that the creators of "Life is Strange" placed heavy emphasis on player customization in the world presented in the game. With the freedom of choice that you can wield, I felt that I could effectively use Max as a vessel to exert my own personal values and thereby create my own reality within the game, which I thought was incredibly refreshing. Often times, in the beginning, I thought: "What would Max Caulfield do in this situation?" and followed through with what Max would have done. However, as the game progressed, I found myself questioning my own personal values, my own beliefs, and my own discretion at a subconscious level. An example to prove this fact would be the one choice you have to make in one of many alternate realities -- whether you choose to euthanize your best friend, Chloe, or not. The fact that somewhere during the game it was me who was making the decisions and not Max implies the extent to which the makers of this game attempted to personalize it to each player-base level that makes it so absorbing.
Another aspect that really shines within "Life is Strange" is the authenticity and the effect of the interactive nature of the game. Having played Quantic Dream's "Heavy Rain" as well as Telltale's "Walking Dead", "Life is Strange" does a spectacular job in tapping the interactive medium that a video game can offer. Each decision you make truly does have a consequence on the happenings within the stories, and despite the intricacy of plot and character development, the producres of this game clearly did not slack off with the narrative and follow-throughing of the tale and path you choose to take. This helps accentuate the delivery of the overall storyline.
As with all stories, the conclusion of the story is the most important, regardless whether the plot belongs to a game, a novel, a movie, or a TV show. The penultimate scene featuring Max's "nightmare vision", and the final decision making choice were definitely memorable and also extremely nerve-racking. From the choices of sacrificing Chloe or Arcadia Bay, I personally chose sacrificing Arcadia Bay for my best friend, Chloe. In the statistics screen, I discovered that the split was almost 50-50, and I think this indicates how tough of a decision the scenario presented, and the extent to which the developers of the game worked to mold the friendship between Chloe and Max.
Playing the game also sparked my interest and rekindled my knowledge on things such as chaos theory, and the question of fate. Having also played "Bioshock Infinite" (PLEASE SKIP THIS SECTION IF YOU HAVE NOT PLAYED THIS GAME), the debate between free will and fate is always a captiviating topic. While I do want to believe that each and every action we make is a conscious doing to create our own future, the narrative of "Life is Strange" made me question whether these actions are actually just a comopsite illusion of free will. Anywho, I'd like to believe that fate, to a certain degree, can be controlled by each and every one of us.
While my experience with "Life is Strange" was certainly amazing in the least, there were (as with all games) certain areas I could see which could have improved the overall experience. Having discussed with a friend who have played this game already, we mutually agreed that the voice acting, at times, did feel a little awkward and even fake. However, much of this was compensated for by the overall storyline which we believed were the main focus of the story. In addition, as a person who played this on the PC, the gameplay did feel a little clunky at times with the interaction between the objects. While frustrating at times, I ended up getting used to it and towards the final episodes it didn't seem to matter that much.
All in all, "Life is Strange" presents to us the power of what an interactive medium can offer. If you have not played games like "Bioshock Infinite", "Heavy Rain", or the very famous "The Walking Dead", I highly recommend those as they demonstrate a similar vibe but with also magnificent stories of their own. Writing this review has certainly been a pleasure and helped me reflect some of the highlights of playing the game, and I'll hope to make more on other games in the future!

I've recommended this to several friends alreadu and when I do, I have trouble describing all the great things of this game.  It has an amazing physics system.  For example, on YouTube a player, named HocGaming, had a three part series testing if he could make an artificial gravity ring in space.  When I was watching the first episode, I was doubting it would actually create any gravity, but infact, with the help of a device that measured gravity in game, it created .1+ gravity, pulling a rover to the ring as it spun.  More than that, planets are massive, the ingame representation of Earth, called Kerbin, is only about 1/10.9 of Earth, that is still fairly large for something in a video game, and they do this with all the planets, moons, and natural satellites in our solar system, and they all have gravity.  More then the physics, this game is quite realilistic in other ways, such as how the rockets work and staging.  Beyond that, I think it is just an entertaining game to play and learn, and oh do you have to learn, even for a game only a quarter of the way done.

Let’s be realistic, this game does have an acquired taste. Now that's out of the way, allow me to tell you why I love this game!
First and foremost, it's gorgeous. Seriously, even without the environmental mods it has beautiful scenery. You will launch your first ship into orbit and you will take fifteen screenshots because you love it so much. It's a beautiful game and the mods only make it better.
The ships themselves are also very interesting. I USUALLY use a planned model as a base, but once you run out of use for something you realize you have to be creative (especially in career mode). It's tough and forces you to think you side the box and make new designs. And when you reach that point and get that science, you advance and feel a rush. It's an awesome feeling!
And better yet, I love how simplicity can really be the BEST way to make your ship. I was able to make it to other planets using a basic design with relatively low tech stuff. All because of "physics"! Literally, it uses the realistic orbital physics (most of the time) for the game. You can use Kerbin's gravity to sling shot your way to another planet instead of relying on fuel. It's pretty awesome.
And even if you don't want to play it seriously, you can get mod after mod to give you weapons and armor and new parts to mess around with infinitely. Don't like just going to the Mun? BLOW IT UP! WHY NOT?
The only problem with it is that it does take a LOT of patience and you need to actually think realistically. If you launch on one side of Kerbin it'll be harder than launching on the other side of its rotation. But even if you are not in it for the actual "make a space station and be a great space program" part, oyu can use the sandbox mode and just find interesting ways of destroying ships and havin fun.
It's a great game and I highly recommend it, especially if it's on sale.

Wow...where to start with this game? By far the most impactful and poignant experience in gaming I've ever had. So charming and touching and human is this masterpiece, I barely have words to describe the feelings this game stirs up. The protagonist Max is such a human character, perfect as our eyes into her surreal world. She is like many of us in many ways, afraid of her potential yet so fiercely strong in the face of crisis.  Little moments in this game that seem insignificant really flesh out our characters, weaving them into our hearts and deepening our connection to their conflicts.
This quaint little unassuming story carries one absolute mind-♥♥♥♥ of a plot. It is intense and emotional and for the first time in these "choose how your story goes" type games, I actually felt morally challenged and convicted. I was actually physically tensed up during the climatic parts of the 4th and 5th episodes. The writers did an excellent job at building the tension of the plot in a way that did not make the climax overblown or underwhelming. Everything pays off for the player at the end and I didn't feel "cheated" by the outcome(s) of the game.
The voice acting was fantastic among the main cast. Very convincing, heartfelt performances from the voice talent really drew me in, especially Max in her most intense scenes. Major props to her voice actor for bringing heart, strength and innocence *wink wink* to a beautiful character. Chloe and Mr. Jefferson were the other two standout performances to me. I might as well mention the very moving soundtrack. Gracefully highlighting the tone and mood of the scenes and tensely unnerving in the moments it needs to be, the music adds emotional heft to a presentation that is already so visceral yet tender.
Please, please, please. If you value exceptional characters and an exceptional story in your games, this one will grip you and not let go. A true work of interactive art, this game deserves every bit of praise it's received. A picture perfect (pun intended) experience I'd rate as a 10/10.

A beautiful, very emotional game with a well-told mystery story. Its shortcomings are minor compared to its achievements, and I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who is at all interested in the genre.
In Detail:
Pros
- The story. Once it gets going - about halfway through the second episode - it never stops picking up steam, with the absolute highlight for me being the end of the fourth episode. You know what I'm talking about if you played it.
- The visuals. Compared to Telltale games and the like, Life Is Strange has very high fidelity graphics. They're still subpar compared to what is possible today, but that is offset by the gorgeous visual design. Every location is staffed by loads of unique-looking clutter, and whoever did the editing on the cutscenes clearly knows a lot more about framing/blocking/editing than the average video game artist
- The music. The game mixes a bunch of neat little indie songs into a palette that fits very well with what kinds of emotions they are trying to trigger. I'm not a musically minded person, but I still loved the soundtrack for this game enough to repeatedly listen to serveral pieces from it.
- The characters. It's kinda scary how attached some fans get to the main duo, but I'd be lying to say I can't understand them to a degree. Virtually all of them start out as cardboard cutouts you've seen a million times before - the bully, the alpha ♥♥♥♥♥, the punk rock girl, the peppy cheerleader - but because a lot of time is spent on developing them, you unveil a lot more depth in them over the course of the game. Which feels very rewarding.
- The gameplay. Games in this genre are sort of notorious for being "walking simulators", but Life Is Strange invests a lot of effort in avoiding that stamp. The central mechanic of rewinding time (whithout changing your own position, allowing you to essentially teleport) gives them the opportunity for some fun multi-dimensional puzzles. These come in all kinds of varieties and get complimented with other creative ideas. Of particular note is the big centerpiece puzzle of EP4: In this, you'll have to work with a big whiteboard and garther information from all the evidence you acquired during your private investigation, in multiple steps, and think outside the box to acquire the neccessary info. This kind of stuff needs to be way more common in video games, and Life Is Strange shows how it's done from a mechanical standpoint.
As for the bad:
- The lip-syncing. God, the lip-syncing. It's absolutely atrocious in the first three episodes and makes the bold step towards barely tolerable in the last two. I suppose it's a result of the higher-resolution textures, but the faces in Life Is Strange are way worse overall at expressing emotion than the more comicky style of Telltale. As such, all the weight of the performance rests on the mo-cap and the voice actors - who do a superb job, thus not making this short-coming the dealbreaker it could easily have become.
- The last episode is....controversial. If you are familiar with the works Life Is Strange takes inspiration from (Twin Peaks in particular), you won't be surprised at the style of the ending. Otherwise, it can be pretty jarring.

Brilliant... for anyone interested in the mechanics of space travel or who just want to mess around for ten minutes, you won't be disappointed with this game.
EDIT: The review I left above was when it was still in early access (obviously).. However, it just boggles the mind that Squad think they're able to tinker with the mechanics to the point of breaking their old system and release it as a completed game. They've butchered the update so horribly- ships that have worked well since forever have been broken time and time again by lame attempts at patches. I mean, they even manage to do this over the gap of just one version. All this is just leading to a point where old ships simply explode when placed on the pad or warped. It's quite a big achievement to move BACK from a Beta version, but Squad have done it here.
That's not even getting on to the god-awful memory leaks and crashes. I frequently get ~10 freezes in a few hours of playtime- and many other Mac users have reported the same problem. I've seen zero progress or feedback from the developers here, and am just getting beyond exasperated.
All-in-all, this would be a very good game IF it was still classed as early-access. As I said, I'm simply amazed that Squad think something like this is worth a full release- and even worth £30. Quite frankly, I wouldn't buy this game again. It's completely overpriced; especially considering it runs awfully on Macs. Big disappointment here; hopefully Squad can turn it around.
Would not recommend buying any more; this is essentially a VERY rough Early Access game and you'll likely get more frustration than fun out of it currently.
Edit 2- DO. NOT. F******. BUY. THIS. FOR. A MAC.

Kerbal Space Program is a game about adventure. No, there aren't dungeouns and XP points to gain (although science serves a bit the same function), but really it's a game about a journey across the universe- or killing little green creatures called Kerbals. Vanilla KSP on its own offers hundreds of hours of gameplay, attempting to build rockets to reach orbit, land on moons and even other planets and other planets' moons. Coupled with the enormous community of players and modders, KSP stops being a silly spaceship game, it becomes a NASA simulator, a Star Wars recreation, and even a game about silly robots. This game is more sandboxy and challenging than any Sim City or Just Cause i've ever played, because instead of a small world to build in, KSP gives you the universe.
I wish I bought KSP earlier.

Wow...where to start with this game? By far the most impactful and poignant experience in gaming I've ever had. So charming and touching and human is this masterpiece, I barely have words to describe the feelings this game stirs up. The protagonist Max is such a human character, perfect as our eyes into her surreal world. She is like many of us in many ways, afraid of her potential yet so fiercely strong in the face of crisis.  Little moments in this game that seem insignificant really flesh out our characters, weaving them into our hearts and deepening our connection to their conflicts.
This quaint little unassuming story carries one absolute mind-♥♥♥♥ of a plot. It is intense and emotional and for the first time in these "choose how your story goes" type games, I actually felt morally challenged and convicted. I was actually physically tensed up during the climatic parts of the 4th and 5th episodes. The writers did an excellent job at building the tension of the plot in a way that did not make the climax overblown or underwhelming. Everything pays off for the player at the end and I didn't feel "cheated" by the outcome(s) of the game.
The voice acting was fantastic among the main cast. Very convincing, heartfelt performances from the voice talent really drew me in, especially Max in her most intense scenes. Major props to her voice actor for bringing heart, strength and innocence *wink wink* to a beautiful character. Chloe and Mr. Jefferson were the other two standout performances to me. I might as well mention the very moving soundtrack. Gracefully highlighting the tone and mood of the scenes and tensely unnerving in the moments it needs to be, the music adds emotional heft to a presentation that is already so visceral yet tender.
Please, please, please. If you value exceptional characters and an exceptional story in your games, this one will grip you and not let go. A true work of interactive art, this game deserves every bit of praise it's received. A picture perfect (pun intended) experience I'd rate as a 10/10.

Short of a long, waxed beard; cafes where non-coffee drinks are served in jars; and black, square-rimmed glasses, Life is Strange is the epitome of hipster. The main character, Maxine, uses an old Polaroid camera; gets bullied by a short-haired girl who uses an iPhone and looks like her wardrobe came from the 70s (ironically bullied about being a hipster); and listens to some of the softest spoken, airy-fairy music I have ever heard.
Now that I’ve gotten that out of the way, Life is Strange is an interactive puzzle mystery with a very unique puzzle element. Maxine is able to rewind time and change her last decision or two. The includes any conversations, interacting with the world, and essentially anything where a conscious choice on her part can change the outcome. Maxine has the power of limited hindsight.
This puzzle mechanic ties perfectly in with the setting of late-teens, high school, the point in everyone’s life where they make the stupidest, yet most insignificant mistakes. Life is Strange is set on a northern US coastline (not sure if east or west, probably same place as Twilight as that area of the US seems to spawn teen angst) at Blackwell Academy, a typical American high school (excepting for the boarding part). Kids wear casual clothes and leave classes as soon as the bell rings, rather than being dismissed. The photography teacher really pushes his “life lessons, inspirations, sitting on tables” vibe. Girls are ♥♥♥♥♥es because they can be and Maxine is an outsider because she’s shy or something like that.
While this review is only for the first game, I plan to continue playing. I’m interested to see where it’s going and where it ends. Not to mention I want to see the consequences of my actions (which hopefully aren’t arbitrary). I might do a quick note once I’ve finished the series.
While you shouldn’t expect too much (if any) dynamic game play, Life is Strange is well-worth the price if you enjoy a highly detailed, fleshed-out interactive story … provided you can move past the teenage setting.

KSP is one of the most rewarding experiences I have ever had in my life of video gaming. Drawn by the tongue-in-cheek humor and the ability to blow up massive, grotesque "spaceships" on the launchpad in unpredictable and hilarious ways, I soon found myself cerebrally engaged by the challenge of building small, functional crafts in Career Mode. My ships rose higher and higher, and I learned many different tricks both by myself and from the KSP Wiki that plunged me into orbit, across space to the Mun, beyond to Minmus, and onward to Duna, Jool, Eve, and out to the limits of the Kerbal system. I felt indescribable joy and satisfaction when I put a vessel into orbit for the first time, got my first working satellite, and especially when I landed successfully on the Mun. (See my profile for my photo album.)
Let's compare this game to Skyrim, since that's generally well known. In Skyrim, you charge throughout a gorgeous and multi-layered world, hacking and slashing and persuading and plundering your way to immense in-game rewards. However, when you've played games as long as I have, you start getting bored with the so-called challenges that Skyrim presents. Truth is, you can plow through the entire game relatively easily once you have the mechanics figured out, and I don't know about you, but I didn't feel much of anything when I became the leader of a prominent organization (or several). I wasn't really challenged on the route to that reward, and so I didn't feel like it was much of a victory.
Not so with KSP. In this game, it doesn't matter if you play Sandbox and get all the advanced parts and advantages from the get-go. You still will only go as far as your skills allow. You have to plan, and test, and test, and plan, and you may even need a few pieces of paper to sketch rocket designs. The game rewards you with success as you further your knowledge of astrophysics, rocketry, aerospace engineering, and math. You'll end up thinking of new creations to build as you go through your day, and you'll return to KSP excited to try them out. The challenge is immensely exciting to me, and when I first landed on the Mun, I felt a sense of victory unlike anything I had ever felt in a video game. Here is this device which I designed, built, and piloted, and it's sitting on the Mun with enough fuel to get back. I can't tell you how incredible that feels; you'll just have to find out for yourself.
And then I built a ship made entirely of solid rocket boosters and shot it directly into the sun. Whatever. It's KSP.
And maybe you'll make it harder: Maybe instead of downloading a mod that calculates your Delta-V (ability to change velocity) for you, you'll pull out paper and manually calculate it yourself. Or perhaps, instead of sticking with a basic craft that works, you'll instead improve upon it just for the thrill of the challenge. After I got a working rover to the Mun, for instance, I then built one that had the capability to land itself on the Mun, refuel at a tank I dropped, and then take off and dock with my space station! A far more challenging thing to build, but so rewarding when I got it to work.
That's another point: KSP is extremely mod-friendly. Installing mods usually requires you to download a file into a folder, and that's it. There are mods that can do just about anything, from adding winches to soccer balls to colony parts. There's even one that will force your Kerbonauts to require food, water, and oxygen for an added challenge.
But if I might recommend a course of action, I would advise you to do the tutorials and the scenarios first, and then start a vanilla (no mods) Career mode. Start simple: Build ships that can fly pretty high and land safely. Deploy a Kerbonaut to take a surface sample of the launchpad (yes, you can do that. For science). Then, when you get better, make your ships go higher and feel the thrill of entering space.
Then, turn off the HUD and just admire the view. Take your Kerbonaut for a space walk. Watch the planet below, and the Mun above. Look out to the stars and admire the galactic band stretching across the sky. You made this view possible, with your ship and your piloting. Enjoy the beauty of the game as you enjoy the challenges.
If I could only play one video game for the rest of my life, I would choose Kerbal Space Program. Even though it is still in development, there is so much to do, and to learn, and to experience in this beautiful and challenging game.

Squad, the creators of Kerbal Space Program, have created a golden game for sci-fi lovers or building fanatics. There is many things to do in Kerbal Space Program that it would be impossible to list them all in a review, but possible if you have the mind for it and the time to be sticking parts to other parts in the game.
This is a game that everyone who enjoys building crazy and awesome contraptions should get. There are many different possible things to make in Kerbal Space Program with the included goal of exploring every planet, planting flags and going for a rover ride.
The game is about creating rockets, satellites and space stations but there are other things to do as well. People have created wacky machines in Kerbal Space Program that doesn't even have to go in space to do incredible things. Such as cannons, weapons and helicopters, and this is all without mods.
The modding community for Kerbal Space Program is a very active community, it may not be Steam Workshop supported but adding mods to Curse is just as good, easy to download, easy to install and all the things the mods add can just add to the insane structures people use to kill kerbals, destroy the game or travel around the galaxy.
There are a few hidden secrets through the game such as an abandoned airport on an island near the space centre, and a monolith with Squad's logo imprinted on it. These secrets can be found in many different places and I've only mentioned a few above. Go out and explore, you'll never know what you will find.
With a recent update to Kerbal Space Program, Squad added Asteroids that people can interact with in space, space exploration isn't the only thing now. Grab a hold upon a massive asteroid and pull it back to kerbin, or collect them and launch them at a space station or a bunch of lined up kerbals resembling bowling pins. There is so much to do in Kerbal Space Program, that I'm not done building what my mind holds, and I'll be damned if I stop now.
Squad has created a game that to me will be remembered forever, and it is certainly worth the money spent on it. With more patches and updates being put upon it, Kerbal Space Program is growing in size. From trips to the moon or deep space exploration it's all possible, in Kerbal Space Program.
I rate this game a 10/10. 1 rating equal to 100 kerbals killed and the size of my smile afterwards.

Short of a long, waxed beard; cafes where non-coffee drinks are served in jars; and black, square-rimmed glasses, Life is Strange is the epitome of hipster. The main character, Maxine, uses an old Polaroid camera; gets bullied by a short-haired girl who uses an iPhone and looks like her wardrobe came from the 70s (ironically bullied about being a hipster); and listens to some of the softest spoken, airy-fairy music I have ever heard.
Now that I’ve gotten that out of the way, Life is Strange is an interactive puzzle mystery with a very unique puzzle element. Maxine is able to rewind time and change her last decision or two. The includes any conversations, interacting with the world, and essentially anything where a conscious choice on her part can change the outcome. Maxine has the power of limited hindsight.
This puzzle mechanic ties perfectly in with the setting of late-teens, high school, the point in everyone’s life where they make the stupidest, yet most insignificant mistakes. Life is Strange is set on a northern US coastline (not sure if east or west, probably same place as Twilight as that area of the US seems to spawn teen angst) at Blackwell Academy, a typical American high school (excepting for the boarding part). Kids wear casual clothes and leave classes as soon as the bell rings, rather than being dismissed. The photography teacher really pushes his “life lessons, inspirations, sitting on tables” vibe. Girls are ♥♥♥♥♥es because they can be and Maxine is an outsider because she’s shy or something like that.
While this review is only for the first game, I plan to continue playing. I’m interested to see where it’s going and where it ends. Not to mention I want to see the consequences of my actions (which hopefully aren’t arbitrary). I might do a quick note once I’ve finished the series.
While you shouldn’t expect too much (if any) dynamic game play, Life is Strange is well-worth the price if you enjoy a highly detailed, fleshed-out interactive story … provided you can move past the teenage setting.

Garry's Mod is a pretty good game in my opinion. I would recommend it to any friend that likes community-based games. It is published by Valve, the same people behind many other great game series and, maybe most notably, Steam. It is a good game for it's time and still holds up today. I've logged over 200 hours in it and enjoyed them all.
I bought Garry's Mod for $10.00 USD, it's normal price. Most developers would ask for $15 or more for a game like this. When it all plays out, I'd say this game is at a good price and could only get better by being available for less or free.
The graphics are not the best, but are not terribly awful for it's time. Considering most graphics you'll see are not default, it's really not a big concern, though. But, I definitely wouldn't mind seeing the defaults remastered (I'd even pay for it).
As far as I'm concerned, the game doesn't take a lot to run. It's requirements are decently low and should be able to run on most computers, gaming or otherwise. With most big servers, though, it might be nice to have a good PC.
There isn't a lot of content and most of the content used on servers is made by the community. The creators didn't even bother with making content. Instead, they took it from the game that it was made from, Half-Life 2.
This game is almost entirely customizability, from the graphics to the gamemodes. It not only has a good amount of built-in options, but it is completely open to modding and the Steam Workshop, which is why the content and graphics are so bad.
The community based around the game is quite nice. I wouldn't consider it toxic, but more creative. Almost everything in the game is made by the players, so the community has to be a bit creative. The community has also made entire games.
It is not difficult to play. Anything that you will fight or and challenge that you will have to face, will be made by you. You can edit the health of your enemies and anything of that sort. It is very customizable as far as difficulty goes.
It is not difficult to pick up. It might take a little to get used to controls, but that's why we play PC, right? You can pick up this game and pretty much do whatever you want. It might take a few hours to get used to tool settings, though.
To master this game, I would say you would have to put in quite a few hours, not just playing, but creating for the game. Making items, models, and scripts is a big part of this game. You don't have to do it, but it is definitely a masterful thing.
I have put in over 200 hours, which says something about it's playability. You could definitely find different gamemodes you like and play this game for months. It's like a seperate game marketplace. You could easily play over a hundred hours.

This game/story gave me the fuᴄking chills.
Screw horror games, screw "lifelike graphics". This will
mess you up, and I'm not overexaggerating.
If you happen to know the Butterfly Effect movie - that was nothing.
I'm 23, I'm male, and yes I cried multiple times while I played through this game. Only a total psycho could stay cold on this.
The graphics may seem "simple", but the storytelling, the pictures, the audio, the cutscenes make this game so immersive you completely forget about it. The "movie" part about this game is outstanding. You feel with the characters, you keep getting headaches about the decisions you have to make - even if it's not real and just a game.
As said, this game's story will fuᴄk you up. You better don't play this if you're in a depressive phase or something.
And even the "simple" graphics have something artistic about them. At times, everything looks like it was painted (and the textures actually were, as you can see when you check them in detail), yet at other times the graphic effects like lighting etc. make it feel more "real". The soundtrack is superb and perfectly supports all the rest.
English isn't my native language. I usually prefer to have games and movies dubbed in my own language to better immerse in them, but the English dub is just excellent. Everything felt like it perfectly fits in, and I rarely had to resort to subs in my own language.
And for last but maybe the most important, this game will teach you something.
No, not the "don't mess with time" thing. You learn empathy. You learn to look twice and thrice before you judge people. And you learn (well, you will likely never
this in your whole life, but you can make a few steps at least) about the consequences of your actions, no matter how small or unimportant they may seem to you. If you're ready for it, and only if, it has the potential to make you a better person in real life. Just too bad the audience of this game usually already has many of their bad decisions and actions behind them already... but I'm keeping it like this: still better late than never.

This game is fantastic. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll have kerbals perish in catastrophic ways. I have at least 400 hours on it (The DRM free model allows me to have several copies all modded differently, hence on having 230 hrs on my account.)
The game stock is a great introduction to the mechanics. I highly recommend doing career mode if you're not familiar with how to build rockets as the limited part selection can help you create something that works.
After some time there is a darkness deep inside all of us that requires something a little more... insane. Queue Mods. The modding community for KSP is one of the best I have seen. Prior to patch 0.23.5, 3.75 metre parts were only available through mods and even still they have a much greater variety.
A few mods I would recommend to beginner players are:
- KW Rocketry (More Engines and fuel Tanks)
- MechJeb
- Flight Engineer
(Mods are hosted at
as of this review)
These will allow you to build bigger more insane rockets (and get them in to orbit). After that you can make the game as challenging or interesting as you like.
And remember, if it doesn't reach orbit; more boosters, and more struts.
PS: Some other mods to consider.
- Remote Tech
- Infernal Robotics
- B9 Aerospace
- Interstellar
- Near Future (a series of part mods)
- Lack Luster Labs
- Better Atmospheres
- Deadly Reentry
- Ferram Aerospace
Beyond that point you can really do whatever you like

You want to go to the Mun, then go to the Mun, you want to begin colonizing another planet, you can do that too. It won't be easy, not at all. but its entirely possible. text:
So, wondering if Kerbal Space Program is worth it? I'll answer that for you, and the answer is definitely.
Maybe it looks intimidating at first, unless you have a degree or work at something related to orbital mechanics, but boy if it isn't fun learning how to to a transfer to the Mün. Or just wondering how should you land your craft so the merry Kerbals can return safely. Or heck, starting to remember that maybe having some batteries is useful so you don't end up drifting in the endless space.
And that's just the beginning. You'll start craving for bigger and better projects. A Minmus base? A solar energy farm near the star of the system, Kerbol? All is possible. And then, you end up finding mods. Before you maybe did a launch, went to wherevere and then returned. Then, you started a fusion based energy farm to power your new engines. Maybe a Kethane base to refuel your ships on landing. Or just, packing up snacks on the ships so Jeb doesn't resort to cannibalism.
You started building pancake styled rockets, hoping that it was enough fuel for Jeb&Co to get in space and maybe, return. You'll end planning maneuvers to launch your little green friends into a planet on the edge of the system just for science and setting up a flag there.
And boy, what an adventure it'll be.

Experience an amazing and strange week through the eyes of Maxine Caulfield (Max for short)

Suddenly on a Monday, our friend Max here has a vision of a tornado destroying the small town of Arcadia Bay. After watching that vision Max gained the power of time reversing.
If you play this game, you will find out if you have emotions for other people or even for yourself !
Graphics 6/10

So Max tries to use her powers for the better good, but doing so has actually caused the tornado that's about to wipe the whole town. If you didn't get the point, this game is based around Chaos Theory. If you don't know what Chaos Theory is, pretty much, the swing of a tiny butterfly or even a fart could result to a tornado or earthquake or any type of natural disaster on another part of the world. Basically on the 1st episode when the butterfly flew in and Max took the picture, that triggered the tornado.
Max thought that she used her powers always for good, even though she only used them right but couldn't use them to their full potential when trying to save Kate Marsh from suicide from the dormitory rooftop.

In Kerbal Space Program the player is tasked with managing their own space program. This generally involves building some sort of craft capable of a specific task and/or reaching one or more bodies in the Kerbol system. It has multiple modes to cater to different playstyles, a simplistic but harsh physics system and a lot of parts for you to choose from when making your contraptions.
The characters you control, named Kerbals, are cute and most definitely insane. They are the heart and soul of the game, and they seem to like danger a whole lot more than being alive. The brilliance of Kerbal Space Program lies in the way you approach problems. You’re guaranteed to fail almost every time you launch a new craft, and while on paper that doesn’t sound that fun, the game’s revert button allows you to recover from all the launch mistakes and the quick save feature allows you to recover from fatal mistakes on your longer missions. I’d say that most of the fun even comes from your misfortunes: having to send out a second rescue party to send the first and the people originally in danger is something that never ceases to amaze.
This game is fairly easy to learn, but it will require a lot of commitment to truly grasp everything you can do in this game. While simplistic, the physics are accurate enough to provide a fair representation of ‘true’ astrophysics, and because it’s so close to real life it shouldn’t take too long to understand what is expected of you.
The scaled down solar system means you will be playing in a lot shorter sessions than you’d otherwise have to, but this game is still very long. Missions can take up to ten hours and beyond. This is most certainly not a game that you can just hop into for a bit. This does mean that this game’s value is insanely high if you’re looking for something to spend a lot of time on. There is no clear end-game, so if you enjoy the game enough you could end up playing it forever.
This game is really easy to mod. So any problems you have with it can be solved by installing more mods, and they often also add content: anything from EVA construction to colonisation to FTL drives. You name it, there’s probably a mod out there for it.
The game’s performance is good, with a few bugs here and there. None of them are gamebreaking though, and most of them are due to the engine. I’m hopeful of what Unity 5 will do for this game, but even with Unity 4 this game will run on a lot of systems. Because the game isn’t a graphical powerhouse it actually runs quite well on laptops, but the processor does need to be good to handle all the physics.
+ High value for money
+ A large amount of parts to choose from
+ Simple yet fun physics
- Long play sessions
- A few bugs
Whether you like building insane contraptions, setting up missions to places far away, or just have an unreasonable obsession with space you will find a lot to like in this game. And who knows, maybe you’ll even pick up a thing or two about how spaceflight works.

The greatest scientific achievements of the 20 and 21st centuries have been -and will be- ones carried out in the final frontier: space. Human space flight is a delicate, highly intricate, and high-stakes endeavour.
It seems as though, however, as much as human's enjoy space flight, the Kerbal's enjoy it tenfold.
Welcome to KSP, where the name of the game is learning through failure and, unlike the real world, failure is always an option. And, despite how the saying goes, if you shoot for the moon and miss, you're more likely to be in a lonely orbit around the sun. For those looking to understand rocketry and spaceflight a little better while having a tremendous amount of fun, look no further. Build your rocket, and fly it; simple as that.
However much time I've spent playing on steam, I've played it long before that; easily clocked another hundred or two aside what Steam says. It's come a ways since it was in it's alpha stage. While there are definitly some things I'd personally like to see in the base game, KSP is pretty great sans mods (though it is often suggested you try some out). The learning curve is a bit steep, but there are lots of tutorials and the community is very Dwarf Fortress-like in it's surprising civility and supportiveness.
KSP has helped me understand the universe more than before I had played it. For that, I can't help but be greatful. It opened my eyes to the importance and beauty of space exploration, and I feel as though I'm better for that.

KSP is one of those games that make you feel like you are privileged to live in the times when you can experience it and play it. It is perhaps the biggest achievement in the field of combining perfect and enjoyable gameplay with educational value. No wonder that NASA has endorsed this game really.
The game made me love physics and learn the basics of orbital mechanics and rocket science. It makes learning those things fun, because you can apply them straight away, and achieve some space exploration of your own seeing how the theory works in practice. It is also proving that given the right tool for putting it into practice, rocket science can be accessible even to a complete physics (idiot) layman like me ;)
But all science aside, this is just a fun, satisfying experience. Clever also by being emotional at the same time. The feeling like placing a foot of the most precious and cute pilot - Jebediah Kerman on a new celestial body is, in one word, awesome. Or managing to fly and land your first airplane. You will feel like a true conqueror of space, that's a promise. Building and flying rockets has never been more fun.
Possibilities for expansion of gameplay are endless thanks to the awesome modding scene and community. I recommend a playthrough of career mode without any mods to master the game, and from there you can take it in many directions using countless mods - more realism, new planets, multiplayer, weapons, hundreds of new parts and rocket types, you name it.
The game gets better and better. The Squad team is continuously working really hard to improve it (letting the community know of the progress on a weekly basis). At the moment the only downside is the limited engine. At some point, when your rockets start getting really big, there is a lot of graphical lag. But, a 64-bit client is on its way, and hopefully the engine will be improved even further.
Buy it. I consider the money paid on KSP as the best money I ever spent on a game.
P.S. There is a learning curve. Watch Scott Manley's tutorials.

The game gets better and better. The Squad team is continuously working really hard to improve it (letting the community know of the progress on a weekly basis). At the moment the only downside is the limited engine. At some point, when your rockets start getting really big, there is a lot of graphical lag. But, a 64-bit client is on its way, and hopefully the engine will be improved even further.
Buy it. I consider the money paid on KSP as the best money I ever spent on a game.
P.S. There is a learning curve. Watch Scott Manley's tutorials.

The greatest scientific achievements of the 20 and 21st centuries have been -and will be- ones carried out in the final frontier: space. Human space flight is a delicate, highly intricate, and high-stakes endeavour.
It seems as though, however, as much as human's enjoy space flight, the Kerbal's enjoy it tenfold.
Welcome to KSP, where the name of the game is learning through failure and, unlike the real world, failure is always an option. And, despite how the saying goes, if you shoot for the moon and miss, you're more likely to be in a lonely orbit around the sun. For those looking to understand rocketry and spaceflight a little better while having a tremendous amount of fun, look no further. Build your rocket, and fly it; simple as that.
However much time I've spent playing on steam, I've played it long before that; easily clocked another hundred or two aside what Steam says. It's come a ways since it was in it's alpha stage. While there are definitly some things I'd personally like to see in the base game, KSP is pretty great sans mods (though it is often suggested you try some out). The learning curve is a bit steep, but there are lots of tutorials and the community is very Dwarf Fortress-like in it's surprising civility and supportiveness.
KSP has helped me understand the universe more than before I had played it. For that, I can't help but be greatful. It opened my eyes to the importance and beauty of space exploration, and I feel as though I'm better for that.

The characters are well-written and likeable, even Max the protagonist (And I'm not usually one to warm to predefined protagonists so quickly). If I had to make any sort of criticism, it would be that there are bugs when rewinding certain actions, and that when you come out of the rewind you can't progress and have to reload your last checkpoint, and one bug where I tried to enter a new area but ended up somehow 'jumping' up into the air and walking partially through the ground in the area I should have been in. However, these bugs are very rare occurences.
The scene that really got me though was at the end of Episode 3. I won't spoil it for anyone but that scene really hit me right in the feels.
Although now since Episode 1 became free to play, I now can't get on the game at all! Hopefully they'll fix this soon but I'm still going to recommend it because it is one that must definitely be experienced.
Edit to add: The community have been very helpful and I've now got a workaround, so if you're having issues then definitely check out the community forums.

Some games have a learning curve. Others have a learning cliff.  KSP has one nice cliff.  But this isn't a bad cliff.
Within five minutes of owning the game I was laughing at disasters.  I have never played a game where disaster and failing a task is so fun that restarting isn't an issue.  I've restarted just to watch disasters over again.  Safely ejecting just to watch a spent stage kill 3 kerbals at once?  Yup.  Putting a man into orbit without a rocket? Yup.  Sending a rescue mission to rescue the rescue mission for the rescue mission for the real mission?  Yup.
Nothing in this game is easy. Death comes frequently and without much warning.  The first round trip moon mission will leave you feeling like a champion.  Pulling off your own Apollo 13 on accident will leave you feeling like a king.
I know the early access game tag requires a little bit of faith.  After spending 250 hours playing KSP, I would not feel ripped off if development stopped tomorrow.  KSP keeps getting better.  Why wait?

Kerbal Space Progarm, also known as KSP, is an amazing space exploration game. It also allows for the creation and customization of space crafts. The game starts you off at the Kerbal Space Center where you can observe space, build ships, hire crew, and fly said ships. The physics in the game also seem to be realistic and could even teach you a thing or two.
The most enjoyable part of the game in my opinion is experimenting with what works and what doesn't to build a working ship. At first it may be a bit frusturating, but once you have the basics figured out you are on to bigger and better ships. From reaching orbit for your first time, to landing on a distant planet, each one is a challenge building the perferct ship.
It doesn't stop there. Then go on from ships to build rovers used to explore the planets you land on. Also with the spaceplane hanger you can build air breathing engines for use on planets with atmospheres. The question is, how do you get them there. Thats for you to figure out.
With the recently added career mode you can perform science experiments to gain science points which are used to unlock parts for your ships. If that is not your style there is always sandbox mode. In this mode science doesn't matter and all parts are unlocked. With this game still under developement we are bound to see more added to the game.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys space, planes, and exploration. It has provided me endless hours of fun.
The ginormus amouts of exploration and customization is amazing. The game has a few bugs, but they are sure to be fixed during its development. I highly suggest playing this game. The game does have a demo which can be found at the game's website. The demo is quite a few patches behind the full game, but it gives you a good feel for the game. I recomend picking it up if you are unsure about this game.

Life is Strange is a flawed game, and yet, with all of its flaws, it still managed to get me hooked and have a really fantastic "Telltale" like experience.
What are these flaws? Well, there is two main aspects that make it flawed: the writing and the gameplay.
The writing imo can get quite cringy at time, because the developers attempted to make the teenaged characters believable by making them say slang. How they executed it makes for a bit of cringe at times.
The gameplay is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥sometimes. There is a scene where you are in a junkyard, and you have to find five glass bottles. This was really frustrating because the developers lacked to skill of making the level design guide you to the bottles, and instead, the bottles blend in with the background. This took me 30 minutes to find all of them. There is maybe four moments like this in the game.
Where this game really shines is in its story. You play as Max, a student that learned that she has the power to go back in time. It is limited by only being able to go back in time around thirty seconds and no further than that. You meet the characters and soon get into a mystery to try and find out where a student at the school has dissapeared off to. The story gets emotional at times, and makes you pick multiple choices. The choices do not affect the ending though, but I still think that the choices are effective, even when knowing this fact.
In conclusion, Life is Strange is a flawed game that has a fantastic story. You can pick this one up at full price without any worries.

If you're a rocket enthusiast, interested in spaceflight and/or the mechanics behind it or just want to throw some junk at the moon, this is the game for you.
The game utilizes real-world physics to create a remarkably accurate yet still highly accessible aerospace simulator. You don't need to calculate anything if you don't want to- you can 'eyeball' a moon landing if your really want to and look up a diagram as to how orbital transfers work. It's also a lot of fun to build hilariously excessive rockets and watch them sail out of the solar system or explode dramatically.
If you're considering this game but are daunted by the fact that it uses a few real-world rocket science mechanics, consider looking up Scott Manley's videos on youtube. He has videos on every conceivable aspect of the game, including the most basic ones. If you like what you see, buy it!

If you're a rocket enthusiast, interested in spaceflight and/or the mechanics behind it or just want to throw some junk at the moon, this is the game for you.
The game utilizes real-world physics to create a remarkably accurate yet still highly accessible aerospace simulator. You don't need to calculate anything if you don't want to- you can 'eyeball' a moon landing if your really want to and look up a diagram as to how orbital transfers work. It's also a lot of fun to build hilariously excessive rockets and watch them sail out of the solar system or explode dramatically.
If you're considering this game but are daunted by the fact that it uses a few real-world rocket science mechanics, consider looking up Scott Manley's videos on youtube. He has videos on every conceivable aspect of the game, including the most basic ones. If you like what you see, buy it!

(Still not better than the game)
What you need
•1 1/4 cups sweet biscuit crumbs
•70g butter, melted
•500g block PHILADELPHIA Cream Cheese, softened
•400g can condensed milk
•juice of 1 lemon
•1 tablespoon gelatine, dissolved in 1/4 cup boiling water
•250g punnet strawberries, roughly chopped
•1/4 cup red currant jelly
•2 teaspoons water
•sliced fresh strawberries
How to make it
•COMBINE biscuit crumbs and butter, press into base of a lined and greased 20cm spring form pan; chill.
•BEAT PHILADELPHIA until smooth. Add condensed milk and lemon juice and beat until smooth. Fold through the gelatine mixture and chopped strawberries. Pour into prepared base, chill 3 hours or until set.
•HEAT redcurrant jelly and water in the microwave for 30 seconds or until runny. Cool. Arrange sliced strawberries over the cheesecake, brush with redcurrent glaze and serve.

What can you say about a mod that has about a million servers and infinite replay value with it's own workshop and fanbase?
Well, for starters. this game has everything to offer due to its unbelieveable amount of mods and mod authors, you want to blow things up? Go download a c4 charge and plant it in a fully destructable building if your computer can handle it.
Want to watch youtube videos in a theatre? Go to a Gmod theatre server.
Want to live a life in a game? Go to a RP server.
Want to roam around a nuclear wasteland filled with zombies and bandits? Go to a dayz server or another end-of-the-world server.
Want to play sherlock holmes and find the traitor among the innocent? Or be said traitor? Find a TTT server.
My point is, you want something? there's probably a mod for that. If you have a friend that can play with you on a LAN server or just a private server, get creative in sandbox. you could make something, you could create scenarios, you could pose some ragdolls for some funny or gruesome screenshots, or even just send armies of rebels against two antlion guards. The choice is yours!
Overall, this game gets a ten out of ten from me unless you have friends, The servers can be hostile. (especially the TTT and DarkRP servers, you can get pretty paranoid in TTT )
And singleplayer is only so much fun, you really need to be creative to find fun in singleplayer.
I'm a bit on the un-creative side so give the game a try yourself, just make sure to bring a friend.
