This game is addicting to gamers who adore open world, physics/engineering games.

Imagine, if you will, a space program created by you, driven by you, and fulfilled by you. That's KSP. You throw parts together like a kid with a container full of LEGOs, sometimes with disastrous, sometimes with spectacular, sometimes with wonderful results. Want to see what happens when a plane has its rudder at the nose? You can find out. Want to see what happens when a bunch of hot burning solid rockets are placed right next to liquid fuel tanks? You can find out. Necessity is the mother of invention, and you'll need to be inventive to enjoy the game, but you could find yourself learning some things along the way too. The physics are mostly realistic, scaled down so they're more forgiving of mistakes, but the principles are mostly the same. This doesn't mean the game is hard - it just means the world works by a consistent set of principles. This makes it a lot easier than the "physics" in other games, which cheat and flub their way through physics using a cobbled-up set of exclusions and special cases to try and approximate a realistic engine.
Word of advice: If you're new to the game, start off in sandbox mode. The other modes are for when you've already learned how the world works, which you'll do by playing in sandbox for a while. Once sandbox is no longer a challenge for you, then start off a new game in career mode. You'll be a hell of a lot happier this way.

Garry's mod is an open world sandbox for those who want to make a game using the Souce engine, yet do not want to mess with Lua Coding, scripting, ect.  When I play singleplayer, I find this game a little anti-stimulating, yet however after booting up some mods from the workshop, this game becomes very fun and ecstatic.  However, the workshop has gone from fresh and exciting the cesspool that is the Five Nights at Freddy's fanbase (shots fired).  I use the game to create scenes of either a high-adrenaline chase or an epic war between two factions.
GAMEPLAY:
The game puts you in an open world, gives you some tools, and leaves you to play.  This allows the creativity in some people to shine out, which is why this game can be lost on some.  However, this isn't the end for these players.  With a massive list of servers with a list of gamemodes to choose from, you can play almost anything; whether that be disquising as a tiki girl running around a laboratory to surviving a CoD WaW-like zombie apocolapse, you have enough to play for hours.  For gameplay, I'll give a 7/10.
GRAPHICS
The graphics on this game are enough to see what  things are, yet the very visualing limiting Source Engine stops this from becoming the millenial's picasso.  Nonetheless, the graphics are good where they need to be.  For graphics, I'll give a 6/10
COMMUINITY
This is where Garry's mod takes a massive blow to the overall score at the end of this review.  I've been avoiding talking about the community in the previous entries because I knew I had to deditcate a whole section to it.  The community is pure filth.  See, in gMod, there are these things called Saves and Dupes.  Saves are things you can upload to the community, and they are copies of your world.  This means you can upload virtually. Anything.  Mlp orgy, anyone? (Yes, I'm petrified to say that that exists.)  But, the most common thing to see on the front page of the workshop is some FNaF garbage, or some Undertale litter.  In order to find a decent and useable mod, you have to have some sort of mod in mind to search, then make sure you have Dupes and Saves disabled, then click on subscribe on it.  However, this isn't all.  The online community from multiplayer servers is awful, I can tell you first-hand.  First, there are the roleplayers.  These are 9-12 year old kids who want to live in a world with rules that make living practically impossible.  They get aggrevated just for interphering with their special little bubble of a world.  You can expect kids like this in every other gamemode out there.  The community get a 1.2/10.  This was very dissapointing to see from a game like this.
The overall score for this game is a 6/10.  If you're looking for a sandbox that allows you to create virtual scenes from the source engine, then this game is for you.
Thank you so much for reading, and please reccomend this!

The only game I have ever played that, when successfully building and launching a rocket to then deploy a lander on the moon followed by an elaborate docking process once back in space led to an ambitious return to the home planet without killing any of my crewmen, gave me a TRUE sense of personal accomplishment that has rivalled real-life accomplishments.
That may sound lame to some of you who are not hardcore about gaming, while it may sound strange to you hardcore gamers who find accomplishment in successes from other games. I tell you this being a 29-year old gamer veteran of 25 long years (Tandy PC jr., TI Home Computer, Amiga, Commodore 64, and Atari 2600 for starters) who has seen many games come and go. I'm sure that Kerbal may not be a true pioneer of the sandbox sim, yet I have never met a game that has kept me riveted to my PC for as long as this one.
Kerbal can create an experience never lived for most of you who grew up wanting either to be an astronaut or a rocket scientist (or both!) and presents it in a fashion that is otherwise unattainable in any other media form. The creation process can be frustrating and unforgiving, between the thrust/mass/control coefficients and the staging management ensuring your success/demise right at the paddock, yet always gives a personal sense of enjoyment when your self-concocted combination of (loosely) held together parts engineered for home plumbing/rocketry when it finally does work out and you break that atmospheric threshold between Kerbin and space.
The graphics are solid; with a moderate gaming laptop or mediocre desktop PC, this game can still shine. The only time I have run into issues with my Ivy Bridge i7 with 670MX GPU laptop running all features @1080p is when I created a six-part space station with lighting fixtures in low orbit (125 km). This causes some choppy camera effects which can easily be resolved with lowering res or AA.
The physics are unmatched; the way each rocket adds mass with thrust, providing an unnerving sense of realism to having too much or not enough on either of these factors. This is a mechanism that other space games should take note of.
The story is unnecessary and therefore (so far) omitted. This is an exploration game with no prome directive. If Squad does finalize the game and provide any type of a campaign, it will only be a plus on an already incredible design.
The gameplay is certainly something special; you build, launch, stage, deploy, land, and dock to your heart's content! There are also some other great features Squad has done with the R&D facility and science points (it provides a heck of a challenge starting with very little to promote a scientific approach to your exploration and desire for more research). The full solar system exploration will provide countless hours of efforts to send unmanned satellites to the farthest reaches, and perhaps even manned vessels of you are REALLY amibitious.
Overall this game, as it stands, is a 10/10 even though there is still so much left for it to improve on but the foundation of what is the single greatest Early Access Game released on Steam certainly surpasses the expectations I could have ever had of it.

Garry's mod is an interesting game.  I love the creative aspect of it, how you can do whatever you what, download and/or create mods to enjoy.  I love the sandbox gamemode.  It allows you to do anything and you can spawn limitless props, npcs, and more.  However, the multiplayer option isn't my cup of tea.  Keep in mind that I have an apple computer so it wouldn't be that great, but all the multiplayer games I joined took forever to load, and when I "joined" the games I would be stuck in spectator mode.  I like how the game is simple, where you can pretty much get on and off frequently, and pick up right where you left off.  It's a casual game for casual gamers.  It's not super involved and time consuming like other games.  A couple examples would be Counter Strike Global Offensive (CSGO) and World of Warcraft (WOW).  I know that WOW isn't a steam game but it is still a good example for an involved game.  In WOW, a lot of leveling up, attaining gear, and overall making any progress is questing and/or dungeons.  In WOW, quests are tasks a player has to fulfill to attain EXP points, which are instrumental  in leveling up.  In most cases, quests tend to become part of a storyline and become more involved throughout the storyline.  However, the harder quests usually yield better gear and more EXP points.  As players move up through the 100+ levels, the quests become more and more involved.  Dungeons are a different story.  In WOW, dungeons are small areas that players go through in groups killing enemies that are stronger than enemies they would encounter in the normal world.  There are usually quests and objectives to go along with these dungeons which result in large amounts of EXP as well as strong weapons or armor upon completion.  These usually take about 30 minutes to an hour and have a lot of bang for their buck.  This is an example of how WOW is a very involved game, contrasting from Garry's Mod.  When WOW players reach the maximum level, they have the option to do raids, which are like dungeons but are longer, with more players, and a hell of a lot more redo's and screwups.  There are usually bosses the group has to defeat, and these bosses are usually painstakingly difficult to beat.  The only real reason players do raids are for epic rewards.  Bosses will typically drop 3 to 4 incredibly powerful weapons or armor pieces.  There is about a 2 in 40  chance that you get an item that is compatible for you, but it's lucrative, like gambling.  Players try to get a complete item set or weapon from a raid and it takes hours.  Even the team making process is irritatingly long, but like I said, it's lucrative.  Now the game is still great and I've had three years of it to know what i'm talking about, so don't think I'm trying to talk♥♥♥♥♥♥abou the game.  CSGO isn't much different.  The concept of CSGO is simple.  It is entirely multiplayer.  Two teams are put together in a fast matchmaking process, and the teams engage each other in combat through a number of different scenarios.  Players earn EXP from playing in matches, but the amount varies, determined by their performance.  Leaving matches before they concluse ususally results in a loss of EXP a player would have earned.  If they perform well enough, players may get rewarded with gun skins.  These "skins" do nothing other than decorate the guns they use. This is one of the ways CSGO is an involved game.  Players get involved in the game so as to perform well, level up quickly, and earn skins for performing well and/or leveling up.  Now we look at the competitive aspect of CSGO.  Competitive is a way to rank up quickly and is very rewarding.  However, competitve games are much like raids in WOW.  The matchmaking process is HELL unless you're on a team, which you need to play a lot to be on.  The games themselves last forever and their is a penalty of being banned from CSGO for a certain amount of time for leaving.  This penalty time ususally increases every time a player leaves before the match is over.  With this in mind, CSGO may not be AS involved as WOW, but it's certainly not like you can get on and off the game as you please.  This is another great example of how CSGO contrasts from Garry's Mod's casual nature.  Garry's Mod is so relaxed in comparison to WOW and CSGO.  Another thing I like about Garry's Mod is it's goofiness.  In the game you can do things like make ragdolls of other game characters float in the air.  You can freeze them into funny positions.  You can drive around a fricking chair.  You can download mods that do things like shoot fricking shrek out of a bazooka.  The limits are endless with Garry's Mod.

There are only 5 or so games, films, or TV shows that have moved me as much as this game, Life Is Strange has. It is a hard feeling to deal with. The characters feel very real. You come to know many of them, and love them almost like real friends. Then the game is over, and those characters are gone. This causes a hurt inside you. Very much like losing dear friends, because there is no continuation for these characters.
This game is VERY emotional and deals with some very dark, and unfortunately very real things in our world. If you feel for other people, and nature, and the things only humans can cause, whether they are good or bad, this game might make you feel very sad at times, because it puts these things right in your face.
I cried so many times going through this game. I'm a pretty emotional person, but I think these feelings are totally intentional, and so I think the people who made this game did a damn good job. I wish to explore that world and those characters forever, because they seem that real. But, you can't. Much like the themes in this game about how little control we all have over time and events we can't foresee, this game ends and I have to find a way to move on.
The world in this game is pretty to look at. The graphics aren't amazing, but they are done in an artistic way that reminds me of watercolors or something. The gameplay is very similar to Telltale Games style, in that it is mostly walking around areas interacting with a limited number of objects, and talking to other characters. The real point of the game is the storytelling, and they do SUCH a good job in this one, as I've been over and over here.
I would recommend that if you do play it, take it slow, take long breaks if you need them. I took almost a year break and then several week breaks in between some parts, and it is still messing with me that I can't see anything more from these characters. Only replay the game again. Which, much like replaying a moment in the game with the unique rewinding power, only allows me to see that world again, and not live in it forever.
This review isn't much of a review, I know. But I don't want to reveal much and I just wanted to put my thoughts on this game out there somehow, even just to help me get through it. Thanks for reading if you do, though, and I hope you can enjoy this game that it seems to me a lot of work and love went into. :)

What is KSP? Well, imagine a box of Lego with a detailled universe right next to it. Your goal is... actually there isn't a goal yet. You're free to do what you want. Want to send some
volunteers to Mun (some might call it moon) or do you prefer deep space missions to the last known planet in the solar system?
It's all up to you in Kerbal Space Program! You are the engineering department, you are mission control, you are responsible for success or the big explosion on the launch pad/during the launch itself.
KSP comes with two modes these days, one of them being the sandbox. Every little piece of equipment is right there when you need it. And there's the career mode where you have to do science to earn new parts for your rockets, (space) planes, rovers or satelites.
Oh and you don't have to be the science space geek to enjoy Kerbal Space Program. I've started "playing" this game blasting those little green men to smithereens. When I stumbled across some Youtube-videos I became quite more interested and now, well. There's planets and moons I've got to visit...

After playing this game twice, I feel the need to review it. So here it goes!
+ Rewind time, change your decisions. I love interactive storytelling, but this adds a whole new layer of fun to it.
+ Your decisions, for the most part, make some impact throughout the story.
+ Possible, implied lesbian relationship. Good to see games including LGBT scenarios, however it falls short and has little focus. Don't expect a romance game, that's not what this is.
+ Some characters are unique and interesting.
+ Dialogue sounds inspired and interesting.
+ Some really good twists!
+ First episode is free now. Give it a whirl!
~ Sorta buggy. Often saw characters talking without moving their lips. Game crashed once or twice through my 2 playthroughs.
~ Rewinding time can be finnicky, and sometimes it's hard to figure out what you need to do to progress, but overall this is a very minor issue.
- Terrible ending. Nothing is explained. One was obviously focused on more than the other, which pisses me off in any game with a "True Ending" in these scenarios. Especially♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off because the ending I initially picked was god-awful. I feel disrespected as a player knowing the choice was there, but the developers seem to think that my choice doesn't matter and spent 5 minutes on it just to have it there. Ugh.
- This dialogue...if you like saying "Hella", "Wowsers", "insert ____ here", and verbal acronyms, then maybe this game is for you, but...I'm not a cringey teenager, so it sorta bothered me.
- Town is oblivious to literally everything.
-
- I didn't care about most of the characters. At all. I don't remember half of the people's names, they introduced so many.
- Soundtrack is small and mostly uninteresting. Pretty much 80% indie music the creators bought to put in their game.
-
Overall: Solid game! I enjoyed my time with it. May not play it again, but I do recommend it, especially with the first episode being free. I had a few things throughout the game bother me, but the biggest thing that made me angry was the ending, which can be forgiven perhaps by a sequel that may expand on some things.

Then of course the whole story and plot is fantastic. It will surely open your eyes to what life is truely about.
So my recommendation is you get your camera ready, start taking some cool photos, for when you need them. Because to rewind time, you'll be relying heavily on past events (especially late in the game) to carry on with your journey. Finally I will say, it has an ending that will test your humanity to the extreme.
This game is not for everyone. Obviously those who like story based games will enjoy it the most, but if you are looking for a really fun and different experience, then I suggest you play this.

This game is excellent, though not for everyone. The game is challenging, and features realistic space flight and orbital mechanics. There is certainly a steep learning curve early on, but the difficulty makes the reward when you succeed that much greater. Beyond that, the game makes failure FUN! So don't think that you're going to get frustrated. If you have any interest in space flight, you will enjoy this game. The game will teach you about rocket science and the challenges of interplanetary travel.
Build crazy rocket-powered contraptions, launch them into space, travel to moons and other planets throughout the system (an analog to the solar system). What's to dislike?
Modes: there is currently a sandbox mode (all parts unlocked) and a Career mode (earn Science points by carrying out missions in order to unlock parts in the tech tree).
The state of the game as it stands is very playable. There are some bugs, but it does not hinder the gameplay. The game is early access, so new content will be added in the future.
Be warned: development is slow. However, SQUAD makes sure that each update is polished and robust before release, so the updates are worth the wait.
Modability: there are TONS of mods for this game. Mods that add parts, mods that enhance the atmospherics, mods that turn the entire system in to the Solar System and scales it up to size, and more.
TLDR: This game is loads of fun, even when your rockets are blowing up on the launchpad. Play sandbox and goof around with crazy contraptions, or play career for a fulfilling experience exploring, earning 'science' points and unlocking parts. Enjoy realistic orbital mechanics -- learn about real space flight!

After playing this game twice, I feel the need to review it. So here it goes!
+ Rewind time, change your decisions. I love interactive storytelling, but this adds a whole new layer of fun to it.
+ Your decisions, for the most part, make some impact throughout the story.
+ Possible, implied lesbian relationship. Good to see games including LGBT scenarios, however it falls short and has little focus. Don't expect a romance game, that's not what this is.
+ Some characters are unique and interesting.
+ Dialogue sounds inspired and interesting.
+ Some really good twists!
+ First episode is free now. Give it a whirl!
~ Sorta buggy. Often saw characters talking without moving their lips. Game crashed once or twice through my 2 playthroughs.
~ Rewinding time can be finnicky, and sometimes it's hard to figure out what you need to do to progress, but overall this is a very minor issue.
- Terrible ending. Nothing is explained. One was obviously focused on more than the other, which pisses me off in any game with a "True Ending" in these scenarios. Especially♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off because the ending I initially picked was god-awful. I feel disrespected as a player knowing the choice was there, but the developers seem to think that my choice doesn't matter and spent 5 minutes on it just to have it there. Ugh.
- This dialogue...if you like saying "Hella", "Wowsers", "insert ____ here", and verbal acronyms, then maybe this game is for you, but...I'm not a cringey teenager, so it sorta bothered me.
- Town is oblivious to literally everything.
-
- I didn't care about most of the characters. At all. I don't remember half of the people's names, they introduced so many.
- Soundtrack is small and mostly uninteresting. Pretty much 80% indie music the creators bought to put in their game.
-
Overall: Solid game! I enjoyed my time with it. May not play it again, but I do recommend it, especially with the first episode being free. I had a few things throughout the game bother me, but the biggest thing that made me angry was the ending, which can be forgiven perhaps by a sequel that may expand on some things.

This is possibly the best sandbox game since SimCity 2000. Props to Squad for building up the core of the game and letting us all go mad with it before they even add the "meat" of actual objectives and management aspects... although, those things will certainly only add to the depth of the experience when they do arrive.
This isn't a particularly newbie-friendly game, though I imagine the in-game tutorials and information assets will improve as time goes on. If you want to actually get anywhere, the learning curve is fairly steep, but there is a wealth of fantastic videos on Youtube that will have you flying your rockets to the Mun and beyond in no time.
Even if you have no interest in serious exploration of the Kerbals' solar system, it is a blast (often literally) to simply build ridiculous contraptions and see if you can get them to fly. Or, to deliberately crash them and make the biggest explosion possible!
TL;DR version: This game is so much fun even in its current developmental state, and it's only going to get better. Buy it!

Game overall is.. mediocre. It's a game that's obviously inspired by Telltale-games and they've attempted to implement a gameplay option to make the game more lively, but ultimately it just fails to shine in any area besides story.
The world looks weird and bland while being described as "calming" by some. I personally don't think there's anything much to it besides it looking plastic-like and incredibly off-putting. In the forest with the rain hitting the ground, it looks like wet and shiny tiles instead of ground. What..?
Animation is kind of B but still acceptable. It's fine! But what I have a problem with is that it's so obvious that the developers are trying to touch real-life issues such as gun control, weed and climate change. While I personally don't mind too much, it starts snowing while being eighty-degrees fahrenheit and Max blames it on Climate change. Really? That's not climate change, let me tell you. This certain effect is pure fantasy, not real science. Climate change would make the weather only more extreme, not.. this.
Additionally, it all gets worse as it's based on high-school drama. It's super cringy and badly made. Who in the world acts like Victoria does; gets paint and water splattered all over their expensive clothes and then while seeing Max going somewhere and coming back immediately after the incidents starts acting like the most humble person ever? Horrible.
It's an okay game. Overrated, in my opinion. I'm glad I never paid money for the first episode. The episodic system doesn't make things better either, because I might've gotten a bad taste from the first episode and first one alone, but I'm not willing to pay €20 for more high-school drama, really. Sad to say.

TL;DR: This game is extremely nerdy, fun and you can totally brute force your way through whatever crazy trial-and-error ship designs you can come up with, so don't be intimidated. Get it. 10/10
This game is deeply intriguing. If you're not careful, you might accidentally learn how to
navigate space. You don't fly at things in space, so much as you mostly speed up and slow down (at the right times) to gracefully fall between orbits. Once you start to grasp orbital mechanics and maneuvers, things can get
interesting. The first time you successfully touch down on the moon, you might just squeal a little bit with pride and satisfaction. Eurekas and epiphanies are abound in this game.
I like building things, like science rover delivery systems, that can safely return my kerbals to kerbin (after letting them drive around recklessly while collecting science data). I could use automated control modules more often, but I like the added challenge of having to build my spacecraft with the return trip in mind. I save the AI cockpits for things like satellites and probes. I play vanilla (no mods), btw.
I enjoy science mode (it's like career mode, but without worrying about funds or reputation). Sandbox mode was fun at first, but you won't learn anything about all the different parts while playing in sandbox mode. Things like scientific instruments and labs just won't do anything. That's no fun. Therefore, I highly recommend science or career mode, so that you are actually working towards something (by collecting data, transmitting it at a minimum, working hard to bring samples back, or even hauling a mobile lab out there to do research in the field).
At one point, I was building landers designed to fall onto their sides, turning them into rovers that snapped together to form big modular labs (delivered in pieces). That was fun. After that, I got into airplanes and other things that use the runway.
Currently, my setup is a cluster of rockets that deliver a lander, with a mobile lab and a rugged detachable rover, to any celestial body. Once undocked, the lander can descend to the surface, detach the rover, do tons of science across multiple nearby biomes, and then bring my kerbals safely back to the mother ship afterwards (which has enough fuel to get them home).
The rover has wheels on both sides, so it's basically indestructible. It has two seats and all the measuring devices. If you bring a scientist, you can remove data manually, reset modules (like mystery goo) and therefore visit multiple biomes to collect data (without making multiple trips with multiple landers). My rover also has ion engines and generators, so technically it can fly (on low gravity celestial bodies, like moons). The engines are nice when you can't get traction for the tires.
The idea with my detachable/re-attachable lander is that I don't want to land my entire craft on a planet or moon when I could instead leave most of my mass in orbit. This is because the fuel for the return flight is heavy and would cost me
of additional fuel, if I were to bring it along for the landing. Instead, I take a smaller craft down to the surface and then rejoin with the main craft later (after leaving the surface) to get home afterwards. I like to do a rendezvous where my scientist and engineer dock the remaining parts of the lander with the main cluster (which is controlled by my pilot). After that, they all head home leaving behind any excess mass or components.
That setup is also beneficial because the ship I leave in orbit houses a relay antenna that often provides my lander with the only available signal that I can use to send data back. For example, if you land on the dark side of the moon (because it's in a synchronous rotation with kerbin), you'll never get line of sight, without something to bounce the signal off of.
You can customize your craft for every destination (and your lander could easily be the entire return craft, for simplicity). If you want to get fancy, you could calculate exactly what you'll need based on your mass, thrust and fuel requirements. You can also use mods for shortcuts or handy readouts.

As of - 22/7/2016, this game's Episode 1 goes free.
If you see the reviews overall as Overwhelmingly Positive - it's right. The game is THAT good.
Life is Strange (LiS) is split into five episodes, this style is very strikingly similar to The Walking Dead series. After each episodes you'll see choices you've made and overall players' aggregated scores. Heck, even the gameplay is the same, plus LiS' time rewind feature - which doesn't exist in The Walking Dead. Throughout the game, you only control Max in third person view, solving some simple puzzles, collecting pictures, and taking advantage of her accidentally gained time rewind power. Apart of some quick QTEs, there's no action involved. You may need help for getting all pictures, though, as some are well hidden. Optional but if you want  to get all achievements this is necessary.
Story, this is where LiS shines most. The game starts very slow, at least in the first two episodes. It's getting darker in nature as you progress and discover Max's mysterious power background. Throughout the game you again and again feel yourself questioned of the choices you pick, whether it's right or wrong, whether it's really our self-conscious decision or just our whim. The fact that we can rewind the time only causes us to question ourselves more. The game really teaches us many things, from strong friendship, family bond, honesty to deceit and lies, many of which dangerously try to poke into our own inner self. In my opinion this is what makes the game appeals for many, aside of it being casual that attracts wide type of players.
And of course voice acting is so incredible. The actress for Max and Chloe, in particular, really did outstanding jobs in making these characters feel so life-like. Too bad stiff graphic animation is rather bad so sometimes the lip sync doesn't feel right.
Well, that voice acting enhanced by amazing soundtracks. Really really amazing, I can listen to Morali's Golden Hour all day long (it's Main Menu music).
The game, although it is marketed as 'choices matter', only has two endings, depending on what particular choice you pick at (almost) the end of the game. You can always use your previous saves so you don't have to replay from the start. This is where LiS falls short, but I can't explain further as there's obviously spoiler involved.
The quality standard of the game, technical wise, is up to par. It has Steam Cloud, proper controller support, Achievements and Trading Cards. Cards can't be unlocked if you have only free version, though. Playing with controller is recommended, but using KB/M is also alright. Game performance is fine, it is not that demanding, and can run with stable FPS on my laptop.
With its Episode 1 coming along free, there's no reason for you not to try this great game.
9/10 - because choices don't matter, and the other poorly made ending. Had it been, it would have received an even higher score from me.

I absolutely LOVE this game.  I definitely recommend it if you love space/space exploration as much as I do.  The physics aren't exactly 'real world' but for a simulator they are phenomenal.  If you're a trial and error kind of person, you'll enjoy it.  If you're a patient person, you'll enjoy it.  If you're a person able to learn things, you'll enjoy it.
There really aren't any full tutorials in game, but the kerbal wiki is rich with material.  It's still early access, but for an early access game it's definitely blown me away.  You start off at a space center on an earth-like planet 'Kerbin.'  You can then either build a rocket from scratch or load a pre-made one; I recommend the latter just to get a feel for the game.  Once you know what you're doing, you can pretty much decide what you're doing from there.
They've added a career mode recently, and I think it holds some promise.  So far you perform launches with a limited amount of parts for your rockets and conduct experiments at different altitudes and locations.  Those experiments will get you 'science points' which are spent to research a new technology on a tech-tree.  The said techonology will unlock more parts for your ship to further your launches which in turn further your experiments.  More points, more parts, more research.  It goes on.  Career mode is still in development so I expect a lot more from it in the future.

Neat visuals, a good base idea to build a story on.. but that's where the problems started for me.
This game wants you to feel like everything you do has an impact on the world, and that everything has consequences on events later, big or small.
Like I said, it want's you to "feel" like you're actually changing a lot, but it's basically a linear storyline that splits up at the end. Some people love this game and see it as a masterpiece. Others, like me, see through the smoke and mirror stuff instantly and get insanely annoyed by all the "illusion of choice" stuff. I understand that you can't have a million outcomes in a game, that would be way too hard to make and might not even add that much to the game's feel. But basically not letting me do stuff that I thought made sense, or letting me ignore stuff that I find completely uninteresting get's on my nerves.
Not even mentioning the cringeworthy "teen kids" jokes thrown in. I might be a European kid, but I hope that nobody has ever said "Go ♥♥♥♥ your selfie" outside of this game. These things kept pulling me out of my immersion, the completely over-the-top use of "memes" and "pop-culture" references made me instantly cry a little because this game could've been a great visual novel like the game "Dear Esther" only that this is neither a game, neither a novel. It's a novel trying to pretend like you have a lot of choices and sort of acting like a game. But it's too linear and scripted for me to be called a game.
Buy it if you're really into doing nothing except reading a ton of things that vaguely add up to a story. Buy it if you enjoy hearing people say "Are you cereal?" and people texting you "BTW THANX BUT WERE NOT FRIENDS."
For me this is steam sale material, but only when all episodes are under 10$.

Buy this game right now, and hope they make more like this.

“Why the hell didn’t I play this earlier?”
Life is Strange is definitely a video game everyone must at least try and experience for themselves. It has a great gameplay, amazing story & characters, and memorable soundtrack. Worth every penny!
I got the first episode of this game from the Square Enix Humble Bundle, and didn’t immediately play it. It wasn’t until around the time for the 2016 summer sale, I finally got to install and played this game. And after finishing the first episode in one sitting, the first thing I thought was, “Why the hell didn’t I play this earlier?”  I knew I have to buy all the remaining episodes, which I did immediately. A lot of people said that the first episode is probably the weakest out of the rest, but it certainly got me hooked instantly.
Life is Strange is a story-rich episodic game, where you get to control Max Caulfield, a high school senior who just returned to her hometown of Arcadia Bay, to enroll at the Blackwell Academy to study her long life passion, photography. Max is a shy and quiet girl, but also very caring towards people and what’s happening around her. One day, she discovered that she has the power to turn back time when she saw her best friend, Chloe Price, get shot at the school’s bathroom.
Much like other story based choice and consequence games, you take control of the main character, in this case Max, as she embarks in Arcadia Bay, make speeches decisions for her and also big decisions which can alter the way the story progress. And you can also explore small segments of maps to interact with objects and other characters. What makes Life is Strange has a unique gameplay is Max’s ability to turn back time. Whilst other games make you live by or regret the decisions you make in game, Life is Strange strongly suggest you to turn back time and try other choices. But there is no correct decision, thanks to Max’s indecisive mind, and it certainly makes it harder to choose.
This is the main strength of the game. Life is Strange is a story full with emotion. Sometimes it’ll make you laugh, but most of the times it’ll make you cry. After finishing the last episode, I was left genuinely sad and emotionally drained, which is the first time a video game can make me feel this way. Even after weeks of finishing this game, the story still floats in my mind. Props to Dontnod Entertainment.
I love the story so much. As I said before, the first episode got me hooked instantly although a lot of people said that the first episode is the weakest one because it’s filled with high school teenage drama, but I’m a sucker for this kind of story. The episodic nature of this game feels really good, like you are genuinely watching a good TV series. And the way they present the intro and the ending of each episode is great. A lot of people also commented that they didn’t like the last episode, which also kinda not what I was expecting, but I certainly still enjoyed it and it still makes it a great storytelling in my opinion.
I love the characters too. They are very detailed. I got really attached to them, especially Max because you get to know everything she’s thinking and feeling every time you interact with objects and other characters, and I especially love that you can read through Max’s diary. Every character has their own unique personality, which certainly helps with the great voice acting, which I think is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a video game. Every line feels genuine. Every interaction feels meaningful.
One of the best, if not the best soundtrack in a video game in my opinion. Dontnod really did their research for this one. It suits the game’s vibe and story perfectly. The songs really put you to feel in the moment of each scene of the game. The timing of these songs are also great, which makes the scenes stronger and definitely gave me goosebumps. And after weeks finishing the game, I still listen to the soundtrack regularly, and each song instantly takes you back to Arcadia Bay and its people.
What a journey it is to play Life is Strange. Great gameplay, amazing story & characters, and memorable soundtrack. I’m thankful to have experienced it. It is definitely high on the list of top games I’ve played, and will recommend it to everyone who just generally love a great story or want to experience something unique in gaming. Please try this game guys! :)

I can't say that I have ever played a more moving game- even though I can't tell you how it's moved me. I guess I could say that it's made me think about the decisions I make in life. How do they affect others? What consequences do they have? What do they lead to?
We've all felt different after seeing the movies we consider to be our favorites. And this game is no exception. The main character, Max, is a teenage girl who comes back to her hometown, 5 years after leaving to go to a highschool where she hopes to develop her dream of being a professional photographer into reality. What she doesn't hope for (or know, for that matter) is that she will soon become in control of time, allowing her to rewind time, to a relatively short degree. Long story short, this is the biggest plot device within the game and the story develops around it. And wow, what a story. (possibly somewhat spoilery)The story of Life is Strange seems to borrow from several sources within popular culture, including The Butterfly Effect, Twin Peaks, The Girl with the Dragon tattoo, and a little bit of Groundhog Day. And it does it well. Playing through all 5 episodes, i was able to feel the influence of all of them. But more importantly, I felt emotionally attached to every character, as if the game as a whole was some sort of 15 hour super movie. Every emotion is there, from happy, to angry, to sad, to devasted. But the most common and terrifying feeling in the game is indecision. Yes, you can always travel back in time, but it only goes so far. Progressing in the game means making a choice and sticking with it, and you WILL regret some of your choices. Yes, you could always restart the game, but you quickly get so emotionally invested in the characters that it's can almost be guaranteed you won't. I promise, this game will speak to you in some way, and that, plus the ~15 hours you get of amazing graphics, storytelling and voice acting, not to mention decisions, is well worth the 20 dollar price tag for all 5 episodes.

Kerbal Space Program isn't a game everyone can enjoy. But if you're the type of person who CAN enjoy it, you're in for one hell of a ride.
When I bought the game, I didn't enjoy it at first. I was extremely confused by all the parts and options and I couldn't even seem to get a 3 part ship right. So i quit for a few months, played other games, and then I came back. It seemed so different from the first time I played it. I did a little bit of research and soon I was designing orbital ships, sending Kerbals up into space and even landing on the Mun. Now I've put nearly 500 hours into this game and I haven't even delved into mods. And the modding comunity is strong with this game, oh yes it is. Tons and tons of new stuff to do can be gained trough mods.
To some, this game may seem hard, but it's really not. You need to calculate things like DeltaV, acceleration and thrust, but you can completely ignore aerodynamics, making the game a whole lot easier. And if you start simple and build up, insted of making a 200 part ship for your first mission, things aren't hard to understand. Add in some utility mods and you'll see just how easy this game can be.
This game makes you feel proud of yourself, as you send little green men to walk on a tiny moon, millions of Kilometers away from home, you can say that it was you who came up with a ship that could fly all the way over there, and maybe even come back. It was YOUR ship that flew back from Eve's extremely thick atmosphere, defying all odds, and it was YOU who came up with the new staging method, in order to be able to make it into space alive.
All I can say is that I would reccomend it to anyone that enjoys space, and that whoevers reading this needs to buy it. Get it at normal price, get it on sale, it doesn't matter, its a great deal either way.

Kerbal Space Program is all about, well, your own space program.
It is an increadibly fun game. If building impossible space crafts, shooting them into space and killing innocent Kerbals is your thing, I can definitely recommend this game.
The base game lacks some performance here and some features there. However, the latter can easily be fixed by installing mods which add a lot to the game - not only parts but also actual game play mechanics.
The graphics are *fine* for this sort of game. Don't expect AAA-like super realistic textures, though.
As mentioned before, KSP does have some slight performance issues. Don't get me wrong here, the frame rate is definitely at an acceptable level. However, the more crafts you have near you in space the longer physics calculations seem to take which will lead to some degree of lag eventually. Talking about physics, *do not expect super-realistic physics*. KSP is based on Unity which is a great engine for casual-ish games but its physics simulation sucks. I think I read an article stating that Squad had to heavily modify Unity's physics engine in order to make KSP possible. - From my observations: orbital physics seem totally fine but your creation tends to start wobbling without reason from time to time.

Life is Strange is an episodic game that focuses on you making decissions that can affect the game later on. What makes Life is Strange so special, is your character's ability to control time, and being able to change what happened in the past. You play as an 18 year old girl named Maxine Caulfield, who has recently started attending Blackwell Academy in a town called Arcadia Bay, where she grew up. She is also a lover of photography, and throughout the game you are able to pictures of certain things, giving you an achievement for each one.
At the beginning of the game you witness a vision of the future of Arcadia Bay being wiped out by a tornado. You wake up to find yourself in class. Not long after this you discover your ability to control time, as you save your best friend, Chloe, which you haven't seen in five years from being shot. The game then points you towards a missing person named Rachel Amber, which was friends with Chloe during the 5 years of Max being away. You team up with Chloe, using your powers, to find Rachel Amber.
The gameplay is a lot similar to TellTale games. There are instances where you control your character, but most of the game is in cutscenes and decission making. There are times where you rely on your ability to control time. For example, there are instances where you may have to rewind time to stop something bad from happening, or maybe you made a choice that you regret making, and want to do/say something else instead, giving you the chance to explore the different respones.
You will very likely bond with the characters on the first episode. Each one has an interesting back story, and a unique personality. A lot of your decissions you make can affect these characters, and how they feel about you, making decission making quite tough at times. These characters, along with the script, make a powerful impact on you.
If you've looked through the screenshots, you will see that this game has a very cartoonish look to it. Looking through some of the reviews, there are people that think the graphics could've been better or they are "outdated". In my opinion, it never really bothered me that much. I do look at some bits and think it could've used a bit more detail, but it hardly comes to the point where it bothers me. One thing that did bother me was lip syncronization. I didn't notice it all the time, but when I did, I was kinda disappointed that it couldn't of been done better.
Another thing that made this game an amazing experience was it's soundtrack. It was always perfectly fitting with the scenes, and made an amazing ending to each episode. Not to mention how it makes it immensely atmospheric and immersive.
Life is strange has easily made it's way to become on of the best games I've ever played! Each episode made me want to find out, whats next. Voice acting is spot on, story is great, the writing is amazing, characters are interesting, soundtrack is beautiful.... The list goes on. With episode 1 becoming free to download, I would highly recommend trying it! Life is Strange has been an amazing experience for me, one that I shall not ever forget. Worth every penny!
- Rich story

- Interesting characters
- Beautiful soundtrack
- Atmospheric
- Good voice acting
- Some textures could use a tiny bit more detail
- Lip syncronization could've been better

“Why the hell didn’t I play this earlier?”
Life is Strange is definitely a video game everyone must at least try and experience for themselves. It has a great gameplay, amazing story & characters, and memorable soundtrack. Worth every penny!
I got the first episode of this game from the Square Enix Humble Bundle, and didn’t immediately play it. It wasn’t until around the time for the 2016 summer sale, I finally got to install and played this game. And after finishing the first episode in one sitting, the first thing I thought was, “Why the hell didn’t I play this earlier?”  I knew I have to buy all the remaining episodes, which I did immediately. A lot of people said that the first episode is probably the weakest out of the rest, but it certainly got me hooked instantly.
Life is Strange is a story-rich episodic game, where you get to control Max Caulfield, a high school senior who just returned to her hometown of Arcadia Bay, to enroll at the Blackwell Academy to study her long life passion, photography. Max is a shy and quiet girl, but also very caring towards people and what’s happening around her. One day, she discovered that she has the power to turn back time when she saw her best friend, Chloe Price, get shot at the school’s bathroom.
Much like other story based choice and consequence games, you take control of the main character, in this case Max, as she embarks in Arcadia Bay, make speeches decisions for her and also big decisions which can alter the way the story progress. And you can also explore small segments of maps to interact with objects and other characters. What makes Life is Strange has a unique gameplay is Max’s ability to turn back time. Whilst other games make you live by or regret the decisions you make in game, Life is Strange strongly suggest you to turn back time and try other choices. But there is no correct decision, thanks to Max’s indecisive mind, and it certainly makes it harder to choose.
This is the main strength of the game. Life is Strange is a story full with emotion. Sometimes it’ll make you laugh, but most of the times it’ll make you cry. After finishing the last episode, I was left genuinely sad and emotionally drained, which is the first time a video game can make me feel this way. Even after weeks of finishing this game, the story still floats in my mind. Props to Dontnod Entertainment.
I love the story so much. As I said before, the first episode got me hooked instantly although a lot of people said that the first episode is the weakest one because it’s filled with high school teenage drama, but I’m a sucker for this kind of story. The episodic nature of this game feels really good, like you are genuinely watching a good TV series. And the way they present the intro and the ending of each episode is great. A lot of people also commented that they didn’t like the last episode, which also kinda not what I was expecting, but I certainly still enjoyed it and it still makes it a great storytelling in my opinion.
I love the characters too. They are very detailed. I got really attached to them, especially Max because you get to know everything she’s thinking and feeling every time you interact with objects and other characters, and I especially love that you can read through Max’s diary. Every character has their own unique personality, which certainly helps with the great voice acting, which I think is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a video game. Every line feels genuine. Every interaction feels meaningful.
One of the best, if not the best soundtrack in a video game in my opinion. Dontnod really did their research for this one. It suits the game’s vibe and story perfectly. The songs really put you to feel in the moment of each scene of the game. The timing of these songs are also great, which makes the scenes stronger and definitely gave me goosebumps. And after weeks finishing the game, I still listen to the soundtrack regularly, and each song instantly takes you back to Arcadia Bay and its people.
What a journey it is to play Life is Strange. Great gameplay, amazing story & characters, and memorable soundtrack. I’m thankful to have experienced it. It is definitely high on the list of top games I’ve played, and will recommend it to everyone who just generally love a great story or want to experience something unique in gaming. Please try this game guys! :)

Life is Strange is an episodic game that focuses on you making decissions that can affect the game later on. What makes Life is Strange so special, is your character's ability to control time, and being able to change what happened in the past. You play as an 18 year old girl named Maxine Caulfield, who has recently started attending Blackwell Academy in a town called Arcadia Bay, where she grew up. She is also a lover of photography, and throughout the game you are able to pictures of certain things, giving you an achievement for each one.
At the beginning of the game you witness a vision of the future of Arcadia Bay being wiped out by a tornado. You wake up to find yourself in class. Not long after this you discover your ability to control time, as you save your best friend, Chloe, which you haven't seen in five years from being shot. The game then points you towards a missing person named Rachel Amber, which was friends with Chloe during the 5 years of Max being away. You team up with Chloe, using your powers, to find Rachel Amber.
The gameplay is a lot similar to TellTale games. There are instances where you control your character, but most of the game is in cutscenes and decission making. There are times where you rely on your ability to control time. For example, there are instances where you may have to rewind time to stop something bad from happening, or maybe you made a choice that you regret making, and want to do/say something else instead, giving you the chance to explore the different respones.
You will very likely bond with the characters on the first episode. Each one has an interesting back story, and a unique personality. A lot of your decissions you make can affect these characters, and how they feel about you, making decission making quite tough at times. These characters, along with the script, make a powerful impact on you.
If you've looked through the screenshots, you will see that this game has a very cartoonish look to it. Looking through some of the reviews, there are people that think the graphics could've been better or they are "outdated". In my opinion, it never really bothered me that much. I do look at some bits and think it could've used a bit more detail, but it hardly comes to the point where it bothers me. One thing that did bother me was lip syncronization. I didn't notice it all the time, but when I did, I was kinda disappointed that it couldn't of been done better.
Another thing that made this game an amazing experience was it's soundtrack. It was always perfectly fitting with the scenes, and made an amazing ending to each episode. Not to mention how it makes it immensely atmospheric and immersive.
Life is strange has easily made it's way to become on of the best games I've ever played! Each episode made me want to find out, whats next. Voice acting is spot on, story is great, the writing is amazing, characters are interesting, soundtrack is beautiful.... The list goes on. With episode 1 becoming free to download, I would highly recommend trying it! Life is Strange has been an amazing experience for me, one that I shall not ever forget. Worth every penny!
- Rich story
- Superb script
- Interesting characters
- Beautiful soundtrack
- Atmospheric
- Good voice acting
- Some textures could use a tiny bit more detail
- Lip syncronization could've been better

“Why the hell didn’t I play this earlier?”
Life is Strange is definitely a video game everyone must at least try and experience for themselves. It has a great gameplay, amazing story & characters, and memorable soundtrack. Worth every penny!
I got the first episode of this game from the Square Enix Humble Bundle, and didn’t immediately play it. It wasn’t until around the time for the 2016 summer sale, I finally got to install and played this game. And after finishing the first episode in one sitting, the first thing I thought was, “Why the hell didn’t I play this earlier?”  I knew I have to buy all the remaining episodes, which I did immediately. A lot of people said that the first episode is probably the weakest out of the rest, but it certainly got me hooked instantly.
Life is Strange is a story-rich episodic game, where you get to control Max Caulfield, a high school senior who just returned to her hometown of Arcadia Bay, to enroll at the Blackwell Academy to study her long life passion, photography. Max is a shy and quiet girl, but also very caring towards people and what’s happening around her. One day, she discovered that she has the power to turn back time when she saw her best friend, Chloe Price, get shot at the school’s bathroom.
Much like other story based choice and consequence games, you take control of the main character, in this case Max, as she embarks in Arcadia Bay, make speeches decisions for her and also big decisions which can alter the way the story progress. And you can also explore small segments of maps to interact with objects and other characters. What makes Life is Strange has a unique gameplay is Max’s ability to turn back time. Whilst other games make you live by or regret the decisions you make in game, Life is Strange strongly suggest you to turn back time and try other choices. But there is no correct decision, thanks to Max’s indecisive mind, and it certainly makes it harder to choose.
This is the main strength of the game. Life is Strange is a story full with emotion. Sometimes it’ll make you laugh, but most of the times it’ll make you cry. After finishing the last episode, I was left genuinely sad and emotionally drained, which is the first time a video game can make me feel this way. Even after weeks of finishing this game, the story still floats in my mind. Props to Dontnod Entertainment.
I love the story so much. As I said before, the first episode got me hooked instantly although a lot of people said that the first episode is the weakest one because it’s filled with high school teenage drama, but I’m a sucker for this kind of story. The episodic nature of this game feels really good, like you are genuinely watching a good TV series. And the way they present the intro and the ending of each episode is great. A lot of people also commented that they didn’t like the last episode, which also kinda not what I was expecting, but I certainly still enjoyed it and it still makes it a great storytelling in my opinion.
I love the characters too. They are very detailed. I got really attached to them, especially Max because you get to know everything she’s thinking and feeling every time you interact with objects and other characters, and I especially love that you can read through Max’s diary. Every character has their own unique personality, which certainly helps with the great voice acting, which I think is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a video game. Every line feels genuine. Every interaction feels meaningful.
One of the best, if not the best soundtrack in a video game in my opinion. Dontnod really did their research for this one. It suits the game’s vibe and story perfectly. The songs really put you to feel in the moment of each scene of the game. The timing of these songs are also great, which makes the scenes stronger and definitely gave me goosebumps. And after weeks finishing the game, I still listen to the soundtrack regularly, and each song instantly takes you back to Arcadia Bay and its people.
What a journey it is to play Life is Strange. Great gameplay, amazing story & characters, and memorable soundtrack. I’m thankful to have experienced it. It is definitely high on the list of top games I’ve played, and will recommend it to everyone who just generally love a great story or want to experience something unique in gaming. Please try this game guys! :)

*TRY TO PLAY WITHOUT ANY INFORMATION FOR BETTER EXPERIENCE!*
Telling you that the overwhelmingly positive reviews are more than justified should be enough for you to start playing. I dove in without any knowledge (other that it's an episodic adventure game), and it was a great experience. Stay away from the screenshots and trailers Steam provided, they contain (minor?) spoilers.
If you need a little more info (or you already saw the trailers), feel free to read the rest.
Life is Strange is more of an interactive story than an actual game. If you're a Telltale fan, you know what I'm talking about, this game is definitely for you. I dare say this title is an upgrade. There are no quick time events, it mainly consists of walking around, interacting with people and observing your surroundings.
You play as Max, a teenage girl who returns to her childhood town to attend a prestige school in hope to become a photographer. After you meet up with your childhood friend Chloe, the two of you try to find Rachel, a student whose missing posters are all over the place. There's also this vision about a tornado...
From the start, the game introduces a neat mechanic: Max is able to rewind time. You don't like a decision you just took? Rewind! (bare in mind this is not always possible, the game uses auto save and when this happenes you cannot go back).
Being in school setting, there is some teen drama involved, but there is something greater ahead. There are 5 episodes (one lasts for about 2-3 hours), each one a little darker and more gripping. To avoid a bigger wall of text, lets brake the game down with pros and cons:
+ Story
Being this type of game, this is essential, and Life is Strange succeeds to draw the player in. You want to know what happens, you get shocked, you experience empathy. A proper emotional drama.
+ Voice acting
The're is not much to say, it is superb. Especially the two main heroines. Max is shy, Chloe rebellius... It makes the characters believable.
+ Soundtrack
Oh my god, the soundtrack fits so good it probably makes half of the game. Got me hooked from the main menu.
+ Visuals
The graphics aren't top notch but they fit the game perfectly if that makes any sense. The camera direction, the colors, the whole style makes it beautiful to look at, screenshot enthusiasts will definitely be happy.
+ Decisions do matter
What you do will matter/have effect throughout the game although it will not affect the game ending possibilities. (well, not all decisions, for instance I don't know if my choice for breakfast affected anything :D). I think that's fine. ''Its about the journey, not destination'' can be applied.
- Lip sync
Possibly the only 'major' negative I can find. Severely lacking, denying the ultimate immersion.
- A bug
Couldn't advance the story, had to reload (it then pushed me through).
- Boobs
18 year olds don't have any it seems. :)
Final thoughts:
1.) Games can trully be art.
2.) I want season 2.

I'm going to start off by saying that for the most part I did enjoy this game, but I think that if you compare it to other games of similar genre, it really falls flat. I can't say your money would be poorly spent on Life is Strange, but I think it would be better spent on other titles.
I'm not going to talk about every part of the game, only the parts that really stood out to me and pointed me to the "would not recommend" selection.
Story: 6/10
From what I've read in other reviews, my opinion of the story doesn't jive with most other people's opinions. Frankly, I was underwhelmed by the heavy-handed coming-of-age tale. Riddled with cliches, the story only glimmered with originality a few times throughout the episodes. From the misunderstood main character who is unpopular because the plot demands it, and for no other well-explained reason, to the mean girl who is secretly sensitive and unsure, the story generally falls predictably into its groove. This isn't inherently a bad thing, it is just frustrating when a plot-based title has so little original thought.
Characters: 7/10
Much like the story, our protagonist fits neatly into her archetype and never once tries to bend or break the ideas that define her. In fact, there are very few characters that don't seem to be drawn straight out of a late 00's throwaway teen flick. With shoehorned pop-culture references that will age poorly and were already out of date before the game was even released, the population of the game felt less like youths in revolt and more like what older people think of youths in revolt.
From the beginning, the protagonist is labelled by the game as an "artsy, misunderstood teen". From the reviews, I expected this to change, for her to gain depth in a way that made her less angst, and more teen. To my chargin, Life is Strange doubled down. With every character interaction, they cemented her into the cast the set, and never seemed inclined to remove her from it.
Art: 8/10
In terms of quality, the art was quite nice. I think it will be the part of the game that ages the best. Realistic enough to make the game tangible, but stylzed in a way that keeps it out of the uncanny valley. Some of those sour pop-culture references and cliche artsy teen vibes pervade into the art, especially in menus. Which bitters, but by no means ruins, the asthetic of the game.
Overall Feeling: Nothing Special
Maybe it's because I have never met anyone who acts the way any of these characters act, but I had a hard time connecting emotionally to the game, which is what games like this are supposed to built around. to me, it seemed that Life is Strange put more effort into building the veneer of originality than it did anything else. Althought I ultimately did enjoy the game, if you have 20 dollars and wish to buy a game, look elsewhere before coming here, there are far better titles than this one.

Having played this practically since the game came out---long before it was ever decided that KSP would be on Steam---I can most certainly vouch for this taking at least a thousand hours out of my life, and I can also certainly say that
In
, you have an entire solar system at which you can throw any space-worthy vehicle you concoct in the vehicle assembly building (VAB), provided you can get it off of the planet, much less the launchpad. Back in the good old days, it used to be that you had an entire planet and its moon, and before those days, a flat square chunk of terrain. The game certainly has made monumental leaps and bounds in its development, and nonetheless thanks to the dev team that (used to) comprise Squad. HarvesteR, NovaSilisko, c7, Porkjet, and many others I can't name off the top of my head, they made it happen. Quite a few were just modders of the early game, and then they were offered dev positions because of their relentless talent.
Speaking of modding, there is an entire forum section and some websites dedicated to KSP mods that either expand on the vanilla game, or transform your solar system into an ungodly manifestation of the Kraken, a previously-killed bug of the game engine that caused the spaghettification of countless Kerbal souls.
Yeah, those green guys and gals you have at your
service? Those are Kerbals, and they tend to be the subjects of your (and the Kraken's) many doings in the game. Provided you put them on the front-end and not the business-end of a rocket, you'll see them off into whatever endless void they find themselves. Or, you know, the business-end is also a lot of fun, shooting them off like a cannon.
Seriously, go and try out the game if you think anything I've bothered to type sounds like your types of shenanigans that would make you laugh, jovially or sadistically.

My number score (out of 10) for this would be a solid 8. I can't give a perfect score, even though it was one of the more amazing games I've played. There are two major sticking points that prevent me from rating it higher:
1) Even though this is a game of choices, too many of them are not true choices, in that you are forced to make plot-driven decisions that prevent real immersion. The most obvious ones involve Chloe, particularly when she first appears on the scene. Since there are other things going on that require Max's attention from that point onward, Chloe's death (especially since Max didn't know how much Chloe had changed) wouldn't have been that big of a deal necessarily. Also, a few choices were just window-dressing, and while some were a little fun (and funny), having them matter more would have been awesome.
2) While the twists in the tale (especially in Episode 4) changed the entire ways in which previous choices mattered, some things didn't quite add up, including a few major holes that were not adequately explained nor dealt with properly. The one that stuck out that wasn't earth-shattering was what happened with Frank's dog and trailer in the diner parking lot. Why didn't Frank react differently when he came out and saw his dog outside, chewing on a bone he didn't give to him? Also, where did he get the keys to drive the RV since Chloe disposed of them?
Other than those two main issues, I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and will be playing it through at least once more. I want to see how evil I can make Max seem, even though the game won't allow certain things to happen (see the aforementioned issue with Chloe). I like Max as an Angel of Justice, but I also want to see if I can make her seem even worse than Victoria.
Sure, the game will seem a little twee for many, but for those wanting depth and a fascinating look into the human condition (even if within the late-teen, private-school, self-involved set), Life Is Strange is one of the best games of this kind ever released.

Max, despite coming across as a fixed personality displaying shyness, kindness and a bright view of the world around her, is influenced by decisions left, right and centre, probably in more ways than the player realises at the time. This makes Life is Strange's game world a hugely authentic work, with many twists and turns that may encourage the player to do the right thing, but hardly make it straightforward. Thus, the player is constantly questioning themselves, did they make the right choice or didn't they? And it's that word that I must emphasise. Choice. An all round amazing game. I mean we are talking about a mod of a game, where you are actually modding a game. In Garrys mod you as a player are able to do everything. You can make your own death match maps, customise them. Make zombie survival maps. Hell, you can make weapons, to use them in your death matches. You can be what ever you want in this game literally. Be a bit creative, and make a game by yourself, a game that you would enjoy yourself.

However! That being said, if story-based games are your forte, and you would take an interest to them, please continue reading....
Enter Arcadia Bay, a beautiful town on the coast of the Pacific Ocean, and meet Max, an 18 year old girl who has just started her first semester at Blackwell University. But something strange is going on in Blackwell, and it's up to Max, and her time changing abilities to figure out the puzzle, along with the help of her friend, Chloe. Your choices and actions will affect you at a different point in the game, so make sure that you choose wisely, because unlike TellTale games, your choices DO matter!
Overall, I really enjoyed this game, but I would like to try and break it down by part just to give a little more depth into the game.
Probably my favorite episode in the game by far, like a good novel, this is the start of the story, you get a better understanding of the characters, and a feel for the town.
Also another episode that I really enjoyed, this is where the the story really begins to take off, and you learn some of the secrets to what is going on here at Blackwell.
My second favorite episode, the end of this episode combined with the beginning of Episode 4 really made me love this game even more. In episode 3 is probably where a big part of the story surrounding Chloe and Max take off and you get to find out more and more about what is happening.
Good, in fact, really good, almost perfection at its finest. The peak of the story, where your decisions will ultimately unfold, as you see the result of your behavior through previous episodes.
Overall, I realy didn't like episode 5, it had a different feel than from the previous four episodes. It can be argued, that in this episode, your choices ultimately didn't matter.
I also didn't like it, because you spend a lot of time in this episode erasing timelines, wherin decisions and relationships that you built up will not matter after they have been erased. This episode just didn't have that overall Life is Strange feel to it, and felt more like a mandatory book reading.
That being said with all that in mind, I still really loved this game. The soundtrack, the visuals, and the voice acting (with the exception of pretty terrible lip syncing) made this game really quite beautiful.
This game really inspired me, and changed the way I feel about video games. To put things in perspective, I am an 18 year old male, and this game nearly made me cry, it was an emotion journey, and episodes 1-4 are an 11/10, however with the addition my least favorite episode, number 5, I'd give this game a solid 9.5/10.
This game will easily go down as a top 5 game for me, and I HIGHLY recommend you buy it and play it thoroughly. And even though there were things about this game that I didn't really like, and choices that weren't all that fair, honestly, Life is Strange like that...

While I've only played the first episode, this was a stunning story with incredible gameplay elements thrown in. I think as far as characterization, there are very few games that "nail it" and completely involve you in the people's lives at a deep level. If someone told me a story about "teenage girls in private school" would end up being on my "best games ever" list, I probably would have laughed in your face.
Very, very rarely do I get drawn in so quickly to a story, and even more rarely do the gameplay mechanics nail it. It's unobtrusive, but on a story-driven game, the dynamic is simply genious. Aside from this, there is a lot of depth to characters I would normally write off as "dear god, I just can't". This... this is brilliant story telling.
In short, while I've been hearing about this game for quite some time, I was never QUITE interested. I thought it to be more along the likes of Telltale Games episodes, with quicktime events and all the other standard dross that gets put into games "critically acclaimed for story".
All I can say is, play the first episode. It's worth the playthrough. If you haven't gotten grabbed in the first thirty minutes, then feel free to refund. But PLAY THAT FIRST THIRTY MINUTES, if you haven't. This is a gem of a game and I'm kicking myself in the♥♥♥♥♥because I hadn't played it earlier.

However! That being said, if story-based games are your forte, and you would take an interest to them, please continue reading....
Enter Arcadia Bay, a beautiful town on the coast of the Pacific Ocean, and meet Max, an 18 year old girl who has just started her first semester at Blackwell University. But something strange is going on in Blackwell, and it's up to Max, and her time changing abilities to figure out the puzzle, along with the help of her friend, Chloe. Your choices and actions will affect you at a different point in the game, so make sure that you choose wisely, because unlike TellTale games, your choices DO matter!
Overall, I really enjoyed this game, but I would like to try and break it down by part just to give a little more depth into the game.
Probably my favorite episode in the game by far, like a good novel, this is the start of the story, you get a better understanding of the characters, and a feel for the town.
Also another episode that I really enjoyed, this is where the the story really begins to take off, and you learn some of the secrets to what is going on here at Blackwell.
My second favorite episode, the end of this episode combined with the beginning of Episode 4 really made me love this game even more. In episode 3 is probably where a big part of the story surrounding Chloe and Max take off and you get to find out more and more about what is happening.
Good, in fact, really good, almost perfection at its finest. The peak of the story, where your decisions will ultimately unfold, as you see the result of your behavior through previous episodes.
Overall, I realy didn't like episode 5, it had a different feel than from the previous four episodes. It can be argued, that in this episode, your choices ultimately didn't matter.
I also didn't like it, because you spend a lot of time in this episode erasing timelines, wherin decisions and relationships that you built up will not matter after they have been erased. This episode just didn't have that overall Life is Strange feel to it, and felt more like a mandatory book reading.
That being said with all that in mind, I still really loved this game. The soundtrack, the visuals, and the voice acting (with the exception of pretty terrible lip syncing) made this game really quite beautiful.
This game really inspired me, and changed the way I feel about video games. To put things in perspective, I am an 18 year old male, and this game nearly made me cry, it was an emotion journey, and episodes 1-4 are an 11/10, however with the addition my least favorite episode, number 5, I'd give this game a solid 9.5/10.
This game will easily go down as a top 5 game for me, and I HIGHLY recommend you buy it and play it thoroughly. And even though there were things about this game that I didn't really like, and choices that weren't all that fair, honestly, Life is Strange like that...

This game is a phenomenal work of art and you shouldn't miss it. But, be prepared. To avoid spoilers, the truth of Life is Strange (LiS) is best explained through metaphor.
Once you've gotten the introductions out of the way, LiS becons you with a beautiful blue flower in one hand, and a knife in the other. Maybe you've played some games before and you recognize this sort of knife, you know how it works and you're ready for it. So you warily check out the flower, keeping one eye on the knife, and soon enough LiS stabs you with it. "Ow" you say, and LiS says, "yeah, sorry", and pulls out the knife and tosses it away. "Well, at least that's done with" you think, it wasn't so bad, and get back to that blue flower. It's a bejeweled masterpiece, a real pleasure to behold with intricate and unexpected details. This is a marvel, you think, and move in closer, only to suddenly find yourself flat on your back, something big and heavy and sharp projecting from your chest. Blinking away tears you look up to see LiS standing over you - somehow you failed to notice that the bejewled blue flower is actually the hilt of a ferociously honed two-handed sword, you've never seen anything like it, and LiS put it right through your sternum so fast you didn't even see the motion. "Wow, jeez, can you pull this thing out?" you plead, but LiS dallies. "Just try to appreciate the moment here." So you lay there a while, trying to enjoy the sensation of blood cooling as it runs down the side of your torso. "OK, that's enough" says LiS, giving the blade a sharp, painful twist before extracting it and helping you back to your feet. "Good grief!" you cry, "What is this game even about?!"
LiS pauses while you both admire the extraordinary blade, then lifts it firmly and prepares to strike again. "This." LiS says, "This is what it's about."
