This game takes the concept of cause and effect, e.g. seen before in The Walking Dead, and takes it to a new level using the rewind mechanism, where you can undo most of your actions and even use knowledge and items you didn't have before. The consequences often come back to you.
It's great fun! Some character animations aren't as refined as in comparable titles, but the environments more than make up for this. And visual details. Effects (the edge of the screen is blurred and mimics chromatic aberration by a camera lens). Various nods to other works. Ambient sounds. Storytelling devices. Even psychedelic dream sequences, like e.g. in Max Payne. An achievement system where you have hints to optional photos you can take in your diary, and can look for those hints in the world to get the shot. It even lets you solve riddles by assembling and sorting clues on a corkboard, which worked exceptionally well for me.
Also, it's unexpectedly intense. Few games emotionally captured me like this and also made me think about life, the universe and everything. For a college-themed game, it's been quite creepy in places.
Alas, although the last episode kept me hooked until late at night, the endings are bloody unsatisfying to me. The adventure lacks purpose and explanations, and the endings feel a bit rushed. Your choices from before don't seem to matter anymore.
Maybe it's just me. Personally, I do like endings that wrap it up coherently, a closure, sad or happy. I'm afraid Life is Strange failed to deliver this to me. I don't feel at rest, but not in a way to play again, but to try to forget.
On a side note, I thought I had hit a bug when I couldn't get up from the first "sitting spot". Turned out you can only get up using one special key (skip scene, space).

In the 2-3 years that I've owned this game, I've wasted god knows how many hours of my life shooting traitors, arresting thieves, blasting mutants, killing aliens, stacking props about 20 feet in the air, and shooting possessed objects.
But it was so worth it.

Pretty much a testament to why I like story and choice-based games. Yes, you can argue that the choices don't have a huge impact on the main story but it's all the little details that matter, and some of them I'd say are pretty damn big choices that affect who lives and dies.
And the story itself is quite engaging, kind of a rollercoaster of emotions, mystery, and suspense. Episode 1 is maybe a little weak overall and all the high school drama kinda gives me anxiety but it's necessary to set the stage for the rest of the episodes.
Visually the game is pretty good, not great though, some moments where the style really showed its weakness but as a whole good enough. The soundtrack is pretty great, a decent number of licensed songs alongside a pretty pleasant original score. A few of the songs really work for starting and ending each chapter well, like, just great music choices.
Gameplay-wise it's pretty much the same as a telltale game. Walk around, talk with people, examine the environment, occasionally solve a puzzle or two. The rewinding mechanic is used cleverly enough throughout the game, though there's only so much that can be done with it before they have to start repeating themselves.
This is a pretty short review since I'm not really feeling a huge review for this one, but suffice to say that it's quite good and that saying much more would probably give away major plot points, so just go play it yourself.

Review 3: This review will be my personal feelings about "Life Is Strange." Alrighty, so let's start off with saying that "Life Is Strange" is definetely a unique game. It's special. That's not supposed to really mean anything but I want to say that. I played this game doing an episode per night, but the review was delayed because on the penultimate episode I got frustrated with something and turned it off.
So, let me give you a little history here, because that's the key to understanding. I first learned of Life Is Strange when I saw friends posting screenshots and talking about the game. My first impression was "Lesbian time travel drama" (which, by the way, isn't even off-putting really.) When the sale came along, I picked it up because I thought "this should be interesting." Because I saw a lot of friends talking about it, and some also seeming to have deep feelings for the game, I thought this would definetely be a good thing to write a review about personally.
So, let's start talking about the game. I saw some people who reviewed it on here saying that they totally identified with the characters. I'm gonna tell you that it wasn't the case for me at all. Don't percieve that as "I don't have feelings for the characters." I just don't identify with them personally. For example, a line from the game:
"You do know I believe in gun control?"
E
e
eww let's not get political with this review whatsoever please for the love of god. Okay, so let me clear that up. Of course I'm not saying this game is trying to push any of those things, views, political agendas. It's not an ideologically charged game at all. Like I said, I just don't identify with the main characters "Chloe" and "Max" That's NOT bashing the game.
Now, keeping that in mind, I found one thing particularly "not nice" regarding the characters. There's a character in this game called "David" he's Chloe's stepfather. Now, the game never gives you a choice, (untill the final episode), to not bash his♥♥♥♥♥constantly and side against him. Now, saying that I need to point out something. You always play as "Max Caulfield" no matter what choices you make in the game. Ho ho ho, I bet now you're saying "Of course dumbass, she's the character you play as in the game, what do you want, ♥♥♥♥ing GTA?" What I mean is, no matter what choices you make, she'll still keep the same views, the same everything. Her perception doesn't really change of people and events.
Now, of course in this review it's mostly my personal feelings but I need to tell you something about the GAME. Here's the biggie. I think it sucks as a game. As a GAME. I think it would have worked better generally and for me, if it was a miniseries, something of that sort. I say that because, every time the "game" came into play, it was such a drag and just felt like it had to be there to justify "game" Some examples:
"Hmmm...the HiFi's unplugged, I should go plug it in."
"Hey, can you grab me the ingredients I need to make this breakfast from the fridge, hon?"
"We need at least five bottles, go find some"
Those are examples of why I thought it didn't work. Whenever it tried to experiment with other game mechanics, it never worked and it was always a drag and made me angry. It's like I was deeply into this movie when suddenly it went "Can you complete that scene by walking to the other side of the room? Thanks."
Now, if you're still reading this, which I hope you are, I need to tell you that I'm only bashing the "game" aspect of "Life Is Strange" I've told you my view of the characters beforehand, so I got that out of the way. I really wish i could have recorded my immediate reactions to little things in this game because that would have had infinitely more value than what I'm offering you right now. And that's something maybe nobody really wants to know anyway, personal feelings about the game.
During conversations, you usually get two very vague dialogue options to choose from that will decide how the whole conversation goes. Again, why weren't you a miniseries? You'd be just as emotional and you wouldn't have to put all these dumb things in here that add nothing.
Let's talk about choices, going back to the "game" part. Choices are placed everywhere, but as you may already know from looking at other reviews, they don't affect the ending. There are two final choices that can change the ending. Now, that's something that really didn't make me angry. But, the final choice I decided in about 2 seconds and then I found out the majority of players actually chose the other one! C'mon guys. Anyways, no spoilers about that.
I should really wrap this up, okay. Summary! Queue Interstellar Overdrive

I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes the type of story games such as those produced by Telltale; however, this game is so much more artfully crafted than many of Telltale's games. The music used throughout the game fits perfectly, the animation (despite the horrible lip-syncing XD) is pretty enough to visually please you, and the story is the best of all. It's such a creative, interesting, and fantastical story, yet somehow they make it seem so real. You truly gain the sense that you are the one and only Max Caulfield. It also really makes you reflect on how the small decisions in life have changed it majorly. Overall, it's hard to describe how good of a game it is without spoiling anything, so just buy the dang game already! An emotional adventure of friendship and time-warping awaits you!
TL;DR: I recommend EVERYONE to play this, but if you find games like Telltale's The Walking Dead or Wolf Among Us lame, you should probably just pass this one up.
P.S. Have fun listening to Jefferson's lecture on selfies.

This is possibly the best game I have ever played. I'm not willing to go ahead and straight-up say it's my #1 favorite game ever, but it is really up there for consideration.
It was thoughtful, intelligent, heartfelt, well written, and beautiful, in a way that I have never experienced in a videogame before. The choices and character interactions felt meaningful and the story kept you on the edge of your seat the whole time. At the same time, the game moved at a fairly slow pace and let you think about things and the ultimate implications of your decisions. It encouraged exploring your options, talking to everyone, and learning about things on your own.
I should also note that the music is quite good, and I really wish that they would sell the OST - I downloaded it from somewhere else for myself, but if they actually sold it on their site or on Steam, I would absolutely buy it right away. If any devs are reading this, please please please make the OST available. I understand that many of the songs are licensed, but they could at least sell the ones that were original for this game.
The gameplay can be a little bit slow at some parts, but it is also brilliant at times. There were a few item-collection type of parts that I really didn't find that engaging, but the times where the game really makes you think with Max's time powers were fantastic - although, in my opinion, the game is a bit too fast in giving you hints when you get stuck. Anything that involved decisions while talking to people and time traveling back to say something else was fantastic, though. (I also want to note that I am very thankful to the devs about not including QTE's in this game, as this game really didn't need them. Glad this wasn't made by Telltale, lol.)
On a more personal note, I wanted to write that this is the second to only videogame I recall playing that has made me actually cry. One of the popular reviews here mentions being a grown man who cried several times through the game, and I 100% relate to that. The only other game that I cried to was Telltale's The Walking Dead Season 1, but even that wasn't like this. There was a segment a good way through this game that, to me, was absolutely heartbreaking. No movie, book, or game has ever made me feel so strongly about a fictional scenario with fake people as that segment in this game has. I don't know if everyone would feel the same about this game, but I do advise you purchase a small box of tissues alongside it. While it isn't really a tearjerker, it is still quite an emotional ride.
---
I did have some issues with this game, though, primarily concerning its performance. To me, as amazing as I thought this game and its overall presentation was, it didn't quite have the polish or sheen that I expect from AAA titles.
In the ~13 hours it took me to finish this game, here were the primary issues I had:
- Throughout the whole game, I had an issue where the audio would randomly cut out for half a second, making people's words sound choppy and disjointed. Even after googling about it, I never found a viable fix for this. It seems that if you have this issue, there's nothing to do about it. It wasn't too big of a deal, but it did affect my immersion at some parts of the game.
- The animations are so strange sometimes that I'm convinced they are unfinished at certain parts, or at least very glitchy. There was one scene towards the end where for me, people were talking but their lips weren't moving, and they weren't emoting like they were supposed to. That sort of thing only happened twice as far as I remember, but it was tough to really keep my immersion while it was happening.
- Five or six times in the game, there would be these strange rimmings of light on the right and bottom sides of my monitor, as if there were some kind of light effect. They would cut in and out depending on the scene, and sometimes the effect would overlap a fairly noticeable segment of the screen. Each time only lasted about a minute but it was quite strange.
- There were two times where the game passively crashed, forcing me to restart it. For both times, instead of fading to the next scene, it faded to black, leaving me to stare at the screen, wondering if that was supposed to happen or not. Luckily, this game autosaves every minute or so, so I didn't lose any actual progress, but I thought it was worth mentioning this because of how confused it made me. I've never seen a game crash quite like that before, just kinda fading to black and waiting until you figure out that that isn't supposed to happen.
---
But for whatever issues or glitches there were, I still consider this to be one of the best games I have ever played. It is certainly the best story-based decision-based game I have played. This is the one that sets the bar. I really, really, really hope to see more games of this style and this quality popping up as time goes on. I cannot possibly recommend this game enough.
My only regret with it is that I waited so long to play it, being the sale-waiting cheapskate that I am. Dontnot deserved more than my $7 during a Steam sale for this.

Life is strange is a playable story of Max and her ability to randomly be able to rewind time.
It's never truly explained why Max randomly gets these powers, and ultimately I feel a little hurt and shocked the ending portrayed how useless the time control really was. To be honest there is no real reason you get these powers and in some "Thats So Raven" esque fashion the game seems to imply that it doesnt matter if you can change time, it will happen anyways.
Dont get me wrong, if you love story. This is a great game. There will be choices that you will have to pause and stop before being able to answer them. There are consequences for certain actions that wont seem very impacting, and then some choices that can completely change the various episodes the game has to offer.
If you get Life is strange, buy the BUNDLE I cannot stress that enough, episode 1 is barely enough to satisfy and the bundle ultimately is cheaper anyway.
If you are unsure about the game wait for a sale.
If you never heard of this game before I do warn you its a rather dark story that has plenty of death and inappropriate themes such as swearing, drug references, and typical/stereotypical bad teen scenerios that some may be uncomfortable with. Which I learned immediately after reccomending this game to someone else.
The story is compelling and has you wondering whats going to happen next, Square Enix shows no trouble at all in hooking you to the story almost immediately. I suggest you explore as much as you can in each episode just so you dont miss any actions or decisions. Trust me asides from some crucial points where the game tells you that you are running out of time, you literally have all the time in the world.
So relax, walk around, and immerse yourself in the story. If you really enjoy story, and choice/consequence games this is definitely one of the best games I've purchased. It reminds me alot like Beyond two Souls, if you enjoy the thematic story telling of that game, you will most definitely enjoy this one. I myself found myself in tears at certain points of the game, because my decision was too hard to make and I really connected to some of the key characters.
There is a little misconception with the "multiple endings" bit so I am going to make this clear.
There are two "endings."
but choices you make in game will impact the game as you continue through the episodes. Your choices for example, could impact a life in the story and maybe the next episode will show the consequence for that action.
I was disappointed by the ending honestly, but I still wanted more.
Yes I do like the game, yes I recommend it, do I want a better ending or maybe more episodes to show aftermath? Yes of course, because I dont feel fully satisfied with not knowing what happens, whats my consequence for choosing ending A over B for example? It never tells you.

Originally i was not impressed with this game. I'd been a prominant user of Source FilmMaker beforehand and i greatly appreciated it for being easy to use once i knew what did what, And having lots of options in case something went wrong. Move someone's arm the wrong way? Undo-able. And placing things into a scene is a breeze.
Taking a test run at Garry's Mod and being stripped of some abilities i had in SFM initially frustrated me so much that i uninstalled the game, Vowing never to touch it again. I felt disappointed that i couldn't get something cool to happen like everyone else did.
Finally one day, I came back after i got tired of the SFM community (Not enough workshop items for what i wanted to do) and decided to fool around more. Maybe i just took it too seriously, I thought; I've only scratched the surface of what it had to offer. Sure enough i was right...
While G-mod still has its share of drawbacks, Its unique elements for game-making adds an even deeper art experience. There's a certain freedom not seen in SFM. I've come to love both equally, But i now also consider the impact G-mod has had on the gaming community since the beginning. It should be given its due, And perhaps, A try-out on your own dime.
I give Garry's Mod a 7/10.
One more thing to note: If you decide G-mod is a keeper, You might want to hit the workshop early on. You'll deplete your spawnlist of new items over time, So it's good to keep adding to it and keeping your playtimes fresh. Needless to say, Lots of the community items are FANTASTIC.

The choices and character interactions felt meaningful and the story kept you on the edge of your seat the whole time. At the same time, the game moved at a fairly slow pace and let you think about things and the ultimate implications of your decisions. It encouraged exploring your options, talking to everyone, and learning about things on your own.
I should also note that the music is quite good, and I really wish that they would sell the OST - I downloaded it from somewhere else for myself, but if they actually sold it on their site or on Steam, I would absolutely buy it right away. If any devs are reading this, please please please make the OST available. I understand that many of the songs are licensed, but they could at least sell the ones that were original for this game.
The gameplay can be a little bit slow at some parts, but it is also brilliant at times. There were a few item-collection type of parts that I really didn't find that engaging, but the times where the game really makes you think with Max's time powers were fantastic - although, in my opinion, the game is a bit too fast in giving you hints when you get stuck. Anything that involved decisions while talking to people and time traveling back to say something else was fantastic, though. (I also want to note that I am very thankful to the devs about not including QTE's in this game, as this game really didn't need them. Glad this wasn't made by Telltale, lol.)
On a more personal note, I wanted to write that this is the second to only videogame I recall playing that has made me actually cry. One of the popular reviews here mentions being a grown man who cried several times through the game, and I 100% relate to that. The only other game that I cried to was Telltale's The Walking Dead Season 1, but even that wasn't like this. There was a segment a good way through this game that, to me, was absolutely heartbreaking. No movie, book, or game has ever made me feel so strongly about a fictional scenario with fake people as that segment in this game has. I don't know if everyone would feel the same about this game, but I do advise you purchase a small box of tissues alongside it. While it isn't really a tearjerker, it is still quite an emotional ride.
---
I did have some issues with this game, though, primarily concerning its performance. To me, as amazing as I thought this game and its overall presentation was, it didn't quite have the polish or sheen that I expect from AAA titles.
In the ~13 hours it took me to finish this game, here were the primary issues I had:
- Throughout the whole game, I had an issue where the audio would randomly cut out for half a second, making people's words sound choppy and disjointed. Even after googling about it, I never found a viable fix for this. It seems that if you have this issue, there's nothing to do about it. It wasn't too big of a deal, but it did affect my immersion at some parts of the game.
- The animations are so strange sometimes that I'm convinced they are unfinished at certain parts, or at least very glitchy. There was one scene towards the end where for me, people were talking but their lips weren't moving, and they weren't emoting like they were supposed to. That sort of thing only happened twice as far as I remember, but it was tough to really keep my immersion while it was happening.
- Five or six times in the game, there would be these strange rimmings of light on the right and bottom sides of my monitor, as if there were some kind of light effect. They would cut in and out depending on the scene, and sometimes the effect would overlap a fairly noticeable segment of the screen. Each time only lasted about a minute but it was quite strange.
- There were two times where the game passively crashed, forcing me to restart it. For both times, instead of fading to the next scene, it faded to black, leaving me to stare at the screen, wondering if that was supposed to happen or not. Luckily, this game autosaves every minute or so, so I didn't lose any actual progress, but I thought it was worth mentioning this because of how confused it made me. I've never seen a game crash quite like that before, just kinda fading to black and waiting until you figure out that that isn't supposed to happen.
---
But for whatever issues or glitches there were, I still consider this to be one of the best games I have ever played. It is certainly the best story-based decision-based game I have played. This is the one that sets the bar. I really, really, really hope to see more games of this style and this quality popping up as time goes on. I cannot possibly recommend this game enough.
My only regret with it is that I waited so long to play it, being the sale-waiting cheapskate that I am. Dontnot deserved more than my $7 during a Steam sale for this.

Though it does have quite a few technical flaws and a couple questionable design choices in its storyline, I will not hesitate to give this game a hearty positive recommendation simply for the experience it conveys. It is an engaging, gripping, touching story that will affect anyone who is capable of feeling emotions at all. In fact, I can think of perhaps one game I've ever played that's touched and affected me as deeply as Life Is Strange after its ending. That alone is a compelling reason to get this game, in my opinion.
To briefly describe the other perks of the game, your main character Max develops a time-travelling power, allowing her to rewind time. The rules of this ability are both overpowered and somewhat inconsistent, but that is not a problem - the game is a bit campy as far as time travel is concerned. There is no fighting (at least not with your character) and little sneaking - most of the game involves character interactions and finding clever ways of using your rewind power to break the world, with a smattering of logical puzzles indeed (most of them not too hard, but there are a few which require a bit of thinking).
Life Is Strange is a "choices and consequences" game, and it is true that your choices affect the storyline - to some degree. The story will develop in different ways depending on the choices you make, but generally the game does eventually railroad you back onto the main storyline (in many cases, all you get are different lines in conversations), so a lot of the times the world doesn't change much. Only a few of your choices are truly monumental as far as altering the world goes. This is a bit of a weakness on the game's part, admittedly. A lot of reviewers bemoan the ending - I don't think it's that bad, though it does have certain problems. However, at this point I must enjoy that the rewind power fits the "choices and consequences" playstyle very well. Instead of having to reload like in other games if you regret your choice and want to pick the other one, here you can just use the rewind function to spare the hassle in almost every instance... it actually makes for very stress-free gameplay. Genius!
Overall, I don't think you will regret buying this game if you are interested in this type of game, but perhaps those who enjoy it most will be those kinds of players who enjoy just immersing themselves in a story, and do not compulsively feel the need to nitpick every minor flaw they find - as well as those who enjoy the theme of angsty teenage drama (or at least, a storyline that starts off as such) in general.

Life is Strange is a five-part episodic "choices matter" adventure game.  The game being split into episodes only affects the narrative in the sense that there are movie-like story arcs and cliffhangers when you reach the end of an episode.  However, you don't have to wait to jump right into the next one (thank goodness!). It also employs a unique "rewind" feature that allows players to test out different dialogue choices and solve puzzles in an interesting fashion that separates LiS from all other adventure games.
You play as 18-year-old Max Caufield, a photography student at a private high school in Arcadia Bay. This coastal Oregon town has its fair share of secrets - secrets that Max sets out to uncover with her mysterious new temporal rewind abilities, and her old childhood friend and rebel child Chloe.  It's a story of nostalgia, coming of age, and self exploration.
This game isn't really something you just click and play through.  It's an experience of emotions and visuals.  There are hours of world exploration, making the game great for those who like to take time with the details and really immerse themselves in the game.  The story is great.  Prepare for dark concepts, swearing and emotionally trying moments.  I think the greatest thing about Life is Strange is that as you play through, you learn a lot about yourself, and what you think is important.  It is a choice-based game, and it features consequences that are as unpredictable and devastating as consequences can be in life.  Each major choice has a large impact later on, and even the little decisions have an effect on relationships and the side story lines.  I really suggest playing with little-to-no outside guidance.  Just see where your choices leave you.
This game has great replay value.  There are lots of little hidden goodies, like picture collecting.  It is worth replaying just to make the opposite choice every time and see where it leads you.  The soundtrack is perfectly fitting, and just adds to the ambiance.  The animation is gorgeous and paint-y, with warm sunsets and peaceful moments of scenery observation. The characters have compelling personalities and backgrounds, and you get to determine what relationships Max forges with these characters.  Will you be a good friend?  Will you take risks and make enemies?  It's all up to you.
I suggest this game to those who are looking for a new kind of video game.  It's like a cross between a movie, book and video game - very story heavy and cinematic, but utterly beautiful.  I hope that you will give Life is Strange a try, and I hope that it makes you think.

It's very hard to put into words how deep, spirited, and unique this game is, but i'll try.
As someone in their late teens who's been playing games since i could talk, there's never been a game that has resonated with me like life is strange has. Dontnod brings the emotional and misunderstood ephemeral halcyon days of late teenagehood to life in life is strange. The uncertainty of everything, finding one's self, little moments that you'll remember forever, wasted chances and time, and events that you can't seem to recover from. Life is strange captures all of these things brilliantly and effortlessly; with engrossing and breathtaking art direction and visuals, a soundtrack that laments the game's atmoshpere and story better than any game released in the last decade, and characters that force you to care for them.
Max: a quiet, introverted photographer willing to take on the world, but needing that extra push to get there.
Chloe: a brash, stubborn girl that's stuck and unhappy with her life. Through these two the story grows from just another game, to a beautiful narrative that's up there with any story across any medium.
In the era of disappointing aaa titles, failed IPs, and wasted potential; dontnod brings a very special game that defies all expectations, transcends it's medium, and stands as the best game i've ever played.
You'll cry, you'll laugh, you'll wish you had played this sooner, and you'll cry some more.

Most games have a learning curve based around mastery of gameplay mechanics, improving reflexes and situational awareness, or problem solving. KSP is an altogether different beast: you'll need to learn orbital mechanics and some basic rocket science to succeed, but unlike most games, this knowledge is directly applicable to (and derived from) real life situations.
Building rockets is hard. Getting rockets into space is harder. Landing your Kerbals on the Mun, visiting different planets, and bringing them back alive is a singular achievment. Yet KSP never makes the learning process tedious; miserable failures - usually explosive in nature - often elicit laughter and joy, and every mistake is an opportunity to learn something new.
Despite being early access, KSP is remarkably polished, and each update adds meaningful, useful content. The developers are engaged with the community to a terrific extent and the community itself is among the best around. There are mods for just about everything, in case the core game ever starts to get stale.
You can't go wrong with Kerbal Space Program. It's a wonderful, gorgeous game.

I'm by no means an expert, but I've played enough to land more than a couple of these tenacious green frog-men where they were never supposed to walk, so I feel at liberty to share my thoughts.
There are very few games like this, probably no other. There's no real goal set here, no objectives or hand-holding or guides or anything. You're really just left to your own devices to do what you want to do with what you have and figure out a way to pay for it.
AND IT FEELS TERIFFIC. You want to put yourself on the Mun? You can do that. You wanna blow all your starter cash on rockets designed deliberately faulty so as to crash them down on your own HQ? You can do that too. The game won't stop you, you just have to make it work for you.

This is like a Zen Garden... in Space.
The lack of clearly defined goals and objectives and the virtually endless possibilities makes this the open-world heir of minecraft. In this regard there is no better game to compare Kerbal Space Program to.
However, this is a simulation, and a rather serious one while we are at it. Of course you won't have nearly as much challenge as a NASA engineer designing rockets, but don't think this is something you jump right into like an arcade game. It will demand you to learn from other players or by trial-and-error. The latter can be frustrating sometimes because you might not understand at first why your plane is flipping like crazy, or your rocket can't make it into orbit even though you have all those big tanks on top of that big engine. After a while, words like Periapsis, Center of Lift, Prograde, Gravity Turn, delta-V, Specific Impulse and many others become second nature and there is no denying it is quite satisfying to know you learned all that stuff playing a game. You will feel slightly smug when watching footage of rockets launching into space and actually understanding all the technical lingo; all because of this amazing little game. And don't worry, even if you do "everything" the game has to offer, there is an amazing modding community that puts out incredible mods that'll keep the game fresh and interesting no matter how experienced you are.
There is hardly anything to complain about. It is fun; it is developed by dedicated individuals that update and support it constantly; it has an amazing community and virtually endless gameplay. It is a bit overwhelming to learn your way around it, but there is hardly anything more rewarding than mastering the concepts required by this game's mechanics. If you are remotely into anything space themed, this game is a must. If you are into science and engineering this game is for you. If you are into bizarre creations blowing up in espectacular ways, go for it. If you want to learn rocket-science without even noticing it, look no further.
Final remaks: Best money I ever spent on a game.

Kerbal Space Program is a simulation of modern and past space programs.  You take control of little green men, Kerbals, and try to do whatever it is you decide to do with them.  If you want to reach space,  you can do that.  Do you want to crash rockets into the sun?  Can do that too.  Try to put a flag on every planet in the know solar system?  Can be done.
Modding makes the game even more fun as you can add more parts or gameplay mechanics to the game.  Want a life support system?  There is one.  Want to fly remote control ships with Line of sight required?  There is one.  Harvest resources and make a space program that is green-centric?  There is one.  Want to shoot lasers and missles at stuff?  There is one.
There is no multi-player however but it is to be expected with a game that has time controls.  You don't want to run the game for a year just so you can get closer to a planet.
Kerbal Space Program is a game you should really play.  Try the Demo, see for yourself.

This is like a Zen Garden... in Space.
The lack of clearly defined goals and objectives and the virtually endless possibilities makes this the open-world heir of minecraft. In this regard there is no better game to compare Kerbal Space Program to.
However, this is a simulation, and a rather serious one while we are at it. Of course you won't have nearly as much challenge as a NASA engineer designing rockets, but don't think this is something you jump right into like an arcade game. It will demand you to learn from other players or by trial-and-error. The latter can be frustrating sometimes because you might not understand at first why your plane is flipping like crazy, or your rocket can't make it into orbit even though you have all those big tanks on top of that big engine. After a while, words like Periapsis, Center of Lift, Prograde, Gravity Turn, delta-V, Specific Impulse and many others become second nature and there is no denying it is quite satisfying to know you learned all that stuff playing a game. You will feel slightly smug when watching footage of rockets launching into space and actually understanding all the technical lingo; all because of this amazing little game. And don't worry, even if you do "everything" the game has to offer, there is an amazing modding community that puts out incredible mods that'll keep the game fresh and interesting no matter how experienced you are.
There is hardly anything to complain about. It is fun; it is developed by dedicated individuals that update and support it constantly; it has an amazing community and virtually endless gameplay. It is a bit overwhelming to learn your way around it, but there is hardly anything more rewarding than mastering the concepts required by this game's mechanics. If you are remotely into anything space themed, this game is a must. If you are into science and engineering this game is for you. If you are into bizarre creations blowing up in espectacular ways, go for it. If you want to learn rocket-science without even noticing it, look no further.
Final remaks: Best money I ever spent on a game.

This is an awesome game! It's a space simulator sandbox. You can launch probes into deep space, build insane rockets to fly into the sun, or build a dune buggy and just drive around the kerbin launch pad. There's a lot of creativity to throw into your game. When you start adding mods into this game, it gets even more intense. You can have your rocket autopilot itself to the "mun" or land. You can create a transformer (pretty much) and have it invade another nearby planet. It takes a bit of learning to get into the game. However, they have a few basic tutorials in-game and a plethora of them outside of the game. Once you do get the hang of it, it's fantastic.
There's a career mode with skill tree progression. You basically have to work your way up the ladder of greatness. This is done by science experiments, reporting, exploring, sampling, scientific stuff, and safely bringing it all back (or transmitting) to your home base on Kerbin. This is the mode that I enjoy using the most.
If you just want to jump into the game and have everything given to you, then the sandbox mode is probably what you'd go with. I had started with it at first, but found the career mode was quite a bit more fun to play with. In sandbox mode, you can basically do the same things you would in career mode, but without any scientific cost to research anything and no credits needed (future version) to purchase parts.
The only thing I have an issue with is that it is 32 bit. With all the mods you would want in this game, you would need to tweak them all a bit to cut down on memory useage due to it being 32 bit. If not, you will crash your game at certain points. I really hope this game goes 64 bit soon.
Running the game vanilla with no mods at all is smooth as butter. If you like flight sims, space sims, sandbox games to build things in a persistent world, then you should check this out. One of the mods that made this game so much better was the Texture Replacer and a few packs that replaced the sky, planets, kerbins, and clouds. It gave the game more life than it already had.
On a side note, they do have a mod for multiplayer, but it is a little buggy.

I don't typically play these kinds of games, but I actually became quite interested in it about half way through the first episode. The characters are realistic and the storyline actually has me interested in purchasing further episodes. The characters and story represent a very popular genre, coming of age, which is a genre I actively avoid in stories, but my desire to finish puzzles and see what kind of consequences unfolded from my actions actually overcame all that. As a whole, I generally disliked most every character, which in my case is a very good thing. They're all quite human and I felt as though I was interacting with actual people, people who who are hiding both good and bad qualities. As a story driven game goes, this one is quite top of the line, and the added ability to completely shift the narrative in various ways, makes it all the more engaging.
That being said, it does have a few quirks which aren't inherently a part of the game itself but a limit of its engine. Character expressions and character movements are in two completely different leagues. At moments I felt like some characters' body language was above average and very realistic, while other times, the movements came out stilted and robotic, not matching up with the dialogue at all.
Facial expressions on the other hand were sub par, which is unfortunate, considering the number of highly emotional scenes in the game. It looked as though most characters felt neutral about what was occuring around them, their expressions remaining dead or only changing just enough to show suspicion or suprise.
As a whole, I would definitely recommend Life Is Strange if you're into deep storytelling and branching narrative. It definitely delivers, and its story is engaging enough to keep you playing.

I definitely recommend this game to everyone who bothers with a great story to be put into the shoes of.

I don't typically play these kinds of games, but I actually became quite interested in it about half way through the first episode. The characters are realistic and the storyline actually has me interested in purchasing further episodes. The characters and story represent a very popular genre, coming of age, which is a genre I actively avoid in stories, but my desire to finish puzzles and see what kind of consequences unfolded from my actions actually overcame all that. As a whole, I generally disliked most every character, which in my case is a very good thing. They're all quite human and I felt as though I was interacting with actual people, people who who are hiding both good and bad qualities. As a story driven game goes, this one is quite top of the line, and the added ability to completely shift the narrative in various ways, makes it all the more engaging.
That being said, it does have a few quirks which aren't inherently a part of the game itself but a limit of its engine. Character expressions and character movements are in two completely different leagues. At moments I felt like some characters' body language was above average and very realistic, while other times, the movements came out stilted and robotic, not matching up with the dialogue at all.
Facial expressions on the other hand were sub par, which is unfortunate, considering the number of highly emotional scenes in the game. It looked as though most characters felt neutral about what was occuring around them, their expressions remaining dead or only changing just enough to show suspicion or suprise.
As a whole, I would definitely recommend Life Is Strange if you're into deep storytelling and branching narrative. It definitely delivers, and its story is engaging enough to keep you playing.

Wow! This game is head and shoulders over any other game I've played, and I've played a lot:
- Role playing is central, but it's not a conventional RPG: no active combat, no monster-riddled dungeons, no looting and levelling. Just amazing story and character development.
- The game is fairly linear, yet somehow doesn't feel like it. There's just enough control and decision making to keep things riveting.
- It's a mystery, but where the main character in most mysteries is a disinterested third party, this main character here is in the middle of everything, both physically and emotionally.
- Once you accept the premise of being able to rewind time, the rest of the story is all too believable, as are all of the characters. Although I'm far from being 18, and not female, as many of the characters are, I had no trouble feeling what the characters were feeling.
- You have to make a lot of choices, and some of them are very gut-wrenching. All are believable. After finishing the story last night, I did not sleep well.
The upshot of all of this is that you are forced to do a lot of self-examination: "What would I really do in this sort of situation?". This can be disturbing, and possibly even dangerous to someone already in an emotionally fragile state. The authors recognized this, and inserted a message between episodes offering a help line to call if you need it. This is not tech support!
I have very few criticisms:
- The polygons in the graphics are quite apparent. However, the overall feeling makes this not a problem - the graphics are beautiful anyway.
- Many of the puzzles require you to rewind time. In itself, this is not a problem. The problem is that sometimes certain physical events are not rewound in the process (providing the otherwise unavailable solution to the puzzle), and there seems to be no logic as to how and when this will happen - you just have to experiment. In some cases, but not all, the game prompts you to try this. Being lazy, I reverted to a walkthough for several of thse. (Thank you, walkthough writers!)
- Two major decision points in the game, indirectly determining whether a significant character lives or dies, cannot be rewound. The only way to get a different result is to replay the entire episode. While this is closer to real life, it seems inconsistent with the rest of the game, and an unnecessary frustration.
Bottom line: the good points completely overwhelm the bad, I'd love to see more games like this, but don't expect to.
My rating: 9.5/10

- Role playing is central, but it's not a conventional RPG: no active combat, no monster-riddled dungeons, no looting and levelling. Just amazing story and character development.
- The game is fairly linear, yet somehow doesn't feel like it. There's just enough control and decision making to keep things riveting.
- It's a mystery, but where the main character in most mysteries is a disinterested third party, this main character here is in the middle of everything, both physically and emotionally.
- Once you accept the premise of being able to rewind time, the rest of the story is all too believable, as are all of the characters. Although I'm far from being 18, and not female, as many of the characters are, I had no trouble feeling what the characters were feeling.
- You have to make a lot of choices, and some of them are very gut-wrenching. All are believable. After finishing the story last night, I did not sleep well.
The upshot of all of this is that you are forced to do a lot of self-examination: "What would I really do in this sort of situation?". This can be disturbing, and possibly even dangerous to someone already in an emotionally fragile state. The authors recognized this, and inserted a message between episodes offering a help line to call if you need it. This is not tech support!
I have very few criticisms:
- The polygons in the graphics are quite apparent. However, the overall feeling makes this not a problem - the graphics are beautiful anyway.
- Many of the puzzles require you to rewind time. In itself, this is not a problem. The problem is that sometimes certain physical events are not rewound in the process (providing the otherwise unavailable solution to the puzzle), and there seems to be no logic as to how and when this will happen - you just have to experiment. In some cases, but not all, the game prompts you to try this. Being lazy, I reverted to a walkthough for several of thse. (Thank you, walkthough writers!)
- Two major decision points in the game, indirectly determining whether a significant character lives or dies, cannot be rewound. The only way to get a different result is to replay the entire episode. While this is closer to real life, it seems inconsistent with the rest of the game, and an unnecessary frustration.
Bottom line: the good points completely overwhelm the bad, I'd love to see more games like this, but don't expect to.

Kerbal Space Program is a must for anyone who loves space and space exploration. The game features realistic physics and surreal views. The systems are complicated and accurate enough that PHD canidates in Areospace Engineering, Astronomy, and Physics love to play it, yet it is simple enough for an eight year old to figure out and enjoy. The game gives you the opportunities to create elaborate single stage to orbit space planes, massive rockets with twenty stages and enough Delta-V to leave the solar system, or a science lab space station. If you can imagine it and figure out how to launch it, you can build it!
This game encourages you to learn by catastrophic failure. While it's reamarkably satisfying to get your eight stage mosnter into orbit, it's just as entertaining watching it fall to peices on the launchpad. When this happens, you get to figure out how to fix it (More Struts!) and get the satisfaction of seeing it finally launch in one peice, only for it to run out of fuel on a sub-orbital trajectory. Now you start over until you get it it right and enjoy every second.
This game also makes you want to learn about space flight. You quickly learn why pretty much every space movie and game can't work because of real physics. You learn what a geosynchronous orbit it and why its important. You learn about terms like periapse and apoapse. You learn about hoffman transfer orbits and hundreds of other terms that I would have never thought of prior to playing this game. However, learning about these things doesn't seem like the hard boring things you learn in physics class, you get to quickly put these things into practice so they make much more sense. This game tricks you into learning while you're having fun.
Another plus to this game is the asthetics. The game is beautiful. The sunsets, eclipse, landscapes, planets and lots more have all had a lot of time put into them. Some aspects are quite cartoonish by design, but the game lookes reamarkable. I have occasionally set up lauches in such a way where I can see the sunrise or an eclipse or some other event just for the view.
Anotther amazing aspect of this game is the wonderful modding community. The game developers encourage modding and as a result there have been some amazing new features added to the game. The are mods that add new parts and mods that  remodle things like reentry (making it potentially deadly) and mods that make planets more pleasing to look at. There are mods for alsmot anything hosted on the official
site. (The official mod site, Kerbal Spaceport, has been shut down and now redirects to the Curse site. For now this is the new official mod site for KSP.)
I gave this game a solid 8/10 when I first played it and it's earned a new rank with every update since. It's somewhere around 14/10 now. It's well worth the $26.99. Don't believe me? Try the free demo. It has cut out most of the parts and planets but you can still get to the moon and back without any trouble. If you've read this far then rest assured that KSP will make it into your top favorite games in no time at all.

This starts off so.... slowly.... I...... very........ nearly........ quit...............................................
But I persevered.
If you want a technical review this is not it. This is just some emotional stuff about how it 'feels'.
There's a heavy emphasis on cinematics and photography, angles, framing, compostion - in theory and practice.
There's also a heavy emphasis on cool white pop culture, refernces to cult TV, literature, movies, art, (Six Feet Under, Quantum Leap, Buffy, Twin Peaks, X-Files, Ray Bradbury, Koushun Takami, Annie Leibovitz, Dali, Robert Cornelius, Diane Arbus(!), Ginsberg, Richard Avedon, Wolfe. Even Gaiman, Hobb, Zimmer Bradley, etc, etc. It almost feels like a lesson in 'how to be cool like a geek' or nerd or dork or whatever it is supposed to be.
So, all that trendy 'buy our game, we're really cool white people' crap aside.
This thing has some intensely dark themes: bullying, guns at school, verbal and physical abuse, sexual assault, teen pregnancy, lying, manipulation, revenge, drugging and, of course, (the one every human on earth has experienced) ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with authority. And there are so many moral and ethical decisions that go right along with those themes. I haven't had a hard time deciding what to do (yet), morally speaking, but I'm 35, I'm cool with my choices, I've had 35 years to figure stuff out. For someone a heck of a lot younger this could be really hard, trying to understand the impact and implications. There's an impossible never-ending butterfly effect just waiting to unleash hell on your backside. It's probably a good 'lesson'.
And that's just the first episode.
Yes it feels slow, but as they say in the game 'you're young, you've got all the time in the world' (literally, she's like 19 or something) so explore everywhere, double check things, it's slow but in the end it's worth it. I've tried really hard to not rewind any decisions, I figure if it were real life I'd only get one chance so let's see how it plays out. If it sucks I can play it again.
Though, I hate Max, whingey nosey wannabe geek. All she does is goes through other peoples things, fidning out everyones highly private stuff, not cool. I feel like the devs tried too hard with making her like 'cool' stuff and she just comes off as a poseur.

This is by far one of the best story-centered games I have played in a long time. The episodic approach to the game allows for deep emersion into both the storyline and characters in a unique way that traditional first-person storytelling cannot. I went through all five episodes in a few days; once started, the story compells to you complete each episode. It just won't let go of you until you do.
In my mind, the only barrier to experiencing the emotional highs and lows through the course of gameplay is the abbility to literally step into the game. I do love the fact that there are still so many questions that are unaswered in the game (I don't think it was ever the writers' intent to provide answers in a concrete manner). How did Max get her power? Does she still retain them after the story's ending(s)? What happens to all the alternate realities she's possibly created?
My hope is that this story continues in some manner; a difference place, different time -- same characters? Until such a time, there's also the fact that it has an awesome OST.
Play this game. It doesn't disappoint.

Its a simulator more than a game, although the developers are continuing to add features which bring it closer to being a game. I used to say that its Minecraft in Spaaaaaace! It still is, in the sandbox mode, where you start off with access to all the parts, and you can build whatever your heart desires. The career mode places restrictions on access to parts, which is better for a new player, since it prevents them from being overwhelmed by all the choices, and teaches the basics of designing a functional rocket.
This falls in the same category as Spore to me, where through playing the game and progressing in the game one inadvertently gains a practical knowledge of the underlying principles being utilized in these games.  For Spore, it was evolution, and for KSP it is orbital mechanics, and to a wider degree a knowledge of gravity, forces, inertia, or how to do stuff in space!

This starts off so.... slowly.... I...... very........ nearly........ quit...............................................
But I persevered.
If you want a technical review this is not it. This is just some emotional stuff about how it 'feels'.
There's a heavy emphasis on cinematics and photography, angles, framing, compostion - in theory and practice.
There's also a heavy emphasis on cool white pop culture, refernces to cult TV, literature, movies, art, (Six Feet Under, Quantum Leap, Buffy, Twin Peaks, X-Files, Ray Bradbury, Koushun Takami, Annie Leibovitz, Dali, Robert Cornelius, Diane Arbus(!), Ginsberg, Richard Avedon, Wolfe. Even Gaiman, Hobb, Zimmer Bradley, etc, etc. It almost feels like a lesson in 'how to be cool like a geek' or nerd or dork or whatever it is supposed to be.
So, all that trendy 'buy our game, we're really cool white people' crap aside.
This thing has some intensely dark themes: bullying, guns at school, verbal and physical abuse, sexual assault, teen pregnancy, lying, manipulation, revenge, drugging and, of course, (the one every human on earth has experienced) ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with authority. And there are so many moral and ethical decisions that go right along with those themes. I haven't had a hard time deciding what to do (yet), morally speaking, but I'm 35, I'm cool with my choices, I've had 35 years to figure stuff out. For someone a heck of a lot younger this could be really hard, trying to understand the impact and implications. There's an impossible never-ending butterfly effect just waiting to unleash hell on your backside. It's probably a good 'lesson'.
And that's just the first episode.
Yes it feels slow, but as they say in the game 'you're young, you've got all the time in the world' (literally, she's like 19 or something) so explore everywhere, double check things, it's slow but in the end it's worth it. I've tried really hard to not rewind any decisions, I figure if it were real life I'd only get one chance so let's see how it plays out. If it sucks I can play it again.
Though, I hate Max, whingey nosey wannabe geek. All she does is goes through other peoples things, fidning out everyones highly private stuff, not cool. I feel like the devs tried too hard with making her like 'cool' stuff and she just comes off as a poseur.

I have never felt so emotionally connected to characters in any other game, or so connected to their story.
The way the story was told was so immersive and interesting, I literally couldn't stop playing. I started and finished the first 3 episodes in 12 hours straight, 4pm to 4am. I played this game for the first time longer than I have played most games in a year. That's a hella big deal for me. But even if I tried to stop, I know I wouldn't be able to. It really is that good.
The characters themselves were so well created and had so much depth and development through the five episodes, especially Max for the latter. I loved, LOVED, Max and Chloe and how their amazing friendship returned, and turned into something deeper than just friendship. They became inseparable and unbreakable; that not even death or fate could keep them apart. I made sure of that.
This game, this experience, made me burst out laughing and burst into tears (which isn't a common occurrence). It had me staring at a screen trying to decide the right thing to do, my hair in fists as I tried to make the right choice, only to scream in frustration in later episodes as I realised I should have chosen different. I lost sleep over this game, not just playing it but thinking about it. During the day when I couldn't play it, I would find my thoughts drifting to it, I would drop out of conversations only to realise the other person was waiting for me to respond. I neglected my friends for 3 days, they asked me if I was okay by the second day. I told them the truth, no. This game completely consumed me.
And I loved every second of it.
I feel so privileged to be able to play this game for those 23 amazing hours. Anyone who is debating whether to buy this game like I was, or anyone who doesn't think it's 'their thing', I beg you, buy this game and play it. It is your thing. Soak up every moment, every second until you finish it. And then, like me, if that’s not enough, play it again. And again. Because trust me, this game will never leave you, even if you want it to. But really, why would you?
I know it never will leave me, and I am 100% okay with that.

PROS:
Modding support.
The developers encourage modding and the modding community for this game is pretty big. While modding extends a game's life and increases enjoyment you can easily have fun with the stock unmodified game. I would reccomend Engineer, MechJeb and Kerbal Attachment System to start.
Easy to start.
You don't need to know a thing about real world rocketry to play this. There are in-game tutorials for most of the game aspects and the community has written out details about the advanced stuff.
(Mostly) Friendly community.
While every community has its share of "not nice" people, KSP has an invested fan base who will help and support each other. Don't know about a certain thing in the game? You won't be ridiculed for not knowing everything.
Quicksaving and reverting are enabled.
Afraid to take some of the Kerbal crew you have grown attached to on a dangerous mission? Have no fear, saves are here! F5 quicksaves the game while F9 reloads the quicksave. Need to take a few tries before you successfully do a powered landing? Just quicksave. Crash terribly before you had the chance to save? Revert to the launchpad. For people who don't like to quicksave it is 100% optional.
Not stuck to one flight.
Don't feel like time accelerating while waiting for your deep space probe's course correction? No problem! Just switch to another ship, your probe will still make progress. A mod called "Kerbal Alarm Clock" is great for letting you know when your ships need to be paid attention to.
NASA street cred.
For KSP's 23.5 update they actually worked with NASA to add things to the game. While the game isn't 100% realistic you can tell that the developers are balancing realism with unrealistic things.
Demo available.
More games should come with a "try before you buy" feature and demos are a great way of giving that. If you are really unsure about if the game is for you, get the demo.
Rewarding gameplay.
Knowing the ship you created landed on the Mun, or even made it into Kerbin orbit, is a great feeling. Being able to bring your crew home safely is also great. I remember my first attempt at a crewed landing on the Mun. I didn't have enough fuel to land on the Mun so I sent an unmanned ship to refuel it using the KAS mod. After refueling I landed on the Mun after several tries. I planted my flag and launched back into orbit only to realize that I didn't have enough fuel to get back so I rendezvoused with the refueling vessel. When I finally made it back to Kerbin and splash downed in the ocean it was a great feeling.
CONS:
Not everyone can pick up and play.
Some people will not be able to figure out the game and will think it is too complicated. There is online material to help with understanding the game but that might not be enough.
==
I have spent more time on this game than any other game. I enjoy it that much. More than half my time is spent designing vessels but I am learning more and more. Often I will not have played the game for a few days when I feel it pulling me back in. I definitely recommend this game.

I'm not sure what I would say to convince anyone to want to play this game, because it seems to me that you either hear about KSP or watch a video and immediately want to play it, or you do those things and it does not interest you. This is very much a simulator for realistic Newtonian physics and orbital mechanics, with some cute frumpy alien creatures goggling in wonder at the universe thrown in to make you smile.
I've played a whole lot of this game. Several orders of magnitude more than it would appear from my profile because I originally purchased the non-steam version (for easier Linux support). I recently purchased a second steam copy, if that says anything about the game. I've played it on all three supported platforms and it works perfectly, even under Slackware Linux. From that I assume it's very distro agnostic.
When I started out with the game, the only mode was the Sandbox mode. This can be a little overwhelming to the uninitiated due to the sheer volume of parts to play with. Since then the Career mode has been added, which limits the parts that you can use and requires you to run missions and gain science to research new parts. This allows you to slowly gain an understanding of all of the parts, and is something that really enhanced my enjoyment of the game.
In the end, you get out of the game what you're willing to put into it. Even in the career mode, the only objective you have is "gain science", so it's up to you to conceive of missions that take you to new places to do that. The game is very much not a guided experience.
Do note however that there are a few short training missions that give you the basics of how to build rockets and fly them. What you do with that knowledge is up to you.

I can't say anything about this game that hasn't already been said so i'll tell you the story of my first trip to the moon(mun).
After managing to get Rodrod Kermin into orbit and getting him home again in one piece(unlike his craft) my space program created an even more ambitious goal.  Land a kerbin on the Mun.  Naturally our most successful kerbalnaut was chosen to make this giant leap for kerbalkind.  Rodrod was so excited for this mission that he never inspected his craft prior to launch.  Placing his trust, and life, in the hands of the engineers(me) would be his undoing.
Rodrod Kerman launched the Luna 1 spacecraft on a beautiful clear day.  All conditions were optimal.  Liftoff was smooth and the craft was easily controlled.  A gravity turn was started at 10km altitude till the apoapsis reached an alttude of 80km.  A long burn was performed about a minute before reaching the apoapsis to circularize the orbit.  Now in a stable orbit Rodrod conducted a few spacewalks to collect science data which was then transmitted back to the space centre to unlock better rocket parts.
Rodrod, eager as ever, plotted out a course to the Moon.  Not a simple task since you can't just point towards the moon and hit the gas.  You need to arrive at your destination at the same time that your destination gets there.  In space location is a very relative thing.  A hoffman transfer manouver was performed bringing us into a stable low orbit of the moon.  Rodrod peered through the capsule window at what would be his new home.  A return trip just wasn't in the cards for my low tech level at this point in the game.
Rodrod then burned the last of his fuel in order to slowly decay his orbit; slowly bringing him towards the surface.  Once completed the moon slowly became larger and larger till it was all he could see through his capsule window.  Realizing the moment of truth was at hand he grabbed the checklist and gave it a once over.
...
-Circularize moon orbit
-Burn retrograde till trajectory touches the moon surface
-Deploy parachutes
...
Rodrod: Umm, Kerbal Space Centre come in.  Someone has been messing with checklists again.  Remind me what to do to keep the landing from being a crash.
KSC: Use the parachutes
Rodrod: Why did I have to bring a spacesuit if there is air on the moon?
KSC: Are you feeling ok Rodrod?  Obviously there is no air on the moon.
Rodrod:  Then how are the parachutes supposed to work?
KSC:...
Rodrod gave his life for the knowledge that parachutes need air to work.

Before getting into the review, you need to be a gamer that loves the narrative of games because the gameplay here is pretty basic like the Telltale Games, but if you are a person who can get involved into characters and emotion driven story, this is a must buy.
Pro: The graphics here aren't there to steal the show or anything but they all had up to the charm of the game. I know I'm gonna compare this again to the Telltale Games (honestly what do you want me to compare it with) but the facial expressions and the movements of characters seems WAY less clunky and fake in Life is Strange. But we got to speak of the elephant in the room which is the story and damn: your first impression of the game will leave a bad aftertaste because of the cheesiness of the setting and characters (the ♥♥♥♥♥, the nerd, the cool teacher...) but don't let this fool you because the most interesting stuff comes later.
For me, the game really clicked in Episode 2 because the game makes you realize your actions really have consequences even if some are scripted but they're still nice to see unfold and leave in a genuine state of WTF sometimes (some will say everything is predictable and I admit 75% of the game is but the movies we see nowadays are too and they're still fun, where is the bad in that). After this, the game just keeps getting better and better until the final moment. For some the end of the game was a total let down, but I saw it coming miles away because of hints throughout the episodes and I survived Mass Effect 3 ending, sooooo I can survive any ending now.
Con: When I said the gameplay was pretty basic, I meant it: you move around you click a bunch until you find what you need and cutscenes/choices and next scene. Even if it's just point and click mecanics GOD is it tedious sometimes (Chloe **** your bottles) and you will lose a lot of time in a completely not fun way. In some cases, the search takes so long the character starts to give hints and you will lose your patience as I did. In other cases, you will resolve problems that in no way a normal human being would solve this way (yeah, cutting live wires.. you're dead) and your rewind power will come in handy because you won't understand Max's logic sometimes. Also, they're a lot of boring conversations with uninteresting characters in this game and choices that end up in nothingness that will make wonder why it is even in it.
Verdict: For any fans of great story even though the teenage cheesiness can make you roll your eyes at times and the gameplay is pretty meh, it is an absolute gorgeous game. If you can see through its flaws, it is a game you will remember and recommend to your friends just to share the experience.

This game is without a doubt the best game I have ever played. And that is a big statement for me to make. But it isn't really just a game, it's an experience; one that makes you seriously think and makes you conflicted, questioning your own morals. It delved into strong themes, many which I could relate with, or at least understand on a strong level. I have never felt so emotionally connected to characters in any other game, or so connected to their story.
The way the story was told was so immersive and interesting, I literally couldn't stop playing. I started and finished the first 3 episodes in 12 hours straight, 4pm to 4am. I played this game for the first time longer than I have played most games in a year. That's a hella big deal for me. But even if I tried to stop, I know I wouldn't be able to. It really is that good.
The characters themselves were so well created and had so much depth and development through the five episodes, especially Max for the latter. I loved, LOVED, Max and Chloe and how their amazing friendship returned, and turned into something deeper than just friendship. They became inseparable and unbreakable; that not even death or fate could keep them apart. I made sure of that.
This game, this experience, made me burst out laughing and burst into tears (which isn't a common occurrence). It had me staring at a screen trying to decide the right thing to do, my hair in fists as I tried to make the right choice, only to scream in frustration in later episodes as I realised I should have chosen different. I lost sleep over this game, not just playing it but thinking about it. During the day when I couldn't play it, I would find my thoughts drifting to it, I would drop out of conversations only to realise the other person was waiting for me to respond. I neglected my friends for 3 days, they asked me if I was okay by the second day. I told them the truth, no. This game completely consumed me.
And I loved every second of it.
I feel so privileged to be able to play this game for those 23 amazing hours. Anyone who is debating whether to buy this game like I was, or anyone who doesn't think it's 'their thing', I beg you, buy this game and play it. It is your thing. Soak up every moment, every second until you finish it. And then, like me, if that’s not enough, play it again. And again. Because trust me, this game will never leave you, even if you want it to. But really, why would you?
I know it never will leave me, and I am 100% okay with that.

SInce you can get most of the positive points in other reviews, let's get to the part where I say what I don't particulary like. And why it's a 10/10 nonetheless, no spoilers.
People that dislike LiS often say that the most of the game's plot is something a sensitive and insecure 16 year old French male must think of american highschools. And my inner 16 yo sensitive French male must definitely, but not happily agree. that they do have a point at times, when he's not busy making sure his fringe stays in place.
You have the b*tchy popular girl and her minions, the nerd that is SO SECRETLY in love with you, rebel girl that you adore, sporty ars*hole and his friends that beat the other chubby nerds when they are not busy insulting each other, and for your confirmation, I'm not reviewing a Glee season, we're still in Life is Strange universe.
But I like what the game's doing with that, it seems to be self-aware enough to juggle with those cliches in a manner that places you gently in the comfort zone of something known, TURNING YOUR COMFORT ZONE UPSIDE DOWN IN EPISODE 3.
The game has a few major plot twists, few subplots that you are craving to learn about at some point, more than enough stuff to read in the journal to put all the missing pieces together yourself.
Do not expect Bioshock* / Interstellar** type of mind blow, but then again, I won't be comparing a fridge to a microwave in terms of which one is better to wash your clothes in, as the game is doing perfectly fine storywise in it's own genre.
Thing definitely worth mentioning is music, as my inner sensitive 16 yo French male was enjoying it to the fullest. If you put your beard away, and leave mascunility in other pair of jeans to actually admit that you enjoy it, not being ashamed of your friends judging your newly discovered love to sad guitar indie tracks, you are going to have a good time.
The dissapointing factor, is that you are left with a binary choice at the end of the 5th season, but by the time you get there, you will discover you got so emotinally attached to some of the characters, that belive me, it would not matter, because it would be the hardest choice of all.
If you disagree with what I wrote, my inner sensitive 16 yo french male would not be bothered, as nobody understands him anyway. The end.

A space exploration simulator that makes you want more.
Kerbal space program (KSP) allows you to built your own rocket from many different parts and send it out to space and distant planets/moons. The steering of the rocket is completely up to you (no autopilot) and that makes you truly appreciate the difficulties of flying space rockets manually. You will blow up a couple of rockets in your first 10 minutes of the game purely by accident.
Not only can you fly to distant planets/moons, you can also fly out to asteroids, capture them and bring them in an orbit around a planet.
KSP has a great modding community with a lot of mods that extend the many, many days of game time that you will spend.
The realism of the orbital mechanics is stunning, however, for people who are not good at physics it can be a bit of a learning curve. Although there is a bit of a learning curve, if you hang in there KSP will definitely introduce orbital mechanics in the best of ways: through a fun gaming experience.
KSP is prone to updates and new content regularly pops up (about once every 1-3 months).

One of the most engaging series I have played in a long, long time...
In the first five minutes of the game, I thought I was playing some dumb girl who got powers and turns to superhero. By the end of the first episode, I thought it was worse; it is about a dumb girl with powers and got involved in some stereotypical anime stuff.
The second episode then took me really into the game; I was able to make more choices and see how my previous choices affect the current and future choices (I saw the warning before the start of the game told me so, but I was still amazed at how it goes).
When it came to the third and fourth episode, my emotions were brought up and down so intensely that I felt my everyday life was affected. The start of the fourth episode was what broke me, and I had to take a day of leave from work just to recover myself.
Then it came to the fifth episode where it is exactly like how many Square Enix games come to end; a major ♥♥♥♥♥torm (in this case no♥♥♥♥♥♥ with mind-pounding, everybody-saying-goodbye kind of "finale" before you take the final shot (hehe). I would say while it provides a closure for all the decisions you have made, it COULD use a little more details and in-depth consideration for the endings.
For example (without spoiling anything), Max would probably write a thing or two regarding the endings, state how she felt about it (or did I miss it?). Alternatively, perhaps the developers could let us go into the perspective of each major character and watch how they are affected by Max.
Nonetheless, I would very much to see an epilogue, considering how this is one of the more emotionally-intense games and the endings do not serve sufficient satisfaction to the community.
If you have 24 hours of game time, play all 5 episodes, preferably leaving a night after each episode for your mind to settle down.

One of the most engaging series I have played in a long, long time...
In the first five minutes of the game, I thought I was playing some dumb girl who got powers and turns to superhero. By the end of the first episode, I thought it was worse; it is about a dumb girl with powers and got involved in some stereotypical anime stuff.
The second episode then took me really into the game; I was able to make more choices and see how my previous choices affect the current and future choices (I saw the warning before the start of the game told me so, but I was still amazed at how it goes).
When it came to the third and fourth episode, my emotions were brought up and down so intensely that I felt my everyday life was affected. The start of the fourth episode was what broke me, and I had to take a day of leave from work just to recover myself.
Then it came to the fifth episode where it is exactly like how many Square Enix games come to end; a major ♥♥♥♥♥torm (in this case no♥♥♥♥♥♥ with mind-pounding, everybody-saying-goodbye kind of "finale" before you take the final shot (hehe). I would say while it provides a closure for all the decisions you have made, it COULD use a little more details and in-depth consideration for the endings.
For example (without spoiling anything), Max would probably write a thing or two regarding the endings, state how she felt about it (or did I miss it?). Alternatively, perhaps the developers could let us go into the perspective of each major character and watch how they are affected by Max.
Nonetheless, I would very much to see an epilogue, considering how this is one of the more emotionally-intense games and the endings do not serve sufficient satisfaction to the community.
If you have 24 hours of game time, play all 5 episodes, preferably leaving a night after each episode for your mind to settle down.
