This game...
I was always hesitant to pick this game up due to it being in episodes, but during the summer sale I decided to bite the bullet and purchase episodes 2-5 due to the amazing reviews that have been left.
From the first episode I was hooked into the story and the mechanics of the game, the characters that developed over the course of the story and the interesting puzzles that you have to face. This game reminded me of the movie 'The Butterfly Effect' and due to the consequences of the butterfly effect and messing with time, you have to carefully think about your actions and what they might lead to. In certain cases, if the immediate outcome isn't something you wanted, you can simply rewind time and try again (or replay the story from a checkpoint in the episodes menu).
At the end of each episode you are presented with a stats list, indicating each of your choices and how many people who played the game also chose each of the outcomes (With the press of a button you can also see your friends choices). Whilst it may not have a ton of replayability, there is still the option to go the completionist route and obtain all the hidden photos by replaying the episodes. You can also play out individual parts of an episode to see what the other choices might have lead to.
This is a game that you can come back to, months after completing it, and just get stuck back in. Never over the course of my playthrough did I get a feeling of boredom or wanting the story to progress that little faster and I feel that this is a perfectly told story with a perfect execution from Dontnod Entertainment

Not only is there no other spacefaring game like Kerbal Space Program, KSP is really unique in the simulation world.
In KSP you are essentially the designer, director, and astronaut crew of a space program. You can design your own type of spacecraft (or, for that matter, aircraft) with multiple stages and many different functions using an array of standardized interchangeable parts. This includes very simple single stage rockets, to massive lifters and space vehicles, rovers, orbital stations, planetary bases, and you can even design and fly re-useable aircraft capable of entering orbit and beyond (known as SSTOs). All of this happens in an imaginary solar system much like the real one, except that everything is 10 times smaller and the distances equally reduced - except the challenge.
You will never forget designing your first spacecraft, getting into orbit the first time, or landing on the Moon (in the sim, the Mun), or sending a probe or crewed vehicle to another planet. The sim is an open sandbox, and people who play it design all kinds of vehicles - every person who plays has their own vision for a spacecraft, every design is practically unique. You can even share your designs with the larger KSP community, or fly a vehicle designed by someone else.
The game has two basic flavors, career mode and sandbox mode. In the latter, all equipment is available - in the former you have to 'earn' new technologies with successful flights and recovery of science. The career mode will be, eventually, the 'game' part of the sim.
That said, the game is still in alpha. There are some annoying bugs that, we are told, will be worked out eventually. For example sometimes during design a spacecraft can get 'bugged' and become useless. There's a stage separator that doesn't work properly which, though a known bug, hasn't been fixed in months. Spaceflight, too, is pretty complex and can be too much for some. There are plenty of mods to assist with design, looks, and flight, but the game doesn't officially support mods.
There are updates to the game about every 3 to 6 weeks, the next one will introduce budgets and contracts to career mode. The game will be close to out of alpha by the next release, and there are plans (and code) to support multiplayer - presumeably people will be able to run KSP servers with up to a certain number of people inhabiting the same world.
I would recommend this game, but the forum staff banned my forum account for having a forum name of a political nature, even though this wasn't against the rules (the name was LTrotsky - which incidentally is a real name for thousands of people in the world today). This suggests some issues with community management.

Score: 9/10
Let me begin by saying that I do not usually write reviews for video games. I am not a very eloquent writer (my punctuation is atrocious) nor exceptionally good at putting my thoughts into text, but I'll try for the sake of this game.
Boiling this game down to it's most influential and important aspects, you would find an emotional rollercoaster of a story showcasing the power of choices on our destiny. This game seeks to show that our lives are defined not only by the big important decisions in our lives but also by the seemingly insignificant as well. I am personally against spoiling anything about this wonderful story, so I will not give any details about the plot or decisions you will face; but just know that I had to make some of the most difficult choices I have ever had to make in a videogame.
I would sometimes sit for minutes straight staring at the screen with the game paused racking my brain to choose the best option; with the most fruitful outcome. I would occasionally turn off the game entirely and do something else to give myself time to contemplate these choices. If this doesn't speak to the amount of investment this game creates in it's story, I don't know what will.
Speaking of investment, I found myself thouroughly invested in nearly every person the main character comes in contact with. They are all very well voiced and their performances help to convey emotions more intimately than any game I've ever played. I am a person who does not easily bond with video-game characters but when it came to some of the most important decisions in the game, I actually felt the gnawing feeling of regret and sorrow depending on who was affected.
The music in this game is also superb, and complements the game as a whole masterfully. Many times I found myself just relaxing and listening to the opening theme before I continued through the game. The music helps make the more intense moments truly nervewracking while during some of the more peaceful moments I wanted to crawl through my screen and join the main character for a relaxing afternoon.
Overall, this game is one of the best I've played in a very long time and really affected me emotionally. Enough so to take my time to write this review. While it may not be the most succinct or well composed review I hope that it will convince others to at least try this game and see what I've written about for themselves. I applaud Square Enix and DONTNOD Entertainment for this wonderful journey and I hope that I will see more titles like this in the future.

... As long as  you are my partner in time."
Life is Strange (LIS) is an episodic game (5 episodes) developed by DONTNOD entertainment and published by Square Enix. The game focuses deeply on human emotions, relations, sacrifice, love, friendship, conspricy, betrayal and bonding between souls. EACH and EVERY decision you make throughout the game has an impact on how the plot/storyline will proceed affecting present, past and future. "Can you actually fight against destiny and fate and emerge victorious?" That's the question LIS ask the players.
-: PLOT:-
LIS takes place during the week of 7th october, 2013 and is told from the perspective of Maxine Caulfield, a shy, introvert American girl whose dream is to become a photographer. In 2008 she along with her family moved to Seattle. She came back to her former hometown Arcadia Bay after 5 years to study photography in Blackwell Academy. The game opens with Max having a nightmare of a storm/tornado wiping out Arcadia Bay!. When she wake up from her nightmare she finds herself in the class attending a lecture. After the class Max has to use the bathroom where she found out that she has this ability to rewind time while trying to save a girl (and succeeded) being shot there by a boy using a gun. That girl was later revealed to be Chloe Price, Max's best friend whom Max has unwillingly abondened for 5 years when she moved to Seattle.
At first Chloe was angry at Max for abondaning her but it takes little time between them to settle all disputes and again becoming best of friends. While spending time with Chloe, Max learns that during her absence from Chloe's life, Chloe has changed significantely. From being a well mannered girl with excellent academic results she was transformed into some sort of "punk" with blue hairs, tattoos and gets involved with smoking, driking, blackmailing, rebelling, drug dealers, debts, guns and whatnot! During Max's absence from her life she made another good friend with Rachel Amber (student of Blackwell Academy) but something strange happened as she has been missing (suddenly dissappeared) from Arcadia Bay for almost 6 months and no one has any clue whatsoever! Chloe was desperate to find her; posting "Missing person posters" around almost in every part of Arcadia Bay. Max decided to help  Chloe in her search. During this period the pair discovered many mysteries and dark side of Arcadia Bay and get to know the motives and ideologies of many people. Also during this time Max made many friends in her High school (although not as close as Chloe) and some unwanted enemies. She always tried to help her friends even she has to use her power.
Due to her frequent use of "Rewind" power, Max is changing the original fate and destiny so much that it is disturbing the balance of nature, realities and timeline. And soon Max realized that changing the original timeflow and reality or altering the present and past can lead to a devastating future and in the end Max has to pay the ultimate price for constantly manipulating time and space.

-: GAMEPLAY:-
Gameplay is simple and straightforward. You will be controlling Max from 3rd person view.The mechanic of rewinding time allows the player to redo any action that has been taken. The player can examine and interact with objects, which enables puzzle solving in the form of fetch quests and making changes to the environment. Items that are collected before time travelling will be kept in the inventory after the fact. The player can explore various locations in the fictional setting of Arcadia Bay and communicate with non-playable characters. Dialogue exchanges can be rewound while branching options are used for conversation. Once an event is reset, the details provided earlier are permitted to avail themselves in the future. In some instances, choices in dialogue will alter and affect the story through short or long-term consequences. For each one of the choices, something good in the short-term could turn out worse later.
-: GRAPHICS:-
Graphics is good. The environment and the world of LIS has an artistic theme. Outdoor settings have vivid blue skies and autumn foliage, with sunlight and shadows cast over the grass and concrete, while the interiors are believably cluttered. Depicting “real life” in games can be difficult since even the best 3D models don’t look like real people, but Life Is Strange does pretty well, especially with the characters who get the most screen time, Max and Chloe. Of note in a game about high school, the artists have done an admirable job depicting different ethnicities and body types. Only complain is bad lip syncing of characters.
-: VOICE ACTING/ SOUNDTRACK:-
Voice acting in LIS is one of the best I have experienced in a long time. The way Chloe's (Ashly Burch) and Max's
(Hannah Telle) character was acted was simply outstanding. Soundtrack is equally good and perfectly fitted according to the situations in the game. Great sound effects, too: snippets of conversation as you walk past other students, birds chirping when you’re outside. This all contributes to a lively world.
-: AWARDS WON:-
These are some notable awards won by LIS...
(1) Golden Joystick Awards : Performance of the Year : Ashly Burch as Chloe.
(2) The Game Awards: Games for change.
(3) Vulture's Top 10 video games of 2015 : 1st position.
(4) Game Developers Choice Awards :	Audience Award : Won.
(5) The Games for Change Awards : Most Significant Impact : Won.
-: OVERALL:-
LIS is one of those rare game that has made a mark upon me. It's an emotional rollercoaster ride for me which made me laugh and cry. The concept of "time travel", "multiverse"(parallel universe), and "rewinding" time is not a common element one could find in every game and LIS executed these things perfectly. Although I felt the endings (which was good) could have been a little better. Anyway I would recommend this game to all the gamers. Try to play the game spoiler free otherwise you might not feel the real emotions and experience this game has to offer.

-: MY PERSONAL RATING:-  9 / 10 (Outstanding).

Now first off i wanna say that this is the first review i have ever written in here on a game.
You play as a teenage girl names Maxine Caulfield (Max short). Max is 18 years old and as of currently she lives with her parents in Seattle, where they moved when she was 13 years old. She then decides to go back to her birth city Arcadia Bay, Oregon to study Photography at Blackwell Academy. This is mainly due to the fact that her idol Mark Jefferson will be tutoring the students in his art at the school.
Then the journey begins. The game begins with max sitting in a classroom, and as your usual teenager (no offence, it's just cliché), she is not really paying attention to class even though Mark is teaching. That day the 7th of October 2013. Max' life changes. She discovers in an event that she has time reversing powers, and this changes her life dramatically (obviously) from here she go on an epic journey as your average akward teenager, but now with what every akward teenager wanted the most during they late teens and start twentys. Time Reversing powers.
Now i could make a lot longer resume of th egame, but o wont do that, since the plot will be so much more interesting if you don't know anything from the beginning.
That being said, this game is unbeliveable. It WILL make you cry, even more than once. I am not the type of person who cry a lot in games or movies, it frankly happens very rarely. But this game got me. It got me good. The story is so good, and even though it becomes a bit strange in the end (No spoilers), it still makes sense everything considered.
Now i have seen some reviews stating that all your choices doesn't actually matter other than the last one. Now this is true in the form of the actual games outcome, but all the choices you make throughout the whole game matters. To you. You become so attatched to the characters in the story, that even though it has no affect on the outcome, it can't help but to affect you.
I found myself several times getting angry at the various characters being a prick to Max, because i got so attachted to her. One of the main things you will also realize about Max (probably long before i did), is that she's got some of the most interesting character development you'll see in a game.
Lastly i wanna say that this review is not written to praise the game/fanboy it, or tell you that you HAVE to buy it otherwise you'll get [Insert randon horrible disease...], but rather to tell you exactly what it will do to you. It got me good. It makes you feel a lot of different things throughout the game, and even though you can reverse time. you realize very quickly that when you change time, you change a lot of things. even things that didn't seem to have anything to do with anything you changed.
Oh and of course, the game comes with all the regular teenage drama you'd have at a school ;)
You will not regret buying this game. But your heart will.

Of course there's a few weird/cringy spots, as this is revolving around a person in highschool (though she's 18 and there's dorms, which would make it seem like college, but no clue on that), and the gameplay can be a bit irritating at points, so I'd be stingy as ♥♥♥♥ and call it a 9.9/10

This game is a great example of storytelling and character development done right. Many decisions you make will force you to contemplate your morals and will influence future events and interactions. The plot is interesting and unravels with many shocking events. The soundtrack is wonderful.
That being said, the game has its flaws. Some of the events are really mundane and irrelevant, and I feel like they were added just to make the game longer (example: find and collect 5 bottles in a junkyard – we World of Warcraft now). Parts of the plot heavily resembled the movie “The Butterfly Effect,” though thankfully there were enough differences to keep the game from being predictable. The endings are powerful and effective, but after all is said and done, you’re left wondering whether your previous decisions really mattered all that much. In a game requiring many tough choices, you’d expect there to be numerous different outcomes resulting from the culmination of those different decisions, but it turns out this is not really the case. Also, a few plot elements that persisted throughout the game were left unexplained.
With just a bit more care, I feel like this game would have been an absolute masterpiece. Though overall I still really enjoyed playing it and think it’s an amazing game as is.

I absolutely love this game!! Even being in early access, this game has a lot gong for it and even more to do.  While the pre-defined challenges are still coming along, I'm constantly pushing myself ot the next goal.  First I landed on the moon, then I landed on the moon AND got the guys back safely.  You can constantly push on to greater goals.  And with the new content that is always coming forward (like asteroids in the latest patch) there are always goals to be had!
There is already a huge robust modding community for this game as well where you can find ships, parts, and add-ons to really impact game play.  Not that it needs it, the vanilla KSP is pretty feature packed!
The one word of caution I might place on this game is it does take some thought.  You can't just haphazardly throw pieces together and suddenly have a rocket capable of interplanetary travel and return.  You've got to think smart about fuel, the amount of thrust, and even timing.  You don't just wake up one morning and say, "I think I'll fly to Mars (or the Kerbal equivalent)" to do it right, you'll likely have to advance time in game to wait for the best alignment of Mars to make the launch.  So, don't expect an arcade game - this is cloer to a simulator.

I absolutely love this game!! Even being in early access, this game has a lot gong for it and even more to do.  While the pre-defined challenges are still coming along, I'm constantly pushing myself ot the next goal.  First I landed on the moon, then I landed on the moon AND got the guys back safely.  You can constantly push on to greater goals.  And with the new content that is always coming forward (like asteroids in the latest patch) there are always goals to be had!
There is already a huge robust modding community for this game as well where you can find ships, parts, and add-ons to really impact game play.  Not that it needs it, the vanilla KSP is pretty feature packed!
The one word of caution I might place on this game is it does take some thought.  You can't just haphazardly throw pieces together and suddenly have a rocket capable of interplanetary travel and return.  You've got to think smart about fuel, the amount of thrust, and even timing.  You don't just wake up one morning and say, "I think I'll fly to Mars (or the Kerbal equivalent)" to do it right, you'll likely have to advance time in game to wait for the best alignment of Mars to make the launch.  So, don't expect an arcade game - this is cloer to a simulator.

Veronica Mars meets Donnie Darko. I can't think of a more fitting description. It's at times over-the-top in the drama department and the storyline can get a bit ham-fisted, but the game was so compelling, I basically gave up a weekend to play it nearly non-stop. The story overline is very well told, the play mechanics are excellent, and most of the characters are very interesting and engaging.
The story will move you, whether it makes you cry, get angry, laugh, like the show and movie I referenced at the beginning of this review, you will be thinking fondly about this game for a while after you play it.
Does this game have its shortcomings? Of course, most do. But the complex storyline, (overall) excellent script and voice-acting, completely overshadow the niggling issues with the game. The choices you make do feel like they matter. The changes can be small to cataclysmic. However, do not be fooled, the narrative is taking you down a singular path, no matter what choices you make. I do not personally have a problem with this because I think the designers made the right choice to limit the endings so that the story can be kept tight.
From a technical standpoint, this game shines overall. I like the dreamy, painted look to the town of Arcadia Bay. Everything is hand-painted. Animations are all motion captured, and while some suffer from the jerkiness and shaking that motion capture can introduce, overall the animation is believable. Sometimes facial expressions are wonderful and at other times characters look like store mannequins. It's very common, no matter what the budget of the game. I do wish that more attention was paid to characters' facial expressions as the vapid looks in various faces starts to break the immersion. With that said, the actresses playing Max and Chloe, especially, are fantastic. The voice over work, overall, is top-notch, which goes a long way to making the characters believable, even when the story spins off into crazy town. Hey, it's a super-hero origin story, a little crazy is more than acceptable.
The interface is very easy to use. I used an XBOX 360 controller, not keyboard/mouse, and I highly recommend playing this game that way. It was designed for a controller. My only gripe is the tight, over-the-shoulder camera made it difficult to move Max around at times.
Gamplay is good overall and helps move the narrative along. This really is a narrative game, there is not a lot of actual gameplay. There are not lots of puzzles to solve. Mostly, the interaction revolves around how you relate to the other characters - the choices you make when engaging with them. However, there is a point in Episode 5 that feels like filler and annoyed me quite a bit. You'll know it when you get there. I guess the designers had less story to tell by the time the fifth episode came around so they felt they had to pad it with some lame gameplay that broke the narrative for a while. But, things quickly right themselves and once you get through that silly section, the story concludes nicely.
The story is quite good overall. Some (like myself) may find it too obvious, as I knew the predicted the ending even before all the games characters had been introduced. I'm ok with knowing the ending if getting there is a fun experience. In this case, the experience was a roller coaster ride. It was very fun and emotionally gripping, so I thoroughly enjoyed the journey even though I knew where it would ultimately end.
Overall, I was very impressed with this game and I hope that DONTNOD (I love palindromes) makes a sequel. It could be with Max but I'd like them to do something along the lines of the Cloverfield movies - a totally new, loosely connected narrative that doesn't involve these characters. Not that I don't want to see these characters again, but the story feels accomplished by itself and doesn't require more telling. However, I'd like to revisit this world and the ingenious time-rewinding mechanics.
Overall score: 9/10.

Okay. Where do I begin.
Garry's Mod, freedom to those who know how to use it.
I began this game with sandbox and a bunch of nuke add-ons. Hours, I would spend spawning NPC's and then blowing them up. In my younger mind, it was fun. Now that I've aged a tad, I understand more.
I'd like to start with the community.
I was an admin for a TTT (Trouble in Terrorist Town) server for awhile, and I met some people. Of course I rarely speak to those people in todays day and age, but they were awesome people. However, there were other people too, like Mr. Pug. Oh yes I remember you, teased, blown off just because you sounded below the age of 13. Actually followed me like a lost puppy for a long time. Seriously, if you haven't hit puberty, don't use a mic. Everyone will hate you for no reason. There's also other people, who are horrifically toxic, and their only goal is to ruin the game. "Oh he walked in front of me, it was accidental mass RDM." It isn't a big deal, but some people take it way too seriously. REPORTED, REPORTED, REPORTED, it's always the same. But that's mainly TTT. Another excellent choice is Prop Hunt, whom I also moderated. Theres people like me, who knows every spot on every map, like a no life, but theres also people who just want to have a good time. Be that person if you purchase this game. Run around as a banana, tease other players, don't sit there in silence under a car. Ok, DarkRP, I have hate and love for this mode. It's horrible community, mixed with it's try hards and gameplay really doesn't make it seem like it'd be fun, which it isn't for a lot of people. However, if you make enough money you can purchase fire arms and lead a small crusade and then get banned because no one can take a joke. I didn't plau much else so that's a lot of what I have to say.
Playing with friends.
If you don't have friends to play with, you'll make tons here. After a year, I was cool with plenty of people, I used to play CS:GO with a lot of them. It's a great place if you want to make friends. Don't be toxic, just play and enjoy the game and maybe you'll make friends with them.
Playing adventure maps
This is one of my favorite things to do on this game. I used to have to start a hamachi server to play with friends but they just added a feature recently that saves you the struggle. There are thousands of maps to choose from, horror, funny, whatever.
The only way to keep this game great, is to treat everyone and this game with a little respect and positivity. I don't care if you make suicide jokes all the time don't get me wrong, just don't be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Life is Strange is one of the episodic series in the short history of the genre. The game has a great story, skillfully takes on serious issues and has a really good soundtrack. What's more - there is at least as much gameplay as there is simple viewing, and the entire game can take more than a dozen hours to finish. There are some minor flaws here and there but they won't overshadow the fact that this is one of the best stories of the year.

This game changed my notions of what you can do accomplish with video games.  The story is amazing, and the gameplay mechanics that are established and developed during the game are tailored to serve the immersion and impact of the story.  Unlike many games in the genre, Life Is Strange uses the narrative structure not to try to hide the limitations of adventure games, but rather uses them subtly to support the narrative.  The dialogue is some of the best in adventure gaming, starring what is perhaps the most believable and impactful friendship I have seen in games.  The game also acts as a commentary on the player's playstyle through in-game dialogue--if your character blows through her life without taking time to notice people around her, the people around her will notice and act accordingly.  And the soundtrack is amazing.  I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600...and this is, without a doubt, in my top three all time list of games.  I can't recommend it enough.

Veronica Mars meets Donnie Darko. I can't think of a more fitting description. It's at times over-the-top in the drama department and the storyline can get a bit ham-fisted, but the game was so compelling, I basically gave up a weekend to play it nearly non-stop. The story overline is very well told, the play mechanics are excellent, and most of the characters are very interesting and engaging.
The story will move you, whether it makes you cry, get angry, laugh, like the show and movie I referenced at the beginning of this review, you will be thinking fondly about this game for a while after you play it.
Does this game have its shortcomings? Of course, most do. But the complex storyline, (overall) excellent script and voice-acting, completely overshadow the niggling issues with the game. The choices you make do feel like they matter. The changes can be small to cataclysmic. However, do not be fooled, the narrative is taking you down a singular path, no matter what choices you make. I do not personally have a problem with this because I think the designers made the right choice to limit the endings so that the story can be kept tight.
From a technical standpoint, this game shines overall. I like the dreamy, painted look to the town of Arcadia Bay. Everything is hand-painted. Animations are all motion captured, and while some suffer from the jerkiness and shaking that motion capture can introduce, overall the animation is believable. Sometimes facial expressions are wonderful and at other times characters look like store mannequins. It's very common, no matter what the budget of the game. I do wish that more attention was paid to characters' facial expressions as the vapid looks in various faces starts to break the immersion. With that said, the actresses playing Max and Chloe, especially, are fantastic. The voice over work, overall, is top-notch, which goes a long way to making the characters believable, even when the story spins off into crazy town. Hey, it's a super-hero origin story, a little crazy is more than acceptable.
The interface is very easy to use. I used an XBOX 360 controller, not keyboard/mouse, and I highly recommend playing this game that way. It was designed for a controller. My only gripe is the tight, over-the-shoulder camera made it difficult to move Max around at times.
Gamplay is good overall and helps move the narrative along. This really is a narrative game, there is not a lot of actual gameplay. There are not lots of puzzles to solve. Mostly, the interaction revolves around how you relate to the other characters - the choices you make when engaging with them. However, there is a point in Episode 5 that feels like filler and annoyed me quite a bit. You'll know it when you get there. I guess the designers had less story to tell by the time the fifth episode came around so they felt they had to pad it with some lame gameplay that broke the narrative for a while. But, things quickly right themselves and once you get through that silly section, the story concludes nicely.
The story is quite good overall. Some (like myself) may find it too obvious, as I knew the predicted the ending even before all the games characters had been introduced. I'm ok with knowing the ending if getting there is a fun experience. In this case, the experience was a roller coaster ride. It was very fun and emotionally gripping, so I thoroughly enjoyed the journey even though I knew where it would ultimately end.
Overall, I was very impressed with this game and I hope that DONTNOD (I love palindromes) makes a sequel. It could be with Max but I'd like them to do something along the lines of the Cloverfield movies - a totally new, loosely connected narrative that doesn't involve these characters. Not that I don't want to see these characters again, but the story feels accomplished by itself and doesn't require more telling. However, I'd like to revisit this world and the ingenious time-rewinding mechanics.
Overall score: 9/10.

The soundtrack is great and the visuals are well done with almost a painterly expression.  If you like good fiction and enjoy story over action, this game will captivate you.  If you value games for game play and intense action, you will not enjoy this series.

This game was interesting, and pulls no punches when it comes to emotional gut punches. It stabs you with a Knife of Feels and twists it mercilessly. The best way I can sum up this game is this: This is how Heavy Rain should have been. Life is Strange is a not so typical coming of age story, that involves time travel. If any of you fellow nerds know anything about movies or books or games about time manipulation, you probably already have an idea how this turns out.
The Characters.
The characters in Life is Strange are a varied array of believable folks with various personality quirks and problems. You may think you've figured certain characters out within 10 minutes, but I assure you, you have not. The main character, Max, is a self admitted, socially introverted geeky hipster whos obsessed with photography. She more or less represents the playerbase that will be playing this product. This is not meant to be insulting to that playerbase, as I am, obviously, part of said playerbase. Pretty much all of the characters that get significant screen time are all very well written and voice acted.
The overarching plot is fairly standard Time Manipulation stuff and Mystery Solving. However something being standard does not mean something is bad, of course. Even the most generic of ideas can be executed masterfully. This is one of those situations.
Music
The music in this game fits very very well with this games set up and enviroment. It's exactly what it should be here, not much else to say about this honestly.
Choices
Tons and tons of choices, big and small. I realized about halfway through most of these likely wouldn't amount to much a whole lot by the end, given the track record of recent games.
Some choices had an impact in ways I didn't expect, others didn't have enough impact in my opinion. Weather or not they all satisfy is up to you.
Cons
Yes, this game actually has a few cons for me.
1. Several times I encountered technical hiccups and glitches that halted my progress, requiring me to quit the game and restart. This happend about 3 times over a 12 hour session, easily acceptable to me, but it's still worthy of pointing out.
2. This is the last, and most important con, imo. Honestly only 1 single choice in this game ever actually matters, in the end. Every other choice is more or less window dressing, due to how that 1 choice is handled. Spoilers below to go into some detail about this, if you are curious.
I am of the mindset that unless the developer intends for all major choices to have a lasting consequence, choices should not be given. Choice for the sake of choice, is never a good thing, in my opinion. In the end this does not really affect just how -good- this game is. Were I to score it, it would be a solid 9/10. The positives of this game greatly outweigh the negatives, and am curious to see what game this developer releases next. I recommend Life Is Strange, to any and all who love and value Story and Characterization.

This review contains no spoilers that are not already revealed by the game's official trailers.
=Summary=
This is a very obviously a narrative-based game, and the premise and "big reveal" were superb. However, there were many details along the way that weren't well executed, and the conclusion also left a lot to be desired. I still recommend the game, but I am forced to admit that it had the potential to be much better. If you do purchase the game, I recommend that in your very first play session, you attempt to save the game as early as possible, quit the game, restart it, and attempt to load your save file again. There exists a bug that prevents the saves from working, and it's better for your to check if you're affected and Google for the workarounds after only being 5 minutes in, than to be forced to replay hours.
=Narrative=
As made obvious by the game trailer and the first five minutes, this game involves a girl who has the ability to travel through time. Unfortunately, like so many time-travel stories, this one suffers from an "Idiot Plot": there are a handful of times when the game throws a conflict at you, and with the intended (and often, only) solution being to rewind time and avoid the conflict with your acquired prescience. The problem is when the game then throws an almost identical conflict with perhaps only a shuffling of people involved, except this happens during a non-interactable cutscene, and the main character does not think to use her time rewinding powers to resolve them, leaving her in a mess that the player then has to deal with. Very few time-travel stories don't fall victim to the Idiot Plot trope. It's unfortunate Life Is Strange failed to evade that fate.
=Execution=
The game generally "works": It's entertaining, the controls are straightforward, and immersion-breaks are few, but unfortunately non-zero. "Choices matter", the game brags, but it is a bit too heavy handed in signaling this to you. In the dramatic moment where you'll find out whether or not a character will take your side, the character will enumerate every choice you've made and how those choices made them feel towards you, both the good and the bad. This sometimes leads to the unintended hilarious effect of making the character seem schizophrenic: in one sentence, they'll smile and talk about how good a friend you were when you stood up for them in one situation, and then in the very next sentence yell at you for having failing to have helped them in another situation. The results are disjointed, as if each line were voice acted and recorded separately, and then just pasted together with no transitions to smooth out the emotional tone.
Every episode save for the first starts off with a "Previously on..." segment that quickly flashes scenes from the previous episodes to jog the player's memory a bit. What's strange is that given how much effort the game put into making sure you understand that your choices really do matter, every scene chosen for the "previously on..." segments are always the "forced" scenes which occur regardless of what choice you make. The Walking Dead series by Telltale games did this much more effectively by having your actual choices show up on these recap segments.
One very interesting and well designed mechanic was "sitting down". Few games allow the protagonist to just sit down and relax for a while, and for the few that do, they almost never serve a narrative purpose. In Life Is Strange, Sitting down allows the protagonist to gather her thoughts, narrate, and give some exposition on her emotional state. Sitting down is completely opt-in, and so players who prefer a "show don't tell" approach can skip sitting down altogether and just get on with the action. In other games, a similar purpose is filled by journals or audio logs: Characters just speaking their thoughts out-loud to reveal more after their personalities and the world around them. That technique itself has some pitfalls, so it's nice to see this new technique explored, and it'll be interesting to see if other future games pick up on it and expand it further.
As a technically less well-executed display of introspection, the protagonist will sometimes comment on objects as you walk by then. Unfortunately, if you walk by two or more objects within quick succession of each other, both of her internal monologue sound files will trigger, one cutting off the other.
=Writing=
The writing of the dialog is generally convincing. There are a few cringe-worthy lines, but we might chalk that up to the speaking characters being teenagers: I know I've said a lot of things that I had thought sounded deep and wise at the time, only to be embarrassed about it now that I'm older.
That said, one place where the dialog really falls flat is how self-aware some of these teenagers are. When a teenager character is being a brat, and you confront them "the right way" (rewinding and exploring other conversation branches makes this very easy), they'll admit that yes, they were being a brat, and it's because they're jealous or insecure of you or whatever. No very believable, in my experience.
Finally, a mixed bag is in the explanation of how the protagonist gained her time-bending powers. Simply put, the "explanation" is completely incoherent. Jargon is thrown around with a clear indication that the characters speaking them have no idea what those terms mean: One of them describes chaos theory as &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥that can happen, will happen". The saving grace here is that, again, these are all teenagers speaking, and so it is actually quite "realistic" to see teens thinking they know or understanding something when they clearly haven't the clue. Unfortunately, there's no lamp-shading or nod from the authors that they, actually, do know what any of these terms mean either (save, perhaps, for the symbolism of the butterfly and the tornado), and so we're left with the uncomfortable position of being forced to give them the benefit of the doubt, that "yes, it's completely idiotic, but that's because they're teenagers! It was all intentional!" Really, I think the writing would have worked better (as in, not been as distracting from the plot) if they had simply not attempted to explain the powers at all, and left it at magical realism.
Cringeworthy Dialogue, stupid teenage drama at every turn, terrible solo hipster guy with an acoustic guitar soundtrack, and overall the most pretentious game I have ever played.

Kerbal Space Program is a game where you can build all manor of contraptions, mostly rockets, strap a very happy little green man into it, and send him to his inevitable demise. That demise may come several in game years after launch as you slam mercilessly into a distant planet because you miscalculated your landing. It may come several seconds after launch as you slam mercilessly into your own planet because you miscalculated your take-off.
Whenever your Kerbal's shortened lifespan comes to an end you will have found yourself having great fun getting him there! Real actual physics and rocket science are well simulated, so there's a steep learning curve to even get into space, but the hilarity of Jebediah Kerman smiling into the ocean on your fourth attempt to leave your home behind will help make it easier to learn.
Once you've found your space legs and can reliably jet around space, and maybe even visit the two moons your mind will start turning with all sorts of crazy ideas for space stations, and Munar rovers and space ships that maybe this time might just get you to Duna! When you eventually reach the point of being a space hero, and can jet to the furthest planets with ease the game has plenty of mods to extend the fun!
I reccomend this game to anyone who has some patience to learn, and isn't going to be too crushed by shattering a hopeful Kerbonauts dreams against a mountain range.

This is an amusing aerospace engineering simulator. The gameplay generally involves designing spacecrafts by assembling different components together. You can then test the crafts by trial and error, and refine their designs, and eventually launch them to space and (possibly) return back to base.
Pros:
- Plenty of options to build different crafts, probes, spacestations etc
- Decent use of physics principles; you will learn some basic rocket science
- Sandbox mode: enables a lot of wacky and/or impressive designs and activities
- Career mode: gives an RPG experience, as you operate a space agency with limited resources and gradually improve your technologies based on your own self-directed exploration missions
- The Kerbals (the crew and mission staff) have an endearing Pixar-like quality, yet they are totally expendable
Cons:
- Early access = unfinished product (and in almost all cases don't deserve the full asking price)
- Wind resistance is not fully implemented as far as I know, ie. while in the atmosphere, a block-shaped craft has the same drag as a streamlined craft of the same mass
- Some advanced components are confusing to build and control correctly although it is nice they are possible and could be a fun challenge (eg. "Mars rover" vehicles)
- Sometimes tricky (if using the mouse only) to glue components in the desired locations/angles, or to get different parts properly aligned
Edit: final score 6.5/10

I don't want to give a negative review to Life is Strange because I love the first couple episodes, but the ending is awful. The game revolves around a story and structure which is pretty much Twin Peaks. The similarities between the two are blatant, there is even a Red Room scene. That is one reason why I love the beginning. I adore Twin Peaks and while this may be very close to it; it is it's own story and earns it's own merits. However, where the story falls apart is when it tries to do too much.
This too much is in the later uses of the time travel mechanic. The time travel is a main mechanic of the game and it is used well... Errr well until you get to some major points of use that is not a choice. You are forced to do them and they have consequences that you are meant to feel responsible for but without choice why should you take responsibiliy. This is where the illision of "choice matters" really breaks down and why I feel so let down by this game. This specific use of the time travel power is also not intrdouced until the very last minutes of episode 3. The biggest problem is when you are finally given a choice about using this power. SPOILERS
If you can overlook the normal pitfalls of the "choice matters" types of games then play this. If you are the type of person to analyze what your choices ultimately did in retrospect then avoid this. I am the latter, and that is why I can ultimately not recommend this game.

I don't want to give a negative review to Life is Strange because I love the first couple episodes, but the ending is awful. The game revolves around a story and structure which is pretty much Twin Peaks. The similarities between the two are blatant, there is even a Red Room scene. That is one reason why I love the beginning. I adore Twin Peaks and while this may be very close to it; it is it's own story and earns it's own merits. However, where the story falls apart is when it tries to do too much.
This too much is in the later uses of the time travel mechanic. The time travel is a main mechanic of the game and it is used well... Errr well until you get to some major points of use that is not a choice. You are forced to do them and they have consequences that you are meant to feel responsible for but without choice why should you take responsibiliy. This is where the illision of "choice matters" really breaks down and why I feel so let down by this game. This specific use of the time travel power is also not intrdouced until the very last minutes of episode 3. The biggest problem is when you are finally given a choice about using this power. SPOILERS
If you can overlook the normal pitfalls of the "choice matters" types of games then play this. If you are the type of person to analyze what your choices ultimately did in retrospect then avoid this. I am the latter, and that is why I can ultimately not recommend this game.

I have owned KSP for over 2 years now and I still love it to this day. It is truly a marvel of a game. You start out with only a few basic rocket parts, you fly a bit, then you try hitting the upper atmosphere, and finally space! The real challenge is staying there though, because contrary to what you might think if takes more than just going up to achieve orbit. That's where the fun is at in this game, because even though it can be a bit frustrating at the beginning, once you get the ropes, you can start planning complicated missions, build your space station, etc. and the feeling you get when  you suceed is pure magic! You can find enjoyment in your failures as well. For example if one of your kerbals is stuck on a planet after a failed landing, you  can start planning  a rescue mission to save him. The game can be hard at times, but that is what makes it so fun, because when you succeed, it is because you rock! not because the game was holding your hand all along.
You unlock more advanced parts by spending your science points and funds you earn when doing contracts and experiments. You start small by exploring your own planet, but as you get better and better, the whole solar system opens up for you and the possibilities are HUGE! Oh and if you get bored, there are mods! They can change your experience completely by adding new parts, new planets, new funtionalities, etc.
Back then I paid the game 20$ and there was much less content than there is now. Even if it was currently 60$ it would still buy it without hesitation. Especially knowing the devs are awesome and hardworking. They haven't stopped adding content and perfecting the game since the beginning. They are a shining example of the early access model done right!
TL:DR : KSP is awesome, what are you waiting for? Buy it!

One of these days I'll actually do a round trip to another planet, until that day though I'm left looking at Mun (The Kerbal equivilant of Luna) with a prang of guilt. I know full well that Jebediah is still up there in his command module, unable to return to the warm embrace of his homeland because for whatever reason that is foreign to all non celestial mechanics, astronauts, cosmonauts, and indeed kerbalnauts the rocket motor on Jeb's ship decided to explode AFTER he made touchdown on Mun. I'll get him back... one day.
The game itself is presented with a near whimsical style and a humorous amount of blurb text for the player, but this is no light hearted affair ladies and gentlemen. KSP is a game that will either get you thinking about how hard spaceflight and travel really is or it will have you just plain confused at how we as humans even managed to do what we have in space. It's tough, and near relentless. You let your guard down and try to slack off in this game and it will reward you with a burning hot fireball of junk on the launch platform.
Graphics are actually stellar for what they are, the style is bound to not to be to everybody's taste, but the love and attention that went in to it as a project is clearly visible. Likewise sound is very well put together, engines and mechanical happenings seem to have all the right whooshy sounds.
The big let downs of this game are that is still unfinished, where budgeting is not currently needed and the career mode is little more than a grindathon of space missions (which is how Jeb got stuck on Mun). Scenarios and mods help to fix this, and indeed even NASA have given the game a mission or two for you to attempt at failing at.
Do I like this game? Yes, it's probably the best example of a space sim out there actually. Do I recommend this game? Yes, Microsoft space flight simulator holds nothing to this gem. Will you get frustrated at how complex transitioning orbits from one celestial body to another really is? Well... don't let me stop you finding out.

Kerbal Space Program (KSP) is a space-sim game which tasks you with sending little green men into the solar system. You design the rockets, space planes, satellites, rovers, etc. and stuff them with Kerbals and pilot them into space. Much of your time is spent improving and redesigning to try and get your Kerbals further and further into space.
The draw of KSP is the excitement of a successful launch, the joy of exploration, and the big boom you make from failure. Or perhaps destruction is your goal, in which case you'll be achieving it often. This
rocket science, or at least a rocket science sim. There is a steep learning curve, so failure is guaranteed and success often comes in small steps rather than leaps. However, with each step forward, your reach into space stretches and suddenly there is a new planet or moon to explore and study.
And that is exactly what keeps you coming back. KSP hands you the keys to a sandbox solar system and says "have fun". It encourages you to explore without telling you exactly how. The only limits are physics and your creativity in overcoming that.
I would recommend this game to anyone passively or actively interested in space and wants to put their knowledge to the test. My only word of caution is that KSP does not hold your hand, but online guides and FAQ's are plentiful, so that shouldn't be a make-or-break for you. The game is also quite mod-able, so there is a lot of value in its price tag.

Garry's Mod. A fun, sandbox-style, do-what-you-want kind of game. At least, that's what it's advertised as, and what people say about it. Garry's Mod, is, however, very unique. The base game is one gamemode and 2 maps, with HL2 content such as weapons and props. That's about it. What provides the magnitude of content is the community itself. Since it's release, there has been a plethora of content added and created for this quite simple mod. So why would I, someone with over 2000 hours of this game, not recommend this game? There's a ton of reasons for this, and I could legitimately write a book about it, but I'm going to boil it down to a set of main ideas.
Gamemodes are, strictly speaking, the heart of Garry's Mod. There are a range of gamemodes available, each with their own interesting rules and gameplay. Or, at least there would be, if it wasn't for the fact that literally only about 5 of these gamemodes are played, and have oversaturated the server browser. These are; Trouble in Terrorist Town, Murder, DarkRP (Or any very mildly modified varient, they all count), Prop Hunt, and Deathrun. I'm leaving Sandbox out of it, because it's Sandbox. Let's boil these down to what they should be, and what they actually are:
1. Trouble in Terrorist Town
Trouble in Terrorist Town, or TTT for short, is a gamemode where you're meant to find out which of your comrades are Traitors, and eliminate them, or kill everyone else if you're the Traitors yourself. On the face of it, it's quite intriguing. You do this by investigating bodies, and determine which of your fellow terrorists are not what they seem, based on location at time of death, weapon, and if they were seen committing the deed. However, what it really is is an oversaturation of addons that do not work together, dropping framerates and killing any sense of mystery (Because they wear ♥♥♥♥ing cosmetics!), overly abusive admins who usually are 12 and paid for it using Mum's credit card, trigger-happy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who thought sniffing the air around them was construed as an attempt on their life, and then yell "RDM" at the top of their lungs to every available admin, who will then ban at request without investigating claims. It takes about 50 hours of
searching through all servers to find an actual decent one.
2. Murder
Oh, boy, did you expect a paragraph? Well, you're out of luck, this gamemode has literally been made for YouTubers, and it is a dumbed-down version of TTT, except there are NO good servers. At all. Next.
3. DarkRP
DarkRP. A place where dreams go to die and people pretend to be someone else. Which is odd, because on the face of it, it looks like people could be extremely creative and have fun. ON THE FACE OF IT. The idea is you can get various "Jobs" in city life, or make your own if you're just a basic citizen. Life is Strange is one of the best games, particularly RPG's, I've played in YEARS.
Admittedly, I was skeptical at first. Don't let the bright, cheerful graphics and perceived age group fool you. Before reading into it and giving it a chance, I made the mistake of letting myself believe this game was only intended for a pretty young target audience. I was sorely mistaken, and found this out the hard way as some very dark subject matter slowly began to reveal itself as I progressed.
This game caused SUCH an emotional rollercoaster, and I found myself experiencing a full spectrum of emotions throughout the story. It's so well written that it's difficult not to become invested in many of the characters, and the thought of losing them can be stressful at times. For me, personally, that's a major characteristic of top-notch storytelling. Knowing your choices will directly affect the past, present and future makes it quite difficult to come to conclusions, and you're often forced to sit for a moment (or two...or three) to look at the situation from a logical standpoint. You're forced to take past events into consideration, while trying to remember who did what/who deserves what, all while playing detective. It was quite the brain exercise!
That said, it wasn't perfect, but no game is, nor can it be (imo). You have to be able to ignore some pretty cheesy teenage dialogue at times, firstly. Some of the puzzles were a bit tedious/frustrating and took up a pretty hefty chunk of time to complete, and I was a little unimpressed with the seemingly limited options when it came to the final choice. It was also VERY open-ended with a few plot holes, and I feel like I was left without full closure, but I do understand why, from a developer's perspective.
All in all, I'm so glad I finally caved and gave Life is Strange a chance. It was a unique and incredibly addicting trip through another world, and I can't wait for Season 2. Highly recommend.

In Life is Strange, you play Max, who discovers after an event happens involving your best friend that you can reverse time. You're stuck in a world of teenagers, with all the annoying teen angst that involves, but if some of the characters and scenes are a little eye-rolling, just stick it out, at least until the end of episode 2. That's when I was truly hooked. And by the end of episode 3, I couldn't step away from the game til I'd finished it.
I love how this game deals with the concept of going back in time. At first, it's just fun and light-hearted. Hey look, someone got hit with a football. I can get her out of the way before that happens! But the drama soon ramps up and you discover that every time you fix something, something else goes wrong. The game touches on the theme of chaos theory, more specifically, the butterfly effect, in quite a mature and realistic way. As the game goes on, for everything you fix, something else goes wrong. You start to see that in fixing things, you are causing unintended consequences, for you and everyong around you.
The game play itself is pretty easy and casual. Think of it as a game version of the "Choose Your Own Adventure" books. Unlike some of the similar Tell Tale games I have played, however, some of your choices in Life is Strange truly do matter, especially in terms of what you decide to change by going back in time, and whether you do it "right" or not.
I had two complaints about the game. One, the music was not my cup of tea. However, it did fit with the atmosphere of the game, so I learned to deal with it. The second complaint has to do with the stealth sections. But then I figured out that, thanks to the time reversing power, they weren't as nerve-wracking as I was making them. When you reverse time, everything around you moves, but you stay in the same place. Move everyone else around in these sections, and go on your merry way. You get as many do-overs as you want, at least in the stealth parts, so while annoying, they're not impossible.
All in all I really loved this game. I don't binge many games, but this one I did. I've only played through it once and am getting ready to do at least one more play-through, if not more, because I'm curious what certain deviations in my choices could bring. I highly recommend Life is Strange, if you've enjoyed any of the Tell Tale games (The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, etc). The basic idea that your choices matter really is true here, and the ending choice of the game and what happens afterward will stay with you for a long time.

Kerbal Space Program is a physics game. That's a term that has been roundly abused and misrepresented, however. Does a mug on a desk fly off when you shoot it? Physics! Does your character fall down stairs like a ragdoll? Physics! Can you twang circular birds at pigs hiding in rickety wooden structures? Yay! Physics! As far as games are concerned, "physics" is now basically shorthand for "stuff that moves kind of realistically".
So let's start over. Kerbal Space Program is a physics game, in the textbook sense of the word. An actual literal textbook, full of real science. This is a game in which you'll need to understand not only an object's centre of gravity, but its centre of thrust. It's a game where you need to know what periapsis and apoapsis mean, and where you'll need to understand orbital eccentricity and inclination.
It's also a game about gormless, wide-eyed cartoon characters who want to be astronauts.
This contrast between goofy cartoon and hardcore science is what gives Kerbal Space Program its distinctive flavour; a game that demands serious thought but is never less than hilariously charming. Though the means by which you achieve it are challenging, the ultimate goal is very simple. You need to help the Kerbals, inhabitants of the planet Kerbin, to reach outer space and land on the Mün and the planets beyond.At its most basic, the game is a construction sandbox in which you put together various rocket pieces before testing them on the launchpad, with a hapless Kerbal strapped inside. Adorable as they are - a sort of cross between the Rabbids and Despicable Me's Minions - it's best not to get too attached. Let's just say this is a job with a high staff turnover.
Even with a high body count, it's fun to muck about with the different bits and pieces, putting together fuel tanks, boosters, command capsules, fins, wings and all sorts of sticky-out bits, before watching the whole caboodle spiral to a graceful yet fiery end. Slowly but surely, you start to work out what's needed to not only get the thing pointing the right way, but also burn long enough and fast enough to escape Kerbin's gravitational pull. And that's when the game gets really interesting.
There are three gameplay phases, in essence. The tinkering design stage, the launch and flight phase where you'll need to master roll, pitch and yaw to keep your rocket stable, and then the not insignificant question of navigating space itself. That's when you need to know how to use the periapsis and apoapsis of your orbit to change course, but thankfully the game comes with friendly, no-nonsense tutorials that somehow make the theory perfectly accessible. Putting that theory into practice is no mean feat, but at least you'll have a broad grasp on the Newtonian forces you're playing with.And it's only once you're in space that you appreciate just how detailed the game really is. That cartoonish exterior is deceptive. The controls are thankfully kept to a minimum, but every button tap matters. If you've seen Gravity you'll know how even small changes can result in massive errors, and Kerbal Space Program doesn't shy away from that. Finding the right trajectory, calculating the correct amount of fuel burn, these are the exact same skills that kept the Apollo astronauts alive. It's no wonder that NASA itself just announced that it's collaborating with the developer on a mission pack for the game. That's how true to life it is.
The game won't dazzle you with its looks, with a graphical style that is functional rather than pretty, but those cute Kerbals inject enough personality to compensate. In a particularly delightful (and ever so slightly ghoulish) touch, you get a little windowed view of your would-be astronauts as they hurtle into the void. Even if they come crashing back down or wind up floating forever in the inky blackness, their wide-eyed faces and daft grins never falter. You'll laugh, and feel like a monster for doing so.
Kerbal Space Program has been in development since 2011, and has constantly evolved from that moment on. Indeed, Squad, the studio behind the game, informs us that "we don't consider KSP to be in Alpha nor Beta. Each update has its own alpha and beta as we originally had no idea when we'd stop development and lead developer Felipe Falanghe wanted to make sure each update could stand on its own as a final version of KSP."In its most recent updates, that has meant the addition of a long-awaited Career Mode, which adds a more recognisably game-shaped challenge to the game. Whereas in the Sandbox Mode every rocket part is available to play around with, when playing a Career game you must research and earn every new gadget or mechanism. It makes an already daunting game even more demanding, but the payoffs are worth it. Experiments can be carried out in space, while permanent bases can be built and maintained on other worlds, all pouring Science currency back to your headquarters from where you can plot your next foray into the cosmos.
It's a real onion of a game, where each successful step forward is hard-earned but reveals a whole new layer of gameplay underneath. The developer's desire to ensure that each new update stand on its own means that at every stage, it feels like a complete and satisfying experience. It's a truly hardcore simulation, but one that is endearingly approachable and eager to get you grappling with the nuts and bolts of space flight.

Kerbal Space Program lacks the immediate pick-up-and-play appeal of Minecraft, but it's one of the few games since Mojang's masterpiece to offer that same combination of boundless possibility and dizzying depth. All this, and it's only on update v0.23. The thought of where it might be when it reaches the lofty peak of v1.0 is staggering.
It is, already, the sort of game you could play for 100 hours without exhausting its potential and yet, even when you're pootling around with doomed-to-fail contraptions, taking the most basic introductory steps, it's never less than charming, engrossing and entertaining. That you can go from such humble beginnings to explore an entire realistically crafted solar system is nothing short of remarkable. Strap yourself in. It's going to be a long and wonderful ride.

A fantastic ravioli recipe.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.

Let me just start by saying, wow.
This is one of the best games I have ever played, and I have played quite a few games. And by quite a few, I mean tons.
Life is Strange is a game that sends you on a journey that is unforgettable, emotional, funny, and moving. I, personally, played this game on the Xbox One, a while ago, and I cannot stress enough how absolutely amazing it is. (All my friends know this, because I am constantly telling them to play it) It does a great job in showing the reality behind many of lifes biggest problems, such as friendships, awkward romance, depression, classes, and the not-so-common problem of being able to reverse time. You fall in love with the characters, and you feel like you really know them. The story is truely something great, and it is delivered in such a way that it is one you will never forget. It has humor, suspense, drama, anger, fear, sadness... Jesus, is there anything this game DOESNT have?
The graphics are absolutely beautiful, and make you really feel like you are there in Arcadia Bay, sitting on the steps of Blackwell and listening to the constant chatter of teenagers as they buzz along, not a care in the world. The music is... astonishing. I have downloaded just about all of it onto my iPod (dont ask me how) and I listen to it on a regular basis... not just because of the game, but because it is so calming, and peaceful, and really is a treat to the ears. The gameplay is crazy good, with parts being cut-scenes and others being the interactive, open-world story where you can move around and do whatever. It challenges you to think, near the end, at least... (No spoilers!) and the choices aspect is great. Sure, many games have the "choices" system, but this game... it is just above all else. There are so many ways to play through the game, and you can so differently alter the story line, so that the game is still entertaining even if you have already played through. This game made me laugh, and cry. And trust me, I do not cry often. I do not think that I will ever forget this game, or the feelings that it put me through. It truely is an amazing game, and if you don't have the cash to go and buy it, well go ahead and work overtime, because this game is a must-play.

Let me just start by saying, wow.
This is one of the best games I have ever played, and I have played quite a few games. And by quite a few, I mean tons.
Life is Strange is a game that sends you on a journey that is unforgettable, emotional, funny, and moving. I, personally, played this game on the Xbox One, a while ago, and I cannot stress enough how absolutely amazing it is. (All my friends know this, because I am constantly telling them to play it) It does a great job in showing the reality behind many of lifes biggest problems, such as friendships, awkward romance, depression, classes, and the not-so-common problem of being able to reverse time. You fall in love with the characters, and you feel like you really know them. The story is truely something great, and it is delivered in such a way that it is one you will never forget. It has humor, suspense, drama, anger, fear, sadness... Jesus, is there anything this game DOESNT have?
The graphics are absolutely beautiful, and make you really feel like you are there in Arcadia Bay, sitting on the steps of Blackwell and listening to the constant chatter of teenagers as they buzz along, not a care in the world. The music is... astonishing. I have downloaded just about all of it onto my iPod (dont ask me how) and I listen to it on a regular basis... not just because of the game, but because it is so calming, and peaceful, and really is a treat to the ears. The gameplay is crazy good, with parts being cut-scenes and others being the interactive, open-world story where you can move around and do whatever. It challenges you to think, near the end, at least... (No spoilers!) and the choices aspect is great. Sure, many games have the "choices" system, but this game... it is just above all else. There are so many ways to play through the game, and you can so differently alter the story line, so that the game is still entertaining even if you have already played through. This game made me laugh, and cry. And trust me, I do not cry often. I do not think that I will ever forget this game, or the feelings that it put me through. It truely is an amazing game, and if you don't have the cash to go and buy it, well go ahead and work overtime, because this game is a must-play.

I've only played the first episode currently, but I'm in love with this game. I love the choices, and characters, and everything else about it! I recommend this game for anyone who likes a Choose Your Own Adventure type game.

Kerbal Space Program is, simply put, the game where you are NASA. You design, build, and launch your own space missions, from orbiting satellites to senting people to Mars -- called "Duna" in the game. The possibilities are endless. And if you ever get bored of building space stations and sending massive rockets out to Jool (KSP's version of Jupiter), KSP has more to offer. Build and fly airplanes to explore your home planet, Kerbin, drive around the launch center in your custom-made rover, or try to exploit the physics engine to get to orbit without any thrusters at all.
Are there bugs? Sure. The game might even crash sometimes. But no more than should be expected from an Early-Access title, and less than even some high-end full-release games.
If 27 bucks seems like a steep price for Early Access, take into account that Kerbal Space Program far exceeds it's AAA competitors in every quality -- especially if you tap into the massive modding community, with parts packs like KW Rocketry and B9 Aerospace to fill your construction needs and Ferram Aerospace and MechJeb to give you even more realistic control of your vehicles.
In conclusion, KSP is my favorite game in my Steam library, and one of very few games that I would give a very enthusiastic 10/10.
Don't waste your money buying hundreds of games when you can have them all in a single game.

I am a pretty hard-core gamer and thought I'd give this game a shot.  At first, I wasn't sure what to expect, but as I went on, I really enjoyed the game. Excellent game design and will keep you entertained for many hours if you get into the game and actually take the time to 'meet' the characters.  Grab it during the Summer sale if possible though so you can get the discount, but it is worth it even at full price.

Note: I bought episodes 1-5 for $10, but I had forgotten I got it on sale, and thought I had spent $20. This game is worth $20, I was satisfied with my purchase regardless.

Overall rating: 9.5/10
What could be better: Lip syncing and Max's voice acting
~Gameplay~
Life is Strange has some interesting gameplay elemts that it will never let you forget. The ability to reverse time allows you to "teleport," by walking forward then reversing time, get information out of people, yadah yadah. It's a fun system, and it doesn't ever go away.
Besides its unique gameplay elements, it handles like  I imagine a Telltale game would. Controlling Max feels smooth, a controller is recommended. Interacting with items in the world allows you to learn more about Arcadia Bay and the people in it. Taking or looking at certain items could have consequences, though.
There are a lot of different scenarios that can happen, though to my knowledge there are only two endings that you can pick from. Throughout the game there are a lot of pictures that you can take and fill up your scrapbook, a sort of collectible system that I plan on completing 100% on my second playthrough.
~Graphics~
Life is Strange has a very nice hand-painted art style. There are a few meshes I wish were slightly higher in polygon count, but overall no problems. If you have a half-decent NVidia card, I recommend playing the game in 3840x2160 DSR, as I had 60FPS throughout and the game was slightly more beautiful in 4K DSR. (I have a GTX 960)
It did bother me throughout the game that many lip movememnts were horribly desynced, but I understand how it would be very difficult to have them by 100% synced in such a freeform game, especially being able to rewind time in the middle of a conversation.
~Audio~
I listen to the game's soundtrack constantly on Spotify. Very good folkish music, calming and really helps set the emotional scene. There are some parts of the game where you can flip on your stereo while doing something in your room, and I loved chilling and listening to the music.
Voice acting is fantastic for all but the main character. Everyone feels real, and filled with emotion, but Max has over-dramatic-protagonist sydrome. She says blantantly obvious things to people that don't care and enunciates every syllable in a super annoying way. It slowly gets better across the seasons, but she's the only character I feel I'm not quite happy with.
~Story~
I refuse to even give a nibble of the story, but play the demo if you're not sure about buying. The demo hooked me and I bough the game then and there.
The story is very appealing to the same people that enjoy John Green books and the "please make me cry" genre of young adult movies. I happen to love that stuff, so I loved Life is Strange!
