Life is Strange Review
Edit: Updated the review now that I have finished all the episodes.
Of all the games I have played over the past year Life is Strange was the one that surprised me and exceeded my expectations the most. It’s hard to offer a comprehensive review of the game since spoilers are so much of an issue with this kind of story-driven experience, but I’ll try and given you an idea of just what it was about Life is Strange that impressed me so much.
First, I have to applaud the developers when it comes to their choice of characters and setting. Life is Strange follows the experiences of a young woman just starting out graduate education as a photographer. It deals with her feelings when first moving away from home, and her interactions with other young adults as they manage the complex social maze that is growing up. This setting and choice of characters is such a fresh change from the usual focus of video games and it has been a pleasure to play.
The characters themselves are very well written, with deep and interesting personalities that develop as the story moves forward. The main character, Max, is herself an enjoyable character to play and offers some very personal and insightful narration in the form of an inner monologue throughout the game. I found myself quickly caring about the characters and thinking carefully about the choices that I made. This is just what you want form a game of this format.
It’s also worth saying that the developers never feel the need to sexualize the female cast. It’s so refreshing to play a game where the women are realistic, interesting characters. Major kudos to them for doing this in and industry that so often fails on this point.
The game itself is familiar fare to anyone who has played modern adventures such as Heavy Rain or any of the Telltale games such as The Walking Dead. You basically guide Max through various scenes where you are given the chance to explore locations, solve some minor puzzles and interact with the various characters. The real meat of the game comes from the various choices that you can make, each of which has both short and long-term impacts upon the story. I’ll not mention any specifics here since I don’t want to risk spoiling the experience for anyone, but I will say that I have been very satisfied with the way that the choices have been presented. They feel as if they have a real impact upon the plot which gives a strong sense of ownership to the story rather than feeling like you are just watching lots of cut scenes.
Technically the game seems very solid too. I run it on a modest gaming PC (for reference: GTX770-2GB/i5-4700k/8GB RAM) and I am able to get a totally locked 60fps at 1080p on max settings. The game looks very nice, with a slightly hand-drawn appearance that reminds me a little of the visuals in Dishonored. The art design is top notch with each of the locations being filled with novel and interesting content. It really feels like the designers have put time and effort into making the game fun.
The sound is also very nice. The voice acting is very good throughout. I am yet to hear a single line that sounds out of place or poorly voiced. It’s certainly right up there with the likes of Telltale’s games, and for the most part is better than many films. The music and sound effects are also very impressive. The music in particular is very well chosen and its placement in the scenes is clearly very carefully thought out and cinematic to the point that it is Tarantino-like in how it affects you.
Finally, I just wanted to say that the game has a certain atmosphere that is really fun. It reminds me the most of the film Donny Darko. Indeed, it borrows a few tricks from that films playbook in terms of the framing of scenes and the clever use of the soundtrack. The overall effect is a feeling of mystery and a sense of being reminded of childhood wonder. It’s a wonderful experience and one that I have rarely found in any media. They really did nail it here.
So as I am sure you can tell I really love this game. From the excellent characters, the interesting story filled with meaningful choices, the great atmosphere and the beautiful visual and sound design Life is Strange just gets everything right. It offers a wonderful experience that is so different from the majority of games that it’s comes as a wonderfully fresh experience. If you have any interest in adventure games at all then this is a game that you should play.
Edit: Having now finished all five episodes of the game I am even more enthusiastic for it. The latter episodes really pay off. Some of the decisions are very difficult to make on an emotional and ethical level which is just what you want from a game like this. I was genuinly moved by the story in a way that I have never experienced in a game before. This is an amazing experience that anyone with even a passing interest in adventure gaming should try.

The things that KSP is capable of dwarfs my interest in the features of other games. Because all the planets are loaded at all times, this allows the player to see them at all times from any celestial body, making it feel more life-like. The rocket building mechanism and customization is beyond any thing that I've ever seen before in a game! The combanation of parts to make your own custom rocket is quite literally infinite, so you can never build the same rocket twice. You can make anything you want, from Lifters to Space Stations to Landers to Probes to SSTOs, as well as much, MUCH more! As you explore the Kerbol system, visiting KSP's analogs for our planets you can collect science and visit easter eggs hidden away from prying Kerbal eyes. you can use the science you collect to unlock more and better parts in Career mode, allowing you to build bigger, badder and laggier Rockets. The modding support lets you make your own custom parts, allowing you to make things that the game does'nt have, or go and download other peoples mods for your use. I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes Realistic Physics, Space, and/or Building.

Kerbal space program is by far the most interesting game I’ve played in a long time. In this engaging game, you are given control of a budding space agency and a pre set solar system for you to explore. You get to design, build, launch and pilot rockets and planes in a realistic space flight simulator and discover just how hard space missions can actually be. As of today (29.03.14) there are no objectives or mission in the campaign mode yet, but that hasn’t stopped me from clocking in over 200 enjoyable hours since release.
As the game is still in development, there is also tons more material to follow and each time I am left really excited by playing and even more excited to hear news of updates, which are quite frequent to give the devs at Squad credit, ranging from three to four months between updates typically. The game has tons of features and is expanding all the time- from figuring out how to launch ever increasing payloads into orbit, to conducting specific experiments in space to basic exploration. You even have to plan in for survival in space by building batteries and solar panels to your ships as without power, they become dead sticks in space. For any science geek like myself or for anyone who is interested in the space programs of the world in general, this game is a must have and is worth every penny of its £20 asking price in my opinion.
Kerbal also gives you a massive sense of achievement as you learn more about the physics of flying space missions.  I still have vivid memories and even a grin while thinking about my very first successful landing on the Mun, the nearest orbiting body to the home planet.
After playing for over 200 hours I can thankfully report that there is  still a huge mass of things for me to do. I’ve still not found a way to explore some of the further most planets- my rocket designs are simply not up to that task yet which is another motivation for me to keep playing. I’ve still not been able to return a man (kerbal) from another planet yet despite several drone and probe landings. All of this, plus the additional updates means that I can play this game after a long day at work knowing that I’ve still only really scratched the surface.
Kerbal at present has 2 modes. There is the sandbox in which you get all the parts to go play with instantly- and there is the skeleton of the Career mode which is fleshed out more in updates along the road. In the career mode, you unlock parts for your space program using a resource called science. Science is generated by doing experiments from certain locations E.G. a crew report whilst flying over some mountains. The game has a great mechanic built in; in which running repeat experiments on the same thing has huge diminishing returns. This means that if you want to generate more science and unlock more parts, your missions need to go further and do something new. You also come across a problem- Science can only be collected on Kerbin, your home planet. So how do you get your experimental results back home? Do you plan for a return trip and build a larger craft with more fuel and re-entry kit or will you sacrifice some of the “science” you could have earned by using the radio to transmit data back to Kerbin- which means you’ll have to go back and do the experiment again to get the rest of the science you could have earned? These kinds of decisions really colour the choices you make,  challenge a player to put time and effort into their designs and to think about their flight plan as with limited fuel and power, missions are not straightforward. For those who don’t like that idea, relax- there is a debug mode in which you can grant yourself infinite fuel so you can look around everything with a little ship- but where is the fun in that?
The moding community for kerbal space program is fantastic. It’s a little harder to integrate mods into the campaign mode, but it can be done even by my severely limited computing skills. As for the sandbox, moding is fun and adds new features and challenges. Want to map planets from orbit? There’s a mod for that. Want to include life support like oxygen/ CO2? There is a mod for that too- hell there is even a radio chatter mod. Pretty much any feature you would like to have will most likely have a mod for it and most of them can be found at the Kerbal space port (Google it, easy to find). The community input into kerbal is phenomenal allowing you to have sci-fi fantasy engines that can fly you out of the solar system on one tank of fuel or delicate life support/ power features for more realistic missions. Another mod I would like to sing the praises of is Kerbal space program multiplayer. Here you can fly missions with other users over the net. Hell yes! But I can’t promise that this will be sticking around as the game engine updates frequently. So if you’re thinking of buying for that reason- wait; as of yet there is not official multiplayer of the game.
Lastly- are there any issues? Well yes, this is a work in progress after all. Some of the larger rockets can wobble strangely and some of the connectors can have issues, meaning that the complicated craft you spend 2 hours designing needs to be tweaked repeatedly.
One of the parts in the core game causes an error as of last update (the hitchhiker support module) but I’m sure this can be and will be fixed- and it's not a majorly inportant part anyhow. But other than these minor teething problems, which to be fair can be expected of a game in development, there are no major issues that I have found or that I can think of that are really frustrating.
If you need any more information before deciding whether this game is for you, check out YouTube- there are hundreds of vids up there with commentary and good examples of game play. Hope this review was helpful in making your choice.

This game has so many flaws. And the last episode, especially, was a huge let down for me because it left too many important plot details unresolved, and nullified all of the choices I've made in the previous episodes.
It even turned quite a believable character in the previous episodes into a typical cardboard villain who does evil things for the evil's sake.
I can go on and on like this, as it is not really hard to find flaws in this game, from the bad lip syncing to dialogues, which sometimes sound unnatural even for a non-English speaker like me.
But what I really like to say about this game is that: YOU REALLY NEED TO PLAY IT!
The game is so masterly done that all those flaws probably won't prevent you from acknowledging its charm. And yes, it's actually that great.
The game feels like a well made indie road movie, and I haven't yet seen any other game in the genre with comparable quality of direction, or showing such depth in personalities of the main characters.
In my opinion, Life is Strange is an important milestone in adventure gaming history, like The Walking Dead is for the similar reason.

Ok, let's get this out of the way. The game is AMAZING. 'Nuff said.
Just kidding (lol), there's more than just that to be said about this terrific game. Well in my opinion anyways. I'd like to mention from get-go that Life is Strange isn't perfect but no doubt, a masterpiece. Many may have different thoughts from this statement; but for a girl with simple tastes, this game definitely satisfies. From the intense story and the intruiging plot, to the gorgeous soundtrack and hand painted artwork; Dontnod does a good job incorporating the littlest things in order to make the biggest impact.
Though I have yet to play the Episodes 2-5 as of 6/23/16 all of my claims and opinions will be strictly based off of my experience with the 1st episode.
Now, for the juicy stuff. One of the things I really enjoyed about this game while I was playing it was the iconic TellTale style gameplay. Having the ability to roam around and interact in the game is great and is something I like personally. Also, being able to make your own choices as a "choose your path" sort of thing expands the story in a way which makes it either thrilling or dramatic due to the decisions your make in either communication or interaction. (Spoiler..? A.K.A Inside Joke? idk) Makes you glad Max's able to "rewind time" dontcha' think? Having complete control on Max's fate on making quick changes to avoid those haunting "consequesnces." lol That's how I think of it at least.
Another factor to point out is the character and story development and how it's portrayed. Every character has this distinct personality which is displayed as the story goes on. If you look at the character Chloe, Max's bestfriend for example. She exhibits several emotions throughout the game and her character really shines when it comes to story development. There isn't really any boring ole' plain Jane character in this game. Everyone in it is equipped with multiple personalities and unique characterisitcs and backgrounds which gives the game it's initial 'special flavor.' Especially since majority of the gameplay is character interaction... Moving on to the story.
Life is Strange doesn't have your usual cliche story, or re-used, watered down plot. It's actually different than the others. In a great way, at that. A unique story of a girl who finds out she is able to reverse time. As the story deepens when you continue on in the game, the current conflicts and events occur like they would in real life. One thing which leads to another, not like some cheesy "oh! this suddenly happens out of no where" story. When you follow the story, "A day in Max's everydaylife", you realize all the events that unravel before you which creates this wonderful plot. Which you get to see through the eyes of Max. Everything makes sense, no confusion or mystery since its just the life of Max nothing more complicated. (Except for the fact her life is complicated.)
I'd get into more details of the game and my thoughts and opinions, but it's getting late and I'm really tired. I can't believe I have already spent 30 minutes re-writing this review... I can do better things, like play the other episodes of Life is Strange or something. Anyway, I may continue making my full review on this game if I remember. Or when I beat the entire game. Whatever comes first.
But before I go, I'd recommend this to anyone. Even if my review didn't sound interesting, give a try. If I hadn't persuade you enough to buy the game, just give the demo a shot and see if you life it. To be specific now, I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a story-drenched game. For those familiar to The Walking Dead video game or any TellTale game, you'd enjoy this very much. Or those looking to getting into a casual episodic game for something to play as you lay back, i'd suggest checking this out .

I have played all 5 episodes of this game and overall I love it. If you enjoyed the Girl Who Leapt Through Time or stories of it's ilk then you'll love the story of Life is Strange. The choices you make in the game do have impact on the story, some of these impacts are subtle and only noticeable if you play the game again in a different way (or watch someone else do so) whereas some have a huge impact on a couple of the major events in the game.

The games character's and themes are relatable and real, and the story will make you cry, laugh and be on the edge of your seat in equal measure. The gameplay feels very much akin to the non-combat parts of Mass Effect, which is on the whole a good thing. And the aesthetic design of the characters and landscapes also dp their part to immerse you in a world that isn't our own, but feels very much like it could be, in a stylistic sense.
The only problems I had with the game is that some parts of the game can be tedious (although Max's internal soliloquys do often help alleviate the feeling of tedium) and the autosaves are occasionally a but further apart than I'd like them. A manual save which restarted you from the same position in an Elder Scrolls like fashoin would not go amiss.
But the good far far outweighs the bad. Do yourself a favour and get this game, preferably before watching the game theory episode revolving around the ending. Which I did. And regretted.

I'm playing with my cousin (We'll call him Jim", and we're using a mod called Dark Multiplayer.

"18 meters, come in at 2m/s and dock at port C5"

Keep in mind he SUCKS at using RCS thrusters and docking
I suddenly see his engines power to FULL THROTTLE, he thought he was in docking mode, and not stages mode. So He pressed Shift...
This spaceplane comes crashing into my space station, modules flying everywhere, poor kerbalnauts being sucked into the vaccum of space... My hardwork was gone in a second.
Fastforward 25 Kerbal Days
I have completed my second space station, as I admire it my cousin says "Whats that object coming towards your space station at 5000 m/s?"

I don't usually leave reviews for games, because I'm a very casual player and am not really good at giving technical critiques. So anything I have to say here is purely based on what I felt about this game.
My mind was blown. The characters were so well fleshed out and so relatable, that I almost felt as if I were watching myself in school again. Even secondary characters who have no bearing on the central plot at all had traits that made them each their own, making them all memorable. The story itself absolutely destroyed me - it was so heart-breaking, and brought to light many of the philosophical issues/questions raised by the concept of time travel, framing them in a way that makes them easy to understand.
There were several points in the game when I was reduced to tears. The mark of a truly great story is when you care so much for its characters, you cannot watch them suffer. Whether or not the actual gameplay was amazing, I couldn't say in detail, but I enjoyed it. It was satisfying to resolve the puzzles, and I've always liked games where I felt I had the ability to affect the story.

If you are one who enjoys space and space ships, as well as crashing said space ships then Kerbal Space Program is for YOU!
It all starts on the planet Kerbin, with its population of "science"-hungry Kerbals, all at your disposal so you can build Kerbin's Best..First....Only..hopefully successful space program!! With a massive amount of parts and billions of configurations you can really make anything! KSP also has an amazing modding community adding tons more amazing additions to the game so it never gets old. And best of all KSP is still in development with much more official content still to come, including parts, space program facilities and more planets to traverse and discover.
Currently there is a sandbox mode with unlimited EVERYTHING all from the START and fairly basic career mode which uses tech trees to unlock parts as you progress your space program and make great scientific discoveries.
Building a rocket and sending it to space or to another planet successfully can prove to be extremely difficult and will often take a great amount of attempts before success. It is rocket science after all :) However after you get the hang of building, launching, maneuvering and docking the rockets you will begin to see the unlimited potential of the kerbal space program. You can build a colony on duna (mars) or the mun (moon), get melted away by the sun, build huge space stations, ships and drive cars on the moon, possibilities are endless! And not to mention the uniqely named army of kerbal astronaughts at your disposal led by the great, Jebediah Kerman.
KSP is, without a doubt the greatest space game of all time!

If you are one who enjoys space and space ships, as well as crashing said space ships then Kerbal Space Program is for YOU!
It all starts on the planet Kerbin, with its population of "science"-hungry Kerbals, all at your disposal so you can build Kerbin's Best..First....Only..hopefully successful space program!! With a massive amount of parts and billions of configurations you can really make anything! KSP also has an amazing modding community adding tons more amazing additions to the game so it never gets old. And best of all KSP is still in development with much more official content still to come, including parts, space program facilities and more planets to traverse and discover.
Currently there is a sandbox mode with unlimited EVERYTHING all from the START and fairly basic career mode which uses tech trees to unlock parts as you progress your space program and make great scientific discoveries.
Building a rocket and sending it to space or to another planet successfully can prove to be extremely difficult and will often take a great amount of attempts before success. It is rocket science after all :) However after you get the hang of building, launching, maneuvering and docking the rockets you will begin to see the unlimited potential of the kerbal space program. You can build a colony on duna (mars) or the mun (moon), get melted away by the sun, build huge space stations, ships and drive cars on the moon, possibilities are endless! And not to mention the uniqely named army of kerbal astronaughts at your disposal led by the great, Jebediah Kerman.
KSP is, without a doubt the greatest space game of all time!

I just finished the full 5 episodes after playing them one after the other and I have to say, what a great game. Well, not so much a game as an interactive story, but still, it's one hell of a story. Playing through it, it reminded me a lot of both The Butterfly Effect and Donnie Darko, but mostly the latter, it really had this strange feel to it along with the music choices that gave me serious flashbacks to Donnie Darko. With that movie being one of my all time favourites, I was quite happy.
The game is quite an emotional rollercoaster and while they handled it well in most places, I thought it started to go a bit over the top in the third and fourth episodes, though, where it entered the realm of cringe worthy. It wasn't completely distracting, but it did pull me out of it a bit as I found it too much, like they were pushing for an emotional response and going overboard with it. The fifth had elements of that but it wasn't as OTT as the previous episodes.
Much like The Walking Dead Telltale series, this game immediately makes me want to start up again with completely different choices. While in the Walking Dead the choices didn't mean much, looking at the choices I made and how they influenced things, even two episodes down the line, really gives me hope that this series will be a lot better in that regard.
So do I recommend it? Yeah, but only if you like story games instead of heavy gameplay. It's a really great story that, while it does go over the top at times, really keeps you guessing all the way along, and the choices you make in early episodes can have outcomes that you really never saw coming further down the line.
Now I'm off to start again...
UPDATE: I went through again and was disappointed to find that the choices really didn't make much difference. A few dialogue changes, a scene or two missing (or added), but nothing that really matters. There's very little reason to actually worry about any of the choices you make, they give a slightly different feel to the story, but no real changes. The game does seem more geared towards Max being a 'nice girl', as in my second playthrough I made her more selfish and uncaring, but the story still had her being friendly and caring to people, so it was a bit jarring.
In regards to the ending, as I see a lot of negative comments about it. As a fan of Donnie Darko, I saw the ending coming from the first episode, so I wasn't bothered at all. To me, the story was more about the search for Rachel, the main story ended when the person responsible was finally caught. After that it was about the overarching time manipulation ability and the trouble it caused while progressing through the plot. The final choice was always going to be about self sacrifice.

One of my favorite sayings is "Always shoot for the moon... but if you miss you'll die horribly in space." Never has this ever been more true in "Kerbal Space Program", a video game exploring one planet's leap into the stars. That ends with crumpled debris and corpses floating in the blackness of the void.
If you haven't caught on to the theme yet, there is a lot of watching in utter defeat as your space vehicles explode into a thousand shards of metal as they slam into the unforgiving ground of an alien planet or moon.
So what is the game all about? Well basically it gives you an entire chest of LEGO-like rocket parts, structural bits, and science-y gadgets to slap together into a spaceship of your own design pretty much only limited by your own imagination. Then you attempt to fly these monstrosities higher and higher into the atmosphere, then into orbit around the Kerbals' home world, and finally to distance alien worlds. Afterward attempting to get your crew back home without them disintegrating during reentry.
While I am sure my frustration is seeping into this article, it's the good kind of frustration. The kind that drives you to design better space vehicles, have a lighter touch with the controls as you pilot your craft, and not make mistakes like decoupling your primary booster engine during take off causing it to cartwheel wildly into the sky before it slams back into your crew compartment (then explode).
There are many broken eggs when making this space omelet, but it's a lot of fun strapping rockets to them and smashing those eggs into the planet's surface at super sonic speeds. This all makes the victories even more rewarding. The perfect orbit and reentry. The first time you slingshot around a planet and get your Kerbonauts back home safety from the vacuum of space. Executing a flawless landing on the moon without tipping over and exploding. And watching with an amazing sense of pride as your spaceship, packed full of alien soil samples and experiments conducted in zero gravity, splashes down into the ocean and is successfully recovered.
All this is kept light hearted with the silliness of the Kerbals, the little green civilization inhabiting the planet you are helping take it's first steps towards the stars. By murdering their citizens in rocket powered death tin cans. Even as scraps of them are raining down over your space center the Kerbals keep it all tongue in cheek with their hilarious screaming faces on their personal monitors, flopping around as they try to waddle across the surface of the moon in their space suits, and running around the hanger like a bunch of little slapstick minions.
It's to be noted that this game is currently in early access 'alpha', but it's constantly being updated and improved. One of the biggest and most recent additions being career mode. Where the sandbox mode gives you the freedom to do whatever you want with unlimited supplies, career mode sets you up with the most basic of items to piece a rocket together, then pushes you to hone your skill and designs while carrying out scientific missions. Upon completion of these, you are rewarded with more bits to attach to you rocket and new missions to tackle. It adds a ton of depth to the game as it makes you feels like you are running your own space race to the stars, rather then just shooting countless Kerbals into space for your own amusement.
Also to give you guys a heads up, the learning curve is a bit steep right now as well. There are some in game tutorials, but to really start murdering a continuous stream of poor poor astronauts of your very own you'll have to do some research on the wiki page and watch some Youtube videos to get some basic knowledge of the controls/interface. I promise that it's worth it though to get a grip on the instruments so you can slam the big red button to go rocketing into the great blue yonder.
I highly recommend this game to anyone that ever once in a while needs something a bit more cerebral then a twitchy shooter or loves a good challenge. Or has a thing for sending cosmonauts to their doom.

Garry's Mod is not a game. It is a physics toy and sandbox style tool. In Gmod, you can reluctantly do whatever
you want to. You can: build things such as cars, buildings, bunkers,
airships, boats, or whatever you can think up, use weapons from other valve games, as well as add-on weapons created by
other people, play with physics, kill NPCs with literally anything, drive a world of vehicles, paint, destroy stuff, spawn props, spawn ragdolls to pose and beat up, make a machinima for use on Youtube or other video websites, listen to music, and MUCH MUCH more. There are addons to download, like maps and player models.
The maps can vary from Counter Strike to Team Fortress, Portal to
Garry's Mod, and Day Of Defeat to Left 4 Dead. A very addicting toy from Team Garry.

Lyfe is Strange is great. A gem. Like Freaks & Geeks except more deep and with time travel. Loved it. Admittedly though some very important moments were spoiled by the pretty bad facial and lip syncing. That was a shame. However the storyline is great, the amount of choices it offers and the way it presents them to the player are remarkable, and for once I actually found a linear video game original story that I genuinley found unique and enjoyable. The soundtrack is great as well, characters well developed ect ect. (A complete hipster photographer with the power to travel into the past? Do I detect irony?) The moral choices in the game are fantastic. They are presented as moral choices in games should be (unbiased and with no 'right' answer defined by the game.) It is remarkable how much choice in plot they managed to fit in without blowing the scope of the game. When it comes to branching narratives, I think of all the ones I have seen this is by far the best at making your choices actually feel impactful(and yes I have played Telltale's The Waking Dead FYI.)
Pros:
-Great story that keeps you interested and not knowing what comes next
-Fantastic character development
-Huge amount of leeway to use your choices to shape the narrative to your liking without sacrificing the overall morals & plot
-Wonderfully chosen soundtrack
-Awesome use of metaphor thoughout the story and through the game mechanics
Cons:
-Poor lipsyncing(as in, character who talk without any of the muscles in their mouths moving, which is pretty frustrating since it happens in some of the most emotionally impactful parts of the story)
-Some conversation transitions don't work too well
-At the end of each episode it shows you your choices from the chapter and what percent of people worldwide or from your Steam Friends List chose that certain option as well. Don't get me wrong, I like this but the problem is it shows you also what COULD have happened if you had chosen something else, and that can take some of the impact out of the decisions you made. airships, boats, or whatever you can think up, use weapons from other valve games, as well as add-on weapons created by
other people, play with physics, kill NPCs with literally anything, drive a world of vehicles, paint, destroy stuff, spawn props, spawn ragdolls to pose and beat up, make a machinima for use on Youtube or other video websites, listen to music, and MUCH MUCH more. There are addons to download, like maps and player models.
The maps can vary from Counter Strike to Team Fortress, Portal to
Garry's Mod, and Day Of Defeat to Left 4 Dead. A very addicting toy from Team Garry.

I just finished the full 5 episodes after playing them one after the other and I have to say, what a great game. Well, not so much a game as an interactive story, but still, it's one hell of a story. Playing through it, it reminded me a lot of both The Butterfly Effect and Donnie Darko, but mostly the latter, it really had this strange feel to it along with the music choices that gave me serious flashbacks to Donnie Darko. With that movie being one of my all time favourites, I was quite happy.
The game is quite an emotional rollercoaster and while they handled it well in most places, I thought it started to go a bit over the top in the third and fourth episodes, though, where it entered the realm of cringe worthy. It wasn't completely distracting, but it did pull me out of it a bit as I found it too much, like they were pushing for an emotional response and going overboard with it. The fifth had elements of that but it wasn't as OTT as the previous episodes.
Much like The Walking Dead Telltale series, this game immediately makes me want to start up again with completely different choices. While in the Walking Dead the choices didn't mean much, looking at the choices I made and how they influenced things, even two episodes down the line, really gives me hope that this series will be a lot better in that regard.
So do I recommend it? Yeah, but only if you like story games instead of heavy gameplay. It's a really great story that, while it does go over the top at times, really keeps you guessing all the way along, and the choices you make in early episodes can have outcomes that you really never saw coming further down the line.
Now I'm off to start again...
UPDATE: I went through again and was disappointed to find that the choices really didn't make much difference. A few dialogue changes, a scene or two missing (or added), but nothing that really matters. There's very little reason to actually worry about any of the choices you make, they give a slightly different feel to the story, but no real changes. The game does seem more geared towards Max being a 'nice girl', as in my second playthrough I made her more selfish and uncaring, but the story still had her being friendly and caring to people, so it was a bit jarring.
In regards to the ending, as I see a lot of negative comments about it. As a fan of Donnie Darko, I saw the ending coming from the first episode, so I wasn't bothered at all. To me, the story was more about the search for Rachel, the main story ended when the person responsible was finally caught. After that it was about the overarching time manipulation ability and the trouble it caused while progressing through the plot. The final choice was always going to be about self sacrifice.

This game is great. At first I was turned away because of previous games that claim that "All your decisions have consequences" have made the mistake of making wildly unlikable characters, not this one though. The characters in the game are great, they all have layers to them, almost no-one is a 2D cardboard cut-out, so when you make a mistake and they die, you feel guilty, real consequences.
The time travel mechanic is handled well and it is used very cleverly in some puzzles. It also makes major decisions different, now you can experience the consequences first hand and if you are unhappy with the results you can return and make a different decision. Although this means that none of them will be the obvious "Right" one.
The graphics are also nice, the cell shaded design gives the game a nice sense of style.
The story is a little bit of a slow boil, starting with teen drama (even though I kinda like teen drama) which can be boring for some people, but it really begins to pick up half way through episode 2 when, without trying to spoil, some crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down.

Garry's Mod is not a game. It is a physics toy and sandbox style tool. In Gmod, you can reluctantly do whatever
you want to. You can: build things such as cars, buildings, bunkers,
airships, boats, or whatever you can think up, use weapons from other valve games, as well as add-on weapons created by
other people, play with physics, kill NPCs with literally anything, drive a world of vehicles, paint, destroy stuff, spawn props, spawn ragdolls to pose and beat up, make a machinima for use on Youtube or other video websites, listen to music, and MUCH MUCH more. There are addons to download, like maps and player models.
The maps can vary from Counter Strike to Team Fortress, Portal to
Garry's Mod, and Day Of Defeat to Left 4 Dead. A very addicting toy from Team Garry.

What is there to say about Life Is Strange that has yet to be said?
The dialogue is super cringey, as in...i feel like it was written by people who have only heard teenagers speaking in English via reading comments or overseeing texts and sarcastic posts on things. Nobody unironically says any of the things that are said in this game in reality, and every time I heard the word "hella" I winced, to the point where I looked like I was having an epileptic fit.
The choices you make, as it is with all of these "choice heavy" games that have come out lately, matter diddly squat. The time travel is inconsistent and used stupidly, the main character is obnoxiously pretentious and seems to be rewarded for that, and the fact that she's bisexual doesn't even matter because any choice made to express a relationship with Chloe ends as all poorly written LBTQ stories do: Death and sadness.
Honestly? Choosing your girlfriend potentially destroys the whole world? That's a bit heavy-handed and a whole new low.
The lip-synching is awful, the controls for PC gaming (using keyboard alone) is obnoxious as hell, and there's very little incentive for achievement collecting.
It makes me angry, because I saw a lot of potential with this game when it started, but each new 'episode' just got progressively worse.
Don't EVEN get me started on that Alt Reality with Chloe either. Honestly? First this game now Me Before You? Life in a wheelchair isn't so horrible that suicide is the best answer folks. Let's try and get a little more creative with our writing here, please.
Again, this whole game's concept and "twist" was something very easily called from Episode One, but I kept playing with the hope that maybe--just maybe--it would prove me wrong and do something different.
If I wanted a story about the butterfly effect, I would just watch the damn movie. This game and Until Dawn are just both so...sloppy about it. Just stop pretending you're giving your players 'so many choices' if in the end things really only end one way or another and that there's really only one "right" ending.
Honestly folks? Save your money and time and just watch a silent Lets Play of this if you really wanna see it.

One of the best games I've EVER played.
It's not complete, but definitely playable, virtually bug-free, and infinitely fun.
In short, you manage all aspects of a modern space program. You build your spacecraft from available parts, hire astronauts, fly the craft to accomplish whatever mission you wish to accomplish, return the spacecraft with interesting scientific data which is converted into science points. Science points are then used to uclock more parts for your spaceship.
There is some trial and error, and in the beginning, you'll crash or leave your poor astronaut forever stranded in orbit. But once you figure out a balance between fuel, thrust and weight, you'll be able to successfully run your missions. You won't need to sit and calculate. Getting the right balance is pretty intuitive after a few mistakes.
Speaking of missions. Currently, in the unmodded 0.23 version, you have to make up your own. The possibilities are pretty much infinite. You can try to reach a certain height or a certain orbit. You can launch a probe to explore your own planet, the moon, or another planet. You can build a space station, which can be used as a staging point for other missions. You can build bases on the moon, or other planets. And so much more, I have not even started to discover.
The parts cost money, but at this point money is not an issue, as the economy has not been implemented yet. So you are free to mess up a few missions before getting them right, losing spacecraft and astronauts in the process.
If you're in for a little challenge, I recommed the MCE mod. This mod introduces an economy, as you have a finite amount of money to build you craft and hire your astronauts. If you mess up during a mission, you can abort the mission and restore to the moment before launch, but you'll be fined.
It also introduces a huge number of varied missions, which give you payout once accomplished, allowing you to build new and more expensive craft for more complex missions. Also, it gives you a sequence of "historical" missions, which start up very easy (reach a certain height, enter orbit, carry a certain amount of fuel to orbit), but become harder and more complex (orbit the moon, build a space station, build a moonbase, etc) as you progress.
If you are not satisfied with the available missions, the mod gives you a tool to create your own and post it for others to try. Similarly, you have access to user-created missions as well.
On my i5 with an Nvidia 650 Ti, the game runs very smoothly, and I've never had a crash. At times, the game freezes, but you can go to desktop with the handy Ctrl-Alt-Del, and then re-enter the game by pressing the game's tab on the taskbar to unfreeze it.
The game may not be complete - or so the developers claim. Even if development stopped here, I would still recommend buying it, as there countless great mods to enhance the game and complete whatever the developers have left out.
The price may seem a bit steep for an early access game, but it's money well-spent. Kerbal Space Program is cheaper than 60-dollar blockbusters that may have better graphics but unoriginal, repetitive, and/or short gameplay. The game will keep you awake many nights, and you'll have played 30 hours, before scratching the surface of what can be done.
Three words: BUY. IT. NOW.
EDIT: I've heard people complaining about the game being slow by adding mods. This is just not true. My computer is definitely not top of the line (see above) and I run 24 mods with no slowdowns and barely a few crashes.
I loved the game at the time of my review. After 100 hour of gameplay I am amazed by it, as there are man mods that add more realism, customization, and gameplay options.

I really regret not getting around to this game earlier, and I'm so glad I was able to avoid most of the major spoilers. Absolute 5/5 for me. Though I can see how some parts of the branching plot aren't the most compelling, my first playthrough had me in tears by the end and on the verge of tears for most of the last two episodes. I clocked in just over 15 hours on that first playthrough and I plan on playing through again to explore some of the alternate choices; you'll definitely get your money's worth.
In terms of gameplay, Life Is Strange is a great take on the Telltale style of adventure/point-and-click games. There's tons of environmental storytelling. Some of it is just for fluff and world-building, but some of it also figures in heavily to the outcomes of some events. Dontnod got a lot of  mileage out of the time powers as well. I would compare the puzzles to games like Portal, because you really do have to think outside of the box ("think with portals", so to speak) in order to solve some of the puzzles.
The writing can be a little cringe-worthy at times, but I definitely became attached to most of the characters. If you can bare with it, then there's a lot to love here. There's so much attention to detail too, with a lot of foreshadowing and clues that really standout during certain sections. The ending relies on a few tropes from time travel stories and you might predict the final choice fairly early on, but I was invested enough that I wanted to believe there was a way around it, and there's still plenty of twists and turns to keep you guessing regardless.
If you even remotely consider yourself to be into story-focsued games, then this is an absolute must play. And even if you're not, Life Is Strange might just change your mind.

I picked this game up on sale and got all the episodes for around $10(So, wait if you can for a sale!) and my god I have to say that the money was well spent.
The art style while very basic looks great even when the character models look awful. The story has been very well written and revised. The choices you make do come back to haunt you in one way or another. One major mistake I made in this game is that I didn't take the scenic route so I missed A LOT, so be sure to look around for everything and think of past events. This game was like a lifetime with friends, you laugh, you cry, you get mad, ect. and I can say I got attached to characters so much that I would talk to my computer screen. This game made me ponder a lot of my personal opinions like the use of doctor assisted suicide and suicide in general.
Now, I do have some bad things to say about this game. It glitches rarely, but when it does it's really annoying as typically it freezes everything around you and doesn't let you countinue. The lip-syncing is just awful at times, there were times that 1. My audio would just straight up stop or 2. Characters wouldn't even be moving their lips. There is no manuel save and while it does auto-save a lot it's annoying when you have to stop in the middle of an investigation and close your game and start over. Random FPS, now this is not a hard game to run and I have a good PC, but it would sometimes just slow down in the middle of a cutscene or while I was walking. This is easily one of the best indie games you can get your filthy moondust covered hands on.
Although the learning curve in the beginning is pretty steep for someone who isn't aware of basic orbital physics or is on par with the navball or rocket construction, it's nothing a couple of videos from Scott Manley (or Robbaz if you intend to just make space a circus) can't fix. If you however know what you are doing and/or have been following someone who knows what they're doing you should have no problem at all getting into this game.
It features many planets, their moons and in the future even an asteroid belt you'll be able to interact with all from the comfort of your own room/NASA mission control centre.
You can build everything from rockets, space planes, landers, probes and god knows what.
The game also features modding support and mods for the game can be found on the KSP site. Mods can add everything from boat parts, weapons, tools for making robots and mechs, new parts to add to the already pretty big library of parts and even customized planets.
The game is however somewhat unstable and building large stations etc can often cause horrible lag on all but the beefiest computers, it is however only a problem when you build VERY large stuff and once the game is finished the optimization will no doubt be better than it currently is.
I truly recommend this game to any and all of you! There is something for pretty much everyone in this game, if there isn't then mods have probably added it.

I really regret not getting around to this game earlier, and I'm so glad I was able to avoid most of the major spoilers. Absolute 5/5 for me. Though I can see how some parts of the branching plot aren't the most compelling, my first playthrough had me in tears by the end and on the verge of tears for most of the last two episodes. I clocked in just over 15 hours on that first playthrough and I plan on playing through again to explore some of the alternate choices; you'll definitely get your money's worth.
In terms of gameplay, Life Is Strange is a great take on the Telltale style of adventure/point-and-click games. There's tons of environmental storytelling. Some of it is just for fluff and world-building, but some of it also figures in heavily to the outcomes of some events. Dontnod got a lot of  mileage out of the time powers as well. I would compare the puzzles to games like Portal, because you really do have to think outside of the box ("think with portals", so to speak) in order to solve some of the puzzles.
The writing can be a little cringe-worthy at times, but I definitely became attached to most of the characters. If you can bare with it, then there's a lot to love here. There's so much attention to detail too, with a lot of foreshadowing and clues that really standout during certain sections. The ending relies on a few tropes from time travel stories and you might predict the final choice fairly early on, but I was invested enough that I wanted to believe there was a way around it, and there's still plenty of twists and turns to keep you guessing regardless.
If you even remotely consider yourself to be into story-focsued games, then this is an absolute must play. And even if you're not, Life Is Strange might just change your mind.

So you wanna fly rockets?
First, you have to build them, and then they have to fly without "expressive deconstruction". Make sure you have enough thrust to get up and away from the planet, hold your course, learn aerodynamics and orbital mechanics. Learn what a Lagrange point is. Learn what Delta-V is. Learn how to maintain a geo-synchronus orbit. Learn to use gravitational slingshots to cut your flight time. Learn to land a can on a foreign body to plant a flag and be proud of that moment! Many Kerbalnauts lost their lives in trial-and-error mistakes to get you HERE! Standing on the Mun! You can go home a hero!
Then you realize you forgot to bring enough fuel to get home.
Do I recommend this game?
YES! You'll learn so much and go so far and crash so many times, but that moment of triumph of planting that flag...

A realistic physics based aerospace sandbox game with the adorable and fearless mascots the Kerbals. If you try to play this game without watching at least 30 minutes of beginners tutorials, you will inevitably kill or strand Jebediah Kerman on your first attempt. Much like watching tapes of the early Apollo program, you are lucky to get off the ground and almost assuradely will blow up your first several attempts.
It is perhaps the only sandbox game I've played that you could say has some measure of linear progression to it, as you will feel a great sense of accomplishment once you get into orbit, eventually the moon, and beyond. The recent story mode gives you some constraint as your feats will allow you to selectively unlock new technology, which is perhaps the most honest guide an inherently sandbox game can provide.
While the learning curve may be steep, you will enjoy every step of the learning process. I cannot reccomend this game enough to anyone who enjoys more than crouching behind objects in first person shooters and firing blindly in an endless grind for reputation.

So, let's get this out of the way. I highly recommend this game to anybody. As long as you're playing a videogame for the experience, for the connections, the immersion, and the memories, Life is Strange is literally the perfect game.
Now, let's talk why. Life is Strange is special. It has that really special spark that gives it life, that causes the player to truly feel connected to the game, to care, and to think about it for hours on end. This game has kept me up at night. But more than that, I will remember this game probably for the rest of my life. I've played a lot of videogames in my time, and there are only a few that I can say will stick with me. The in-game experience (connection with characters, immersion, character quality, etc) really only comprises a small part of why I recommend this game. It makes me rethink choices, appreciate free will, and feel more connected the the real world. It makes me revel in my ability to be involved. It makes me feel digusted for wanting to be removed and apathetic. I don't think I'm exaggerating when I say that this game has been life-changing.
As for the game itself, you play an 18-year-old girl named Max Caulfield who just moved back to her hometown (Arcadia Bay, Oregon) after living in Seattle for 5 years. The game begins with your experiences as an everyday schoolgirl with everyday troubles. Suddenly your world is flipped around when you realize you are NOT an everyday schoolgirl. Things escalate, the story unfolds, and the entire time, you play the game from the perspective of a normal person, not a superhero. The gameplay is very Heavy Rain-esque, in that it's an interactive movie type game. There are detective elements, but really the point is to make choices, interact with the world, and see what happens.
For those of you still reading, there's not much else to say without giving away parts of the story. If I haven't convinced you to buy it yet, then hopefully I will now: This game is worth far more than $20. It's worth more than $60 for what you get out of it. I have played the game for 27 hours, and I plan to play for 100 more, at least. My only regret is that I will never again be able to play it for the first time. So go ahead! BUY IT! Let me live vicariously through you! Four people who watched me play this game keep asking me if I've finished it because they were so engaged in the story, and they weren't even playing! You'd only be hurting yourself by not getting this game.

Okay, that was my early access review. I now have a 4 digit number of hours playing the game and it is in full release, so time to update it...
It is over 2,000 hours later playing it and I'm still liking and playing  this game. It cost me less than $20 when I bought it in early access, so my price per hour of play is less than one cent. I have played this game more than every other game in my Steam account combined.
So what is KSP? It's an open world, do what you want game of building rockets (or space planes) and seeing if they will fly, and if they do, of exploring an entire solar system. The Kerbol System is smaller than ours, to make it quicker to play and more approachable for those of us who don't have degrees in Orbital Mechanics or Astropyhsics. And those little green Kerbals are just so cute, you feel bad when you inevitably crash and burn. And you can do it in sandbox mode, science or career mode, so you can keep going back and trying new things.
Sandbox mode - everything is available from the start and money is not a consideration so you can go to the furthest reaches of the Kerbol System. But if you are new to KSP, better off to start with getting to orbit and then the Mun. But, despite there being a "career" mode, you can play an entire career/campaign in sandbox.
Science mode - no money requirements, but you have only low tech rocket parts at the start. You need science points to unlock new technologies that give you access to new or better rocket parts. You gather science by visiting biomes on Kerbin, the Mun or other planets and performing experiments. So you have to work your way up.
Career mode - you have to balance a budget, every rocket costs you $$$, and you have to worry about reputation and science as well. You can earn reputation, $$$ or science by completing contracts. Contracts include things like setting speed and altitude records, getting into orbit, visiting other planets and moons, building space stations, collecting resources from asteroids or other planets, completing science projects and taking up space tourists. Pretty much all the stuff that people are talking about for the commercialization of space.
Mods - KSP has a huge modding community and there are hundreds, if not thousands of mods out there. Everything from allowing you to build steam punk styled rockets to developing advanced technologies like fusion power, plasma drives and even FTL drive. There are mods that add new planets and new solar systems. Mods that add new contracts, mods that make the game easier and a lot more than make it harder and more realistic. Mods that add life support, that require communications networks and that allow you to build satellites to scan planets. Mods that allow you to build colonies on other planets, and even build roockets there using ISRU (in situ resource utilization). One mode Real Solar System converts Kerbal to Earth and so you can go launch from Kennedy Space Centre (or Baikonur, or many other real space ports) and explore Mars or Jupiter. But Real Solar System needs a lot of mods (aka the Realism Overhaul combo pack) which make the game much more realistically... and that generally means harder, so it's best left for the advanced rocket jockeys only.
Try the free demo, but it only hints at what the full game (and mods) will offer. Hope you enjoy it!

Pretty much all the stuff that people are talking about for the commercialization of space.
Mods - KSP has a huge modding community and there are hundreds, if not thousands of mods out there. Everything from allowing you to build steam punk styled rockets to developing advanced technologies like fusion power, plasma drives and even FTL drive. There are mods that add new planets and new solar systems. Mods that add new contracts, mods that make the game easier and a lot more than make it harder and more realistic. Mods that add life support, that require communications networks and that allow you to build satellites to scan planets. Mods that allow you to build colonies on other planets, and even build roockets there using ISRU (in situ resource utilization). One mode Real Solar System converts Kerbal to Earth and so you can go launch from Kennedy Space Centre (or Baikonur, or many other real space ports) and explore Mars or Jupiter. But Real Solar System needs a lot of mods (aka the Realism Overhaul combo pack) which make the game much more realistically... and that generally means harder, so it's best left for the advanced rocket jockeys only.
Try the free demo, but it only hints at what the full game (and mods) will offer. Hope you enjoy it!

tl;dr: Kerbal Space Program is a game that involves a lot of thought and is massively improved with mods. Get it if you want that kind of experience and don't mind poor performance or the occasional bug.
KSP is focused around space travel, and as such, you have a lot of time that's just waiting for things to happen. In Vanilla, this means that you have to play close attention to everything going on, but with mods, you can pretty much let the game play itself. The game is divided into two main sections; construction and flight. The construction system in KSP is intuitive and easy to use, but can become frustrating when you unlock a large amount of parts due to the organization of the parts. Flight is as complicated as you'd think it would be - in Vanilla, you only have maneuver nodes to make things easier, which allow you to plan maneuvers before you make them.
Vanilla KSP is missing a few key features that are made up in two mods - MechJeb and Kerbal Alarm Clock. MechJeb is an autopilot system that can do anything from planning and performing maneuvers to automatically landing or docking spacecraft, and provides a large amount of essential information about your spacecraft, and Kerbal Alarm Clock allows you to set alarms that are triggered from various things. Without these two mods, KSP is far more frustrating and based on far more guesswork.
KSP is notorious for its bugs and poor performance. If you want to build a colony or large station, or if you want to just make a really big ship, you can expect sub-20 fps performance even on beefy computers. Bugs mostly have to do with physics simulation, and can sometimes cause parts to break when they shouldn't or cause your ship to control oddly.
All in all, KSP is a great game for just sitting and relaxing with music or a video playing while you explore the Kerbol system. Mods dramatically improve and expand the experience, and installation of mods is made easy with the Comprehensive Kerbal Archive Network program. The physics simulation is top-notch, but as a result, performance can be  worse than expected.

Firstly, this game has a great learning curve, especially if you're like me and want to learn the game by doing it yourself. With only 32 hours on this game, I'm not an expert, however the vastness of the Kerbol System is beyond belief. 7 planets and 9 moons make this game sound small. However, the challenge of planning the route, the right lander and the right spaceship make the game much longer than you might expect, but not tediously; it makes the game feel much more grand. Every celestial has different gravity strength and a different place and surroundings and require different spaceships. For example, a Mun landingcraft, which is designed to land somewhere with little gravity and no atmosphere and is close to Kerbin, will be much different than an Eve landingcraft, which has high gravity and lots of atmosphere. Personally, I'd recommend it mainly if you're interested in rocketry, physics and simulators, although the game can be quirky and fun amd is fun for most ages, although it can be boring and tedious at times. 8/10. Tl;dr Play this game if you want an accurate presentation of space travel, but can cope with some frustration.

The narrative driven, choice based adventure game has been a pretty big hit ever since Telltale made The Walking Dead. Lots of other studios have taken a crack at creating uncomfortable and trying scenarios for gamers to rack their minds with. Those studios usually forget to make choices have deeper meaning or create decisions that exist within a binary function of "right" and "wrong."
Life is Strange attempts to tackle the problems these games typically face. It doesn't quite nail the impact of decisions (deciding to go with an all or nothing type ending), but it certainly sidesteps the issue of viewing the world in terms of black and white.
The main plot follows a week in the life of Max Caulfield, an 18 year old art student studying at a prestigious school in a fictional Oregonian town. She witnesses the death of a punk rock girl and, in a moment of desperation, turns back time. She doesn't know what happened or how she did it, but manipulation of the very fabric of space and time is within her control.
The tale then follows her path to uncover the source of her powers, the reason behind the murder she originally witnessed and the problems facing Blackwell Academy. Lots of the story deals with a coming of age type narrative arc, before giving way to a murder mystery straight out of Law & Order.
The real meat and potatoes comes from all the different branching choices you're given. Life is Strange deftly handles choices without falling back on "right" and "wrong." Most decisions will never seem better or particularly easy. It's all about figuring out how you would react or what causes the least amount of harm.
Max's power of time control is also wonderfully worked into the gameplay. Once you make a choice and see the impact play out, you can immediately rewind to attempt the alternate option or just to tinker around with different outcomes. Instead of relying on the player to keep different save files or playthrough a second time, you can see basically all of the decisions first-hand.
There is one key part of the story that rips control away from Max and creates a heartbreaking encounter that can potentially end in tragedy. There are also story arcs that tackle the implications of getting a "do-over" and changing "destiny." It's not entirely original, but its application is very well done.
What’s not so great is the dialog in the earlier episodes. Until around the mid-point of Episode 2, the writing is a bit wonky. Things like, “hella amazeballs” and “for cereal” are uttered without a hint of irony. It feels like an adult was trying to remember what being a teen was and mixed up some memes online.
The acting is also stilted, at first. I’m guessing no one was exactly sure how the game was going to pan out during the development of the first episode, but it just feels like a lack of direction was going on. Some of the lines are either a bit too soft or lack any dramatic weight. This does eventually pick up and turn into genuinely great performances (save for the final episode fizzling out), but it’s not thoroughly mesmerizing.
There are also some uncanny valley moments with the presentation. While this runs on the Unreal 3 engine, the characters are stiff and the environments feel detached. There is a very touching scene in a pool, but it looks like two dead mannequins floating in nothingness. I couldn’t get around that image, either.
What I did truly love was how gameplay elements were organically woven into the story. There are a lot of puzzles sprinkled throughout Max’s adventure and it’s awesome to not feel like you’re simply a spectator. You have to use critical thinking to figure out solutions based on the powers you’ve been given.
One scene has you gather chemicals to create an IED, blow open a door and then rewind so you end up on the other side. It’s a really awesome accomplishment. It truly feels like you came up with the answer on your own.
Chapter 4 is where this really shines. You have multiple pieces of information you’ve gathered over the course of the game that you’re required to piece together. You have to take a long look at any correlation and connect the dots. Even if you fail, the game has a few work-arounds to get you back on track (excluding your rewind).
The final chapter drops the damn ball, however. There is a stealth section that is entirely pointless. Since you can rewind and remain in place, there is literally no reason to have characters searching for you. You cannot fail and pressing forward serves no repercussion. I understand it was a narrative device, but it utterly fails as a piece of gaming.
Honestly, the game was building up to a crescendo that Episode 5 never delivers. The definitive ending is certainly gut-wrenching, but the 2 hours leading up to it feel like a cop-out. It seems like DONTNOD had no idea how to really make your actions take affect or just wanted to impose their own will on the story. Regardless, Episode 5 does away with all of the good that the rest of the game exhibits.
There are some light puzzles, but everything is a forced, linear path and the dialog amounts to nothing more than expository exchanges with main characters. Some beats will tug at the heart strings, but most will just bore you (do I need to see that damn picture changing cutscene each time?).
That doesn’t destroy all the good that Episode 3 and 4 bring, but it does bookend the game with average scenarios. It starts slow and ends with a whimper. If you chopped out a little bit of the first episode, you could honestly combine it with the second and get the same result.
In all honesty, a lot of these games seem to crumble under marketing hype. Developers never know when to chill out with how cool their games are (or publishers pressure them into overselling their creations). Life is Strange is more about the relationship between two friends and how choices aren’t the end of the world (until they literally are).
I hate to be so harsh to a game that tackles such dark, dramatic and realistic topics like sexual abuse, stalkers, suicide and bullying, but most of the elements drag down the experience. The ridiculous twist of the real villain is also completely out of left field.
The game creates characters that feel like 3 dimensional beings and demands you look at them as more than caricatures, then the final chapter ends up labeling you a hero and the main bad-guy a psychopath. Dammit.
Still, Life is Strange is absolutely worth a playthrough. It’s not the best thing around, but it has an excellent mixture of gameplay and narrative heft to feel like a really important piece of gaming history. It will also resonate deeply with people who have suffered through similar tragedies in life.
I just wish DONTNOD nailed every aspect. This could have been a stone cold masterpiece.

Life Is Strange is an episodic narrative that evolves and develops around the choices you make in each episode.  In each episode, there are big choices you have to make which can cause a somewhat significant change in the overall narrative while other minor choices alter fairly inconsequential points of their own.  A big thing to get out of the way is that your choices in the episodes don't affect the ending in any major way but rather, shape the narrative that leads up to the ending.  I feel the need to mention this since most might be going into this game thinking all their actions will affect the ending in some major way, when in truth, it is used as a device to shape your personal narrative and experience.
Life is Strange is a great entry into the “interactive story” genre because while it tells a compelling story that shapes around the choices you make, it also has a great cast of major and minor characters each with their own unique personalities and stories.  However, the story is really about Max (you) and your best friend Chloe.  While much of it is central to them, all the major characters also become central to your own story in various ways as each episode plays out.  This means that your choices when interacting with them, or avoiding them completely if possible, will oftentimes greatly alter how they play into your own story and future interactions with them.
Very early into the game, you discover you have the ability to time-travel or rather, rewind time.  This mechanic is pretty fun as you can often talk to someone and learn something about them then go back in time to use this information in new dialogue options to gain new insight on the character, or change their perception of you.  This can often award you unforeseen benefits in later episodes or possibly unforeseen consequences, depending on your choices.  The rewind mechanic also allows for some great puzzles which, while a but under utilized, are fun to figure out when presented with them.  As Max's ability with time-travel evolve, it'll introduce you to some crazy scenarios.
I thoroughly enjoyed Life is Strange and I think the narrative doesn't hold any punches when explaining itself.  It can be incredibly sad and tragic at points but also has moments of heroism and humor.  By the time you get to episode 5, you'll be wanting to know how it all wraps up and that is where things, in a way, start falling apart with the game.  Episode 5 is, in my opinion, the weakest episode in the game.  It does wrap things up but much of it felt like padding to extend the play-time for an entire episode.  It sharply deviates from the established mechanics leaving you with very little choices to be made and instead, seems more interested to just push the story forward without your input.  There are big choices in this episode but the very linear path you're guided down as well as this being the final episode, your choices seem moot at this point since you really won't get to see the effects it has on the narrative later in the game.
The ending, which I'm not going to spoil, is
the culmination of all your choices coming to a head, but rather one last choice you have to make.  I can't say how or if you'll enjoy the different endings but to me they felt like the logical conclusion to the story.  I was initially dissapointed with the ending I got but after thinking about it, I felt it fit perfectly into the story, a story that provides a great sub-text that may not be greatly apparent right away.  I feel games like these shouldn't be taken at face value because there are often undercurrents and themes that show themselves when you stop to think about the experience and the story it's trying to tell.  To me, doing so has greatly enriched the story and certainly gave me pause to admire how (for the most part) well constructed it all was.
I can say that it's been an greatly enjoyable ride and I would recommend it to anyone who might be intrested in it.

Like I said in another review of mine, you should stop right now.  Don't look at any screenshots, ESPECIALLY the ones on the store page; watch no videos; read no story details; if you have any intention of getting this game, know that it is excellent and that you will get so much more out of it the less you know about it.  If I can only offer two words, let them be this: Twin Peaks.
Luckily, I didn't play it until I had pretty much forgotten everything I knew about it and my experience with the game was so much richer for it.  Thus, this review won't talk at all about the story or the characters or anything like that.
So what is it?
(LiS) is a modern adventure game in the vein of a Telltale game (Walking Dead being an extraordinary example of the type), but this one is by Dontnod, developers of
, which you probably didn't play, but that's no matter.  Like most Telltale games out there, the big hook for LiS is presenting players with several choices, with the promise that they will impact the game as episodes (of which there are 5) play out.  However, if you've played any Telltale game out there, you'll probably shrug your shoulders as most of them are pretty deterministic and the curious-minded will go back and find out that their choices didn't really amount to anything.
Similarly, player choices in LiS won't affect the overall plot of the game, but unlike the typical Telltale, your choices can have a deep impact on the
you take to the game's inevitable conclusion.  In LiS, you have several opportunities to affect how the story plays out, in a sense personalizing it for you even though everyone playing it will inevitably reach the same place, and this amounts to much more than simple dialog cues that change.  More than that, whether or not you live with those outcomes is also a choice you make.  It's pretty meta, but I'm not going to explain why.
Some nitpicky stuff - anything that isn't specifically motion-captured is clunky; while this doesn't take away anything from the game, it does render a few otherwise-strong scenes a bit awkward and lessens the emotional impact (unless you're really good at suspending your disbelief).  Voice acting is pretty good, but the dialog is ripped from Y2K despite taking place in the present.  Still, the actors/actresses do a great job of rolling with it and the writing is strong enough to really build character from the principal actresses to the supporting cast.  There is an odd thing, too, when going through your dialog trees where a character's lip sync totally fails; you just get to watch them bob their head as words hauntingly make their way out of their throats without a single twitch from the mouth.  Not a deal-breaker by any means, but it does have a jarring impact on the immersion.
At any rate, you have an extremely well-developed story to experience in LiS, with very significant choices to be made, populated by lovingly-written characters that truly feel like they live in this world.  This is a fantastic piece of fiction, regardless of the medium, and it should be enjoyed by as many people as possible.  Dontnod did a phenomenal job here.
