New players may be at a loss as to what some of the parts are used for, thus forcing them to go searching for explanations on these parts.

The narrative driven, choice based adventure game has been a pretty big hit ever since Telltale made The Walking Dead. Lots of other studios have taken a crack at creating uncomfortable and trying scenarios for gamers to rack their minds with. Those studios usually forget to make choices have deeper meaning or create decisions that exist within a binary function of "right" and "wrong."
Life is Strange attempts to tackle the problems these games typically face. It doesn't quite nail the impact of decisions (deciding to go with an all or nothing type ending), but it certainly sidesteps the issue of viewing the world in terms of black and white.
The main plot follows a week in the life of Max Caulfield, an 18 year old art student studying at a prestigious school in a fictional Oregonian town. She witnesses the death of a punk rock girl and, in a moment of desperation, turns back time. She doesn't know what happened or how she did it, but manipulation of the very fabric of space and time is within her control.
The tale then follows her path to uncover the source of her powers, the reason behind the murder she originally witnessed and the problems facing Blackwell Academy. Lots of the story deals with a coming of age type narrative arc, before giving way to a murder mystery straight out of Law & Order.
The real meat and potatoes comes from all the different branching choices you're given. Life is Strange deftly handles choices without falling back on "right" and "wrong." Most decisions will never seem better or particularly easy. It's all about figuring out how you would react or what causes the least amount of harm.
Max's power of time control is also wonderfully worked into the gameplay. Once you make a choice and see the impact play out, you can immediately rewind to attempt the alternate option or just to tinker around with different outcomes. Instead of relying on the player to keep different save files or playthrough a second time, you can see basically all of the decisions first-hand.
There is one key part of the story that rips control away from Max and creates a heartbreaking encounter that can potentially end in tragedy. There are also story arcs that tackle the implications of getting a "do-over" and changing "destiny." It's not entirely original, but its application is very well done.
What’s not so great is the dialog in the earlier episodes. Until around the mid-point of Episode 2, the writing is a bit wonky. Things like, “hella amazeballs” and “for cereal” are uttered without a hint of irony. It feels like an adult was trying to remember what being a teen was and mixed up some memes online.
The acting is also stilted, at first. I’m guessing no one was exactly sure how the game was going to pan out during the development of the first episode, but it just feels like a lack of direction was going on. Some of the lines are either a bit too soft or lack any dramatic weight. This does eventually pick up and turn into genuinely great performances (save for the final episode fizzling out), but it’s not thoroughly mesmerizing.
There are also some uncanny valley moments with the presentation. While this runs on the Unreal 3 engine, the characters are stiff and the environments feel detached. There is a very touching scene in a pool, but it looks like two dead mannequins floating in nothingness. I couldn’t get around that image, either.
What I did truly love was how gameplay elements were organically woven into the story. There are a lot of puzzles sprinkled throughout Max’s adventure and it’s awesome to not feel like you’re simply a spectator. You have to use critical thinking to figure out solutions based on the powers you’ve been given.
One scene has you gather chemicals to create an IED, blow open a door and then rewind so you end up on the other side. It’s a really awesome accomplishment. It truly feels like you came up with the answer on your own.
Chapter 4 is where this really shines. You have multiple pieces of information you’ve gathered over the course of the game that you’re required to piece together. You have to take a long look at any correlation and connect the dots. Even if you fail, the game has a few work-arounds to get you back on track (excluding your rewind).
The final chapter drops the damn ball, however. There is a stealth section that is entirely pointless. Since you can rewind and remain in place, there is literally no reason to have characters searching for you. You cannot fail and pressing forward serves no repercussion. I understand it was a narrative device, but it utterly fails as a piece of gaming.
Honestly, the game was building up to a crescendo that Episode 5 never delivers. The definitive ending is certainly gut-wrenching, but the 2 hours leading up to it feel like a cop-out. It seems like DONTNOD had no idea how to really make your actions take affect or just wanted to impose their own will on the story. Regardless, Episode 5 does away with all of the good that the rest of the game exhibits.
There are some light puzzles, but everything is a forced, linear path and the dialog amounts to nothing more than expository exchanges with main characters. Some beats will tug at the heart strings, but most will just bore you (do I need to see that damn picture changing cutscene each time?).
That doesn’t destroy all the good that Episode 3 and 4 bring, but it does bookend the game with average scenarios. It starts slow and ends with a whimper. If you chopped out a little bit of the first episode, you could honestly combine it with the second and get the same result.
In all honesty, a lot of these games seem to crumble under marketing hype. Developers never know when to chill out with how cool their games are (or publishers pressure them into overselling their creations). Life is Strange is more about the relationship between two friends and how choices aren’t the end of the world (until they literally are).
I hate to be so harsh to a game that tackles such dark, dramatic and realistic topics like sexual abuse, stalkers, suicide and bullying, but most of the elements drag down the experience. The ridiculous twist of the real villain is also completely out of left field.
The game creates characters that feel like 3 dimensional beings and demands you look at them as more than caricatures, then the final chapter ends up labeling you a hero and the main bad-guy a psychopath. Dammit.
Still, Life is Strange is absolutely worth a playthrough. It’s not the best thing around, but it has an excellent mixture of gameplay and narrative heft to feel like a really important piece of gaming history. It will also resonate deeply with people who have suffered through similar tragedies in life.
I just wish DONTNOD nailed every aspect. This could have been a stone cold masterpiece.

I am going to try to nuance my opinion.  I love story-driven games, Mass Effect, Walking Dead, Game of Thrones are some of my favorite and I don't mind the lack interactivity when playing that kind of games, so after reading the great reviews, having my tumblr dashboard flooded, I thought this game was certainly a "must play" and must be worth it.
But in the end, I found myself bored and felt kinda of ripped off. Something was missing and made me feel all along that Life is Strange was not a bad game but way OVERRATED.
The game has good points, some interesting characters, a good concept but as a story-driven game, you'd expect the writing to be subtle and well constructed.
But in this case, the characters are caricatures of american highschool movie stereotypes who act like 15 yo while supposed to be between 18 and 22 yo.
Plottwists are so obvious that you know from the 1rst episode that the "main suspect" is too suspicious to actually be the bad guy and this is all unveiled via a ridiculous forseeable plot-twist, that contains a 180 degree turn from a character that goes from cool and collected to sadistic and heartless, a change of personality coming out of nowhere to the point that makes it hard to believe. There is no coherence.
About the ending :
Gameplay wise, the concept of rewinding time and butterfly effect was nice but the pace of the game being too slow made redoing actions several time a real chore. The least you can have when you handle a game with so much dialog is to have the possibility of skipping sentences (like in most story rich games) which is not the case here and is a real problem. Advancing in the game becomes tedious.
So I wouldn't recommend this game. It had certainly qualities but I really don't understand how all those bad points got overlooked....a real disappointment that didn't live up to its hype nor price!

There are only 5 or so games, films, or TV shows that have moved me as much as this game, Life Is Strange has. It is a hard feeling to deal with. The characters feel very real. You come to know many of them, and love them almost like real friends. Then the game is over, and those characters are gone. This causes a hurt inside you. Very much like losing dear friends, because there is no continuation for these characters.
This game is VERY emotional and deals with some very dark, and unfortunately very real things in our world. If you feel for other people, and nature, and the things only humans can cause, whether they are good or bad, this game might make you feel very sad at times, because it puts these things right in your face.
I cried so many times going through this game. I'm a pretty emotional person, but I think these feelings are totally intentional, and so I think the people who made this game did a damn good job. I wish to explore that world and those characters forever, because they seem that real. But, you can't. Much like the themes in this game about how little control we all have over time and events we can't foresee, this game ends and I have to find a way to move on.
The world in this game is pretty to look at. The graphics aren't amazing, but they are done in an artistic way that reminds me of watercolors or something. The gameplay is very similar to Telltale Games style, in that it is mostly walking around areas interacting with a limited number of objects, and talking to other characters. The real point of the game is the storytelling, and they do SUCH a good job in this one, as I've been over and over here.
I would recommend that if you do play it, take it slow, take long breaks if you need them. I took almost a year break and then several week breaks in between some parts, and it is still messing with me that I can't see anything more from these characters. Only replay the game again. Which, much like replaying a moment in the game with the unique rewinding power, only allows me to see that world again, and not live in it forever.
This review isn't much of a review, I know. But I don't want to reveal much and I just wanted to put my thoughts on this game out there somehow, even just to help me get through it. Thanks for reading if you do, though, and I hope you can enjoy this game that it seems to me a lot of work and love went into. :)

If a game manages to be in your mind days and weeks after you finished it, then you know it made many things very right. I’ve played a lot of games, some which hit me emotionally hard (for example The Last of Us, Mass Effect), but I’ve never experienced something like Life is Strange. Life is Strange an emotional roller coaster. Sometimes it makes you happy, sometimes angry and sometimes very sad and leaves you heartbroken.
Without spoiling too much, this is a story-driven mystery game, which you witness through Max, an art student in the fictional town Arcadia Bay. She discovers that she can rewind time. This is going to be your main tool to influence conversations, events and solve riddles. If you ever watched a movie or a tv-series where time manipulation plays a role, you know that this always comes at a price and the longer the game goes on the more you will see that this is also going to happen here. Although there were maybe two or three chapters which were a little bit annoying, because they force you through “research” and “stealth-sections”, every episode as a whole are absolute fantastic. The story keeps you on edge and there are some twists and turns, which will leave you shocked and surprised.
In the end, this is maybe the most beautiful game I have ever played. I love the music, art style, the symbolic and especially the characters. I will never forget Max and Chloe. It is weird how fictional characters can affect you emotionally. They are portrayed in such a good and relatable way that they will always have a place in my heart. In all my years of playing games, this may be the one, which made me reflect on my own life the most.

Like every other episode, your choices only impact about 1% of your game; it's TOO linear.
If this company ever makes another story game or continues this one, they need to keep the story intriguing; moments like Max and Chloe on the train tracks, seeing Kate in the hospital, etc. Instead, for episode 5, it was a dream-filled chaos that made no sense at all.

And if you are prepared for a game that refils your tanks, amps up your thrusters, teleports you to planets, and softens your re-entries, you should rethink EVERYTHING. This game is an amazingly hard, yet amazingly satisfying experience. Speed equals thrust divided by drag and mass. Understand? If you did, you may be ready to go far. If you didn't, though, you can still have a blast by going to the spaceplane hangar and building anything you want. And remember, you can always Alt F12 if you need that extra little push. So all in all, this game has something for everyone. Pick it up, and you wont regret it.
Edit: The 'full' release is out, contracts and such, and I love this game even more. 750 hours later, I still reccomend it above all else. Looking forwards to future updates!

If a game manages to be in your mind days and weeks after you finished it, then you know it made many things very right. I’ve played a lot of games, some which hit me emotionally hard (for example The Last of Us, Mass Effect), but I’ve never experienced something like Life is Strange. Life is Strange an emotional roller coaster. Sometimes it makes you happy, sometimes angry and sometimes very sad and leaves you heartbroken.
Without spoiling too much, this is a story-driven mystery game, which you witness through Max, an art student in the fictional town Arcadia Bay. She discovers that she can rewind time. This is going to be your main tool to influence conversations, events and solve riddles. If you ever watched a movie or a tv-series where time manipulation plays a role, you know that this always comes at a price and the longer the game goes on the more you will see that this is also going to happen here. Although there were maybe two or three chapters which were a little bit annoying, because they force you through “research” and “stealth-sections”, every episode as a whole are absolute fantastic. The story keeps you on edge and there are some twists and turns, which will leave you shocked and surprised.
In the end, this is maybe the most beautiful game I have ever played. I love the music, art style, the symbolic and especially the characters. I will never forget Max and Chloe. It is weird how fictional characters can affect you emotionally. They are portrayed in such a good and relatable way that they will always have a place in my heart. In all my years of playing games, this may be the one, which made me reflect on my own life the most.

Kerbal Space Program packs a ton of fun and learning into a surprisingly polished alpha. The game isn't even done yet! They also encourage the mod community and boy have they delievered. The forums are abuzz with must have mods that enhance your KSP experience.

If this company ever makes another story game or continues this one, they need to keep the story intriguing; moments like Max and Chloe on the train tracks, seeing Kate in the hospital, etc. Instead, for episode 5, it was a dream-filled chaos that made no sense at all.

Space has always been a wonder to me. From my early childhood I have gazed at stars, watched documentaries and played space themed games without ever getting bored. Space is infinite.
KSP gives you that Sandbox feel while adding some complexity just from the nature of the game. You set yourself an objective, starting by actually getting out of orbit, visiting the closest astral body, setting up a satellite network around your home planet, establishing a colony on Duna (our equivalent of Mars). Then you repeat until you get the largest and most efficient thing possible out into space.
Building a ship or plane is made in a way that could remind some of Spore, where you start from scratch and design a contraption to your liking. The engines you chose, the way you stage your ship, the size of everything... there's so many things you can change so not one ship is the same and not one ship reacts the same.
To some degree Kerbal Space Program is easy once you get the basics down, there is an immense amount of mods out there to make your life easier, harder and more realistic. I highly recommend researching around the web for the basics of spaceflight in KSP as it is quite hard figuring out what best way to attain orbit without proper explanation. When you think you can handle everything in the game, once have landed in the furthest planet and came back, it's time to grab a realism overhaul mod which makes everything much harder and more satisfying.
- Realism overhaul"
I have had countless hours of trial and error, managing plane designs, attempting to make viable space planes, researching everything through the career mode and realising halfway through my mission that I forgot to install proper energy regeneration on my ship. I do not regret one second spent playing this game, even if it's not perfect yet and even if it never will.

It may be rocket science, but at least it's not brain surgery.

'Life is Strange' is BY FAR one of the best story driven games i've ever played. At first, the game felt like a stereotypical high school game, which left me with very few motives to continue playing. However, after speaking to a few people who had finished the game, I decided I would give it another chance. 'Life is Strange' immediatley felt more enjoyable by the second episode, and I was becoming hooked.
I moved swiftly on from
and began episode 3. Episode 3 was arguably one of my favourite episodes, period. When I first began playing, I had no idea of the depth and intricacy provided by 'Dontnod Entertainment'. I was left in shock at the ending of episode 3. I was truly spechless. All I can recommend is that you play the game youself, and then you'll realise how powerful the ending truly was.
I would argue that episode 4 & episode 5 are on par in terms of quality. Yes episode 5 provides closure to such a great game, but season 4 was filled with perfectly executed moments that were so unexpected. All in all, I can't differentiate between episode 4 & 5, as both were of such great quality.
Overall, I would highly recommend for you to play this game if you haven't already. 'Life is Strange' reminded me of Naughty Dog's 'The Last of Us', as both had an incredible story, backed by some very enjoyable gameplay. Now please do yourself a favor, by purchasing a copy of 'Life is Strange'.

In Life is Strange, you play as Max, a teenage girl who discovers she has the ability to rewind time. She and her loose cannon friend Chloe use this power to try and unravel the mystery surrounding a missing girl and other strange occurences in the town.
Throughout the game you have to make a lot of decisions, and very few of them are easy. The choices aren't your typical "good guy or bad guy" choices; both outcomes always have advantages and disadvantages, with many potential unforseen consequences. Several of the decisions I had to make in this game were very easily the most difficult I've had to make in a video game.
The story is brutal and doesn't hold back. I don't want to get into this much for the sake of avoiding spoilers.
The soundtrack is excellent, and the art style is good.
If I had to nitpick, some of the textures are bad and the lip syncing isn't ideal. There are some minor plot holes, as is more or less inevitable in a story involving time travel.
It took me over 17 hours to complete my first playthough, and the full game is only $20 full price. If the game sounds interesting to you, I think it would be hard to go wrong when you see it on sale. Life is Strange is an instant favorite of mine.

Everyone's first fifty rockets did.). The first thing I recommend doing is playing around in the Sandbox mode just to get used to the controls.
The first challenge is getting it off the ground. The second is the orbit. The third is making sure you can get back down. From then on, the choice is yours.
From shuttles to rovers, from stations to bases, from planes to SSTOs. KSP is the perfect game for anyone who has had a moment of awe just looking at the moon. For tips on playing the game I recommend checking out Scott Manley on YouTube. It's best to learn some astrophysics from an astrophysicist, isn't it?

The game was overhyped. And if you are looking for an experience like The Walking Dead or other choice based games, then this is not the game for you. At first, I hated this game and was planning on giving it a terrible review. But the key to enjoying this game is to know what you are getting into. The characters are not that unique, neither is the story. But once you temper your expectations and get past the painfully slow and honestly boring first two chapters, the game starts to pick up and feel less like a highschool soap opera.
The story focuses more on long-term choices you make in your social life, and the effects that they have on the people around you, rather than the usual "do or die" survivalist decisions that this genre is known for.
That being said, the game is still aimed at a rather narrow market, so make sure to keep that in mind. One last thing, don't spend too much time examining every little thing you can interact with. A lot of it, ESPECIALLY in the first two chapters, is completely pointless.

I bought this game on a Steam sale, completely expecting it play as most casual indie games do. This game is NOT liek most indie games - it is a challenege with extreme replay value. Let me elaborate:
Objective: None. This is a sandbox game where you attempt to start up your own space program. This includes spaceship design and flight. You can go into orbit, go to the Moon (Mun as its called in this game), go to the a different planet, even try to fly into the sun! If you can dream it, you can do it.
Gameplay: This game is designed to be realistic, but only to a point. The aerodynamics aren't quite right, and up til no reentry and g-forces are not as deadly as they should be, but they could both definately break your spacecraft. THIS IS NOT AN EASY GAME, but the true fun lies in failing. This a game best learned through trial and error, and will consume a large amount of time if you let it. There are actual bits of real life rocket science in this game, including things such as semiaxis, apoapsis and periapsis, delta v caluclations, etc. That doesn't mean you have to be a rocket scientist to play. It took me a long time to write a review for this because.... well the emotions this thing takes you through is both amazing and at the same time just fundamentally overwhelming.
I found myself lost in the character, wanting to see her fix everything, to be happy, to have the cake, and share it with all her friends. The emotional investment I put into this game was beyond anything I felt I would give to a game, and I loved and hated every minute of it.
It made me laugh, made me scared, and utterly made me cry a number of times.
I am not going to go into the story since anyone can google to see more about it, but what I can say is the story drove me to care and any story that makes you really care about the characters is great in my opinion.
I hated it to end, I cried when it did, and I missed it for weeks afterwards.
Luckily you don't now have to wait for all the episodes, but damn the pain of waiting for each episode as it came out was almost like madness to me.
In saying that, there is a couple of flaws, but most of them were utterly forgivable when overshadowed by the story.
To me the graphics sometimes just felt "off". The choice of textures or maybe the lighting just made the scene pull you out of the moment, and you were reminded with a slap in the face that you were playing a game, and not watching the best damn movie/tv series in the world.
Character Movement could also be off sometimes, enough so that things could go wrong and you would have something happen you didn't want to happen and you would restart from a point. However, this was only few and far between and no one enough of an issue to prevent enjoyment as a hole.
The puzzles in the game were also challenging while at the same time fun to work through, and not enough to stall you for too long.
Overall this was a great experience one that I was very happy to buy. I bought the whole thing on full price and felt this was a game that totally deserved my money, and more important my time and emotional investment.
Here is hoping that  DONTNOD Entertainment and Square Enix come up with another story of just as much value and quality to allow me once again to feel the utter joy of the emotional journey this did for me.

As others have said before this is a terrific sandbox game, that lets you play nasa and lets you do anything you want within the limits of the laws of physics.
You can just have a good laugh shooting kerbals into suborbit and letting them crash down or you can approach it scientific by orbiting compleet bases like the iss or refueling bases. You can then launch a two step rocket: first into orbit and dock at your previously launched station, refuel there and then continu your journey to other planets in the solar system.
Also with the release of 0.23 it isn't just sandbox only anymore. The career function is now live too, albeit under construction, but you can gather science points by doing experiments with which you can unlock newer parts etc.
According to the devs update 0.24 will release contracts so you can become a sort of spacex company by launching satellites  into orbit for cash.
When this game will be fully released it will be the most extensive space sim in it's class and can be fun for both casual players as for hardcore gamers who do their own calculations as to how much fuel they need and so on.
One last thing: Did i mention mods?? KSP already has a really active modding community with tons of extra parts and fly ready spacecrafts. Also some of them add the capability of mining resources from other planets for that extra level of depth.

This is highly addictive and quite hardcore space faring sim. I call it NASA sim with kerbals. Having been playing space trading games like Elite or X3 I have always dreamt of game that actually does have orbital navigation and things like that. But this game is really much more than that - You actually colonize the space with Your own custom built space stations, planetary landers, planetary bases, rovers and anything Your imagination can create. And the "building bricks" are based on real world counterparts - no teleporters or stargates here.
Should this game have a story like Mass Effect and space trading economy like X3 series, it would be my dream game come true.
I would highly recommend this game to everyone who dares to test his own creativity in building sophisticated craft that can actually fly and land on distant planets and moons.
And You will have to land there if You are playng campaing mode, because that is a way You gather more science data for Your scientists and You will need that to learn better components for Your spacecrafts.
This game has also a huge modding comunity already that have created a lot of content that can extend a stock functionality.
There are also tons of tutorials on Youtube that will explain a game in detail and a dedicated wiki to learn more.
Try not to be distracted by appearances of those kerbals - they will share Your passion of flying high and far away and they will show their appreciation if You do things right! :)
Have fun and fly safe!

I always liked story-driven games, and I never minded the limited interactivity they usually offer, so naturally, after I read about "Life is Strange", and the stellar reviews it got from critics and users alike, I thought I'd give it a try.
I must have missed something along the road, because I'm nowhere near to agreeing with all the praise Life is Strange has received.
Life is Strange has an intriguing enough set-up: you're Max Caulfield, a photography student in Arcadia Bay, where strange environmental phenomena occur, along with some students' disappearances over at Blackwell Academy that Max and her best friend, Chloe Price, are trying to solve, helped by Max's ability to reverse time.
I guess I put too much faith on the writers, hoping they could successfully juggle all these seemingly unrelated plot points and tell a concrete story.
They didn't.
The main problem here is the attempt to tell multiple stories at once: Max's coming-of-age, the relationship between Max and Chloe, the environmental occurrences and the mysteries going on at Blackwell Academy.
The strange happenings include snow on a sunny day, birds falling dead on the streets, a sun eclipse, whales being washed up on the beach, the appearance of a second moon and, finally, a gigantic tornado. These are mostly on the background, teasing the fact that something big is coming. It's a fascinating plot point, to say the least, and I couldn't wait to see where they were going with it.
Turns out, nowhere. None of it mattered, or is explained in any way. And I don't mind ambiguous storytelling; but this isn't ambiguous, nor fair. It's cheating out on your continuous teasing.
As far as the mystery of the disappearances goes, it's awkwardly brought to an end via a ridiculous plot-twist, that contains a 180 degree turn from a particular character that goes from cool and collected to sadistic and unfeeling, a change of temperament so forced and out of the blue I had a hard time buying it.
Now, let's talk about the ending.
First things first, whatever choices you've made throughout all 5 episodes, big or small, have absolutely no impact on the final choice you're presented with: either to sacrifice Chloe in order to save Arcadia Bay from a tornado (if it sounds illogical, it's because it is), or let the tornado destroy the whole town.
Truth be told, I'm fine with this binary ending. It goes without saying that multiple endings would be preferable, but this is what we got.
And "this" is REALLY problematic, story-and-gameplay-wise.
It's obvious that the "Save Chloe" ending was a quick footnote, a sudden realization from the writers that, hey, we can't have only one ending, quick, let's hastily write an underwhelming conclusion that we hope none of the players choose, because let's face it, it's not the true ending to the story we want to tell.
That's not to say that the "Save Arcadia Bay" ending is a fitting conclusion.
It's not, for a very simple reason: it's unfair. Both to the player and to Chloe.
I understand that the main theme of Life is Strange is the "Butterfly Effect": the minutest of actions can bring about the apocalypse. And I can see why letting Chloe die is supposed to emphasize this. But going all the way back in time, to the first moments you spend in Blackwell Academy, apart from rudely erasing EVERYTHING you've done in the past 13 hours or so, undoes another of the game's main themes: the relationship between Max and Chloe.
With Chloe dead, she's never reunited with Max. She's never redeemed from her problematic lifestyle. They never fix each other's brokenness. Chloe just ends up dead, shot in the stomach, in a toilet in Blackwell Academy. If that's not unfair to a strong character such as Chloe, I don't know what is. All this character development, undone - just for the sake of a bittersweet ending, the emotional power of which is nonexistent once you realize the way Chloe's character was handled.
What's frustrating is that Life is Strange does wonders in some aspects, which only shows the wasted potential - and the game it could have been.
The oil-painting-like art style is beautiful and fits the environment and characters just right. The sound design and mixing is top-notch, and the soundtrack (both the original and the licensed) is superb.
But where Life is Strange truly shines is when it focuses on Max and Chloe. The chemistry they have is incredible, and the interplay between them is, for the most part, natural, honest and, above all, convincing. Chloe, especially, is a surprisingly well-written character, and Ashly Burch's performance is pretty much flawless. This strong chemistry makes the first hour of Episode 4, "Dark Room", one of the most quietly powerful sequences I've experienced in a video game.
It's a shame, having these brief glimpses of strong storytelling, only for them to be overshadowed by the game's inability to organically combine many plot points. By the end of Episode 4, too many loose ends were hanging in the air for them to be resolved in a satisfactory way in the final Episode; it was pretty much inevitable for the story to be hastily ended.
The game crumbled under its own ambition.
A mess of a story that's too ambitious for its own good, with some scattered moments of brilliance that are overshadowed by a lack of clear vision; and an ending that reduces you to two unfair outcomes whilst completely obliterating every single decision you've made throughout the journey.

Life is Strange is one of the most unique episodic games I have played so far, in all aspects of visuals, story-telling, and character insights. A quick brief of what this game is, Maxine Caullfield is a 18 year-old student that attends Blackwell Academy, she has a dream of becoming a photographer, within her first months of attending this school Max realizes she obtained powers that allowed to to alter time and space while also affecting realities. She finds out that a major storm will be hitting Arcady Bay (town) so along side your best friend Chloe Price, which after 5 years of each other's absence after Max had left for Seattle with her parents, you both embark an a journey that will allow you to change everyone's fate, for good or bad. The story is amazing, for being this type of game it is very atmospheric, allows you to interact with the tiniest of details, also achivements for taking pictures along the story is really great. The in-depth of character is really great, talking to others really helps you get a good image of what they are like and what have they been through. And most importantly, the choices, as you seen that I have mentioned the choices you make here are excellent, it really does affect how you progress the story (from the life of a person to petitions being acknowledge to causing conflicts) Overall I would give this game a 9.5/10 due to the stunning visuals, amazing storyline, and character interactions. Having always appreciated story based games, I decided one evening to pick this one up.
I knew nothing about it from the get-go. Only that it had a female protagonist, and that it was supposed to induce plenty of feels.
The story's main protagonist is the young photography student Maxine Caulfield - or Max, as she prefers it. The tale begins with her returning to the hometown she grew up in to study under a famous photographer. During a dramatic event she discovers her ability to time travel and gets reunited with a childhood friend; rebel without a cause Chloe Price.
Things are not all sunshine and butterflies with the two old friends. Max has to rebuild the friendship she neglected while living in the big city, all the while investigating and unraveling a mystery that turns out to be more violent and complex the deeper she gets.
This game is mostly a story driven walking simulator, but the strong characters and the game's attention to character depth and distinct design makes it engaging. You want to keep playing to see the characters interact, to see the events unfold. During your playthrough you will have to make choices. Both big and small, sometimes with larger consequences than you first assumed. The main themes of the game are friendship, family, bullying and bravery. Disclaimers to anyone suffering with a depression, alcoholism, the loss of a loved one or bullying. Life is Strange tackles it all, and it does so with surprising realism. The events in the game are fictional, but the feelings they inspire are very, real.
It's readily obvious to anyone with eyes that this is not Crysis. It doesn't need to be, and I like the way they approached the visuals on this one. It's like cell shading and oil painters got together to create effective locations and models that are very much passable and immersive. This game also targets a more casual audience, so it's probably a smart choice not to make it too demanding on your system. Runs great even on older laptops. One thing that does stick out as a sore thumb is the lip-synch. During more relaxed parts of the action it's easy to forgive a mouth flapping randomly, but it did detract form my immersion during some of the game's more dramatic scenes.
I find the sound design to be quite anonymous in this title, but it is to be expected. It doesn't stand out, but does it's job perfectly well. The soundtrack, on the other hand, is solid, heavily featuring the french band Syd Matters. Whoever was in charge of picking the music for this game did an amazing job, and there are tracks I still listen to in order to relive some of the magic of the game.
I played through the game using a controller, but also tried the m&k, and it works fine. Controls are as responsive as they have to be, and it comes down to preference.
The game's key mechanic is your ability to rewind time. All of the game's decently designed puzzles are centered around this mechanic, since you are able to "teleport." You stand still while time doesn't. Any objects you pick up and carry on your person will also stay on you. Most of the puzzles are quite easy to complete, but they still feel fun and meaningful. Mostly because of the proudful exclamations made my Max once she figures something out.
The most rewarding use of the rewind ability - however - is the dialogue. You can choose to rewind pretty much everything, but that doesn't make choosing what to say that much easier. Oft times you have to make difficult calls on how to approach a problem, and this will leave you wondering about the consequences of other approaches possibly for hours to home. The butterfly effect of time travel is a heavily featured "character" in this game, and it works to great effect. Your choices do have consequences, however not all of them carry through to the game's ending.
You'll spend most of your time walking around, hearing the protagonist comment on the environment or what she has to do. Occasionally you'll be able to take pictures - both optional and non-optional - but all is still done with the push of a button. Some of these optional photos can be quite tricky to find, as you often have a limited time to capture a certain moment.
I finished the game in around four seatings, where the first was a rather short one. It takes between 14-18 hours to beat the game in it's entirety, but this all depends on how much time you spend rewinding, collecting and admiring the beautiful environments. The price is really low, so it definitely brings a lot of value to the table.
I found the story engaging and interesting, but I did not suffer an emotional collapse like many other reviewers did. Admittedly I felt the tears well up at a couple of points, but not at the ending or other "apparent" points. The story did stick with me, though, and I was left thinking about it and processing it for a couple of weeks.

After spending four (straight) hours on this game, and DEFINITELY more, I wanted to write this short review.
Do I recommend this game? Do I need to eat everyday? The answers are the same: yes.
It is amazing, stupid fun launching a tiny Kerbonaut up into space. Whether you actually get them to space is another matter altogether, although it doesn't matter. Big explosion or safe landing, either one gives an amazing feeling. (I believe they call this false accomplishment, but hey, if false accomplishment is this fun, I'd love to falsely accomplish more things.)
There is only really two suggestions I would make:
Firstly, have an option to either grid lock parts onto your space ship to balance weight out, or allow precise measurements of weight distribution. If my rocket has five pounds extra on one side, have a system that allows me to see that. Allow that system to actively display weight changes before I attach objects. If I hover a fuel tank on the other side of the heavier side, allow the system to actively change to the weight distribution that would occur if I attached that fuel tank.
Secondly, it would be amazing to have a list/tree showing objectives. It is amazingly hard to figure out exactly how I need to gain Science points, etc. Maybe have a chart/tree, starting at Objective One: Getting Started, having that tell you your first objective, and then gradually move up/down the tree to the next branch, such as Objective Two: Lifting Off, etc.
Other than those two suggestions, I would seriously recommend this game. As I've stated before, it is amazing, stupid fun.

This is a great pick-up for any rocket science or space buff, or really anyone who loves playing in sandboxes. Building rockets to travel to all of the different planets and moons presents many different (and sometimes difficult) engineering and design challenges. The game models orbital motion based on Newtonian physics, so in most cases real-world rocket science can be seamlessly applied to the in-game world. Exploring each world is a greater achievement than the last, and you can be sure that you'll have many crowning moments of ingenuity, wits, and downright awesomeness.

Having always appreciated story based games, I decided one evening to pick this one up.
I knew nothing about it from the get-go. Only that it had a female protagonist, and that it was supposed to induce plenty of feels.
The story's main protagonist is the young photography student Maxine Caulfield - or Max, as she prefers it. The tale begins with her returning to the hometown she grew up in to study under a famous photographer. During a dramatic event she discovers her ability to time travel and gets reunited with a childhood friend; rebel without a cause Chloe Price.
Things are not all sunshine and butterflies with the two old friends. Max has to rebuild the friendship she neglected while living in the big city, all the while investigating and unraveling a mystery that turns out to be more violent and complex the deeper she gets.
This game is mostly a story driven walking simulator, but the strong characters and the game's attention to character depth and distinct design makes it engaging. You want to keep playing to see the characters interact, to see the events unfold. During your playthrough you will have to make choices. Both big and small, sometimes with larger consequences than you first assumed. The main themes of the game are friendship, family, bullying and bravery. Disclaimers to anyone suffering with a depression, alcoholism, the loss of a loved one or bullying. Life is Strange tackles it all, and it does so with surprising realism. The events in the game are fictional, but the feelings they inspire are very, real.
It's readily obvious to anyone with eyes that this is not Crysis. It doesn't need to be, and I like the way they approached the visuals on this one. It's like cell shading and oil painters got together to create effective locations and models that are very much passable and immersive. This game also targets a more casual audience, so it's probably a smart choice not to make it too demanding on your system. Runs great even on older laptops. One thing that does stick out as a sore thumb is the lip-synch. During more relaxed parts of the action it's easy to forgive a mouth flapping randomly, but it did detract form my immersion during some of the game's more dramatic scenes.
I find the sound design to be quite anonymous in this title, but it is to be expected. It doesn't stand out, but does it's job perfectly well. The soundtrack, on the other hand, is solid, heavily featuring the french band Syd Matters. Whoever was in charge of picking the music for this game did an amazing job, and there are tracks I still listen to in order to relive some of the magic of the game.
I played through the game using a controller, but also tried the m&k, and it works fine. Controls are as responsive as they have to be, and it comes down to preference.
The game's key mechanic is your ability to rewind time. All of the game's decently designed puzzles are centered around this mechanic, since you are able to "teleport." You stand still while time doesn't. Any objects you pick up and carry on your person will also stay on you. Most of the puzzles are quite easy to complete, but they still feel fun and meaningful. Mostly because of the proudful exclamations made my Max once she figures something out.
The most rewarding use of the rewind ability - however - is the dialogue. You can choose to rewind pretty much everything, but that doesn't make choosing what to say that much easier. Oft times you have to make difficult calls on how to approach a problem, and this will leave you wondering about the consequences of other approaches possibly for hours to home. The butterfly effect of time travel is a heavily featured "character" in this game, and it works to great effect. Your choices do have consequences, however not all of them carry through to the game's ending.
You'll spend most of your time walking around, hearing the protagonist comment on the environment or what she has to do. Occasionally you'll be able to take pictures - both optional and non-optional - but all is still done with the push of a button. Some of these optional photos can be quite tricky to find, as you often have a limited time to capture a certain moment.
I finished the game in around four seatings, where the first was a rather short one. It takes between 14-18 hours to beat the game in it's entirety, but this all depends on how much time you spend rewinding, collecting and admiring the beautiful environments. The price is really low, so it definitely brings a lot of value to the table.
I found the story engaging and interesting, but I did not suffer an emotional collapse like many other reviewers did. Admittedly I felt the tears well up at a couple of points, but not at the ending or other "apparent" points. The story did stick with me, though, and I was left thinking about it and processing it for a couple of weeks.

So my personal, spoiler free review of Life is Strange- because Stark couldn't be bothered to sleep after Episode 3. This game was heartbreaking every step of the way. Every choice that you have to make in the game has repercussions on the way the next part of the story will go. But in that respect, every choice that I made brought the final conclusion of the story to a very difficult end. I couldn't choose and I didn't want to have to choose.
If you are like me and you have a terrible case of sonder and an aversion to making choices based on chaos theory and the butterfly effect, this game will be difficult for you and you will end up trying to redo some choices because of that "every choice effects every other choice you make".
In the end, at least for me, there was a lot of moments where there were no good answer regardless of how you answered. There were also moments where it judged me on things that I had no idea were even in the story, until the end of the episode, and those things did not really affect the story for me at all. In the end though, my choices played out as good or bad and I would never know until the end of an episode whether or not what I had done was either. I suppose this is real life though, is it not?
Some things are easily gleaned and some things are not, but the way that these parts are told, regardless of how easy it is to guess the whos and whats, is sensational.
I was left with a morbid sense of longing regarding my final choices in the game, which is what was intended, and a profound sadness because I so deeply preach against any of the similar powers that Max has, but it left me to really think, 'In the end, what would I do?'
And so I did. And so yet I am left unfulfilled, sad, and full of questions. 10/10, might play again.

Game for nerds who want to go to space. Being a wannabe space nerd i found this game extremely intruiging and challenging. The developers are pushing this game to a whole new level. Please tell me of any other space sim that has seamless flight from space to planet. You are a Kerbal engineer and you build all aspects of a spaceship or space plane. Heck you can construct a space station in space if you like. Feeling sadistic? build a spaceship with no parachute and have them re-enter earth at 3000ms. POOF!!!! Running a 2013 MBP with NVidia graphics and 8mg ram. Minor lag when i build an extremely large platform but otherwise no problems. I wouldn't try running this on mac with anything less than these requirements. Finally crashed a Kerbal into the sun which was a major achievement!
All in all if you like the idea of being a project engineer for a space mission this is the game for you. Not your typical simulation game. Physics are certainly a strong aspect of this game and each piece you add contributes to the weight of your overal vehicle thus effecting flight characteristics and survivability!!! If NASA can do it.....so can the Kerbals! I really enjoyed driving an unmanned rover on the moon.....untill i wrecked it!!! Have fun!

Time for a review in my "Hierarchy of importance" fashion, from top as most important (to me) to bottom least important (to me)
~ Story: The story itself is rather simple but charming enough for a sandbox game, especially when some of the most famous sandbox games such as minecraft or terraria have no story to begin with. And yes I know this game has a career mode but as there's no economy for parts I still see it as a sandbox
~ Gameplay: The controls are responsive for what they are, considering you are piloting a hunk of metal strapped together by random struts and you are confused as to why the pieces are jiggling... Though sometimes things grow confusing and there's often no real saying what goes wrong or right and as such repeating successes can be tricky the gameplay itself is fairly strong and consistant.
~ Sound: The music is charming and calming giving a sense of epicness and yet serenity, being in space is among my favorite sound tracks as it's truly as soothing as space seems to be, though long periods have the music fade away to the back of my mind
~ Replayability: Though I have to admit to utterly blowing at this game (Mun and Minmus are my only landing sites) I do have to admit to loving it unconditionally. I keep coming back to it and it makes for quite a good game to play in a smaller window whilst watching a tv-show or something on Netflix
~ Graphics: While the appearance of the ground is nothing too impressive to me, perhaps my low settings, the rockets look genuinely made out of metal rather than plastic and space is... Magnificent! When you get in orbit and look at the white trails and the stars, or moons and planets in the distance you feel as though you are in space
TL;DR A must play, this game is greatly addictive and even though it's very difficult for someone who just wings it, like myself, it is still fun to see the crazy structures to send in orbit and even more bonkers structures to build in space via docking.

Not everyone will like this, but it is the pinnacle of a genre. To those who like story– and character-based gaming or Telltale-style adventures, I cannot recommend this game more strongly. In terms of writing, atmosphere and mechanics, it is the pinnacle of the genre. With only a couple of momentary exceptions, it will draw you into its world and make you truly care about the world and its characters. It encourages exploration with a cool photographic mechanic while keeping you focused on the story and making difficult role-play choices.
I usually avoid wild predictions, but I would wager that 100 years from now, college students will study Dontnod's "Life is Strange" to gain insight into what life was like at the turn of the millennium in the Pacific Northwest. If I'm correct, future professors will teach it similarly to how students today read Thackeray's "Vanity Fair" to gain insight into life in 19th-century Britain.
I can speak with some authority about the area where the game is set as I grew up in Oregon. This game captures many of the nuances of that culture without the broad caricature of a "Portlandia." Sitting down to play one of the game's chapters feels like settling in on the couch with a old friend to reminisce about the vivid experiences you had growing up. The sense of connection, fear, love and possibilities all come through in what is perhaps the most emotionally adept game to date.
For those who don't like story-heavy walking simulators and adventure games, you may not like this either. There is little tono real-time action: it's more about experiencing a story, connecting with the characters and playing a role. If you're on the fence about other adventure games, I'd recommend you give this one a chance, as it's the best of the genre in my opinion. Although it's not an action game, the emotional content is extremely intense and fulfilling. If you're not enjoying it by the end of the first chapter though, you can probably skip the rest.

This game reminds me of a "choose your own adventure" book, but crossed with a motion picture. It has action, emotion, and mystery. It has the ability to awaken dormant emotions within your own psyche, and this I found rather remarkable.
It's not a perfect game - there is the occasional piece of repetition I found to slightly disrupt the story's flow, but this happens only a couple of times, and never did the repetition become frustrating.
The graphics, although not amazing, are beautiful. I understand the choices made by the developer - performance over polygon count - and this I believe was a good choice. I'm sure the game runs well on lower specification machines, and I never experienced a slow down in frame rate or any stuttering. I didn't experience a single crash either.
The soundtrack is truly epic. The song selections fit the mood very well, and although I'm sure they're not to everyone's taste, they perfectly fit mine - Obstacles is my favourite.
It is rare a game has me hooked to the point of neglecting other things in my life. This game is one of those rare beauties.

On a serious note, this is certainly one of the most amazing gaming experiences I had. The story is very immersive (the feels, sigh), it's very easy to identify with the characters, interactions are very natural and the music and art are simply stunning. More than a game, more than a story, more than a movie, sometimes you do feel like the circumstances are happening to you.
The game mostly involves a lot of dialogue, interaction and exploration and long cutscenes. If you are a fan of action packed games, it would certainly not be for you, but if you love a great story and feel like crying like a little ♥♥♥♥♥, then the game is CERTAINLY for you.

Do you prefer technical games that make you think and sometimes tear your hair out but give tons of creativity and lots of satisfaction? Do you like space? Do you want to be (or are) an engineer? This game is loads of challenging and creative fun, and very worth it for the price. So many different parts, ways to put them together and make some crazy contraption, reasons to do so, and ways to use and enjoy them once you've made them. Made a small space rover? Great, now put it on a rocket and get to the moon! Now send an attachable thruster system that allows it to fly. Build a space station in the same hair tearing way we did in real life! A moon colony! Honestly it's just got so much content, along with all the mods you can create for ages.
An awesome story from the start to the end!

Life is Strange, the mechanics are pretty simple. Doesn't take a genius to figure out the game. But is horribly linear and only has two endings, both of which is pretty much ALL Pricefield (Chloe x Max). That was fine the first time, since I actually though Chloe was cool. Punk is cool.
Then the second playthrough and I just couldn't stand Chloe anymore. I simply played it to see how my choices affect the consequences, just ♥♥♥♥ around a little bit cuz the ending was kinda disappointing.
The game overall has a rather... interesting story and the twists are... well.. predictable yet not at the same time. The world is well thought out, graphics are just BEAUTIFUL and the sound track made me want to dig uo all my old AltRock and Country music.
I had really hoped for more character with all the other side charcters dynamic between Max and the rest of the school goes beyond that of most typical teenage drama series. All choices and interactions with the other side characters carry over to the later episodes as well.
And the best part is that it sorta emulates real life, doesnt matter what walk of life you're from, you can be a  regular nobody or some jock or a nerdy science geek but everybody swears and isn't shy about it. It's just, normal everyday life. Not like most other games where saying the word '♥♥♥♥' is like a glorified status that only the creme of the crop does.
If this had a proper rating system, I would give this game an 8.5/10. I liked the game, but I wished that there would have been different endings and more story between the other characters. Maybe even a romance outside of Pricefield because that really is all they give you to work with and it is HORRIBLY lacking in story. But you would think it was okay because you didn't know any better until you've completed the game and decide to go looking for more.
And if you were like me that would be turning to the world of fanfiction. That was where I fell in love with Chasefield and never looked back.
And it made me dislike Chloe even more to the point of actually despising the character and the Pricefield ship.
But that's besides the point.
Bottom line is, paying about 20 for the game isn't that bad a deal, or you could wait for a sale and get it then. It's a good game the first time through, not so much replay value as I would have liked. And figuring out where the collectibles are for the achievements was pretty fun
One word of warning though.. Chloe is... well, to sum it up in one word, VULGAR with a capital V. Horribly RUDE as well to the point I got annoyed and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at her character and skipped through whatever I can skip. She is simply angry ALL THE TIME and flies off the handle at the smallest things and just screams and shouts and swears LOUDLY and... well you get the point.
So if that's not your thing and you cant stand hearing someone say the word '♥♥♥♥' then I would probably recommend you to not get this game cuz EVERYONE and I mean EVERYONE swears. Especially Max.

Believe it or not, we’ve been coddled by super-cute and ultra-tough space-race simulator, Kerbal Space Program. Players who have a ring of dead Kerbals orbiting Kerbin, or who’ve left lonely craft to sink into the canyons of Eeloo because they forgot to add chutes, might beg to differ, but with upcoming update 0.22 more will be asked of you than ever before. No longer is it enough to just make it to orbit and beyond for the fun of space adventures. There will be science to be done when you’re up there.
0.22 is the R&D update. Gathering data requires you to do experiments in space and report the findings back to Ear – er, Kerbin. It currently just involves getting a specific research tool to space, exposing it to the void, and letting it do its thing, but this is the first building block of career mode and I’d imagine future updates will complicate the issue. With the data gathered, you can beam it back to base or take the ship down and manually transfer it to the space base. The point of this is to increase the science payout for your mission. Science is kind of a currency that you spend in the new tech trees, allowing you to add new, experimental parts to your ships.
Shipbuilding is receiving a pretty major addition, enabling players to save sections of their builds. It means you can call up a pre-assembled chunk of parts and add it on to your ship without having to reconstruct it. Very handy.

Well.... kudos for one of the most immersive.... meaningful and entrancing experiences i ever lived with a game.
First of all, if you absolutely hate a game with no gameplay (meaninig the only actual gameplay is just living the game, exploring and interacting) then maybe you won't be able to enjoy a game such as this. But if you don't mind that, this game is simply put.... a masterpiece of story telling.
Never mind that it has awesome characters.... or vividly artistic graphics..... or that the soundtrack is simply so amazing and so right that you will simply get lost in the moments as if you were living the story......... what the game has tackled here is simply too much to describe. Playing with the idea of choices, action and consequence.... and the fact that you can actually rewind and change your choices........ at first it may seem like a safety net where you feel you can't go wrong..... but then you learn the hard way that it's even worse since no matter how many times you try to change your choices you can never feel completely sure about them.
Without giving any spoilers..... ultimately the game guides you into the painful lesson that the more we think we are in control, the harder we get hit by the fact that we never actually were.....
As a final consideration, some people weren't happy with the endings.... but i feel that it's the kind of ending that remains loyal to the story and it's evolution throughout the chapters, again, remarking the fact that we are never trully in control. So i recommend to enjoy it to the fullest with its unique experience, even if one would like a different one.

While it would be tempting to label the game perfect due to its impact as many others seem to be doing, I must also recognize its flaws. The big decisions weren't as relevant as desired and are practically irrelevant in retrospect after seeing the ending which left me feeling a lack of closure. The people who write otherwise in their reviews either haven't finished the game or haven't played other choice-driven games. With time travel inevitably comes paradoxes but one must put this aside in order to enjoy a game on the topic. Definitely play if you like a hipsterish vibe/soundtrack and stereotypical "high school theme" and/or a story-driven slow paced experience based on mystery and character development - you'll love this game. Truly amazing story and a game that is worth every penny of the asking price.
It is so very rare to play a game that keeps you 100% emotionally invested in both the story and the characters. Life is Strange does this flawlessly. Everything about the game draws you into the world in such a way that you feel the characters pain as the story unfolds. The soundtrack is simply wonderful and adds to the emotional feel of the story, almost evolving as the characters complete their story arcs. The game is beautiful too and the use of lighting effects (particularly the sunsets) really add to the feeling that you ARE Max Caulfield and that you are seeing it firsthand.
The story is masterfully done and has twists and turns that are very hard to see coming. Usually I find that games try too hard to add a twist and so it becomes labored and obvious very early on, and yet Life Is Strange manages to send you up a dozen wrong paths before hitting you with something you simply never saw coming. Not to mention the fact that they have really done a stellar job of keeping timeline continuity together too (which in this game could be very tricky!).
I was actually given a code for episode 1 of this game for free and as soon as I played 10 minutes of it, I knew I needed to play more. When the story got going, I was both surprised at it's complexity and intrigued as to where it was going. I immediatly bought the remaining 4 episodes after completing the first. I will never regret this as a purchase.
I can honestly say that this is one of the best written and most well made games that I have ever purchased. I think during the whole 18+ hours that I played, I only noticed one bug and that was a slightly out of sync mouth during one part of a conversation which honestly could have been brought on by lag as I was recording the game as I played and had also been playing for 5 hours straight. Everything about this game is wonderfully tailored to make you feel like you are inside the world of Arcadia Bay, and it makes you feel like you are in control but also (at the same time) powerless to stop the inevitible events that will take place. The game takes you on a journey of emotion in every episode, ranging from happiness, to melancholy, anger and even (at times) shame. I have honestly never played a game that has given me such an emotional roller coaster ride as I progressed through it.
I simply cannot recommend this game enough. If you like engaging stories, buy it. If you like Immersive worlds, buy it. If you like to be emotionally invested, buy it. If you want a game to remember forever, buy it.
Simply put, buy it. You won't regret it.

KSP represents the ultimate sandbox game for anyone that loved/loves space simulators. The learning curve is intense but reaching new personal achievments can be exhilirating. During your first few hours (especially if you play sandbox right away), you will gain a new appreciation for the science and engineering that goes into our real space program. Just don't go emailing NASA and telling them "but it works in KSP". The one downside of KSP is that it feels unfinished in many places. Career mode is just starting to unfold but lacks a few key elements to make it truly engaging. The pacing of the tech tree can be slow and will be almost completely unlocked before you leave Kerbin's sphere of influence if this is your first go around. I expect this will be less of a program when a rigorous budget system is implemented. On the plus side, the modding community and forums are full of some of the most creative and helpful people I've ever encountered in a videogame. Many of the games' shortcomings have been identified and someone has developed mods to improve them. From clouds, to aerodynamics, to realistic universe, to parts parts and more parts. Also, the mods are really easy to install. This is a game worth buying now and following until it's release and beyond.

This is a fantastic game, You get fear when a mission goes wrong, and you immedietally try to stop and do whatever you can to ensure the safety of your kerbals! You feel accomplished when you take those first steps on the moon, and you see your kerbals smile on re-entry, knowing that they are heroes to all of kerbal-kind. You feel a sense of continuaty when your space ship doesn't go as planned, and you rush to find what the problem is.
You start to get addicted, and before you know it, you're writing a 10/10 review on this piece of art.
This, my friends, is a piece of what gaming always wanted to be. A fantasy world, truely in your mind, where you can dream up what you want, when you want, and how you want it. Think Minecraft in space, where you have to make the complex calculations to get to Duna, the kerbin equvilant of Mars.
Now, the thing is, all of this is about x8 easier than what it is in real life.
Once you figure out physics and the complex mojo that really makes NASA's scientists, well, NASA's scientists, you start speaking it aswell, you start reading on and on with the changelogs, and before you know it, It's halloween and you're dressing up as a Kerbal.
This is what I see in this game, a fantastic piece of gaming history that should be carefully monitered, and is one of those games you might find bad, then you play the game. This is the game you want to throw $ at so that it lives.

This is the best game I've ever played in my life.
It's one of those things that leaves you feeling hollow inside so many times all the way up until the end. Absolutely gutwrenching, but so beautiful, this a masterpiece, to call it a "game" seems disrespectful, this is life. And just like this experience, real life is strange too, and has it's ups and downs, sometimes it sucks, sometimes it sucks so bad you just want it to end, and other times you're so grateful to be alive, because you can witness all the beauty that you would've never seen other wise.
I don't say this lightly at all, this is the most real thing I've ever experienced, and it feels like watching a movie, where you get attached to the characters and the story, and you feel like you care about those people, and that's you in that story.
It's been said before, "Did I beat the game, or did the game beat me?" And I can safely say, we all won here, and nobody, depending on how you look at it. I went into this expecting a choice based, story driven game, that would make me think, and leave me feeling satisfied that I got my money's worth; I left thinking I could've never been happy with living my life and having not gone though this. It filled a hole somewhere, and maybe it opened another, because it frakking tore me asunder. At times if feels just like the movie, the Butterfly Effect, because it's the same principle, sometimes it seems like, no matter what you do to try and help, you ultimately cause something else, and keep perverting the natural course of events, until you realize you are the problem, and maybe you're causing more harm than good.
I've tried to be vague, for those of you who havn't gone through it yet. But all I can say is never have I played a video game that impacted me so hard it made me reconsider my own life choices, my life itself. If you're easily saddened or depressed, maybe you should steer clear of it; it literally has an ad that rolls accross the page, saying if you're affected by the content, you can contact them and they'll help you find a support group to talk to. I've played some emotional games, and some intense stories, but I think this is the first one I've ever played that actually made me cry and feel bittersweet as hell, gave me that feeling where your stomach feels weird, and it hurts to swallow, you feel like you've got a swollen throat, just like when I saw the Season 8 finale of Scrubs. You don't know whether to love it or hate it, or yourself for that matter, you question everything at that point.
I'm rambling now, so to wrap it up, it's been a hell of a ride, but I wouldn't change a thing, love is a powerful thing, sometimes it can make you do the wrong thing for the right reasons, it transcends reality... Max and Chloe together, forever...

END OF GAME REVIEW
Okay, so after playing through the entire game and reading other reviews, I decided to do a post-endgame edit.
What IS typical...the PLOT and Character Architypes
This game is not at all about gameplay (at least, combat and controls-wise) or even plot (pretty basic on the surface), its about philosophy and your personal experience, based on your LIFE, and how they influenced your in-game decisions. The story is simplified so anyone can relate and move the story along (assuming we've all been through high-school, and know the architypes) to the more important parts of the game's mechanics...the character development, the empathy you have for them, and the gravity of your in-game choices.
What is NOT typical...the StoryTELLING Mechanics
The story itself doesn't matter, only your relatability to the characters. So when it matters most, the game design makes you feel the FULL weight of your choices. But you'll eventually realize that you are winning battles only to eventually lose the war. So instead of a "Here is yet another game I have to try to beat", I think you eventually realize you can't "beat" it in a traditional gaming sense.
GAMEPLAY and other Game Mechanics
The music is simple, and does its job carrying you through the emotional rollercoaster...while not distracting you. Gameplay (walking around and interacting) is simple and not distracting, no bugs. The visuals are amazing from a cinematic stand point, and whether it was in 120 FPS or 30 FPS, the relatable dialogue, character development, and smart focus on game mechanics is what you focus on.
FINAL COMMENT
I grew up assuming I could always OUTPLAY the game with strategy guides, properly leveling/build the characters, and mastering mechanics. This is not that kind of game. But I thankfuly learned at the end of the game, and feel I've made the right decisions. If you keep trying to play this game to "Win"...you've miss the point of the game and already lost. Once again, a philosophical story...not just another playthrough.

This game, in a nutshell, is the most crazy feat of player control. Most of the things created or even conceived for games are by the gamers behind the game. Despite this game's age--older than a lot of the player base--it is still going strong, with many new ideas coming from us, the players, including gamemodes, maps, and overall new ways to play coming out almost hourly. All in all, I reccomend this game entirely.

KSP is a superb game - the community, modders and players alike are wonderful. To say it's like Minecraft in Space is to do both games a diservice. Working with real-life physics (or near enough) you basically learn the ground laws of astro-physics, in order to progress. Given that this game is still early access, it's going to be so utterly exciting to see this game once it is fully developed.
As with most early access games, there are still a lot of bugs left to iron out, but that in no way harms the playability or the sheer thrill of attaining your first orbit, or landing trusty ol' Jeb on the Mun. There are plenty of mods out there to enhance your experience, either by changing the career science tree or adding new parts and/or physics. KSP has been a gateway game into Greenlight Studios for me, and I now spend quite a bit of time searching for other equally intriguing studios to support.

Within the first episode, you learn that you have rewind powers. Every time you make an important decision, it displays a little message that you can rewind and change your decision if you want to. It really messed with my head at times, but I love that. "Are you SURE that's the decision you want to make?"
o.o No! No, I'm not sure!
>.< Haha...
As the story progresses, each decision gets harder and harder to make, and your choices really do affect the story.
It's truly surprising, and the ending actually made me cry which is a real achievement. The last game to make me cry was.... none? They do a really great job of transporting you into the story. The music is beautiful. It's absolutely one of those games that I wish I had never played so that I could play it again for the first time. To call it a game is selling it short. It has a very deep and emotional impact on anyone who plays it.

This game gets better the more you play. The first episode drew me in but I wasn't sure if I was going to love the rest of it. Part of it, I'll admit, is the voice acting. At times it really felt cringe-worthy, but the performances improved over the course of the game (or I just got used to it--either way, it didn't bother me anymore).
The overall narrative was extremely satisfying to play and I felt very connected to most of the characters and this made me try really hard to do the right thing each step along the way. Episode Two was my personal favourite but that certainly isn't to say that the other ones weren't up to par. I am excited for Season Two although it will have a whole new set of characters--the idea of turning back time is far too intriguing to give up on.
One complaint I do have is that I didn't feel satisfied with either ending option. I wound up playing both of them, but I couldn't figure out which one was inherently better so I didn't get a lot of closure. I also feel that there were some holes as far as the extent of Max's powers went, but hopefully these are things they intended to leave open for the next season.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys heavy emphasis on storytelling and characters. I loved Life is Strange.

Kerbal Space Program is probably one of the hardest games I have played recently and I love it for that reason. I did the first tutorial on launching a rocket then jumped straight into career mode and quickly started to re-live the early days of rocketry watching rockets spin out of control and crash, look like a good launch only to veer off uncontrollably, finally achieving a sub orbital flight, then one orbit. Eventually a multi-day orbit. Now I'm trying to land a probe on the moon! KSP does such a good job of mixing the simulation aspect with fun and humor. Plus, it's not an over the top simulator. Don't get me wrong, this isn’t just strapping some candlesticks to a crew capsule and pressing the "Go" button. At some point you will be racking your brain trying to build a rocket that works, but allows you to have enough fuel once in space to get somewhere besides around the planet!
KSP’s physics are excellent if you lose control there isn't much you can do but watch the thing crash, but I never feel like I need a 100 keys to make things work just the mouse and one hand on the keyboard. Even though this game is "Early Access" the game already has a solid core, and the amount of stuff you can do is already amazing! It’s not perfect, I've seen a few graphical glitches, but nothing that has caused me to get frustrated. I eventually did have to go to the wiki to figure a few things out. Oh, and no need to stress about money in career mode, this is all about science (for now, looks like budgets and reputation are coming)! One last thing, this game can feel serious but it’s all about the fun with hints of amazement (the first time you make it to the dark side of Mun!). Here’s the secret to enjoying this game: build, test, crash (and laugh) or fly, learn (and gather science), rebuild, aim for the next goal.
TO MÜN! (then other planets)
