I've been playing this game since the alpha, and I always have something else I want to do in the game.
So, how to describe it?
Well, it's a mostly realistic space flight simulator that pulls very few punches with the rocketry physics.  You'll need to become familiar with terms like apoapsis, prograde, specific impulse, and delta velocity.  Before you run away screaming, though, allow me to point out that despite all of that it's actually a pretty simple game, especially compared to the only other realistic space sim of note, Orbiter.
Actually, it's a lot like Orbiter with training wheels:  The solar system is a sort of small-scale parody of ours, with many of the planets and moons obviously inspired by our own, although it's not a direct copy.  Out-of-the-box, you don't need to worry about things like life support and reentry heat (yet) though mods exist that introduce both of these things.  Unlike Orbiter, you can create your own rockets from a set of parts.  This sometimes leads to "fun" in the Dwarf Fortress sense as you learn (much to your dismay and potential amusement) that you forgot some important piece of equipment you needed for your mission (or to prevent the thing from exploding.)
There is the beginnings of a career mode, where you fly scientific missions to collect science points and use these to unlock new parts.  This is something I would actually highly reccommend over the sandbox mode because the tech limits serve to guide your early learning and introduce new parts at a steady, predictable rate.  The devs are promising expansions to the currencies of career mode to include budgetary constraints and prestige objectives to increase said budget.
If you're wondering what age this game is appropriate for, I'd say pretty much any.  While completing more complicated objectives will require some maturity and understanding, there's plenty to occupy any kid who likes to make pretty spaceships and crash them into the ground, intentionally or otherwise.

I should start by saying that this game is not for the faint of heart.  My interest in this type of game has come from a childhood growing up watching sci-fi tv shows.  Shows like Star Trek, Star Wars, and my favorite show of all time, Firefly.  But this game more closely resembles the adventures of Apollo 13, which I experienced from the Tom Hanks movie.
In Kerbal Space Program, you'll have to plan your rocket building, and your missions very carefully.  You'll quickly discover how challenging it can be to complete the simplest of missions.  Getting to the moon may be one of your first goals, but before that you'll have to just get into orbit, which can be surprisingly difficult for your first time.  Then, making it to the moon is one thing, but have you planned your rocket well enough to be able to make it back?  Not to mention future challenges down the road such as getting to other planets.
You'll experience realistic physics first hand, especially as you try maneuvers such as in space rendezvous.  Your orbit must line up perfectly, which can be astoundingly difficult.  Then you'll have to learn to maneuver your ship with RCS thrusters in order to easily dock.  You remembered RCS thrusters, right?  Your Kerbal's life may depend on it.  But of course RCS thrusters won't matter much if you forgot a parachute.
While building your rocket(s), you'll have to organize stages (how pieces will be dropped off as you go, like fuel tanks as they empty), consider the center of gravity, aerodynamics, fuel, and weight.  Of course, not to mention everything else, like aquiring science points, and having what you need to accomplish your mission.
The new career mode is fantastic, making goals more clear, forcing you to attempt small steps at a time.
If you like building, strategy, and planning in a very difficult game, and are willing to work through the difficulty, then you'll enjoy success.  Just make sure you keep your beloved Kerbals alive.
Update: March 2, 2014
So, I just built a new computer for work and gaming.  The extra horsepower makes a world of difference in Kerbal's gameplay.
The physics all calculate quick and properly, so I don't get any random explosions anymore, and I'm not limited as much to how big of a rocket I can build.  Before I could only build a rocket with about 150 parts.  After that the physics became unplayable.
Next, the extra terrain detail is immediately noticeable.  I'm excited to go back to the moon and see how much of an impact it has on the experience.  Before with the settings nearly all the way down, everything was as bland as possible.  The core gameplay was the same, so I still found it a lot of fun, but having the extra detail is still game-changing.
And finally, I'm excited because the game will be more playable.  I did a quick test flight and noticed that now, with the shadow quality turned up, shadows render as far as possible.  Which is incredible, and will make landing so much easier.  Before, at first I didn't have shadows on at all, which makes landing much more difficult.  Then, I turned them on, but they were on the lowest settings possible, so they didn't appear until I was already very close to the ground.
Overall, my new computer has been an "economy" build.  So the parts were relatively cheap, but the performance value is unbeatable.  For those interested, my new computer is of the new Kaveri APU chips, the A10-7850k, with 2400mhz, 10 latency ram.
Update: November 23, 2017
This game has seen amazing updates over the years, including some that massively improve gameplay.  My favorite is a complete communications system, with signal strength, relays, and data bandwidth.  This update makes play with drones complete and functional.

KSP is a cute spacecraft building 'sim', featuring an alien solar system loosely based upon our own.  The basic concepts of the game can be split into two main parts: designing (and building) spacecraft (and space planes) and then manually flying them to try and achieve your own space missions.  Your first task will no doubt be to attempt to build and fly a rocket in order to get your Kerbals into orbit around their home planet of Kerbin.
In career mode KSP is a strategic game, featuring scientific research to unlock parts and (soon) budgets for vessels / missions.   Alternatively, the game can also be played in sandbox mode, with all parts already unlocked and unlimited funds.  I'd recommend starting out in career mode, since the unlocked inventory of parts can be a little bewildering to new players.
Either way this is not only a terrifically fun sim but it is also rather educational, since if you want to get anywhere you will need to learn about real-life space-science concepts.  These include: basic orbital mechanics (orbital apsides, velocities, etc.) Newtonian physics, Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, Hoffman transfer orbits, manual docking processes, etc. and so on.
The game is very mod-friendly, allowing all sorts of additional parts (flight computers, aerodynamic parts etc.) and missions (ex. resource gathering) to be added easily to either the career or sandbox modes, in order to expand the game.
The game is still unfinished (thanks Early Access!) but it is very playable.  I've put in a lot of hours to it since you really do get out as much you put in.  During this time, I've built and launched satellites, space stations, moon landers and interplanetary research vessels.
Highly recommended.

Life is Strange to niezapomniana przygoda, pełna trudnych decyzji, bardzo miłych chwil i wspomnień, które pozostaną nawet dłużej przy Tobie i w Twoim umyśle niż się tego spodziewasz. It's a narrative game, more storytelling than game, though it has some gameplay at times.
I'm going to review the whole story, here, episods 1 through 5. It's unlikely that you may want to stop at the end of episod 1 anyway.
The pace of the story is good, you get enough time to become strongly attached to characters (most of them are likable) before the slowly sink into a problems way above their heads (except for a special power that give them a fighting chance). It's emotionally very intense, heartbreaking at times. Graphics are really excellent, not quite photo-realistic, but somehow better than that, they've got their own style and I like it very much.
The story has its twist and turns. Even the most unlikable characters have some reasons to their behavior, and maybe you didn't understand them quite enough when you first disliked them.
It's a fantastic journey.
I concur with others to say that the conclusion of the story, at the very end of the 5th episode is not as strong as I'd like. It's logic is not as sound as the rest of the game, and though it conveniently closes the story, it may not be the best nor the thing that makes the most sense in the game.
I loved the 5th episode though that is really extreme, and rightly so as it's the last one of a crescendo in the story. The 'nightmarish reality' or 'realistic nightmare' of the 5th episode is really interesting. It reminds me of the good parts of early 'Silent Hills' games. (the very conclusion of the game, though, the last two minutes, are less good than they ought to be though, as I already mentioned in an earlier paragraph).
Don't let this deter you, this is a fantastic story and a fantastic time, you'll want to go through it a few times until you've tamed all the 'ugly things' that come your way in the story. You should definitely play it if you're into narrative games. it has a very strong emotional impact, and I think it will be a lasting impact. This game, its characters, its story, has a very strong appeal and the journey through the game won't disappoint, I can assure you.

As long as you have a decent gaming computer, you will have fun with this game. It is about flying into space, but its more fun than it sounds. You add the parts to your rockets, they are not premade. There are two game modes as of .23, sandbox and career. Sandbox, everything is open to you, let your imagination run wild. Career, you start with the least effiecent rocket parts and you must work to unlock more. The game is in deep beta yet it feels finished, Only one crash within 60 hours of playing.There are a few problems (which is expected with a beta) You can make as big rockets as you want to without consequence, but a cost feature is in development.There is a lack of sound when you arent firing rockets, its just awkard until the space music comes in. Science points (which you use to unlock rocket parts) is too easy to get, you can unlock most things going to the 2 moons orbiting earth/kerban. In the creation menu you cant rotate things in a specific way, just 90 degrees, which hinders some designs of rockets. When looking at your path in deep space, you have to zoom out far away so it isnt buggy, and that decreases accuracy. But after all this, the game is amazing fun, i still play it nonstop, its like crack! The developers work hard to make sure the game is great, so far i havent seen a bad update. You add the parts to your rockets, they are not premade. There are two game modes as of .23, sandbox and career. Sandbox, everything is open to you, let your imagination run wild. Career, you start with the least effiecent rocket parts and you must work to unlock more. The game is in deep beta yet it feels finished, Only one crash within 60 hours of playing.There are a few problems (which is expected with a beta) You can make as big rockets as you want to without consequence, but a cost feature is in development.There is a lack of sound when you arent firing rockets, its just awkard until the space music comes in. Science points (which you use to unlock rocket parts) is too easy to get, you can unlock most things going to the 2 moons orbiting earth/kerban. In the creation menu you cant rotate things in a specific way, just 90 degrees, which hinders some designs of rockets. When looking at your path in deep space, you have to zoom out far away so it isnt buggy, and that decreases accuracy. But after all this, the game is amazing fun, i still play it nonstop, its like crack! The developers work hard to make sure the game is great, so far i havent seen a bad update. It's a narrative game, more storytelling than game, though it has some gameplay at times.
I'm going to review the whole story, here, episods 1 through 5. It's unlikely that you may want to stop at the end of episod 1 anyway.
The pace of the story is good, you get enough time to become strongly attached to characters (most of them are likable) before the slowly sink into a problems way above their heads (except for a special power that give them a fighting chance). It's emotionally very intense, heartbreaking at times. Graphics are really excellent, not quite photo-realistic, but somehow better than that, they've got their own style and I like it very much.
The story has its twist and turns. Even the most unlikable characters have some reasons to their behavior, and maybe you didn't understand them quite enough when you first disliked them.
It's a fantastic journey.
I concur with others to say that the conclusion of the story, at the very end of the 5th episode is not as strong as I'd like. It's logic is not as sound as the rest of the game, and though it conveniently closes the story, it may not be the best nor the thing that makes the most sense in the game.
I loved the 5th episode though that is really extreme, and rightly so as it's the last one of a crescendo in the story. The 'nightmarish reality' or 'realistic nightmare' of the 5th episode is really interesting. It reminds me of the good parts of early 'Silent Hills' games. (the very conclusion of the game, though, the last two minutes, are less good than they ought to be though, as I already mentioned in an earlier paragraph).
Don't let this deter you, this is a fantastic story and a fantastic time, you'll want to go through it a few times until you've tamed all the 'ugly things' that come your way in the story. You should definitely play it if you're into narrative games. it has a very strong emotional impact, and I think it will be a lasting impact. This game, its characters, its story, has a very strong appeal and the journey through the game won't disappoint, I can assure you.

Wow. I just finished this game, and honestly I'm speechless. This is a work of art unlike any I've come across, and man does it screw around with your emotions. I will absolutely unequivocally recommend this game to anybody - it paints such a beautiful story of friendship and sacrifice, and you will find yourself having to make choices that are truly heartwrenching. More than once I found myself questioning what I would do if these were situations I came across in real life, and it really questions what you value and prioritize. I also highly recommend that you make the choices on your own!!! Don't look up any guides or playthroughs - it will really detract from the experience of this game when you already know the consequences of your actions from online sources. Don't focus on what will get you to "win" - savor the experience of playing it through not knowing what will happen because that opportunity only ever comes once. I promise it is so worth it. It is full of unexpected twists and turns that are relentless to your emotions. For the 5 nights I've played this I've found myself up till at least 2am just wanting more, and each episode leaves you on such intense cliffhangers. This is one of those games where you develop genuine attachments to the characters, and consequently this game has stuck me on a feels train that will probably go on a few days.
The developers really did an amazing job on all fronts: gameplay, storyline, soundtrack, artwork.  I especially enjoyed the soundtrack, and it really is such a huge part of the whole vibe of the game. I'll probably be playing through a few episodes again to see how the different choices affect the storyline. 10/10, and thank you to the developers for creating this masterpiece.

Kerbal Space Program is pure MAGIC! On the facade it comes across as something with the depth of Angry Birds and the looks of a crappy looking 3d rollercoaster tycoon and the unsuspecting gamer is easily fooled. However, there is a reason this game has a fanbase of millions! There's a reason I'm scoring this game 12 out of 10. I find this game to be the most addictive thing in my library. I even try NOT to play it, but when I do it keeps me awake at night and busy while doing daily chores...
KSP, like the name might have hinted, is a Space Program Simulator Game. There is the career mode, involving missions and research, and there is the sandbox mode that allows you to run free with it. The game is in early access and the career needs work (I find the missions redundant and confusing, but it's already fun), and this review is more about the sandbox mode.
You run the show, so you set out your own missions, like fly to the moon or another planet. Then you have to build your lander, rover, satelite or whatever, the means of manouvering in space and a rocket to get it in space! Then you have to find out not just how to get something off the ground and into space, you also need to learn to make an orbit. Then you learn how to manipulate orbits in order to get around. There are no concessions! By the time you've figured out how to get where you want to go, you will have learned the basics of actual spaceflight! You don't need a science degree to do this and to understand this, the game is brilliant this way. You can get there by trial and error and in a fun way too.
I recommend this game to all people that like simulation games, tycoon games, Lego (the plastic bricks), science fiction in general, science in general, rockets and blowing stuff up, real space exploration or even have slight positive stance on looking at the sky at night willing to learn.
As you set out your own missions, you send your Kerbal individuals (they all have names) on grand adventures. Their homeworld has a cicumference of about 12000km and it comes with 2 moons. The bigger one looks like our own moon and it can even cast a solar eclipse (really a fun and beautifull feature). In the Kerbol (name of the star) system you will also find the planets Moho, Eve with it's moon Gilly, Kerbin with Mun and Minmus, Duna with Ike, then a gas-giant called Jool with no less then 5 moons plus finally the dwarfplanet Eelo. The distances are measured in millions of kilometers when traveling in space. It may be a scaled down planetary system, but that doesn't mean it's small. I have never before adventured through such an immense ingame world. Each planet and moon comes with it's own biomes and anomalies to discover and explore and you'll busy for hundreds of hours before you've done it all. Everyone plays in this same systen so everyone can share their adventures with eachother, you know what the other player is talking about.
When I started playing, I had little expectations. It looked like a mod, but then I reached space. It was like the opening of the movie 2001: a Space Oddisey. The "space whales" ingame music started playing and my contraption was floating in a serene fashion high above kerbin, ever going higher and higher, kerbin getting smaller and smaller, I passed the Mun... lost kerbin, then found the "eva" button.. I found out stands for "Extra Vehicular Activity", or "Go play outside".. so I lost my Kerbal. Hours of my life passed by while staring at this phenomenon called KSP, while drooling over my keyboard.
This game is not done yet. I'm not sure when they aim for a release candidate, but they can't fail this anymore. Nasa has made an addon for it, so now asteroids are also part of the game and can be landed on or grabbed. Nasa also added their own rocket parts based on the new Space-X rocket, how awesome is that! And the developer has even announced multiplayer!!! I don't know how this will work and what we could do in an online game, and It's already more fun if a friend plays this game too, but it's anticipated by me nonetheless.
The educational value of this game is through the roof! I thought I understood the principle of orbits, but boy did I learn a lot. I understood the concept of flying faster horizontally then you fell vertically, but putting it to practice requires more then just going. So, I watched Nasa do it. They pivot the rocket as soon as it has picked up enough speed, so ok... I built a rocket with steering parts and pivotted it correctly after a few try-outs and finally worked out an eliptical orbit to play with. At this point the concept that Isaac Newton put down of "every action has a 'pose and equal reaction" gets a whole new meaning in orbit (you'll see :KSmiley:).
Every run you make in Kerbal, you get more advanced. Your rockets become more stable, because you know how to make them, you get to other planets faster, because you know how to get there. My rockets grew in size from around 60 parts for the rocket with my first moonlander, of which I built a new version every night, to about 1300 in my rocket plus massive oversized truck I landed on Duna, which took me 2 weeks to build! It went from slapping together a simple contraption to a mind-boggling engineering puzzle that even my pc (or the game's engine) found hard to process when launched.
There comes a point where you get stuck on something, like how to dock in space. There are several things to do, but I warn you: this can make or break your experience. Try as hard as you can if you're stuck, play with a friend (you know, together on one pc thinking and building) and if all else fails, then try youtube or a guide. Letting guides take you by the hand can ruin your experience. But when you've reached this point it just means a whole new world of Kerbal opens before your eyes. I think every KSP player has posted screenshots, videos, guides both online and private to friends. The ammount of material you can dig up is staggering.
Also, don't install mods as you just start playing, exept for scan-sat perhaps (but don't, the other mods will lure you). Mods potentially ruins the experience as they can either make it to hard or too easy. I've reached the point where making an orbit has become a boring thing to do and I had seen all the parts ingame. I've reached the point of not getting my ships docked. This was the point where I looked on youtube, read guides and reviews for mods and then installed mods, mods like MechJeb (in flight telemetry and autopilot options, use at your own risk), advanced cockpits (cockpit screens, buttons to press, external cameras, awesome!), more parts, graphical addons, scan-sat (scans planets, awesome!), etc. But with all games in early access, mods can be broken when the game is patched. But when you've reached that point, KSP can be enhanced in such ways it brings about limitless posibilities, as realistic as you want it to be.
This game is 100% quality, dedicated hard work and deserves all credit it can get. When it's done, it just means it has reached a point where the developers can call it a complete game. With more standard parts, more physics, more career, more tycoon and basicly more game then it is now. From that moment this game will only expand as if it were the universe itself thanks to mods and I don't think this game will die out soon. Just buy the game, you'll have fun for years to come I promiss!!!
Now years after release, I stand by my review. This game will stand it's ground.

This game crushed me. It tore out my heart and stomped on it repeatedly. Worth it. In fact, it's tempting to manipulate time a little bit, myself, by starting the story over...
The theme of this game is exploring time travel and causality, and the plot and mechanics lean on this for everything it's worth. In it, you play as a high school senior who suddenly discovers that she has the ability to rewind time and alter the course of history - although every possible course of events has positive and negative consequnces - and often the negative in spades.
Forming the focus of this game is its cast of characters. There is a real depth to each of those who get significant screen time. I found myself lost in trying to figure out what each was thinking; to glean every little scrap of them from every word. Dialogue is occasionally awkward (especially the business-like use of "social media" to replace the names of specific networks, presumably for obvious trademark reasons), but there is an earnest touch to it that shines through - natural inside jokes and teasing between teenagers, and raw emotion when characters are at their limits.
On technical merits and in terms of artistry, this game is beautiful. The visual style reminds me of that of Tomb Raider, another Square Enix title (although one produced by a different studio), except with a painterly, stylized look applied to everything. Arcadia Bay is enchanting, if flawed, and creates the perfect backdrop for the coming-of-age drama - as well as the dozens of photos Max will take during the course of the game. Each character has a memorable, lovingly crafted look.
The ending made me agonize over some parts of my own life and asked me questions I didn't know how to answer. Without going into the specifics, the ending is one of the major parts of this game I take serious issue with: there is no truly "good" answer, and any choice will require some justification on your own part. But, such is life at its worst - without giving too much away, it won't feel fair because it isn't.
It has been a long time since a set of characters in a game have moved me this deeply.* I left with the distinct feeling that, while I knew them all very well, some like old friends, I wished I was able to spend more time with them. Art imitates life.

Life is Strange may have issues with its plot, but it hides most of it well behind great dialogue and touching moments. If you love character drama, this interactive miniseries will surely captivate you and make you care about its characters as they slowly drift towards an inevitable tragedy.
On the surface, Life is Strange is a standard time travel story, presented in an interactive film format: a shy but nosy teenage girl discovers she can rewind time and uses it to save as many people around her as she can, but always ends up in deeper and deeper trouble.
Like with most similar products, there isn’t any gameplay to comment on, the entire thing is the story and its presentation. And in our case, we have somewhat of a mixed bag.
Let’s get the bad side out of the way first: the plot is weak. More than half of it (including an entire episode) is pure filler with no story advancement. It is also riddled with issues like tired high school archetypes that never get past their one-dimensional role, and a B-grade slasher movie serial killer who even has a clichéd bunker hideout.
On top of that, it feels like as if the story was originally written for television, as all so-called interactive elements have no real influence on anything. No matter what you choose, all but two scenes have the exact same outcomes with some minor dialogue changes here and there.
So what is good? The script is. The dialogues are excellent, and the cast made a flawless job at capturing all the wonderful small moments, the tear-jerking character drama that easily elevates this story above many similar products we saw in recent years. These things may seem small compared to the plotting issues, but in reality they make sure that you will hardly regret going through Life is Strange, not even for a moment.

Kerbal Space Program is a spaceflight simulation game developed by Squad. It features a full solar system based off our own, a large variety of propellants, and abilities for free modding. That's not to say that the game isn't difficult, if you just pick the 'God' mode where you have every part unlocked then you likely won't have any idea what you're doing. I find it helps to take the training scenarios before you start. Even though I had a bit of trouble getting started, you can find that orbiting is far easier to control via the map screen. Mods are availible at their website
without any kind of Steam Workshop support.
Modding the game before playing is reccomended, but this just makes the game boot and play far slower. Also, to the people aware of PC architecture, this game
runs on a 32-bit process. A game that is in development that runs with a maximium of 3.25 gigabytes of RAM. That's a huge bottleneck when they don't include direct streaming from the hard drive. It basically means that if you were playing on a GeForce GTX Titan or something to that effect with 64 Gigs of Workstation memory, you'd be running KSP at the same speed as a 4 year old laptop. Also, the majority of people playing this will defend it until the end of time. I questioned about why the hell they still use the same instruction process as the first edition of MS-DOS, and got flamed for it. After a crash (happens often) Windows 7 suggested that it may not be running correctly and enabled compatibility settings. This is the exact reason why I don't reccomend buying early acsess titles. It is like pre-ordering, but the Devs get to just have you play an incomplete title and ruin your experience.
This game is sometimes cited as a Steam sucess story, but I don't think it's too deserving. The people behind this game simply refuse to make this game run well. The fanbase sucks, and it's simply just a loss of potential.

With the addition of a career mode where the components you have access to are limited, Kerbal Space Program has grown from a fun sandbox game to a engrossing challenge to lock everything as you explore the solar system. You really get a sense of progress as you take the first few steps you can to encircle your starting planet and venture further for longer as you unlock more components.
I couldn't help writing descriptions for the rockets I built; explaining their purpose and what differeniates them from previous models.
There's definitely more that can be added to the game, but this is already a game worth investing time in.

This game crushed me. It tore out my heart and stomped on it repeatedly. Worth it. In fact, it's tempting to manipulate time a little bit, myself, by starting the story over...
The theme of this game is exploring time travel and causality, and the plot and mechanics lean on this for everything it's worth. In it, you play as a high school senior who suddenly discovers that she has the ability to rewind time and alter the course of history - although every possible course of events has positive and negative consequnces - and often the negative in spades.
Forming the focus of this game is its cast of characters. There is a real depth to each of those who get significant screen time. I found myself lost in trying to figure out what each was thinking; to glean every little scrap of them from every word. Dialogue is occasionally awkward (especially the business-like use of "social media" to replace the names of specific networks, presumably for obvious trademark reasons), but there is an earnest touch to it that shines through - natural inside jokes and teasing between teenagers, and raw emotion when characters are at their limits.
On technical merits and in terms of artistry, this game is beautiful. The visual style reminds me of that of Tomb Raider, another Square Enix title (although one produced by a different studio), except with a painterly, stylized look applied to everything. Arcadia Bay is enchanting, if flawed, and creates the perfect backdrop for the coming-of-age drama - as well as the dozens of photos Max will take during the course of the game. Each character has a memorable, lovingly crafted look.
The ending made me agonize over some parts of my own life and asked me questions I didn't know how to answer. Without going into the specifics, the ending is one of the major parts of this game I take serious issue with: there is no truly "good" answer, and any choice will require some justification on your own part. But, such is life at its worst - without giving too much away, it won't feel fair because it isn't.
It has been a long time since a set of characters in a game have moved me this deeply.* I left with the distinct feeling that, while I knew them all very well, some like old friends, I wished I was able to spend more time with them. Art imitates life.
*

Life is Strange has vibes similar to Beyond: Two Souls, with the "teenage life" concept. The game tells the tale of a girl named Max, who moved away to Seattle when she was younger.
Recently, Max moved back to her hometown, and joined Blackwell Academy, an art school in the fictional town of Arcadia Bay, Oregon.
While "sleeping", in class, max has a dream of a tornado wiping out the entire town, and when she wakes up, she discovers that she has time traveling abilities.

I'm not too sure how to write a review that does this game justice AND avoids spoilers. Like Undertale, I decided to go in blind with as little knowledge about the game as possible. With that in mind, I really don't think I should mention much for this game.
This is a story game. You won't be playing it for any other reason, so be prepared to commit to that accordingly. It takes roughly 15-25 hours to complete, so it isn't very long (but it is definitely not too short). There are some moments in the game that may be distressing to some, but saying what those moments are would ruin the story.
For me personally, I found myself extremely emotionally invested in the game, possibly more so than any other game. I found myself REALLY thinking about the choices in the game and what they meant to me. At two very key moments, I ended up in tears, and that has never happened in a game before for me. If you're willing to really get into the game, it will hit you pretty hard.
Lastly, the ending does need to be addressed, and while what I say won't contain spoilers, it WILL give away a certain element of the entire game, so read on at your own risk.
A must play for anyone who enjoys a good story.

I`m sorry, but I cannot give this game a positive review. This game was promoted as a challenging adventure where the choices you make change the game, but unfortunately it is a major disappointment.
It is very linear, with no more that 2 choices to choose from. The outcome of your choices is very obvious and I could actually pre-determine the ending just by selecting the path I want.
The adventure is very basic with absolutely no difficulty. You don`t know the answer, reverse time and try a different option until you get it right.
The story is "weird" jumping from objective to objective and leaving entire scenarios unfinished. Your objective is very simple with no mystery and no surprises.
Visual complexity is good, but the screen and the game environment are full of actionable items that are useless and have nothing to do with your mission. Also, object interaction is either "Look" or "Use" and only when critical items are found, you get more... I can access someones laptop and see what is on their screen, but I cannot use it or the NPC does not say anything about it or my action does not influence the outcome of the game.
I could keep going and going, but there is no point.
If you value your money DO NOT BUY this game until is goes on a really big sale.

If you like a game that involves tough choices, great music, amazing voice work, interesting plot, and an overall great setting, you should try this game.

This game is so versatile and attractive to so many people, but at its core is a space focused flight physics game. The game is nearly endless in its challenges to you. Every success is the most exciting success in its moment and the moment you achieve it, you start looking to get further along, which means getting back into the builder and finding defeciencies of your rocket and launching again.
The recent addition of the campaign has added a whole new level of challenge; and in my opinion, is necessary. It forces you to explore everything for currency (science points!). With this currency, you can research new parts for your rocket. This adds a need to visit locations under different circumstances, adding a lot of replay value.
If you love space, flight simulators, or just generally like to fire explosives into the sky, Kerbal is your game. I find myself coming back to this game and getting wrapped up in it month after month and love the direction it is currently taking.

Every so often you find one of those delightful games, KSP is one of them.
KSP is a great game, it rewards failure with humourous outcomes, and rewards effort with a real sense of achievement...your first orbital flight, your first trip to the Mun and back, your first landing on another world (and the return), all will fill you with pride.
I will give another example of pride. I had a bad mission to the Mun, the ship exploded on landing, leaving three kerbals trapped in their capsule on the Mun. I tried a rescue mission, but didn't land close enough to allow them to jet pack to the rescue ship. I aborted and sent another mission. This one was perfect, landed relatively close, rescued all three kerbals. But...when I got home the rescue capsule kept exploding when I landed. So I reloaded, tried again, this time climbing a kerbal outside and jumping into the ocean at low altitude. Amazingly, with the lightend load, or a little luck, everyone survived. It's a classic piece of emergent gameplay, and the satisfaction of bringing everyone home was fantastic.
For failures, my first rocket, I triggered every stage at once, so I fired to boosters, seperated the capsule, and triggered the parachute...the outcome was a disaster, but watching my little kerbal scream in panic, or grin like an idiot still made it a heartwarming experience.
There's a good community around it, good mods, and the developrs keep adding to the game. I recommend career mode so you can progress your technology along with your understanding of the game, and use the wiki and youtube for help when you are stuck.
UPDATE: the new challenges addded to career mode make it easier to progress, and create some interesting challenges to drive more experimentation.

A friend recommended Life is Strange, it turned out to be amazing and one of the best games I played in a long time.
You take control of Maxine (Max) a young aspiring photographer who gets a scholarship at Blackwell Academy, a reputable academy located in Arcadia Bay seaside town in Oregon which has a mixture of students from different financial and psychological backgrounds. You sense early on that despite having a couple of good friends, Max is somewhat lonely in Blackwell.
The storyline is very elaborate, it's about the choices Max makes in life and their consequences. She develops the ability to manipulate time and starts trying to go back in time to "fix" things only to realize that the more she changes the worse the consequences.
After using her powers the first time, Max enters a journey of multiple possible alternative realities depending on the choices she makes (butterfly effect) and the way she manipulates time. The beauty of the choices Max is confronted with lies in the fact that they look very realistic and allow you to explore the journey from different prespectives with some really tough calls to make along the way.
The game does not fall short on "Aha","Wow" and "ooohh" moments, the plot gets more and more complicated as Max uses her powers and discovers new things, including the fact that life is indeed strange in Arcadia Bay and is not as straight forward as it looks.
The game has a very melancholic atmosphere and probably one of the best musical scores I've heard in a video game, which elaborates the gloomy and melancholic atmosphere of the game.
Even the name of the game has a melancholic tone to it if you put it in context of events, "Life is Strange".
The graphics are unique since everything you see on screen was hand painted. The storyline is very good and hooks you up immediately, some complained that the language used in most of the dialogues is overstated "teen" lingo that no one actually uses, that is by no means a deal breaker neither extremely noticeable once you dive into the story.
Life is Strange is a psychological game in nature and it actually allows you to explore your own psychology as you guide Max into making her decisions, it's very interesting to step back after you finish each chapter to think about how your choices evolved the storyline and think about how you sometimes rush into making decisions based on gut feelings, perceptions and paradigms without actually analysing enough. The game does well in placing doubt in your heart about almost every decision you make as Max always reflects with a golden "what if" question.
I cannot recommend this game enough, it really hooked me up to the extent that I binged on it until I finished it. I believe the episodic nature of the game serves the atmosphere and I wouldn't imagine any better form of presentation.
A definite must have for any gamer who likes to try something other than shooting and blowing everything up!
PS: I already finished the game on PS4 and now I'm having a rerun on Steam!

Truly a great game worth every penny, even if it's not on sale. I've had it for a year longer than it's been available on steam, and I'm still playing it regularly. The learning curve is a bit high at first if you're not familiar with orbital physics (and let's face it, most of us weren't before we started playing), but it encourages learning through experimentation - and explosions. If you're like me and couldn't figure out how to get to the moon (or "mun", as planets in KSP are different than our solar system's) or even into space, there are plenty of great community guides and youtube tutorials out there that you'll want to check out (I highly recommend videos by Scott Manley). Whether you find yourself a master rocket engineer trying to land and take off from Eve or if you're a new mechanic trying to just get into orbit, there's always more fun challenges you can take on.
And despite being in alpha, although there are bugs you'll inevitably encounter, it's incredibly stable and they are constantly adding new gameplay mechanics, parts, and other things to help it become more realistic while still fun. The modding community also adds TONS of gameplay enhancements and custom parts that add hours more of fun.

To pick a single word to up Life Is Strange it would have to be perfect, there is never a moment that feels out of place or as if it is there to simply bulk out content in the game.  The world that the developers have created is engrossing, dynamic, unique and truly special, this makes playing Life Is Strange akin to reading a good book and means that you can truly become lost in all that it has to offer.
I would urge anyone that enjoys story based gives to try this

This is definitely in my top 10 favorite games of all time along with GTA (series), Red Dead Redemption, Ghost Recon 1, Rainbow Six 1, Arma (series), FSX, Skyrim (i.e. ES Series), etc. I know that those games may not all sound alike, but they all have been leaders in the open world style gaming and have lots of options on how to solve problems.
Kerbal Space Program is the ultimate in open world...its an open solar system that is fully realized. There are no warp gates, just the massive black void of space between you and your goals. Every mission (campaign or self given in sandbox) requires ships to be built or altered for specific needs using hundreds of parts. In order to reach another planetary body, distances, fuel amounts, electrical storage, atmospheres, landing needs must be pondered and calculated for prior to liftoff. Did you ponder incorrectly and your ship disintegrate into a huge fireball upon liftoff? Did you make it to Duna (Mars) with a Kerbal in a lander, have him do a planet walk, only to realize you forgot to add a ladder for him climb back in?
It's the ultimate in critical thinking gaming. This is without a doubt one of the most challenging games I have ever faced...bar none. Tons of fun.

Kerbal Space Program is the perfect mixture of science, and cartooniness (if that isn't a word it is now). Basically what it is is a rocket simulator where you can build and fly your rockets to different locations. The KSP world has several planets orbiting the sun like our solar system. You start on the main planet, Kerbin, where you build the rocket and launch it. From there you can try to travel to different planets, or attempt to land on one of Kerbins two moons, or simply just try to get into orbit around Kerbin. Though getting there is easier said than done. I still haven't quite made it into full orbit with a few small fuel tanks, yet it is possible. This is one of those games that requires you to watch many videos of people playing online to understand how to do what you want to do. Since this is a sandbox, you can set your own goals and such. When you try to build something and it doesn't work out, you could be sitting there for hours trying to get it to finally work like you want it to.
There is a career mode, which starts you off with very little supplies to build your rockets with. You then earn science by conducting experiments in the atmosphere, space and even other planets. You spend the science on research to get you more parts. That is just the basics of it. Of course it is still in alpha, so it has it's glitches, but they don't affect the overall gameplay.  I would recommend this game to anybody who enjoys a good challenge.

As many have pointed out Life is Strange isn't just a game; it's an experience. I feel this games aim was to test me and really push me to see everything in a different light. Every choice you make has to be taken with caution, care and delicacy. Everything can change in the blink of an eye and the things you thought were right were so very wrong and that's what makes this game so beautiful.
It's an adventure that knows how to make you love, care and want to help the folks of Arcadia Bay as much as you possibly can; it knows how to tug at your heart strings, playing you as if you were an instrument. I, personally became so absorbed in it's story from the first episode. I was sucked into it all with its intresting concept and powerful message leaving me feeling flabergasted and overwhelmed at times.
All the characters (primary) were memorable, likable (or despicable), and were all deep, three dimensional characters each with their own feelings, prospects and agendas and getting to know them all was a very unique and fun experience that I just can't see myself forgetting. On that note I'd like to talk about Max Caufield, maybe I'm a little biased because she reminds me so much of myself but she was just so easily relatable to me. She felt real, like someone I could imagine I would want to have as a best friend (she wasn't the only one but she's very notable), hang out with at home and have legit good discussions with. Maybe it's a little unfair due to the fact that you're the one making the choices but either way I had a blast going on this adventure with her and never once thought of her as boring or plain but rather intresting, having a beautiful soul and seeing her get excited about her craft is just heartwarming.
The story itself is just so good, I don't think a game has ever kept me so invested emotionally, ever. Like I said above it really loves to hit all those highs and lows and it does it hard. A lot of times when something wasn't going the way I envisioned I was left with this gut wretching feeling like my stomach fell and all I could say was "No.." over and over again. It reminds me that I'm human, presenting me with real problems that we have faced or are facing, one of the big themes being bullying and what it can do to someone. But that's not all, it also represents sacrifice and what it takes to really endure. It represents bravery, challenging the player to do what's right or what they think is right. I strongly believe this games message, I really do.
Now we get to gameplay, it is very different from anything I really played and it pays well to have a very observent eye as it requires you to intereact with the enviroment a lot for almost everything like getting information, events where you have to be quickly inspecting everything around you to get the best possible outcome or maybe just to snag that cool photogenic opportunity you're looking for. Another thing I love is the conversations, you need to be able to pick up on small ques and details to figure out what you should be doing and Max's dialogue is always helpful and serves a purpose.
Finally, from me just to sum it up I loved this game from beginning to end, the game was beautiful and is something I feel you should give a try if you haven't. It touched me with it's look on friendship, it's characters, story, everything. I shed tears of both pain and of happiness, things like these don't come along very often and when they do I cherish them very much. Life is Strange is special, a very unique experience worth the 20$ I payed for the five episodes.
Enjoy.

This game is very close to genius. It's not about having the best graphics, but about an involving story that stays with you afterwards, characters that you become attached to, and choices that you have to make that haunt you...and others that make you smile. The animation / motion-capture is some of the best I've seen, apart from the occasional rare lip sync issue. Although weakened a little by the "recycled assets nightmare sequence" towards the end (ala Max Payne, or Far Cry 3), the actual ending itself is smart and very moving - you may be able to tell that it has left me a bit sentimental. I hope the makers of this game keep working to bring more games like this into the marketplace - and the world.
For those who haven't played a branching storyline game like this before, it's best to resist the tempation to replay a chapter when it didn't go your way - it's much more satisfying if you live with the choices you've made through to the end and get the truest outcome for you.

Okay, this is actually one of the first times I write a review.
After having played it through once in a relatively short time, while trying to find everything there is to find and also having watched the Director's Commentary, I have a rather special understanding of this game, I think.
I have seen a few bad reviews and I want to talk about those first. The main problem for many people is that in the end most of your choices do not matter. A lot of those reviews also quote Mass Effect 3. I didn't share this feeling back with Mass Effect 3 - though I could understand their position - but it's a lot less appropriate here, with Life is Strange.
The Difficulty with this "Choices Matter" genre is, that you still can make only one game and I have the feeling people would really like to have devastatingly different endings - wich is not impossible but also not the point of this game. The reason why I said this "Bad ending" attitude is worse here than with Mass Effect 3 is that there is no sequel to Life is Strange and as this is the final decision, there's practically nothing left to influence.
Another reason are the relatively bad graphics - at least for modern standards. But in the Director's Commentary, they explicitly state, that they wanted it like this and also that all textures were hand-drawn. They didn't want to overload the players with graphics, they wanted them to express the atmosphere - and too much detail makes this difficult.
I said before, the decisions in Life is Strange are not about exploring as many difficult endings as possible. Instead, those decisions are about how the character (and also the player) copes with the reactions and the results of their choices as well as getting this feeling, that there is no easy way, maybe not even a right way. Of course, the rewind power gives you some measure of control, but it's not infinite. Sometimes you just spend too much time idling around or gathering information about your current scene, that you can't rewind far enough back to change things you've done earlier in the scene. Sometime you end up having the same dialogue dozens of times and in the end have to rewind one last time and decide wich option was the best in your opinion.
Some people might think that so many choices equal a high level of replayability. Now, I won't exactly argue against it, but it's not as easy as one would think. I got the following idea from another review, so this is kind of a quote: I actually wish I had not played the game, simply because then I could play it again with a blank slate,
. Of course, I do not have the power to alter the past, and this game has taught me, that such power is not even desirable.
One last warning, if you will: This game is hard. Not hard in gameplay or difficulty terms, but hard to cope with, hard in an emotional way. Never before have I been affacted this strongly by a game. I actually thought Mass Effect was the peak of emotional impact I could get, with so much content, so many decisions, so much death. Now, take all that, put somemore emotion on top of it and squash it all in game much smaller, much shorter, as well as put it in a realistic setting, something we can very easily relate to, and you get Life is Strange.

Ok, where do I begin ?
It's an amazing piece of art. I didn't know anything about Life Is Strange before trying it, but the numerous positive reviews (and the humble bundle) compelled me to try. Oh gosh !
Pros
- I hate useless drama. This isn't about useless drama. Story is great, characters are great, music is great, graphics are stylized and nice.
- You are going to be probably broken by this game. But broken in a positive way. Trust me.
As a matter of comparison, telltale games didn't really touched me that way that life is strange did.
- Attention to details is excellent. Immersion is total. Small piece of papers, objects, characters, everything is made to feel real.
- Did I told you characters were amazing ? Even though they are merely pixels we get really attached to them.  And they're going to get through hell with us.
- Excellent price. I mean for this amazing thing 20€ is a very good price, and you'd want to replay once to do all the stuff you've missed.
- Superb voice acting, minus 1 or 2 secondary characters.
- Did I told you the music was brillant ? It really sets up the mood. Would buy the soundtrack.
- If you are or know someone who is into art, this game will definitely speak even more for you. And brings back sweet memories.
Cons
- The ending is a bit previsible. But don't worry, it's not a disappointment.
- Sometimes they might talk a bit too much.
- Sometimes lips syncro is out, or bugged. Not frequent, but might happen. Not a serious issue for 99% of the game.
- Technically graphics are also a bit simple, but the lightning and art design are perfect. So it's highly subjective here. For me it didn't bothered me at all. That said facial expressions are sometimes not very vivid, however the voice acting more than make up for that.
- We need more. Seriously. Make season 2.
- Episode 1 is really... calm compared to others. If you tried it and thought "meh this is just high school drama", I still advise you to get the rest of the episodes when they're on sale. The story really picks up toward more epic action later on.
This game is about story, characters, intrigue. If you don't like talking, exploration... you probably won't like it. Still, take it more like an interactive movie than anything.
And of course if you don't care about people, this game won't do much to you. This game is about the connexion the player has with the characters, if you don't care about them the magic won't operate.
Final verdict : must have. For me it's a 9,5/10. This is not even a game, that's freaking art. Get it.

Life is Strange is a point & click adventure game that offers a great experience as it allows you to follow a very beautiful and interesting story and connect with the characters inside it.
It's is exactly the type of adventure game that is so story-driven that almost feels like you are put inside a movie and able to change the course of events with your choices.
Choices matter. A lot. And with them it allows the player to shape his/her own very special turn of events and actions all related around a very specific core background that follows a chain reaction of actions and consequences through time and space.
You play as Max, an art college teenager that dreams to become a famous photographer and who gets in a college located in a town where she spent her childhood accompanied by Chloe, who used to be her best friend.
Max is a photography geek, a very low profile character and a shy person while Chloe having to go through different circumstances of life has turned out to be a dropout punk chick who gets often into trouble and hides a very sweet core beneath her tough behavior.
The story starts the moment you, playing as Max, find out that you have the special power to rewind time for a few seconds or minutes, allowing you to actually be able to undo and redo actions, choices and dialogues, giving you the feeling of control over reality.
A feeling that turns out to be less and less strong as laws of chaos theory and relativity begin to take over leading you to a climax of events and choices that will even test your consensus and the way you understand the world you have emerged in.
The game, depending the way you play it - and how your own character and ethics are as a person, can turn out to be a unique symbolic corner-stone of what friendship is about and offers you one of the most basic morals that a human brain must cope with in life, that for every action in life, there's always a reaction.
Technical-wise the game has simplified graphics, probably playable by most hardware setups, it is amazingly designed and voice acted.
There's a lot of color, attention to cinematic-like environmental settings and the direction is very well done. And i'm talking about actual direction tricks being used, like camera views well combined with background actions, dialogue combinations, and some times well balanced views.
In addition, during your run you will be accompanied by some very nicely selected music tracks (the OST are indeed amazing).

Okay, this is actually one of the first times I write a review.
After having played it through once in a relatively short time, while trying to find everything there is to find and also having watched the Director's Commentary, I have a rather special understanding of this game, I think.
I have seen a few bad reviews and I want to talk about those first. The main problem for many people is that in the end most of your choices do not matter. A lot of those reviews also quote Mass Effect 3. I didn't share this feeling back with Mass Effect 3 - though I could understand their position - but it's a lot less appropriate here, with Life is Strange.
The Difficulty with this "Choices Matter" genre is, that you still can make only one game and I have the feeling people would really like to have devastatingly different endings - wich is not impossible but also not the point of this game. The reason why I said this "Bad ending" attitude is worse here than with Mass Effect 3 is that there is no sequel to Life is Strange and as this is the final decision, there's practically nothing left to influence.
Another reason are the relatively bad graphics - at least for modern standards. But in the Director's Commentary, they explicitly state, that they wanted it like this and also that all textures were hand-drawn. They didn't want to overload the players with graphics, they wanted them to express the atmosphere - and too much detail makes this difficult.
I said before, the decisions in Life is Strange are not about exploring as many difficult endings as possible. Instead, those decisions are about how the character (and also the player) copes with the reactions and the results of their choices as well as getting this feeling, that there is no easy way, maybe not even a right way. Of course, the rewind power gives you some measure of control, but it's not infinite. Sometimes you just spend too much time idling around or gathering information about your current scene, that you can't rewind far enough back to change things you've done earlier in the scene. Sometime you end up having the same dialogue dozens of times and in the end have to rewind one last time and decide wich option was the best in your opinion.
Some people might think that so many choices equal a high level of replayability. Now, I won't exactly argue against it, but it's not as easy as one would think. I got the following idea from another review, so this is kind of a quote: I actually wish I had not played the game, simply because then I could play it again with a blank slate,
. Of course, I do not have the power to alter the past, and this game has taught me, that such power is not even desirable.
One last warning, if you will: This game is hard. Not hard in gameplay or difficulty terms, but hard to cope with, hard in an emotional way. Never before have I been affacted this strongly by a game. I actually thought Mass Effect was the peak of emotional impact I could get, with so much content, so many decisions, so much death. Now, take all that, put somemore emotion on top of it and squash it all in game much smaller, much shorter, as well as put it in a realistic setting, something we can very easily relate to, and you get Life is Strange.
This game is loads of fun. Just buy it.

I only finished the game yesterday and feelings are still pretty raw, but I think I'll carry this experience with me for a very, very long time. Life Is Strange starts unassuming, in an ordinary US high school in Oregon. There are early hints that something is amiss, foreshadowing the game's time travel elements and a central mystery, but you soon discover that's not why you're playing it. The characters are so well written that you feel absolutely compelled to learn everything about them, to be a good friend to them. You reconnect with the main character's best childhood friend and, despite only just meeting her, you fall in love with her - in as many ways as feels right. You begin to care about just about anyone in the game.
Life Is Strange isn't for everyone. But it is for you if you enjoy games that foster genuine connection with
realistic characters. It's totally for you if you enjoy the vintage photography, autumny, singer-songwriter aesthetic. If you think games
tell stories well but often don't, you will love this piece.
It's not perfect, it's clumsy in places, but it has real emotional impact. A rarity in an industry where most products are, in this respect, polar opposites.

KSP is perhaps one of the most-engaging, challenging, and rewarding games around today. It is neither simple, nor easy, but through a combination of charm, reward, and challenge it tosses us the important pieces of a space program and lets some seriously deep gameplay evolve from that. Building better rockets requires research, research requires funding, which you earn in the form of science, which is basically looking at things from different heights then picking them up to take home. You can also build ridiculous-looking rockets and space planes, then watch them fly apart seconds after launch, Kerbonauts inside screaming their last screams.
Failure is part of the charm of KSP, and that's a good thing too, because you will fail, a lot. That's not to say that KSP is needlessly hard, but it does simulate rocket science (in an arcade-ish sort of way) and the amount of freedom it gives you means that mistakes are inevitable. This is why that charm is built into the game, there's a certain witless innocense about all the Kerbals. Like kids pretending to be astronauts, only with real rockets.
But that just makes it all the more satisfying when you send them up into orbit, calculate a transfer burn and manage to slingshot around the Mun and get them home again. Knowing that all you have to rely on, the only thing between you and the edge of the universe is a rocket engine, Isaac Newton, and how well you managed to time your last engine burn. There's an amazing sense of accomplishment in the successful completion of a mission like that. One that really gives you a small but powerful insight into what space exploration is like and why every time you see Mission control at NASA people always clap when everyone's back on the ground.
I've played KSP since the early Alpha, before Steam, and it's come a long way since then, even at this early stage there is enough game here to keep you busy building orbital habitats and sending probes and crews to other planets for a long time. If you're even partly into astronomy, ever played orbiter, or just love the harder side of Science Fiction, KSP is a worthwhile investment, and one that rewards your success like few other games can.

The best (and only) game in its class, Kerbal space program is a game where goals were only just introduced in the latest expansion pack. Your goal is to collect Science, a currency used to buy upgrades, which are used to build larger and faster rockets, which allow you to collect more Science. The game has a training section that mostly covers flying rockets, but misses a huge aspect of the game: Rocket Design. You are stuck designing these contraptions alone, which is fine if you just want to mess around, but while plenty of errors can be made in a design intended only for orbit or Kerbin's local system, there is little to extremely little room for error in an interplanetary design, particularly one where the crew must return to Kerbin. there are online guides, and mods that add an autopiolet system to the game (MechJeb) but overall, you must still design the rocket yourself. If the idea of designing an interplanetary vehicle and piloting it through a million-meter void to its destination sounds fun and exciting, then this is the game for you.

Ok, where do I begin ?
It's an amazing piece of art. I didn't know anything about Life Is Strange before trying it, but the numerous positive reviews (and the humble bundle) compelled me to try. Oh gosh !
Pros
- I hate useless drama. This isn't about useless drama. Story is great, characters are great, music is great, graphics are stylized and nice.
- You are going to be probably broken by this game. But broken in a positive way. Trust me.
As a matter of comparison, telltale games didn't really touched me that way that life is strange did.
- Attention to details is excellent. Immersion is total. Small piece of papers, objects, characters, everything is made to feel real.
- Did I told you characters were amazing ? Even though they are merely pixels we get really attached to them.  And they're going to get through hell with us.
- Excellent price. I mean for this amazing thing 20€ is a very good price, and you'd want to replay once to do all the stuff you've missed.
- Superb voice acting, minus 1 or 2 secondary characters.
- Did I told you the music was brillant ? It really sets up the mood. Would buy the soundtrack.
- If you are or know someone who is into art, this game will definitely speak even more for you. And brings back sweet memories.
Cons
- The ending is a bit previsible. But don't worry, it's not a disappointment.
- Sometimes they might talk a bit too much.
- Sometimes lips syncro is out, or bugged. Not frequent, but might happen. Not a serious issue for 99% of the game.
- Technically graphics are also a bit simple, but the lightning and art design are perfect. So it's highly subjective here. For me it didn't bothered me at all. That said facial expressions are sometimes not very vivid, however the voice acting more than make up for that.
- We need more. Seriously. Make season 2.
- Episode 1 is really... calm compared to others. If you tried it and thought "meh this is just high school drama", I still advise you to get the rest of the episodes when they're on sale. The story really picks up toward more epic action later on.
This game is about story, characters, intrigue. If you don't like talking, exploration... you probably won't like it. Still, take it more like an interactive movie than anything.
And of course if you don't care about people, this game won't do much to you. This game is about the connexion the player has with the characters, if you don't care about them the magic won't operate.
Final verdict : must have. For me it's a 9,5/10. This is not even a game, that's freaking art. Get it.
The title can not be more fitting : this is about life. And life is strange ! But ehh this is just a review so I won't get into philosophy here. Enough said that this game will make you think. You won't forget it.
Just to add to my point, they put a support page about suicide on their website.
Now you'll excuse me I have to replay it.

I cannot state how overwhelmingly awesome this game is, especially if you have any love for space and/or challenges.  Even if you never leave the atmosphere of Kerbin, it can still be quite fun.  How fast can you make your little craft go on land before it explodes in a fiery death of awesomeness!?  How fast can you make your aeroplane fly before the mach forces tear it to shreds (capping the speed doesn't count!  You have to tear your plane apart. ;D)  How absolutely insane can you make your ship look, and still be able to fly it around!?  I've seen some pretty haphazard looking ships out there fly, and it's always a treat when you make your own!
Of course, going outside of Kerbin offers an even larger avenue of things for you to do.  Explore the planets and moons, build space stations and small colonies on other planets, preform precarious take offs and landings, dock sensitive station components to even more sensitive space stations, even break the laws and make your own weaponry systems!
I would recommend this game to anyone who loves space simulators, flying simulators, space enthusiasts, and/or those who just love making crazy stuff and seeing if it'll work!  Having the availability for mods only adds to the amount of things (and challenge, as some can add things like life support) you can do!

It's like a cross between NASA and Spore, in only the best ways. You construct a giant tank of explosives, attach holes with gimbal adjustment, and hope your Kerbals (the slightly dopey titular characters) make it to space before the thrust runs out. There's a delightful amount of real-life physics to it, and eventually you'll understand why periapsis is important and why comparing a space vessel to asparagus can cause radical developments in spaceflight.
There's not a tremendous amount of parts yet, but there's definitely enough for weeks of fun a nearly infinite amount of mods to keep it going between updates.
Definitely worth most sale prices, maybe even full price if the cash is burning a hole in your Steam wallet.

Kerbal Space Program is a game for the patient. The learning curve is more like a learning cliff, and you will find yourself frequently on YouTube watching tutorials, and maybe even browsing the occasional NASA publication for guidance. It can easily take half an hour just to dock two objects in orbit, and a day of gameplay to carry out a mission to another plant. That being said, the rewards of investing time in this game are frequent and progressive. Greater amounts of knowledge of skill will yield greater satisfaction, as you first put a satellite into orbit, then travel to the moon, and eventually set foot on other worlds. The learning is fun, but standing on a rocky asteroid with a gas giant overhead (and knowing that you have enough fuel to get back as well) is the real payoff. A must-play if you have an interest in spaceflight.

comes together after episode 2. Max Caulfield matures into the young heroine we want her to be, and the residents of Arcadia Bay prove more complex than they first appeared. Even in the last episode, where other stories get mired in dull exposition,
continues to expand on the same nostalgic themes of friendship, regret, and the loss of naivete. This is great storytelling!
Like its characters,
has flaws. I'll mention one here: Max will encounter badly designed puzzles and stealth segments. These are rare, unimportant to the story, and blessedly brief. Do not be ashamed to Google a solution if stumped.
The ESRB rating is well-deserved, but not for blood or violence.

Kerbal Space Program is a game for the patient. The learning curve is more like a learning cliff, and you will find yourself frequently on YouTube watching tutorials, and maybe even browsing the occasional NASA publication for guidance. It can easily take half an hour just to dock two objects in orbit, and a day of gameplay to carry out a mission to another plant. That being said, the rewards of investing time in this game are frequent and progressive. Greater amounts of knowledge of skill will yield greater satisfaction, as you first put a satellite into orbit, then travel to the moon, and eventually set foot on other worlds. The learning is fun, but standing on a rocky asteroid with a gas giant overhead (and knowing that you have enough fuel to get back as well) is the real payoff. A must-play if you have an interest in spaceflight.

This game is best described as if Telltale, Donnie Darko, and Butterfly Effect had a baby. This isn't a bad thing either, unless you like none of those things.
Otherwise, there is not much else to say, as this game is better experienced then spoiled. Episode wise, the plot starts off fairly slow and rather weak. It is only around Episode 3 that the writing behind the various characters begins to properly shine through, and that delay will likely feel like a bad thing. Up through episode 2 mostly feels as if you are playing a high school drama. If you can get through that though, then you will enjoy what follows from 3 onwards. I will echo the statement many had about a rather out of place (and far too long) piece of filler that was in Episode 5 though.
Overall the game is fairly bug free, at least it was for me. I had some small issues here and there, but nothing that would be deal breaking. The soundtrack isn't all that bad either, while the voice acting works well with the characters being presented. The cast is fairly middle ground, with an odd balance of cliche characters, and some characters you may initially hate written with respectable depth as time goes on. The gameplay is about what one would expect from the interactive movie genre, with some welcome puzzles showing up more towards the end.
TL;DR: If you can stand a start with rather rough and cliche'd writing, you will be in for a fun ride once the feel-coaster gets rolling on it's tracks. I admittedly still need to do a second playthrough, so this perspective is from a person who has only gone through once.

While incomplete, KSP has the makings of a great and addicting game.  I would recommend to anyone who has a love for space exploration and engineering.
What is it?  It's essentially a space program simulator, in which you are empowered to design, build, and fly your own space rockets, air planes, satellites, and space plans.  It features single-body gravity physics, multi-stage rocket design, and a full solar system to explore.  The titular Kerbals are cartoony little creatures that help bring levity to the game.
A word of caution: there is a bit of a learning curve, so I would strongly recommend viewing the game's wiki page and/or viewing some video tutorials on YouTube.  Once the basics are grasped, then you should have no trouble designing and building your space program and reaching for the stars.
A note about the fact that this game is still in development: Obviously there are legitimate concerns with buying a game prior to its completion (is it stable? is it playable? will the devs abandon the game prior to completion?).  In terms of stability, the game is quite stable (in fact, I've had less issues with this game than with several released blockbuster titles).  In terms of gameplay, there is quite a bit to do and play in game (and the content grows with each milestone).  I would say the only lacking parts is a comprehensive set of tutorials for explaining how to play the game (there are a few tutorials but they are far from comprehensive) and mission objectives (currently you make your own goals for your program, which--depending on your disposition--could be either liberating or frustrating).  For reference, in less than 6 months, I have poured over 160 hours into the game and have not yet begun to feel fatigued.  Finally, the game developers are very active (they post a weekly dev blog with a summary of the current development progress and release milestone patches every few months that add numerous features and content.
In short, I would certainly recommend this game for the space lover who's always wanted to build and fly your own space program.

Oh KSP, how I both love and hate you. Have you ever wanted to build a rocket, a rover, satellite, space station, base, jet fighter.... a boat? How about one on or around a different planet? Well you can! It'll take creativity, patience, and most of all complete lack of compassion for one, or many, of your astronauts (kerbals) who become stranded in space, left in orbit, or explode on the launchpad! KSP creates a realistic space program while at the same time allowing players to create unrealistic solutions to their problems. Kerbal stuck on the mun? Build a cannon, send it to the mun with a return capsule, and launch your kerbal back to Kerbin (Earth)!
KSP is a growing game, with significant updates every few months. At the moment, there is both career and sandbox mode. Career mode allows to unlock specific parts by using Science. Science is obtained from performing experiments and various observations throughout the solar system. Future updates plan on expanding on this dynamic. In sandbox mode, all parts are unlocked and the only limit is how many parts your computer can handle being on one vehicle.
One of the greatest parts of playing KSP, is being part of an engaging community. From easy to install mods, that allow you to alter the game to your tastes, to dedicated youtube KSP gurus such as Scott Manley that can teach both beginners and pros alike, KSP has something for everyone.
