I have only played the first chapter!
What a great game. I'm very impressed. I will very probably continue this series when I have a moment.
First I would like to say that I'm very much in favor of this kind of busines model. Around 5 bucks or whatever your regional equivalent is very easy to overcome by most, and a great way to see if this game is for you or not. If it isn't, you have not really lost a lot. And I like shorter games in bite-sizes. The first chapter does a good job of setting everything up and getting you hooked and wanting more.
I do suspect that this game is trying really hard to get you into the game in order to sell you the rest (of course), and it may be that the rest of the game is not as great as this initial chapter, but I still think that if this would be the whole game based on this price, it is very much worth it.
If you are familiar with tell-tales games you will feel right at home, but this game also feels more polished and a little different. It feels little more "interactive". You can explore more and look at everything. Quite a few things have a "background story" that greatly adds to the feel and lore of the game.
The game is also and quite pretty and poetic and it is clear that it is the artistic vision, not just the graphical fidelity that is the achiever of this. Writing, characters, music, faces, details, emotions, locations etc all play really great together in a concise presentation.
Even though I don't relate very much to the late teen-angst and worldview anymore today, I still remember the feelings very well through this game. I feel like I am there experiencing the feelings again, I'm seeing the world again through the eyes of that interesting and often special time even though I did not have "special powers".
As I have not played the whole game and don't know the conclusion, my instincts still tell me that the story is not so much about the factual conclusion but about the actual journey in this time of one's life, particularly the emotional worldview, the "growing up" and "leaving old times" behind.
The writing and voice acting is fantastic, and even though one might think that the language is a little "teenage-y" and trying to be cool, I still would say it is quite witty and very fitting. And it also has a depth I haven't seen in most games. Personally I don't feel the game is out of touch at all, and it is even quite aware of itself, pulling quite a few postmodern jokes here and there.
And even more healthy postmodern ideals are found: I mean, female protagonist, the game feels aimed towards women (which doesn't detract a single bit). The game also seems more about feelings, emotions and reflections. The main game mechanic is about "what ifs?" (and I assume, letting go of it). I think most of us have wondered what would happen if we could change things in the past, so this is easy to relate to nomatter your age.
You can even sit down at various locations and just day-dream away. The game also has a quite a dark despairing mood, which is quite typical of this time in one's life, and also quite post-modern. There is a lot of awareness of victims and oppressors, of environmental destruction, of minorities, of class differences and injustices. Life seems to break apart, old values die, and our imortality is becoming obvious.
This game nails this feeling down more than anything I have seen.

But it is not a walking-simulator, you feel involved and active. I also enjoy that you can approach many situations in different ways which affects the game's outcome. I understand this might not have a huge outcome in the end, but I do feel that it does affect you in the moment as you play, which is as interesting and important as having a fantastic conclusion. It does feel like the choices affect the game more than most telltale games I have tried. Also, I'm not too bothered about games not being massvely different in the end because I understand that in order to have a well-written story that takes everything into consideration you simply can't have 345 different endings due to all the choices one makes. But you CAN do small things in the moment that affect the journey and has a big impact in the here and now. So yes, I think that this game does that better than what I have seen in the past. Your choices do matter, even though the end game might still be going towards a certain ending, which I suspect it does. Again, I don't know.

I have played many kinds of games, and have been doing so for many many years.  This game did two things that very very few others games did.  But if you just want to know if I like it, yes I did, I recommend it, even at full price.  And there is a short TLDR if you want a little more than that.
I felt the emotion of the story.  I cried, I laughed, I stared at the screen for an hour agonizing over the decision I was about to make.  There has only ever been one other game that did that to me.  It was the feeling that got me into gaming in the first place.  And this game made me so happy to be a gamer now.  It truly is a piece of art.
It has more game play than a Tell Tale game tends to.  You actually control your character, even if you are still mostly pushed down a linear path.  Giving just the right amount of control kept it interesting to actually play, while also not diverting from the fact that this is a story driven experience.
The story itself is almost like they made a sequel to "The Butterfly Effect".  I don't want to go too much into it for spoiler reasons.  But I will admit that if I was to objectively critique the story I wouldn't have good or bad things to say.  It definitely had it's interesting moments, and I would even describe some parts of the game as intense.  I think it's because it was believeable.  While the events occuring weren't things that happen all the time, the way the characters go about them is very realistic.  They don't make the right decisions, they let their emotions carry them.  It's very easy to get swept up in that in the moment.
I found myself angry when I should have been, sad when I should have been, worried when I should have been.  I would stop playing, and want to play not because it had a great core gameplay loop, but because I really wanted to know what would happen next.
The second thing this game did, is something I dont' think any game has ever done.  I felt 100% satisfied.  I did not in any way feel compelled to keep playing it because if I didn't, I wasn't getting as much value out of it.  I was physically exhausted after finishing it. I felt like I had gone through it all myself.  I didn't feel the need to go back and play again, and see how I could change things.  (I probaly will eventually, but ultimately make your own decision type games are very easy to predict if you know what you are looking for)  There were decisions I felt horrible about.  Decisions where there are no right choices.  So I can definitely see some re play value in the game.  But I didn't feel like I needed to.  I was content at the story I experienced, and felt like part of that experience wouldn't be there if I did play it again.  It wouldn't have the same emotional impact the second time around, when I'm simply making decisions just to see what happens.
TLDR  One of the only games that I would whole heartedly recommend at full price.  An amazing experience, and that is what it is, an experience.  You will not be taking head shots, at least not with a gun, there is no score, there is no RPG like progression system.  It is a complete experience, that is worth the money to partake in.

It ventures into territory that few other games have, and with a delicate tactfulness, showing the deftness of the writers and the team behind this game. There are so many calm scenes drenched in moodiness, artfully cast atop one of the best soundtracks of any game. And for once, the episodic format truly shines, as it gives a chance to reflect at predefined intervals. And reflect, you will.

This game is still in early development alpha stage and yet I have played it more than any other Steam game. Don't let my "low" play time fool you, I must have over 200 extra hours I played before this was released on Steam.
Despite being an alpha, Kerbal Space Program excels well. I honestly could believe this is a released game if it wasn't for the patchnotes and version number!
The game itself alone can be played in sandbox or career mode. This means you can either start out with everything and just build wacky creations (incredible fun) or gradually build up the R&D to develop the different parts (gives way more pride). The feeling you get from completing the technology tree in career mode is incredible. Planning, building and flying missions makes me feel like a true rocket scientist.
But surely that means you need to know rocket science? Well, not really. I started this game without any real knowledge of how spacecrafts get to orbit, how missions are structured or how different engines vary. I started originally by doing silly beginner mistakes, and slowly realised I could do things more efficiently a different way. I taught myself a lot about how orbital mechanics work, and the game inspired me to research more. I would say it's one of the biggest things that has driven my passion for space along with seeing Saturn through a telecope and watching a rocket launch from Kennedy Space Centre.
So is the game centred around physics and orbital mechanics (bleh!)? Nope! While Kerbal Space Program brings many real life effects into account, and does its best to correctly model the physics acting upon bodies, you don't need to really pay much attention to this. For instance, you could build a huge plane and fly to the North Pole, or create a tank and drive around firing at buildings. This game can be as in depth as you'd like it to be.
But what if science is your thing? Well then you're in luck because Kerbal Space Program allows you to whip out the calculator and start crunching those formulas. Several times I have been to wiki to remember the forumla for Delta V or when to make the most efficient transfer burn to one of the several other planets/moons. Mass, thrust, Isp, velocity and fuel quantities are all given to you by the game allowing you to plug them in to whatever equation you want allowing you to create several page booklets on each mission! I like to keep a notepad and pen closeby to scribble down some quick maths to make sure my missions will go off without a hitch.
Not enough? Both the Forum and Space Port have hundreds of user-created (along with a few by users that have since been hired to work on the game itself) mods to install (via drag and drop, no hard installations!) and further expand the quantity and depth of your missions. Currently my favourite mod I am using makes unmanned vehicles need to be connected to Mission Control to be able to move, throttle, operate hardware and send back infomation. This means I have had to set up a telecommunications satellite array consisting of 4 ground stations, 6 geostationary satellites and 3 satellites orbiting each of the planet Kerbin's (your starting planet, similar to Earth) moons. Setting these up required some serious hard work and crazy amounts of logical thinking I didn't think I was capable of, but with it currently running perfectly I'm over the moon! (Ba dum tss)
Remember; this game is still in Alpha: There are bugs, there are crashes, not everything you'd expect to be in the game is here yet. However, and more specifically recently, I have been seeing a huge drop in bugs. The physics engine could do with some work and aerodynamics leaves much to be desired. However, until this is further looked into by the devs, a marvelous user by the name of Ferram has created a mod to more accurately model aerodynamics. That's the way at the moment with KSP; Much like smartphones and apps, there's a mod for anything you'd want to do from going boating to recreating the Mir Space Station.
I would highly recommend this game even if you aren't a huge fan of science or space because of the wacky, original fun you can have from messing around with this marvelous, beautiful game.

Both the Forum and Space Port have hundreds of user-created (along with a few by users that have since been hired to work on the game itself) mods to install (via drag and drop, no hard installations!) and further expand the quantity and depth of your missions. Currently my favourite mod I am using makes unmanned vehicles need to be connected to Mission Control to be able to move, throttle, operate hardware and send back infomation. This means I have had to set up a telecommunications satellite array consisting of 4 ground stations, 6 geostationary satellites and 3 satellites orbiting each of the planet Kerbin's (your starting planet, similar to Earth) moons. Setting these up required some serious hard work and crazy amounts of logical thinking I didn't think I was capable of, but with it currently running perfectly I'm over the moon! (Ba dum tss)
Remember; this game is still in Alpha: There are bugs, there are crashes, not everything you'd expect to be in the game is here yet. However, and more specifically recently, I have been seeing a huge drop in bugs. The physics engine could do with some work and aerodynamics leaves much to be desired. However, until this is further looked into by the devs, a marvelous user by the name of Ferram has created a mod to more accurately model aerodynamics. That's the way at the moment with KSP; Much like smartphones and apps, there's a mod for anything you'd want to do from going boating to recreating the Mir Space Station.
I would highly recommend this game even if you aren't a huge fan of science or space because of the wacky, original fun you can have from messing around with this marvelous, beautiful game.

short version:
Amazing game, which I would recommend for everyone to play.
tl;dr version:
-Sound:
Amazing 11/10, devs made great OST and chose correct voices for every character (imo). Add to this background sounds (like birds singing behind the window) and you'll get a huge piece of unique atmosphere.
-Graphics:
Sadly, I always sucked at describing graphics. Let's say in my opinion this graphics is pretty much alright, but yeah, since game is built on 'unreal' engine, I don't really see potential issues with it anyway.
-Storyline:
uhhhhhhhhhh... 7/10. No offense, story is awesome, but maybe that's just my personal preferences which make me hating game stories including thousands of alternative realities and so forth. Let me put it this way: I seriously enjoyed first two episodes, ep. 3 and 4 was okay and fifth... Fifth went a bit tough for me.
But yeah, I believe I have to admit story makes few unexpected turns and you may find yourself pretty much surprised.
-Gameplay:
uhhhhhhhhhhhh... Yeah... 6.5/10. Now there's a dilemma: On the one hand I like the way of story being told through questions and answers you can choose during dialogue, BUT(!) there's one thing I stongly dislike, however: most of answers don't mean anything and serve only for visual 'distracting of an eye'. For instance if you replay dialogue and choose reply C instead of B, you'll still have same answer, except first sentence would be different. That somewhat kills the wish to re-play dialogues. Plus, big part of game the only thing you do is choose answers. By the ep.5 you start feeling pretty much bored and annoyed of stuff like that.
-Overall description:
I love this game, I really do... Yeah, despite the fact I gave it 6.5 out of 10 for gameplay and said I disliked idea of several realities, I still keen on thinking everyone should play this game. At least first two episodes. You see, it's nothing like CoD or Battlefield. It's more like interactive movie. If you ever played 'Fahrengheit', 'To The Moon', 'Heavy Rain', or 'The Walking Dead', then you should pretty much know what to expect from this game. It's pretty cinematic and has good storyline. Ingame dialogues only help you to immerse into whole thing which is just awesome.
One more part I should tell you about, as I think, is game's philosophy. Even despite antagonists who would love to kill your character, game still teaches you that there's no absolute&ultimate evil and good. Life has way more gray patterns and even if someone hurts you, it doesn't necessary mean he or she does not suffer from doing so.

This is a tough one to review, as I have very mixed feelings about the game.  On one hand, it is a very good story.  On the other, it is a very poor game.
Story:  A
This is a story of a young woman struggling to rebuild a lost friendship.  The relationships feel real.  It is easy to have feelings about most of the characters in the story.
Soundtrack:  A+.
Lots of acoustic guitar and vocals.  Don't know who it is, but it is good.
Graphics:  B
The style is fine, but the animation can be hit-and-miss.  I witnessed dialogues where one of the character's lips were not moving when they spoke.  The first time it wasn't too bad, but it really through me off in a dramatic scene near the end.
Gameplay:  D
This is where it breaks down to me.  Apart from a few mundane simplistic puzzles, the game is nothing but choosing dialogues.  That is fine if that is what you are expecting.  It works for the first 4 chapters.  Your choices seem to have impact.  Some characters die or are put in danger because of your decisions.  It all breaks down in the 5th chapter, though.  The fifth chapter plays like a two hour long Dear Esther.  Story on a rail and all you have to do is walk forward and gawk at the visuals.  At the end of it all you make one decision--ONE--that determines the outcome of the game.  To make it worse, no matter what decision you make, all your previous decisions are for nothing.
Good story, but ultimately unsatisfying game.  I bought it on sale.  I would recommend it on a 50% off, but not worth the full price.

- Serves 4

INGREDIENTS:

- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and
sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then
drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or
wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the
ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the
chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the
meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around
2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture,
bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat
through. Serve with noodles.

'Thanks for crying!' say the credits for Episode Four of Life is Strange, replacing the traditional 'Thanks for playing!'. It's an apropos message, because I absolutely did cry. A raw, shuddering, and terribly viscous affair. Life is Strange is that kind of game. However, the subversion of 'playing' is germane in another way, which DONTNOD probably didn't intend. Because they clearly prioritized the story, and its emotional impact, over engaging gameplay. The reciprocal message encountered at the beginning of each episode declares the game to be about meaningful choice, and, at the risk of being crass, that's marketing BS.
Truthfully, the decisions you make are mostly window dressing. You will experience nearly the same story as everyone else, with minor nuance. The game only occasionally attempts to leverage its identity as a video game to its advantage, and in most cases, it is clumsy and halfhearted. The majority of puzzles are weak, usually being arbitrary in conception, and insubstantial in implementation. There are few occasions where the decisions made have real, lasting impact, and you are never given agency to act outside the narrative corridor you are forced down. This is not uncommon to certain genres, but that's not what most players felt they were promised. However, it is my belief that if you are prepared to forgive the game its shortcomings, and set your expectations appropriately, you will be rewarded with a rich, incisive, moving, and eminently worthwhile experience. If you're into that kind of thing.
The story revolves around Max Caulfield (Hannah Telle), an 18 year old girl returning to Arcadia Bay, the small Oregon town where she grew up, after having moved to Seattle five years prior. She has returned to enroll in a prestigious private High School, Blackwell, hoping to kickstart her passion for photography into a burgeoning career by enrolling in the program directed by the acclaimed artist Mark Jefferson (Derek Phillips). But Life is Strange (
), and it seems that God, destiny, chance, the Spirit of the Land, or the Flying Spaghetti Monster have decided Max be granted the ability to alter time, as she discovers in a moment of frightening duress.
She soon reunites with her childhood friend, Chloe (Ashly Burch), and together they begin an investigation into the disappearance of Rachel Amber, a local girl who vanished 6 months prior. But as they learn more, and Max experiments with her new powers, things only become more complicated. Who can they trust? What is the meaning of the impossible phenomena that plague the town? Who are the Prescotts, and what are they up to? Why did SquareEnix think it was a good idea to plug a terrible fourteen year old movie, in one of the most ham-fisted attempts of petulant propaganda I've ever seen?
The game is nominally a mystery, but truthfully, it's more science fiction tale, and in my estimation a damned good one. It hearkens back to a lot of the books I read growing up (it's no accident Ray Bradbury is name-dropped repeatedly), and has a lot of similarities to similar explorations of time travel, memory, or both. Touchstones include Donny Darko, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, the Butterfly Effect, and To the Moon. It explores intriguing and provocative ideas in an intelligent way, but with a strident focus on character development.
I initially cringed at Max's character, but by the end of the game, I was deeply invested in her. If there is a benefit to Life is Strange being a video game rather than a TV show or movie, the proof is in Max. She is given personality and life by blending the intimacy of text, the expressiveness of animation, and the empathetic characterization of voice acting, while allowing you to co-habitate the space she does. You can't do all of that in any other medium, and it works well.
Her dialogue is good, but even more effective is the journal, where she writes her personal thoughts on the plot, as it develops. It's a more compelling read than a summarization of events you just experienced has any right to be. The graphic artists are able to give her character mostly through broad body language, as they simply don't have the tools for facial nuance, but it is still an effective presentation, and one that succeeds due to Telle's portrayal of Max's pain, anxiety, joy, and eventual growth. These all come together to give the game the emotional core it needs. Because you can only guide her, Max ends up as one of the stronger protagonists in gaming, simply because she has her own personality, rather than being a blank slate for the player to inhabit. There is little more bittersweet about Life is Strange than that we probably won't ever see any more Max Caulfield.
Playing Lois Lane to your Superman is Ashly Burch's Chloe, who is difficult to countenance for the first two and a half episodes. It's a tall order to present a petulant, irresponsible, and selfish teenager, and expect the average player to identify with her. Incredibly, Burch does accomplish this, persevering until  given the chance to redeem the character with some truly raw and deeply affecting performances. The end result is a character you like not just because of who she is, but of who she clearly will be. You want to watch her to grow, and achieve the great potential she has.
The rest of the cast is comprised mostly of one-note characters, such as the nerds, the jocks, the preppies, the hippies, the conservatives, the punks, etc. etc. A few stand out, like the performance of the drug dealer Frank (Daniel Bonjour), or that of Phillips' Jefferson, but even more important is the town of Arcadia Bay, represented by greasy spoons, woods both dark and adventurous, cold beaches, and comforting domiciles. I have to say that I certainly would not mind more games set in the Pacific Northwest during Fall.
The graphics are not flashy, but they are emotive, focused more on lighting, color, and mood, than verisimilitude. Very much like a movie. The sound design is especially persuasive, featuring an unusually potent implementation of diegetic music. The soundtrack was carefully selected to provide a calm, contemplative ambiance appropriate to the quiet, nostalgic, connotation most people ascribe to the Pacific Northwest. This introspective mood is closely entwined with the introverted Max, as she uses the music to center herself, or to bond with others. This gives a casual feel to the majority of the game, inviting you to set your own pace while you unravel the mysteries of Arcadia Bay.
While it would have been nice for the game to have a few more ideas on how to engage the player with meaningful interaction, I feel the story and humanity imbuing it to more than make up for this, making it easy to recommend, regardless of its flaws. However, before I finish this review, I must briefly discuss the ending. Episode Five was the dealbreaker for a lot of players, so I feel a warning is in order. Remember, your decisions do not truly matter. Do not expect they will. If you are prepared for this, perhaps you will appreciate the story as much as I have. It's not perfect, but I think it's efficacious, giving additional meaning and depth to the entirety of what came before, and completing Max's character arc. I even think it's rather clever for a game that explores the possibility of predestination to have the ending be circumscribed.
Life is Strange is not a uniformly cheerful game. It's full of loss, regret, and darkness. But darkness is only given meaning by light, and so those moments of pain and powerlessness give rise to lessons of acceptance, perseverance, and the importance of memories, good and bad. 'Don't take people for granted' the game tells you. 'Live life to the fullest.' It's a story worthy of the telling, a powerful memory in which we call can share, left to us by the creativity, imagination, emotion, and hard work of those who gifted it to us.

Kerbal Space Program may be one of the best sandboxing games I've ever played.  The premise is simple.  You lead the planet Kerbin's first space program.  You build, design and fly your own spacecraft.  While the campaign mode is being slowly implemented and looks quite promising, the sandbox element of this game is what will keep me playing this game for years.
My first two hours was a glorious trial and error endeavor to put my first Kerbal into orbit.  After that milestone I spent a solid week trying to land and return from the Mun (moon).  I was spending my breaks at work diagramming flight plans and rocket (and spaceplane!) designs in preparation for my second job as the chief pilot/engineer of my own space program.  I was spending late nights watching Scott Manley's Youtube videos for hints on how to achieve the best thrust-to-weight ratios and how to achieve better fuel economy during my ascent.  I learned what dealt-V was and how it related to space travel.  I learned about how apoapsis and periapsis work in relation to orbits and how to adjust them.  I've just learned soooo much from this game.
The community around this game is second to none.  The mods that are available are so well designed and amazing.  There are all sorts of mods that cater to whatever you want to do in this game.  From new theoretical rocket parts, to a ready-built spacestation, to realistic satellite communcation the quality and number of mods is staggering.  On the forums and reddit, the community is extremely supportive and inventive.
The bottom line is this game is engaging and highly educational.  The idea may seem simple, but the way this game allows you to learn by trial-and-error really teaches you how spectacular it is that we have gone from the Wright Brothers to landing rovers on Mars in such a small timeframe.
I recommend this game to anyone who is a self-professed "space geek."  Even in it's Alpha state the game is well worth the Early Access price.  This game is only going to get better and better.

Max may at first seem like a stereotypical female protagonist. The not-quite an introvert, girl-next-door teen who initially gains courage extrinsically (through her powers and BFF, Chloe) and later intrinsically after a couple of epiphanies. Relations between Apollo and Dionysus complicated by circumstance and other archetypal teen characters. The story as told by Mighty Max from her humble pedestal.
Fortunately, this is mostly not the case. This game shines because of the script and character development. The way characters are interwoven keeps the player engaged to the story. Props should be given for showing very well the different facets of an individual and humanity through each character (both major and minor).Characters are revealed to Max by conversing, nosing around and reversing time to unravel additional options. Depending on Max's interactions, she is able to find either redeeming or damning qualities with the people she meets.
Time moves on, but is never the arbiter of events. Even so, Max, with her powers, struggles to make the right decisions. All thanks to Chaos theory. I.e. Jerking off can diverge into infinite possibilities that are vastly different from the initial conditions and impossible to predict accurately (dead kittens or crusty pies?). In this case, screwing up time and space somehow equals colossal tornado. Which really needs no explanation because this game is not a sci-fi.
Story-wise, the build-up to episode 5 is done extremely well. The sneaking sequence somewhat broke my emogasm when all I wanted was to sit back and watch what happens next. In the finale, one of the two choices is pretty anti-climatic. The 2nd choice is where got my kick. Maybe it's because I have the habit of getting hard-ons when it comes to tragic but heroic sacrifice or just tragedy in general. Maximum emo, love it.
Second only to Civilization V in time-wasting capability. Making your first Mun shot is downright addicting.

The rest of the cast is comprised mostly of one-note characters, such as the nerds, the jocks, the preppies, the hippies, the conservatives, the punks, etc. etc. A few stand out, like the performance of the drug dealer Frank (Daniel Bonjour), or that of Phillips' Jefferson, but even more important is the town of Arcadia Bay, represented by greasy spoons, woods both dark and adventurous, cold beaches, and comforting domiciles. I have to say that I certainly would not mind more games set in the Pacific Northwest during Fall.
The graphics are not flashy, but they are emotive, focused more on lighting, color, and mood, than verisimilitude. Very much like a movie. The sound design is especially persuasive, featuring an unusually potent implementation of diegetic music. The soundtrack was carefully selected to provide a calm, contemplative ambiance appropriate to the quiet, nostalgic, connotation most people ascribe to the Pacific Northwest. This introspective mood is closely entwined with the introverted Max, as she uses the music to center herself, or to bond with others. This gives a casual feel to the majority of the game, inviting you to set your own pace while you unravel the mysteries of Arcadia Bay.
While it would have been nice for the game to have a few more ideas on how to engage the player with meaningful interaction, I feel the story and humanity imbuing it to more than make up for this, making it easy to recommend, regardless of its flaws. However, before I finish this review, I must briefly discuss the ending. Episode Five was the dealbreaker for a lot of players, so I feel a warning is in order. Remember, your decisions do not truly matter. Do not expect they will. If you are prepared for this, perhaps you will appreciate the story as much as I have. It's not perfect, but I think it's efficacious, giving additional meaning and depth to the entirety of what came before, and completing Max's character arc. I even think it's rather clever for a game that explores the possibility of predestination to have the ending be circumscribed.
Life is Strange is not a uniformly cheerful game. It's full of loss, regret, and darkness. But darkness is only given meaning by light, and so those moments of pain and powerlessness give rise to lessons of acceptance, perseverance, and the importance of memories, good and bad. 'Don't take people for granted' the game tells you. 'Live life to the fullest.' It's a story worthy of the telling, a powerful memory in which we call can share, left to us by the creativity, imagination, emotion, and hard work of those who gifted it to us.

Have you seen Crash (2004)? It's one of the few movies that provides a multiperspective experience of a situation and the consequences of subtle actions. Nothing is quite what it seems until you've seen through all the perspectives at once. Before judging anyone, it's a must to see things through their perspective first.
Life Is Strange is finally a video game that explores this concept. You start out as a high school student with the ambition of becoming a well-known photographer. Suddenly superpowers happen and you end up solving a murder case as well as saving people all around the place. By winding back time and digging through the personal stuff of people, you learn the context of their thoughts and actions .. and wind up in even more trouble.
It's amazing how immersive a video game can be already without a virtual reality setup. The graphics, animation, sound, music, dialogues, narrative -- it's all so life-like and easy to relate to. In fact, it's so easy to relate to, that it can change your personality and the way you see life. Luckily the game is divided into episodes, which makes it easier to take a break and return to the "real life" every now and then. I managed to finish the game without losing my life, even though I'm not sure I even had one.
All in all, this game is very life-like, deep in philosophy, deep in psychology, features good humor and even packs spiritual lessons. Almost everything in the game is scenic and photogenic, which complements the ambition of the main character extremely well. Way too many in-game screenshots =P. The gameplay is rather simple, just WASD and point & click. However, it would be neat if the PC port allowed for typing lock number combinations instead of clicking those spinboxes (which got pretty annoying). Even though I'm really picky about games, Life Is Strange has definitely earned the first place in my favourites (now there are two). That's how awesome Life is Strange is :)

Well, this game was a very interesting one among the "choices matter" type games that are out there.  This just covers a new genre and I wouldn't be surprised if this type of game covered everything.  Going to try and sum it up briefly.
Game starts out with you expecting high school drama seen from the eyes of a girl.  It then deals with some taboo subjects and then gradually turns into high school detective game.  You technically solve the case and then it goes from 0-100 in the feels train and wtf is happening mode.  Then the game ends with a binary choice, almost as bad as Mass Effect's ending.
The plot isn't too bad and your choices kind of matter for the most part during episodes 1-4.  The last episode just throws it all away pretty much.  If you can get over the mediocre voice acting and terrible references, this is a decent game.

This is slowly turning into the best game I have ever played.  It has certainly been the most educational by far.  I strongly recommend (as of ver 0.23) the installation of the MechJeb add-on and that the game be played in career mode.  You will start out with minimal computer (MechJeb) guidance support, and will essentially be trying to make orbit by joystick.  But as your career progresses you unlock greater computer control of the craft, so making your 100th orbit is just routine and you don't have to do it by hand anymore and can spend your focus on things like figuring out how to get to the moons of Jool and back safely.
In the process I have learned a very deep understanding of basic orbital mechanics, something I already thought I understood but really only could do the math.  The gut understanding is much different than what I thought it was before I spent hours happily flinging kermen into space.  I haven't even begun to mess with aircraft construction, but I expect that will be equally eye-opening in the realm of aerodynamics
It's still under development, of course, so there's no telling what it will eventually become.  But right now this game is simply phenomenal.

I really, really don't write reviews usually. This will be in fact my first review ever, I think. But if a game deserves it, then this one.
Firstly, you should know that this game is almost purely story-driven. Therefore, gameplay is mostly easy. You can't really do much wrong, and if you do anyway, your ability to manipulate time makes it so you can easily correct your decisions after you thought them through carefully. However, there are also parts in the game where you have to get a little bit creative to solve a puzzle or conflict as you desire.
But let's come to the part about the game that is, as mentioned before, is the most important: The Story. You are playing as 18-year old Maxine Caulfield, who is returning to her old hometown Arcadia Bay, so she can attend a photography class after 5 years of living in Seattle. After seeing a girl get shot in the bathroom, she discovers her ability to rewind time. From this point on she is trying to find out the truth about a horrible vision she had and other mysterious things that happen in Arcadia Bay and attempts to turn things to the better.
The characters that you will meet are all unique in their traits, and you will once again find out that often the world is not painted only in black and white. Many of them will grow dear on you soon.
This all is set in a wonderfully designed environment, with great lighting and a marvelous soundtrack, altogether creating a beautifully contemplative and dense atmosphere.
Of course this game is not perfect. I have to admit that the slightly painting-like graphic-style might not be everybody's taste and texture do sometimes look really blurred. Also in some rare cases characters act elusively or consequences seem inexplicable.
But how does this all work together as a game? Long story short: For me, it did absolutely great.
I can honestly say that I have never in my life played a game that touched me so deeply and caused so strong emotions in me, from sadness over anger to delightful joy, while at the same time it made me see what really counts in life. This game accomplishes that almost everything you did seems to make sense somehow, associating moments from events early and late in the story.
After each episode, I just sat there and stared at the credits. Not only because I wanted to see what people worked on this masterpiece, but mainly because I needed a few moments to reflect on everything that I just experienced.
For me, this is and probably will stay the by far best adventure and one of the best games I ever played. Thank you, Dontnod Entertainment, for this masterpiece.

- Short -
Kerbal Space Program is a masterpiece of a space agency simulator. It is the perfect combonation of exploration, strategy, building, and open world all wrapped into a neat package. If you ever dreamed of being Elon Musk managing and creating your own space agency, this is it.
- Long -
KSP ranks in my top 5 favorite games of all time. In career mode you take the part as a manager of a space agency, your only directives are placed forth by missions of your own choosing, or you can explore the stars without any mission or clear objective (though you will need funds, which accepting missions helps out with). This game is challenging. My first time playing it, it took me days (real life) to figure out how to land on the moon, or even get there, years of playing after.. I am constructing space stations above the equivalent of mars (Duna), and have a well established tourist route among the planets.
This game requires not just thought or strategy, but a fundamental understanding of real life basics of physics and space flight. Each craft you make must be carefully thought out, planned, and executed in order for your mission or goals to achieve. It is brilliant, and not for idiots (pointing at you reviewers who call this game "too hard").
While I don't typically incorporate addons or mods with a review, some of the modders are actually people who previously worked on the game. I -strongly- recommend adding the UMBRA space industry mods for added realism (food and habitat requirements) and colony development, along with Mechjeb (automated spacial orientation and guidance). The modding community is excellent for this game, just about any addon or feature that isnt present in the base game can be found in the modding community.
Pros & Cons
Pros -
Infinite replayability - I have come back over and over to this game for years, I paid $25? for this game, and that has equalled out to less than $0.02 per hour enjoyed. Making it one of the best valued games I own.
True open world - No borders,  no forced missions. no limitations.
Enormous modding community - Want a feature? Chances are it's been made, from life support, to radio chatter.
Realistic Physics - This game is so accurate to physics that NASA has used it to test basic theories.
Cons -
Physic bugs - While rare (and with most physics games) some absurdly large builds will tend to flop around like jello, in a totally unrealistic way. This however can be counter-acted with struts.
Final
If you are even considering buying this game, and my review sounds tempting, you would be a fool not to at least try it. As someone who is very critical of games (my review history can attest to that), I had a hard time finding any flaw in this game. The devs made a true masterpiece, and this belongs in the library of any space enthusiest.

That's insane right!? WRONG. THAT IS NOT INSANE. THAT IS REALITY, with Kerbal Space Program. Build whatever you want. Nobody's gonna judge you. Who would have though that building your own spacecraft, strapping them to rockets, and then using the resulting contraption to launch little green men (sorry, Kerbals) into outerspace, could be so much fun? With simulated physics (not perfect to real world physics); a wide variety of manufacturing components; and a vast galaxy, with several planets, and countless moons to explore; this game provides hours upon hours of entertainment. This game is still in slow development, and constantly keeps improving with bug fixes and new content, but is still very highly recommended by me, to those who enjoy sandbox type games.

This game looks very damn good. The graphics appear drawn, and often a mere hint results in a strikingly lifelike and realistic picture. It is a joy to watch.
Having said that, faces, and especially eyes can be a bit lacking at times, with eyes appearing milky or looking very odd.
I had some difficulty relating to the main character (an 18 year old rather girly student), but this might be because my teen years are long past me, and I am not American and a male. I found her obviously cute, but sometimes a bit too obvious, and not always believable from my perspective. She also feels a bit meek at times, probably to contrast her with her friend.
The story is good and gripping but one thing that annoyed me was the enormous amount of things you could interect with, 70% of which hardly contributed to the story and was there just for flavor. It gave a slightly *grindy* feeling at times when I entered a new area and I had to click on 20 things and talk to five people, of which only one thing was needed to progress. Of course if a game would only contain the bare essential things to interact with it would also be boring, but maybe some colour hint to differ things of interest from essentials for the storyline would help in this respect.
I read some reviews and saw that people flipped out over part 5, and the way the ending is constructed. I feared the worst and it actually wasn't so bad. It is true that despite all the decisions leading up to the final event stop to matter, but since a lot of decisions didn't matter very much in the first place and you were often lineairy guided towards one course of action, this didn't strike me as very odd.
There is no happy end. Maybe that pisses people off. You get confronted by a heartbreaking ethical choice, with no overall happy option. It is some sort of utilistic ethical dilemma: Do I sacrifice what I love for the greater good? And I have to agree that the necessity of this harsh choice is not clear at all. It comes from nowhere. It does not evolve logically from the rest of the story, so you get a feeling that the makers forced some ultra dramatic moment upon you out of the blue.
And example of a believable true ethical dilemma would be that your best friend had a very deadly virus and you have to choose to kill her to prevent the risk of spreading, or choose for her and accept that risk. Here it is completely obscured why you have to sacrifice your friend to save the city. Hardly any satisfying logic is presented (your use of *powers* caused a massive hurricane). But this did not annoy me as much as some other people.
The story and atmosphere strongly reminds of Twin Peaks, and The Secret History of Donna Tartt. If you are cynical you can say it copies elements, if you are good willing you can say it builds on in the same direction.
All in all a gorgeous looking good solid game, with a female character that can be cute and realistic depending on your outlook and taste. It is smooth, the story is compelling, and I found it fully worth the money.

Life Is Strange is an episodic graphic adventure video game developed by Dontnod Entertainment and published by Square Enix. It consists of five episodes released periodically throughout 2015.
The game's plot focuses on Maxine Caulfield, a photography student who discovers that she has the ability to rewind time at any moment. The story for the most part is extremely engaging and interesting. It starts off strong, and continues to have a very strong emotional narrative throughout most of it. Characters you meet in the game feel believable and voice acted very well, which really adds much into the story.
Graphically, I liked how the characters are designed. They look attractive, act and animate nicely. The main character isn't overly sexualized and she has realistic proportions. (Well as realistic as an 18 year old scrawny teenage girl would look like anyway). Environment art looks very nice, and the whole game makes you feel like you're in a surreal painting. Sound design is superb, with brilliant voice-acting accentuated with a nice grungy soundtrack.
The game itself is very simple to play and progresses in a very linear manner not unlike a Telltale Graphic Adventure. The stand-out mechanic is the method in which you rewind time, which is borrowed from "Remember Me", an earlier game that was also designed by Dontnod Entertainment. It was the most interesting mechanic in that game that wasn't used much, and I'm glad that it was used to a much greater and impactful effect here. You can use it to solve puzzles, or interestingly to go back in time to select a different choice after you've seen the one you've selected.
That said, the weakest part of the game, in my opinion is the final episode. Maybe because the game tried too hard to tie up all its loose ends, certain characters acted completely out-of-character compared to how they were in the earlier episodes and it all feels very phoned-in. Even the puzzle in the last episode felt lazy compared to some of the earlier well-thought and designed puzzles in the earlier episodes.
Don't get me wrong, the ending isn't terrible, but I wished it was more impactful and well thought out instead of the one we got. Still, the weak ending doesn't take away the brilliance of the earlier story that was so well crafted in the earlier episodes.
Overall Rating: 8 / 10
A very enjoyable graphic adventure that starts off very strong, continues to power through with intriguing sub-plots and well-thought out puzzles and character designs but unfortunately fizzled off at the very end. It is still worth the price of entry, and fans of graphic adventures or anyone who enjoys a good story should definitely pick it up.

I am really looking forward to what we get in the future from the Life Is Strange developers.
In Life Is Strange you play as a girl named Max who is back in her home town attending the "prestigious" Blackwell Academy. She is a photographer trying to get a head start in her career and through a strange turn of events she not only meets up with her childhood best friend she has not spoken to in years, but also gains the ability to travel backwards through time.  The story of Life Is Strange starts slowly, but sure does pick up pace quick a few episodes in, as the consequences of the choices you make start piling up towards the conclusion it will leave you second guessing yourself every step of the way.
I highly recommend Life Is Strange to anyone who is a fan of adventure games, sometimes it pays to remember it really is the journey that matters.

Fantastic game. Elegantly quenches a gamer's thirst for some delicious science, while allowing the demon within us to unleash wave after wave of fury onto poor, green little kerbals as ship after ship explodes in ever-hilarious fashions. This game can be played in a myriad of ways, but many people stick to one of the following: Either casually strapping rockets together and seeing what does or doesn't explode, and giggling intensely at the ensuing chaos, or carefully planning out missions, charting amounts of delta-v, and creating expeditions so fantastic that the player feels they should be talked about in a textbook or documentary somewhere but that no one else seems to care about. The habits of most, though, fall somewhere in between. Therein lies the beauty of this title; it can easily be played in a relaxed manner or as something to pour hours and gigawatts of brainpower into. Very few videogames provide such leeway on the type of gameplay they provide, and therefore Kerbal Space Program should be thought of as neither a science game nor a casual one, but as both: as a game whose content, fanbase, and demographic ranges as far as the impossibly distant stars gazed upon by observers in the Kerbol System.

At the moment Unity engine can freeze even high end PCs, but with the current pace of devs, KSP is taking great shape with every update. What you achieve on KSP is fuelled by your imagination, so if you're looking for a linear game with missions and a set storyline, this isn't for you.
In addition to vanilla experience, the KSP community has great deal of skilled modders who have created a plethora of mods to complement the game, easily installed thanks to an official mod-sharing website. For a alpha state game theres plenty to do and great deal to achieve.

I was a bit put off by the first chapter - at first I thought the dialogue seemed like traditional badly translated from Japanese or something, and the gameplay seemed extremely slow, but both improved within the first episode, and the middle few episodes were excellent.  Like some others, I found the ending a little disappointing, as seems quite common in story and character driven games (I'm looking at you Mass Effect 3)(come to think of it, that kinda makes it more impressive how perfect the ending of The Last of Us was), but not enough to put me off recommending the whole experience.
Just bear in mind the kind of game this is, and whether it's the kind you like.  The experience is about the story and characters, and your interaction takes the form of decision making.  There's no skill involved (ie no quick reactions and precision movement required) which I know pits some people off and makes certain people claim "that's not a game".  If you're one of those people, I think you already know this isn't the game for you,
TL:DR I loved it.

This is probably one of THE best indie games out since Minecraft. It is innovative and highly addictive to play once you get going. It is also by far one of my most favorite games to play because of its simple premise: Attempt to build and fly rockets into space and land on other planets.
Despite the label of "Early Access" Kerbal Space Program is by far one of the most "complete" and able games you can get as an Early Access choice.
If you like games that force you to think in order to accomplish a goal, then this is for you. That the game not so much "forces" you to utilize real world aeronautical effects and maneuvers to properly get your ships where you want them to go speaks volumes to the quality that goes into the development of KSP from the guys at Squad. If you are adventurous, the dozens of astoundingly popular and very high quality mods available greatly expand the capabilities of what can be done in KSP in a realistic approach to current and future space flight.
The Career mode allows people to easily approach the game from a beginner's standpoint and slowly gain experience launching into orbit as you gather science in order to further develop new and improved rocket parts on the tech tree.
If you just want to play around and watch the explosions of rockets in the pad or test out designs, then the Sandbox works great.

Wow.  So, I had heard plenty of people talking about KSP for a while now.  I thought it sounded cool, but I had no idea.  Don't get me wrong, this game is not for everyone, and I hesitate to even call it a game.  This is a space simulator that is simple enough to where you aren't designing every aspect of your craft, landers, satellites, etc, but the basic aerospace and orbital physics are the focus.  It's so much fun though.  I've learned a ton, and had a blast so far.  Just had my first successful orbit of the moon, and things like breaking the atmosphere, your first orbit, you're first flyby of the moon, first orbit, etc are all amazing feelings of accomplishment.  I reccomend reading as little as possible, don't just copy and paste someone's design, it's much more rewarding if you don't.  Of course, I'm sure you'll have to look up some basics of spaceflight, and learn al the terminology like retrograde, aphopaphis, etc.
Anyhow, this game is amazing, still a work in progress, and really I see this game as the next big cult hit, like Minecraft.  It won't ever appeal to as wide of an audience, because it does require some brainpower, but the end result is extremely rewarding.  I can't reccomend this game enough.

This game is my pick for 2015 GOTY.
Story: 9.9/10
The writing is fantastic, particularly in the character development. The characters, particularly the protagonist Max Caughfield, are believable and do not embody stereotypes like many story based games.  The plot is thrilling and takes many a turn that if you are invested enough in the story may catch you off guard. There is some dispute as to if the ending lives up to the rest of the story, but regardless of your opinion on the ending, the story is incredible.
Art Style: 10/10
This game has excellent asthetics, but if you're looking for a game with "real life" graphics you may want to look elsewhere. This game is really an excellent example of how a game without flashy graphics can immerse you in this artists world.
Voice Acting: 9/10
The voice acting in this is stellar, there are a few times where the editing was a little sloppy, but hey who can blame them when you have a list of six different dialogue options.
Replayeble?
Uh, yeah! There are so many different choices to make that effect the outcome of the entire story.
Bugs:
There were a few immersion breaking bugs, but they hurt my enjoyment only in one scene that wasn't particularly important to my story any how.
Overall, this game is pretty great and certainly worth every penny I spent on it.

This game has a very steep learning curve but once you master it, the experience is quite rewarding. The mechanism behind this game is not exactly rocket science, but it's probably the closest thing. I'm using this game to teach some science concepts to grade 7-12 students, concepts like gravity and orbital mechanics. I personally recommed getting this for your kid (this game is kid-friendly), it will put them in a place where they have to be creative problem solver.
If you are somehow bored with the vanilla game, there are tons of mods for you to use. They add value to the game experience. Some mods tweaks the planets to be more realistic, some others add parts that you can use to build your rocket. Find it to easy? Install the realism mod (google it).
All in all, it's a great game. It has A LOT of potential (and do note that this game is still in development stage). I bought another copy of the game from the website itself after spending 90+ hours on this game on Steam. The non-Steam version is portable so I can play it in the office (I work as a science educator).

For example, on TTT, people will kill absolutely everyone whether they are an innocent or a traitor and then leave straight afterwards to avoid punishment and move on to the next server. Keeping in mind that this is still in Early Access, I'm extremely impressed with this title. It merges (relatively) realistic space simulation with a freeform ship designer that doesn’t take a rocket scientist to figure out.  I say relatively only because the game is set within a goofy universe full of creatures which remind me of the Minions from
.  But that’s the real beauty of this game: it can take itself seriously, yet when your rocket goes maverick and crashes into Kerbin, you don’t always feel like raging...you just chuckle and remember the look on Jebediah’s face as he realized his eminent demise.  At this point there’s no multiplayer, which is a little disappointing, but I know this is planned for the future, and look forward to revising this review once that’s fully developed.  Barring that, though, I applaud what the folks at Squad are trying to accomplish here, and wish them all the best.

I'm giving this a "Yes", but only as far as buying Episode 1 at first. I certainly like it and own the whole season, but I can definitely see where many would not, even if they are otherwise fans of a story-rich adventure games. It is not a game for everyone, because it is not a game that even tries to be for everyone; and that is what makes it so good for those of us that like it.
I also cannot really talk too much about the game itself, because even talking about the gameplay mechanics will include story spoilers. Let's just say that it starts out as a form of adventure game that flirts with being a visual novel... But soon enough, you will discover that there's more to this game than that. Quite a bit more, in fact.
Of the things I can discuss, is that I think the music is absolutely fitting for the game. Jonathan Morali wrote the original score, and the band Syd Matters (which Morali is a member of) has a few tunes in the game that might as well have been written for the game. And the way these tunes are presented makes them part of the game, which just helps the immersion.
Also, choices. The game has real choices. And the good thing here is that what you don't actually know what's the good choice, for two reasons: One, many of the choices are in themselves not very clear, and you're not sure you're doing the right thing. And secondly, what you thought was a good choice in episode 1 may well come back to bite you in a later episode. So all you can do is try and decide what you think is right to do there and then.
The high school setting contains characters that are, both fortunately and unfortunately, rather believable. I say fortunately because it really makes the gut punch moments (and hoo boy are there some of those) all the stronger. Plus, it actually contains topics that actually happens in high school, including genuine swearing, honest discussions about sex and drugs that goes beyond "Don't do it!". For those of you who thinks that all of this is a good thing, I heartily recommend this game.
But it can also be unfortunate, because it reminds me that there are people out there behaving like that; and thinking about that is not fun. And for those of you who had a crappy high school experience, and who play video games to escape those memories... I do not think you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are usually fitting well for the game's setting. However, there are a few immersion-ripping animations happening every now and then; which is a shame.
What more is there to say? I've given warnings where I can, and if you still think this might be an interesting experience for you, then give it a shot. Get episode 1 if you're still wary; and if you like it, get the rest! And if you don't, then you'll only have spent a few dollars. It's a small risk for a potentially pretty big reward.

This is a difficult review to write, because I loved 4/5ths of the game.  However, the final chapter, and in particular the choice at the end of the game, were so bad that I have to recommend that people avoid this game.
Without going into spoilers, the game tells you many times that "this is story driven game and your choices will have an affect on the [story]"  What's incredibly frusting about the ending is that it comes down to a single binary choice where the ending is completely contingent on what you choose that one time.  None of the other choices or actions that you took in the 4.9 chapters leading up to the ending have any effect on the ending, and both options will completely invalidate a section of the choices, actions, and events that you took throughout the game.
There are other flaws (the main "villian"  in the story doesn't make a lot of sense and there was a better person available for the role), but this is what takes a game I would have recommended wholeheartedly and forces me to not recommend it.
It's really a shame, because this game was straight up amazing prior to the last chapter, and I'll aways remember Max Caulfield, but the ending was so upsetting that it tarnished the rest of the experience.

I have seen a great amount of games trying to pull off a space simulator game, to which KSP does quite well. The game gives you the basics, no background story, and no economy, and no outside force telling you what to do or nagging you that someone died (like a government or weeping families), which means no ramifications when your ship can, and will, mess up. The career mode added in the idea that you had more things to do than to put gravestones on backorder. it added in Science, which gave players progression with their rockets, starting you off with a small rocket instead of the "Death Rocket 9001"
In conclusion. Great Game. Good luck keeping Jebediah Kerman alive, and dont burn the space center down.

Here are my short remarks about this game.
Positive:
- The story catches you and makes you live the life of the protagonist, if you let it. I totally enjoyed the emotions it brought to me, I even cried a little.
- Nice, cute soundtrack.
Negative:
- The plot of going back in time to fix something is overused, nothing special here.
- Characters are also very stereotypical.
- Lips are awfully animated.
- The choices you make don't impact the ending at all.

Neutral moments:
- It's more an interactive movie than a game.
- The game is relaxing and chilling at the beginning, but tension grows as you progress.
- The main character is overly sweet.
- Textures and models lack in detail, but still look stylish.
Conclusion:
I'd make this review neutral, if I could. Life is Strange isn't that good, but it's still enjoyable. I feel like going through the game again later, making different choices to see what will actually change with them.

Let me start off by saying, this isn't so much a game as it is a life experience.  I've played moral decision making games before, but none where it so closely mimics real life in the sense that aside from some supernatural elements, it feels very close to reality.  That being said, if you're someone who really values story and character development, I highly recommend this game for you.  The world is very beautiful and draws you right in.  It also inspires you to want to explore all the objects and people you can interact with.  From playing this game, I discovered a lot about myself, what I value in life, and the kind of choices I would make under duress.  That kind of self-discovery is hard to find in entertainment and even harder to find in a game.  Granted, what you discover about yourself may make you feel uncomfortable at times, it's still an experience I would recommend to everyone.  Whether you're a casual gamer or a heavy gamer, I urge you to try this game and see what you learn about yourself.

This is a difficult review to write, because I loved 4/5ths of the game.  However, the final chapter, and in particular the choice at the end of the game, were so bad that I have to recommend that people avoid this game.
Without going into spoilers, the game tells you many times that "this is story driven game and your choices will have an affect on the [story]"  What's incredibly frusting about the ending is that it comes down to a single binary choice where the ending is completely contingent on what you choose that one time.  None of the other choices or actions that you took in the 4.9 chapters leading up to the ending have any effect on the ending, and both options will completely invalidate a section of the choices, actions, and events that you took throughout the game.
There are other flaws (the main "villian"  in the story doesn't make a lot of sense and there was a better person available for the role), but this is what takes a game I would have recommended wholeheartedly and forces me to not recommend it.
It's really a shame, because this game was straight up amazing prior to the last chapter, and I'll aways remember Max Caulfield, but the ending was so upsetting that it tarnished the rest of the experience.

Here are my short remarks about this game.
Positive:
- The story catches you and makes you live the life of the protagonist, if you let it. I totally enjoyed the emotions it brought to me, I even cried a little.
- Nice, cute soundtrack.
Negative:
- The plot of going back in time to fix something is overused, nothing special here.
- Characters are also very stereotypical.
- Lips are awfully animated.
- The choices you make don't impact the ending at all.

Neutral moments:
- It's more an interactive movie than a game.
- The game is relaxing and chilling at the beginning, but tension grows as you progress.
- The main character is overly sweet.
- Textures and models lack in detail, but still look stylish.
Conclusion:
I'd make this review neutral, if I could. Life is Strange isn't that good, but it's still enjoyable. I feel like going through the game again later, making different choices to see what will actually change with them.

From playing this game, I discovered a lot about myself, what I value in life, and the kind of choices I would make under duress.  That kind of self-discovery is hard to find in entertainment and even harder to find in a game.  Granted, what you discover about yourself may make you feel uncomfortable at times, it's still an experience I would recommend to everyone.  Whether you're a casual gamer or a heavy gamer, I urge you to try this game and see what you learn about yourself.

is a game about choices and their consequences.
The twist here is that you are able to know the immediate consequence before sticking with a choice. This is done thanks to the main character's ability to rewind time, which implementation is a real technical achievement.
,
features really nice design direction. One of the first things to notice is the impressionist style of the textures as well as subtle post processing effects that add depth to the visual scenario. Lightning is another element nicely used to impact the perception and tone of the moment.
Unfortunately, other noticeable features include the stiff facial animations and horrendous lip syncing. The latter took quite a while for me to finally ignore meanwhile being really distracting.
relays heavily on narrative, in which voice-acting plays a huge role. Max comments about a great deal of people, events, and objects -all of which are voiced. Dialogues during cut-scenes are convincing and emotional.
This game features one of the most beautiful licensed
. It's really something to buy and carry around, specially when travelling. Music is another great component of the whole picture, and even some scenes seem to have been crafted around the songs. It really is amazing.
In regards to
there is not much to say.
Camera placement is a bit annoying at times, and there is some stuttering when you move in constricted places.
Developers have put a lot of attention to detail, same attention and dedication that seems to be thrown in by writers for character design and progression. And it's through the aforementioned narrative that you get to know features and distinctions about them if you are willing to invest the time. For instance, there are places where Max can sit and just contemplate about life and the circumstances, and you are given this in a cinematic scene with voiced thoughts and peaceful music.
is beautifully crafted, touching serious themes as family violence, cyber bullying, and suicide. It can get quite dark.

In my opinion, however, some of the parts just felt like fillers. Puzzles -if they can be called that- like the ones with the bottles add totally nothing to the development of the story. I understand the objective was to force the player to explore the junkyard but in the end it just came as a pointless chore. And there are some more moments like that.
The real
was another issue for me. There is a whole arch of the story that could be considered pointless, so the choices trough that part have no meaningful impact despite how hard and emotive those are.
So,
is a nice slow-paced game (with some technical noticeable issues) which I ultimately enjoyed.
It also has
. Achievements being easy to get for the most part and well integrated with game-play. They have also added
in the form of 9 short videos which can be watched from in-game or via streaming.
Do I recommend it? That's a whole dilema.

When I was a kid, I wanted to be an astronaut.  I know that isn't terribly unusual.  However, while my friends grew up and became lawyers and businessmen, I never really managed to drop that desire.  Even now, the one thing that I want more than anything is to see Earth from orbit.
Kerbal Space Program helps to scratch at that itch in the most satisfying way.  The premise of the game is simple: build rockets and launch them.  You can play the new-ish career mode to develop your space agency from the ground up, or you can play in a delightful sandbox that opens up the entire solar system as your plaything.
The play mechanic of build/launch/explore/recover (hopefully) is well implemented.  Possibilities for construction range from landers and rovers to giant rockets and space stations.  While deceptively simple in concept, the nuances of construction offer a respectable challenge on their own.  Flying is simple, though the physics in KSP can lead to some uniquely impossible machines, such as a flying wing with no engine.
The game is challenging (and rightly so), but filled with so much content that it's possible to enjoy simply flying around Kerbin.  The underlying humor of the game also alleviates some of the sting of failure.
I can't come up with any reason not to buy this game.  I honestly don't know why you haven't already purchased it.

TL;DR Liked the game a lot, but not the devs or their support. Insulted me for helping them with THEIR job (actually doing their job since they have no idea how to troubleshoot, it would seem) and don't care to fix or even check into serious bugs.
First, I'll say I really liked the game, but I won't be buying more from them or Square - I don't support companies that treat their customers badly. The devs and especially their "tech support"/"customer service" are worthless. I was insulted by them for pointing out a gamebreaking bug on some systems. I wasn't the first to notice it, but I did the most to troubleshoot it. Another person who didn't even have the bug made a workaround (more than the devs would do), even though he didn't have the bug.
Their first thought about it came from someone who went to their site for support (they sure weren't/aren't "supporting" here) and came back with a canned response saying that it was probably a corrupt savegame. I pointed out that this was unlikely because it probably wouldn't cause this sort of bug (not being able to walk during a scene near the end of the 5th episode, though Max still animated, brushed her face with her hand, etc). A corrupt save would more likely mess up your choices, not let you play that save at all, delete the save, etc, based on all the fun a certain other company created with their problems with savegames. I moved, then deleted my savegame, turned off cloudsave, reinstalled and started a new game with a completely fresh save folder. I jumped to ep 5, as close to the problem point as I could, letting the game make previous choices, and still had the same bug, proving they were wrong.
Then I began more troubleshooting, trying to pin down the cause. After some time of that, a "dev" (tech support/customer service) *finally* got involved and asked everyone to post their savegames somewhere like dropbox so they could take a look at them, lol. I went along with it, being polite, but explaining that corrupt saves weren't the problem. When they got back to us, they said it wasn't a bug and that our systems weren't good enough to run that scene, which they claimed was the most hardware intensive scene in the game. That made no sense because very little was happening in that scene and, in any case, should only slow down the scene (there was no slowdown, just unable to walk anywhere). They ignored me.
They insisted there was no bug and insulted me even though my reasoning, explanations and logic were sound. I eventually proved it to them, but as far as I know, they haven't even looked into the bug (too few complaints and/or systems they don't support - sort of understandable, but...). As anyone who knows anything about programming knows, a bug will be a bug. What I mean is even if they don't think enough people have experienced this bug to lose them many sales, it being a bug, they need to at least look into it because bugs are unpredictable by their very nature and they don't know what else it might affect. Also, insulting customers for ANY reason is bad business, so they won't get mine anymore.

The game's simulation of orbital mechanics is accurate enough that an educational version is in the works, although sadly, you can only be affected by one body's gravitational field at a time.

Starts off interesting but pretty cliche and tacky, based around typical high school ♥♥♥♥♥y drama.  Quickly evolves into an incredibly dark, sad and riveting tale of a town full of mystery.
Choose your own adventure style games often cop a lot of criticism for choices not making much of a difference in the grand scope of the game, which is what the appeal of the genre is (looking at you Game of Thrones TellTale).  While there aren't so many alternate endings based on your choices, the game does a fantastic job of developing relationships with every character based on your choices.  While your ultimate goal may follow the same path, the friendships and enemies you make along the way are completely determined by your actions, which is nice.
The introduction of a 'rewind time' mechanic is a great idea and helps this character/relationship development.  With it, you can really look into the complexity of each character, and both their good and bad side.  Life is Strange isn't black and white, depending on your actions, characters can be very likable or absolutely disgusting.
Have a box of tissues ready when you play to, sad af.

'Life is Strange' is one of the best and most memorable (choose-your-own-) adventure games I've played to date. It has an imaginative and engaging story, well-written dialogues, and good looking graphics. The game's main selling feature is your character's ability to rewind time so that she can affect change in the people she interacts with and in her environment. Implementing time travel in games (let alone in movies) can be challenging, but the developers did a really fine job here. This feature really opens up possibilities in storytelling, character development, and puzzle design.
Although the game was originally released bimonthly in episodic format, it is best experienced if you play it without such gap between episodes. Each episode is tonally different, and while it offers variety in gameplay, it can make the overall gaming experience uneven and jarring when done in parts. Playing through the episodes in as few sittings as possible allows you to appreciate the richness of the game's major and minor story arcs.
How much you'll enjoy 'Life is Strange' greatly falls on how well you can live with the decisions make. Sure, if you believe you've made a bad decision, you can rewind time up to a certain point to change the outcome. However, the impact of your decision may not be apparent until later episodes; so instant gratification may actually result in unsatisfactory outcome down the road. The fact that you are given pretty much all the time in the world to make a decision increases your burden, but also makes each outcome more impactful.
Aside from gameplay and design, I also recommend 'Life is Strange' because it addresses social issues of bullying and peer pressure, and the realities of life and death, as well as touches upon philosophical ideas of being or the present, change, karma and destiny. It's so refreshing to see a video game tackle these topics in a serious and mature manner without sacrificing entertainment. This is one of the games to show people how video games are not just for kids, but can be a powerful medium to bring awareness to different social issues and ideas to the masses.
