Starts off interesting but pretty cliche and tacky, based around typical high school ♥♥♥♥♥y drama.  Quickly evolves into an incredibly dark, sad and riveting tale of a town full of mystery.
Choose your own adventure style games often cop a lot of criticism for choices not making much of a difference in the grand scope of the game, which is what the appeal of the genre is (looking at you Game of Thrones TellTale).  While there aren't so many alternate endings based on your choices, the game does a fantastic job of developing relationships with every character based on your choices.  While your ultimate goal may follow the same path, the friendships and enemies you make along the way are completely determined by your actions, which is nice.
The introduction of a 'rewind time' mechanic is a great idea and helps this character/relationship development.  With it, you can really look into the complexity of each character, and both their good and bad side.  Life is Strange isn't black and white, depending on your actions, characters can be very likable or absolutely disgusting.

I used to play a lot of adventures in the (g)olden days of the likes of Indiana Jones and Police Quest. But the genre mostly lost me when it largely moved to achieve difficulty by designing obscure and counterintuitive puzzles that don't make you open a door by looking for a key, but stuff like using a branch and duct tape to create a fishing rod, using that to fish a salmon to place in front of the door to attract a grizzly to charge at in and break through the door. When adventures started to become basically unplayable without walkthroughs, I moved on, because I don't want to tackle puzzles defying logic and reason.
And then came Life is Strange, which is nothing like that. It's a almost classic approach to adventures, where you can figure out the puzzles by applying logic and common sense and just doing what you would do in the character's place. On top of that, the story was compelling, the characters believable and relatable and the art is fantastic. And on top of the top, it even features a strong female lead character, which is still (sadly) something unsual in the video game industry.
It is probably the best adventure game to get released in many years.
And normally I would stop writing here, but unfortunately this awesome game also features one (actually two) of the worst endings I have ever seen in a game. There is a "good" and a "bad" ending for the sheer sake of giving players a choice, but the "bad" ending is so completely out of character for the main character that you know that she would never, ever have chosen it. The "good" ending, on the other side, is not only a completely uninspired, "have-seen-this-10,000-times- in-time travel-plots-before" cliche way to end the story, but also leaves every single choice you ever made in the game basically irrelevant in a way that you wonder why you even played the game. And the worst thing is that it's completely predictable and obvious from at least the 3rd chapter on that this will be the outcome.
The game is still awesome, and I still recommend it, but it really didn't deserve the horrible, unsatisfying ending(s) they gave it.
A Butterfly Effect wiith less happy endings.

I don't usually write review posts so I'll try my best. It might be a little lengthy as well.
This game is so much more than just a game, it is an experience. This work of art will stick with you for weeks and months after you have finished playing it. I bought the game two days ago, and in those two days I have already beaten it twice. We all know people like Evan, Kate, Chloe, Max, Victoria, and Nathan. That is where the magic of this game lies, it is so relatable. You might even be one of those characters. As the game moves towards it conclusion and you make more and more decisions you slowly start to become part of the world that was crated. A world crafted with so much detail, personality, and vibrancy you could get lost in losts just studying. Every detail had been so thoughtfully and delibrately placed that you start to question the meaning of everything. You begin to get attached to this world as if it were your own. All ages and genders will leave this game changed, some learning a lesson while others possiblity reliving the events which creates a hunger to learn more. In the two days since I've had this game I have laughed, cried, and pndered the meaning of my life. I have read through close to a hundred pages of lore, side research of the symbols, and theories.
However, with that being said, I can not fully recommend this game. I say this after such high praise because I feel deep down that no game will ever feel the same. All my replays will not feel the same as my first playthrough. I have potentially lost a hobby that I love to be replaced by a singular game that I love. I have gained a new outlook though, a different prespective.
You have been warned, and yet welcomed at the same time.
Story/Plot
The story telling in Life is Strange has changed the way I view all games. We all look for that one game to escape reality, but in a way we can relate. A way to view the world, without directly influencing it. Thats why people play video games. Life is Strange has done this in a way that blurs the line of what is part of this world and what is part of Life is Strange. It is a special blend of everyday life layered with the supernatural. The plot hits close to home, yet is fantasic enough to clearly be impossible. It strikes up awe and wonder whether you let your imagination flow everyday or even if you haven't used it in a decade. It makes you want to believe again like a child, even when the plot is so unforgivening you want to unplug the computer. Even in these moments Life Is strange demands your attention.
Music
The music for this game was chosen first, and the scenes were built around those songs. This ensures that every song fits every scene fits perfectly. The lyrics are thoughtful and relate directly to the plot. I still can't listen to obstacles by Syd Matters without crying,
Graphics/Enviroment
The graphics are not the best as some of the lip syncing does not much up. The drawings in this game are not very define in an impressionistic way. Some of the character models look stiff and rigid. With all this being said, I wouldn't have it any other way. The lovable and quirky art style is one third of the personality of this game. The enviroments are so full of small details that you'll spend hours looking at everything. The world feels full and lived in. Natural and comfortable. I can easily said that if the art style or the enviroments were even a little different Life is Strange would feel cold and stale.
Life is strange easily deserves all the praise in the gaming community. Even if you are not into games like this, or even into games at all you really should play this. The flaws it does have are minor in comparison to what it does right. I have beaten this game (as I mentioned) twice in two days already and I want to play it again. I will refrain for now because I don't and couldn't let Life is Strange feel overplayed until it loses its luster.

I had just spent the better part of a half-hour dreaming up a big♥♥♥♥♥rocket to shoot off into space, building it and getting it to the launchpad. When said rocket (which I was sure would be zooming off to the moon in no time flat) turned into a big♥♥♥♥♥explosion, I was flabbergasted. I had forgotten to account for the laws of physics: I had made something too heavy with not enough thrust. But I was determined to try again. The game wasn’t frustrating in the least. In fact, it captured my imagination and my persistence was rewarded with an entertaining, open-ended gaming experience.
… I’m getting ahead of myself, aren’t I? Let me start from the beginning. “Kerbal Space Program” (or KSP, for short) is less of a true game than it is a toy box. There’s no campaign to speak of and no real enemy; just a set of tutorials that teach you the basics with simple text narration and funny pictures. Wonderful game, with a very good and engaging story, wonderful and perfectly fitting soundtrack, and a solid easy-to-get gameplay, despite some very few, not so important bugs.
The story centers on two friends - Max, an aspirant photographer; and Chloe, a young rebel who drops the school - girls who didn't see each other from the past 5 years, and who followed different paths, since one of them moved to Seattle, and the other had to struggle with the loss of her father and her best friend. The story focus on friendship, and the consequences of little actions in our human relations.
To supporting it, the game successfully bring to us a story based, choice and consequence gameplay style, where we can interact with a lot of the environment elements and characters, most of them part of the story or the choice-consequence tree.
Some choices didn't matter, leading at best at different dialogues, some environments have pointing glitches, the skip-dialogue mechanic may bug and freeze (so don't use it), but these are all the "problems" you can find.
I recommend you to jump in this awesome experience prepared to play several hours at a time, chapter by chapter, because you'll get really involved by the game mood and soundtrack, like if you're watching (and playing) a good indie movie.

Life is strange, sure.  Also, it's sometimes a bit disappointing no matter how many do-overs you get.
A review of the game really needs to start at the ending.  After four episodes (a few hours each) of making choices, seeing consequences and constantly double-guessing yourself the game culminates in a final episode that goes completely off the rails.  Setting aside player opinions on the climax and whether or not your choices were meaningful, the ending is bogged down in lengthy cut scenes interspersed with irritating mechanics such as a maze sequence or scenes that try to turn the casual interface into a twitch game.  Your "rewind" power gives you infinite attempts to get it right but timing a kick or a trip just didn't feel right.  The pacing was off as well -- one moment you're leaning back in your chair doing nothing for five minutes as people on the screen talk, the next it's hustle, hustle.  Simply put, I didn't have much fun for the final hours of the game.
Up until that point though, Life is Strange is an interesting enough journey and occasional puzzler revolving around a teenage girl, Max, who learns in a moment of crisis that she has the ability to rewind time, using the power to attempt to solve the mysterious happenings at her school and re-connect with her estranged best friend.  With the plot focusing on the teens, the dialogue is sometimes eye-rolling and Max is a bit too precious and twee for anyone's good but the story has moments of genuine pathos and the mysterious story line has its own twists.  I may be a bit too removed from my teenage days to get "hit in the feels" (as I understand the kids are saying these days) but the story kept me playing despite this not really being my preferred genre of game.
Game play is usually very simple and casual: You walk around, items of interest get highlighted with a circle, you look at or interact with them in some way.  Interlaced with this is your ability to rewind time, allowing you to prevent things from happening or alter the course of a conversation by presenting new information.  Many small instances of choice pop up as you play and each chapter ends with a break down of the decisions you made (or failed to make) and how many others did the same.  It's interesting to make a seemingly obvious decision and then see that only 35% of the players thought the same way.  The art is usually attractive and visually consistent although some parts looked distracting low-res.  The mainly acoustic indie soundtrack wasn't my cup of tea but fit the overall feel of the game.
Ultimately, I give the game a somewhat reluctant recommendation despite its unwieldy conclusion. The road to that ending was interesting enough and had enough bright moments to make it worth taking even if ending falls flat.

It's a surprisingly fun game. If you don't know about it, then KSP (Kerbal Space Program) is a sandbox/adventure/career game where you must build a rocket that will make it to outerspace or a plane that will fly anywhere. There are two game modes, career, where you must research your actions and other planets to advance your rockets, and sandbox mode, where you have access to every piece of rocketeering material and unlimited resources. Beginning can be difficult, but no one said that building rockets and orbiting planets was easy. It definitely takes some thought when making a rocket that will make it to another world without exploding our running out of fuel, but you can also fool around and make some of the oddest and funnest inventions known to Kerbal kind. The game is also completely mod-able, making it a playground for anyone with a 3D art designer and some programming knowledge. There are mods for just about everything, guns, FTL drives, more planets, etcetra, and the community is always growing. The game features some solid sofware, allowing for the rendering of entire planets and a star, but lacks performance with lighting. Turning on a spotlight or floodlight at a great height could cause the game to lag horribly, and there are no ends to how many bugs it has, but it must be tough ironing the kinks out of an entire solar system. All in all, the game features solid gameplay, and values creativity as much as it values logic, go nuts, be careful, it doesn't matter! The Kerbals are always happy to help, whether it's to fly your ship to Eloo, or crash it straight into the ground, its your space program! Do as you please. (10/10 Mighty Magus approved!)

Did you ever sit in front of an early game console and wonder what the future of video games would be like? What the most realistic game ever made might look decades from then? The thoughts going through your head might have been about photo realistic graphics, or virtual reality, maybe both?Some kind of danger room or a holodeck style experience, I know I did.
What I never counted on was that, for all the excellent strides we've made in technology, presentation, interactivity, story telling and delivery, the most tangible, the most real emotional responses in games can -even now- all hinge on the quality of writing and performance.
But when it comes together right, all the captivatingly earnest performances and exuberant writing in the world can never have the same power over the reader or the watcher as it can over the player. A narrative you are forced to move through under your own power can be so much more. A good Video Game doesn't happen in front of you, You move through it, you dive into what is strewn out before you and see what it is for yourself, where it can take you.
I have been in love with games for 23 years or more and for me, for what I want from Games and Art and the future; Life Is Strange is the best example of player driven story telling I've allowed myself to dive in on. Top to bottom, from the almost unfinished art style to the quivering emotion in exceptional voice recording sessions. Life Is Strange is a triumph.
I am willing to overlook any fault in light of what has been accomplished. Dontnod could never make another game half as good as Life Is Strange and they would remain one of the most important developers in front of us right now.

Life is strange is a true treasure for people who like story-driven games with a great atmospere. It is no game you should rush or break into small pieces or you will miss out a good part of what makes the game the possibly most engaging expierence I had when it comes to video games. The plot, the characters, the artistic presentation and the soundtrack all add to a very homogeneous experience that can put you under its spell for an approximate 2.5h per episode. My advice to get the most out of the game would be to play each episode in its own session. This is especially true since life is strange is no game you are going to replay very often (if at all), because it's main allure remains the plot and the tension resulting from the incertainty if or how each of your actions will affect the story.
If I had to rate the game I'd give it a 9/10. The one missing point is for the fact that the game sometimes gave away hints for a riddle too easily and mostly for the final ending. Since I don't want to give too much away I'll stay rather cryptic on that one and only say that I am not criticizing the idea behind it (a final truly difficult choice), but rather that this choice felt a little bit forced since there imho could have been an easy way to resolve that particular last problem.

Nominated for the “I'm Not Crying, There's Something In My Eye” Award.
I can’t think of a time that I have been anywhere near as emotionally invested in a game's characters as with Max and Chloe.  A fact that the game uses ruthlessly to take you on a rollercoaster ride of euphoric highs and truly heartbreaking lows.
The interactive element and the central time manipulation mechanic are used effectively to reinforce that investment in the story by making the player complicit in Max’s choices in a way that books, film or TV simply can’t replicate.
As they should in this kind of “teen” drama all the choices feel freighted with huge consequence; even when they are just everyday interactions.  The game uses this and the time rewind mechanic to initially lull you into a false sense of security before hammering you with horrible, inescapable, “lesser of two evils” moral dilemmas; which occasionally left me staring at the options for minutes before I could bring myself to choose.
The ending seems to be the focus of most of the negative reviews even though to me it felt like a natural, logical and horrible choice that the whole story had been building towards.  Though for me, by the time I got to it, it wasn’t a choice at all; there was simply no way I was ever, ever going to do the “correct”, logical thing.
More than any other game the history you bring with you will determine if/how you connect with the game and its characters - it felt like a very personal experience (hence the harrowingly cathartic comment); However the mark of a great “coming of age” tale is that the framework of teenage awkwardness and lost friendship is so universal that virtually anyone can project something of their own life onto the characters.
It's not quite perfect:
It stumbles most often when it “remembers” that it needs some game elements; which are sometimes seriously annoying speed bumps in the narrative flow (yes - I’m looking directly at you “Episode 5 nightmare stealth sequence”).
Occasionally it hammers home some of its themes where a lighter touch may have had a more lasting impact.
Ultimately: I loved it, it broke my heart, in time I will heal and return for more heartbreak.
If you loved Buffy for the characters and their relationships or Friday Night Lights made you a Panther and then a Lion I think Life is Strange will probably break your heart as well.

Life is strange is a true treasure for people who like story-driven games with a great atmospere. It is no game you should rush or break into small pieces or you will miss out a good part of what makes the game the possibly most engaging expierence I had when it comes to video games. The plot, the characters, the artistic presentation and the soundtrack all add to a very homogeneous experience that can put you under its spell for an approximate 2.5h per episode. My advice to get the most out of the game would be to play each episode in its own session. This is especially true since life is strange is no game you are going to replay very often (if at all), because it's main allure remains the plot and the tension resulting from the incertainty if or how each of your actions will affect the story.
If I had to rate the game I'd give it a 9/10. The one missing point is for the fact that the game sometimes gave away hints for a riddle too easily and mostly for the final ending. Since I don't want to give too much away I'll stay rather cryptic on that one and only say that I am not criticizing the idea behind it (a final truly difficult choice), but rather that this choice felt a little bit forced since there imho could have been an easy way to resolve that particular last problem.

I have only completed chapter one. But here is my review of Life Is Strange.

Nominated for the “I'm Not Crying, There's Something In My Eye” Award.
I can’t think of a time that I have been anywhere near as emotionally invested in a game's characters as with Max and Chloe.  A fact that the game uses ruthlessly to take you on a rollercoaster ride of euphoric highs and truly heartbreaking lows.
The interactive element and the central time manipulation mechanic are used effectively to reinforce that investment in the story by making the player complicit in Max’s choices in a way that books, film or TV simply can’t replicate.
As they should in this kind of “teen” drama all the choices feel freighted with huge consequence; even when they are just everyday interactions.  The game uses this and the time rewind mechanic to initially lull you into a false sense of security before hammering you with horrible, inescapable, “lesser of two evils” moral dilemmas; which occasionally left me staring at the options for minutes before I could bring myself to choose.
The ending seems to be the focus of most of the negative reviews even though to me it felt like a natural, logical and horrible choice that the whole story had been building towards.  Though for me, by the time I got to it, it wasn’t a choice at all; there was simply no way I was ever, ever going to do the “correct”, logical thing.
More than any other game the history you bring with you will determine if/how you connect with the game and its characters - it felt like a very personal experience (hence the harrowingly cathartic comment); However the mark of a great “coming of age” tale is that the framework of teenage awkwardness and lost friendship is so universal that virtually anyone can project something of their own life onto the characters.
It's not quite perfect:
It stumbles most often when it “remembers” that it needs some game elements; which are sometimes seriously annoying speed bumps in the narrative flow (yes - I’m looking directly at you “Episode 5 nightmare stealth sequence”).
Occasionally it hammers home some of its themes where a lighter touch may have had a more lasting impact.
Ultimately: I loved it, it broke my heart, in time I will heal and return for more heartbreak.
If you loved Buffy for the characters and their relationships or Friday Night Lights made you a Panther and then a Lion I think Life is Strange will probably break your heart as well.

So after clocking in 2k hours on my account I feel I need to leave a different review, before I start let me explain that I have been playing gmod since gmod 9. And I have really 4k hours if you count the hours that I clocked in on my brothers computer. I started really likeing gmod during the death of Gmod 9. There was not a single server up, but I played single player and built. At the time I did not know how to use the tools, I did not know how to use the thruster. What I did know was how to build, and I knew how to build well. By brother after watching the first idiot box decided to purchace Gmod 10. My god, the second he did that I found the hover ball, and I wanted to know how to use it. I quickly hop on the internet and google it. You can bind keys to it. I was estatic. I made massive gun ships with elevators, and I made robots that are bipedal. It was a good time for me.
At this time I clocked in 300 hours into my brothers copy of Gmod 10. Then went gmod 11, 12 and by this point I was an addict sitting at about 1000 hours of gmod on his account. My brother worked at this point and I had even more time to experiment. I found a mod called "Wire mod" I downloading from the addon site anyone back in gmod 9-12 days would remember and got it. Jesus christ I was lost. I had no clue what to do and I got so frustrated I stopped playing gmod for a solid year.
On my 13th birthday I was given a steam account, Hl2, ep1-2, a new computer, and of course, gmod. I looked at it with disgust. I did not like feeling as confused as I did. I played and beat half life many upon many times. It got old. But I heard a rumor that Garry was giving out Gmod 13 beta keys with real workshop support. I might as well just♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. After a couple days I got a key and was amazed at the speed in which I picked up my old habits and skills, and the workshop support made it easier, and safer to get addons than ever. Soon after that gmod 13 was given out as an update to the public.
It was weeks into the games proper release when shopping the workshop I found a good ol' friend. "Wire mod." I was determined, with my newfound age and slightly better IQ I went and tried. I just could not get it to work. Luckly on the server I was on, somebody I met was willing to teach me, and they did, I could not beleive how amazing this was. I had a new era of gmod. From there I am where I am now, a freelance LUA programmer, wire mod master, and Gmod nerd. Buy this game, and if you can make me laugh I will even teach you wiremod.
TL;DR: Buy it, please.

With the level of improvements they've made with each point release, I imagine KSP is going to be the most awesome game ever made by time 1.0 comes out.   With the latest, .23, we see some massive load time improvements, far less lag with high-part-count vehicles, tweakables *in the ship editor* and best of all, only one of my mods had issues, but it didn't crash the game - it simply didn't function at "go time".  That's already been fixed, it just hadn't been released officially as of this time yesterday.
If you like space ship games, you will want this game - it's pretty damned hard if you're coming in with zero experience with rocketry, calculus and / or orbital mechanics.  You'll walk away with some if you put in the effort in career mode in this game.  I have a far better understanding of how something gets into orbit - and far more respect for the men and women who engineer those feats.
If you like educational games, this one is for you as well - it's not for all kids, but I could see a bright middle school or high school student picking this up quicker than most adults.  And adults could all learn a thing or two by playing this game - NASA engineers play this game in their free time.
And most importantly, if you like to tinker AND play video games, this game was quite likely made for you.  The mod system is incredibly simple to work with - but if you know the right languages, you can make whole new features in the game!
At any price, $10 or $60, this is a game worth every penny - and it's not even done yet!
UPDATE for Beta 0.90:
Since this review was written, Career mode has been added, the old Career mode renamed to "Science".  In addition, further features have been added - Contracts, better joints, new parts, way easier navigation and the career mode actually feels like you're helping the Kerbals march their way to the planets!  You have to balance science with your contracts (money!) and grow things carefully.
It truly is educational in every sense - engaging, teaching and adjusting.  This game is whatever you want it to be - the mod ecosystem is growing and with CKAN, it's even easier to install and remove mods with a push of a button.  Check it out if you haven't yet!

With the level of improvements they've made with each point release, I imagine KSP is going to be the most awesome game ever made by time 1.0 comes out.   With the latest, .23, we see some massive load time improvements, far less lag with high-part-count vehicles, tweakables *in the ship editor* and best of all, only one of my mods had issues, but it didn't crash the game - it simply didn't function at "go time".  That's already been fixed, it just hadn't been released officially as of this time yesterday.
If you like space ship games, you will want this game - it's pretty damned hard if you're coming in with zero experience with rocketry, calculus and / or orbital mechanics.  You'll walk away with some if you put in the effort in career mode in this game.  I have a far better understanding of how something gets into orbit - and far more respect for the men and women who engineer those feats.
If you like educational games, this one is for you as well - it's not for all kids, but I could see a bright middle school or high school student picking this up quicker than most adults.  And adults could all learn a thing or two by playing this game - NASA engineers play this game in their free time.
And most importantly, if you like to tinker AND play video games, this game was quite likely made for you.  The mod system is incredibly simple to work with - but if you know the right languages, you can make whole new features in the game!
At any price, $10 or $60, this is a game worth every penny - and it's not even done yet!
UPDATE for Beta 0.90:
Since this review was written, Career mode has been added, the old Career mode renamed to "Science".  In addition, further features have been added - Contracts, better joints, new parts, way easier navigation and the career mode actually feels like you're helping the Kerbals march their way to the planets!  You have to balance science with your contracts (money!) and grow things carefully.
It truly is educational in every sense - engaging, teaching and adjusting.  This game is whatever you want it to be - the mod ecosystem is growing and with CKAN, it's even easier to install and remove mods with a push of a button.  Check it out if you haven't yet!

Cons (just minor):

Conclusion:
If you want some chill game with good background music and perfect storyline set into modern high school environment, there you go!
